questions.setup: My driving lesson is from two to three.

a journey you make to work
a time when someone teaches you
a break before you start work
questions.explanation: A lesson is a period of teaching, here learning to drive.
feedback: Repair work fixes something; a driving lesson teaches a skill.

questions.setup: At the end of the language course, we have a short test.
questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the test?
options: to check what we have learned
to choose our next teacher
to buy our course books
to arrange our lesson times
questions.explanation: A course test checks learners' knowledge or skills.
feedback: A course test checks learners' knowledge or skills.
Choosing staff is not what 'test' means in this course.
Buying books is preparation, not a test of learning.

questions.setup: Tutor: 'Where do you live?' Learner: 'In Lima.'

options: Tutor
Where do you live?
Learner
In Lima.
questions.explanation: An answer responds to a question; 'In Lima' gives the requested place.
feedback: 'Tutor' names the person asking, not the reply.

'Learner' labels the speaker, not the words of the answer.
An answer responds to a question; 'In Lima' gives the requested place.

questions.setup: After work, Mei studies English at home.
questions.prompt: What does 'studies' mean here?
options: teaches other people
works to learn something
stops learning a subject
chooses a different language

feedback: Teaching helps others learn; this sentence describes Mei's own learning.
'To study' is to spend time learning a subject, for example by reading and doing exercises.
'Studies' means 'works at learning', not 'stops'.
Studying does not mean changing the subject she chose.

questions.setup: Our talk is about food. Its title is 'A Taste of Home'.
questions.prompt: What is the topic of the talk?
options: food
A Taste of Home
the person speaking
the room for the talk
questions.explanation: The topic is what a talk is about; here it is food.
feedback: The topic is what a talk is about; here it is food.
These words are the title, the name given to the talk.
The speaker gives the talk; 'topic' names its subject.
The room is its location, not what it is about.

questions.setup: Our English class has twelve adults from five countries.
questions.prompt: What does 'class' mean in this sentence?
options: the room where we learn
the book we use to learn
the group learning together
the time when we have a break
questions.explanation: 'Class' can mean the learners taught together, as it does here.
feedback: The room holds learners, but 'twelve adults' describes the group itself.
A book contains material; it is not the group of adults.
'Class' can mean the learners taught together, as it does here.
The number and countries describe people, not a break time.

questions.setup: The course book has printed lessons and exercises. I need a second book with empty pages for my own writing.
questions.prompt: Which book do I need?
options: a dictionary
a textbook
a guidebook
a notebook
questions.explanation: A notebook has space for your own writing, such as notes from class.
feedback: A dictionary gives word meanings; it is not a book of empty pages.

A guidebook gives information about a place or activity rather than empty writing space.
A notebook has space for your own writing, such as notes from class.

questions.setup: The tutor says, 'Turn to page six in your book.'
questions.prompt: What should you look for?
options: the sixth book on the shelf
the side of a sheet numbered 6
the sixth word on the cover
the sixth lesson on the timetable
questions.explanation: A page is one side of a sheet in a book; its printed number helps you find it.
feedback: 'Page' refers to part of one book, not a separate book on a shelf.
A page is one side of a sheet in a book; its printed number helps you find it.
A word is much smaller than the numbered page requested.
The instruction names a page inside the book, not a lesson time.

questions.setup: On the board is the sentence 'I work here.'
questions.prompt: Which choice is one whole word from the sentence?
options: work
w
work here
I work here.
questions.explanation: 'Work' is a complete word between the spaces in this sentence.
feedback: 'Work' is a complete word between the spaces in this sentence.
'W' is one letter from 'work', not the whole word.
This contains two words, 'work' and 'here'.
This is the whole three-word sentence, not one word.

questions.setup: Rosa helps the adults in our cooking course learn new skills. She plans the lessons.
questions.prompt: What is Rosa's role in the course?
options: a visitor
the teacher
a customer
the receptionist
questions.explanation: The teacher plans and leads learning, as Rosa does here.
feedback: A visitor attends a place; the sentence gives Rosa responsibility for teaching.
The teacher plans and leads learning, as Rosa does here.
A customer buys something; that is not the learning role described.
A receptionist welcomes people and handles enquiries, not necessarily their lessons.

questions.setup: Ben is 54. He works in a shop and goes to a college course on Fridays.
questions.prompt: At college, Ben is a student. What does that mean?
options: He sells the course books.
He is learning on the course.
He teaches the Friday course.
He cleans the college rooms.
questions.explanation: A student is someone studying; students can be adults of any age.
feedback: Selling books is a job; 'student' describes his learning role.
A student is someone studying; students can be adults of any age.
Teaching is the teacher's role; a student attends to learn.
Cleaning is not the meaning of 'student', even if a student also has a job.

questions.setup: The worksheet says, 'Match each word to a picture.'
questions.prompt: What does 'match' ask you to do?
options: write each word three times
draw a new picture for each word
put each word with the right picture
read each word to the class
questions.explanation: 'Match' means connect things that belong together, here words and their pictures.
feedback: Repeating the word practises writing; it does not connect words and pictures.
The instruction uses the pictures already provided.
'Match' means connect things that belong together, here words and their pictures.
Reading aloud does not show which picture belongs with each word.

questions.setup: The notice says, 'Final exam: Monday, 10 a.m. Bring a pen.'
questions.prompt: What is happening on Monday?
options: the first lesson of the course
a test at the end of the course
a meeting to buy new pens
a break from the course
questions.explanation: A final exam checks learning at the end of a course or stage.
feedback: 'Final' points to the end; 'exam' names a test rather than a lesson.
A final exam checks learning at the end of a course or stage.
'Bring a pen' tells you what to take, not the purpose of the event.
An exam is an assessment activity, not time away from learning.

questions.setup: For this activity, read the message silently.
questions.prompt: Which action follows that instruction?
options: Say the message so everyone hears it.
Listen while someone says the message.
Look at the written words without speaking.
Write the same message on a new page.
questions.explanation: 'Read silently' means take in the written message without saying it aloud.
feedback: 'Silently' means without speaking; this would be reading aloud.
Listening uses another person's voice; the instruction asks you to read.
'Read silently' means take in the written message without saying it aloud.
Writing it again is copying, not the requested silent reading.

questions.setup: The online exercise says, 'Write a short answer in the box.'
questions.prompt: What should you put in the box?
options: words that answer the question
a recording of your voice
a picture of your face
a link to the next exercise
questions.explanation: 'Write' asks you to produce written words, here by typing in the box.
feedback: 'Write' asks you to produce written words, here by typing in the box.
A recording is a spoken answer; 'write' asks for written words.
A photograph does not provide the requested written answer.
The box is for your answer, not a way to move to another exercise.

questions.setup: Close your books and listen to the recording.
questions.prompt: What should you pay attention to?
options: the words on the next page
your partner's written answer
the pictures on the cover
the voices you can hear
questions.explanation: Listening means paying attention to sound, here the recorded voices.
feedback: The books are closed; this is not a reading task.
A written answer is something to read, not the recording named here.
Pictures are visual; 'listen' directs attention to sound.
Listening means paying attention to sound, here the recorded voices.

questions.setup: The piano teacher says, 'Ten minutes of practice every day will help.'
questions.prompt: What does 'practice' mean here?
options: time spent choosing an instrument
time spent watching a concert
time spent waiting for a lesson
time spent playing to improve
questions.explanation: Practice is activity done to develop a skill, here playing the piano regularly.
feedback: Choosing is preparation; it is not working on the playing skill.
Watching may be useful, but 'practice' here means doing the playing yourself.
Waiting does not involve the repeated work the teacher recommends.
Practice is activity done to develop a skill, here playing the piano regularly.

questions.setup: The quiz gives one point for each correct answer. My score is 8 out of 10.
questions.prompt: What does my score tell me?
options: how many minutes I used
how many pages I read
how many quizzes I took
how many points I got
questions.explanation: Your score is the points awarded: eight from a possible ten.
feedback: A score measures points here, not time.
Page count is not what the quiz awards points for.
'Eight out of ten' is the result of this quiz, not a count of quizzes.
Your score is the points awarded: eight from a possible ten.

questions.setup: I borrow course books from the college library and bring them back two weeks later.
questions.prompt: Which description fits this library?
options: a shop where I buy my lunch
an office where I pay my course fee
a place where I can borrow books
a room where I sell my old books
questions.explanation: A library provides books and other resources for people to use or borrow.
feedback: Lunch is bought at a food shop or cafe, not borrowed as course books.
The sentence describes borrowing books, not paying for the course.
A library provides books and other resources for people to use or borrow.
These books must be returned; selling books is a different activity.

questions.setup: After the evening lesson, our tutor gives us two exercises to finish before the next class.
questions.prompt: What is this homework?
options: course work to do outside the lesson
cleaning the rooms in our homes
work we do for our employers
a lesson taught in our homes
questions.explanation: Homework is work set for learners to complete outside class; it can be done in a library too.
feedback: Homework is work set for learners to complete outside class; it can be done in a library too.
Cleaning is housework, not work set by a tutor.
Paid job tasks are work, but not homework set on this course.
Homework is a learner's task, not necessarily a lesson or something done at home.

questions.setup: One learner remembers new words with pictures. Another uses short recordings.
questions.prompt: They use different methods. What does 'methods' mean here?
options: reasons for joining
subjects to learn
results of learning
ways of learning
questions.explanation: A method is a way of doing something; pictures and recordings are different ways to learn words.
feedback: A reason explains why they joined, not how they learn.
Both learners are working on words; 'method' describes their approach, not a different subject.
Results come from the activity; the methods are ways of doing it.
A method is a way of doing something; pictures and recordings are different ways to learn words.

questions.setup: For my local-history project, I found the year the bridge opened in a newspaper article.
questions.prompt: The tutor asks for my source. What should I name?
options: the title of my project
the day I finished writing
the newspaper article
the place where I sat to read
questions.explanation: A source is where information comes from, here the article you read.
feedback: Your project uses the information; it is not where you found it.
That is your work date, not the source of the bridge information.
A source is where information comes from, here the article you read.
Your reading location does not identify the material containing the information.

questions.setup: A course page gives two statements: 'The building opened in 1998' and 'It is the nicest building in town.'
questions.prompt: Which word describes the second statement as a personal view?
options: a date
an opinion
a measurement
an instruction
questions.explanation: An opinion is a person's view; 'nicest' depends on what someone likes.
feedback: A date tells when something happened; 'nicest' expresses a judgment.
An opinion is a person's view; 'nicest' depends on what someone likes.
A measurement gives an amount or size, not a personal judgment of beauty.

questions.setup: During a talk, Sam writes 'bus: cheaper; train: faster' to help him remember.
questions.prompt: What are these notes?
options: short pieces of written information
the exact words of the whole talk
questions sent to the speaker
marks showing his test result
questions.explanation: Notes record useful information briefly, often without full sentences.
feedback: Notes record useful information briefly, often without full sentences.
Notes can be short reminders; Sam has not written the complete talk.

questions.setup: The course aim is to help adults use email. At the start, many learners cannot send a message.
questions.prompt: What does 'aim' mean here?

how long each lesson lasts
what the course wants to achieve
how much the course costs

feedback: That would be an actual result; an aim says what is intended.

An aim is an intended result, even before learners have reached it.

questions.setup: A dictionary entry says: 'island: land with water all around it'.

land with water all around it
the name of the dictionary
the page number of the entry

feedback: 'Island' is the word being explained, not its explanation.
A definition explains what a word means; these words explain 'island'.
The dictionary's name identifies the book, not the meaning of 'island'.

questions.setup: The tutor says, 'Some courses teach practical skills. For example, this college offers bicycle repair.'
questions.prompt: What is the example doing?

explaining why the college opened
telling learners to repair their bikes
giving one case of a practical course
questions.explanation: An example is a particular case used to make a general idea clearer.
feedback: One course is named; the tutor has not provided the full list.

questions.setup: Your report has three separate blocks of writing. Each begins on a new line and develops one point.
questions.prompt: What do we call these blocks of writing?
options: paragraphs
headings
letters
titles

questions.setup: On this course, written work receives A, B, C or D. My essay received a grade of B.
questions.prompt: What does 'grade' mean here?
options: a rating of my work
my current year level at school
the number of words I wrote
a comment about one spelling error

feedback: A grade shows how work was assessed; this course uses letters for its ratings.
'Grade' can refer to a school year in some varieties, but here it rates an essay.
'B' is the assessment result, not a word count.

questions.setup: Marta is choosing between history and computing at college.
questions.prompt: These are subjects. What does 'subjects' mean here?

pieces of work she must hand in
rooms where lessons take place
areas she can study

feedback: 'Subjects' can mean participants, but history and computing are not people.

questions.setup: Learners tested two paper designs. The result was that the folded design held more weight.

What do we hope will happen?
What happened in the test?

questions.explanation: A result is what an activity or test produced, here the difference in weight held.
feedback: That asks about preparation before the test, not its outcome.

A result is what an activity or test produced, here the difference in weight held.

questions.setup: For a project on local shops, we read old records and ask long-time residents questions. Our research takes a month.

options: the final talk we give
the work we do to find information
the pictures on our front page

questions.setup: The college sends learners six questions about their journey to class. It collects the answers in a survey.

questions.explanation: A survey gathers information or views; these questions ask about people's travel experiences.

A survey gathers information or views; these questions ask about people's travel experiences.

questions.setup: The report shows each course's learner numbers with bars of different lengths.

a timetable
a dictionary
a questionnaire

questions.setup: Four learners came in the morning and six in the afternoon. The total was ten.

the number from both groups together
the number in each group
the difference between the groups

questions.setup: The task says, 'Compare the two college websites.'

options: Copy the words from one website.

'Compare' means examine things in relation to each other, including similarities and differences.

questions.setup: The tutor asks for a summary of a long talk in three sentences.
questions.prompt: What should the summary contain?
options: the main points in a short form
the exact words of the whole talk
only your opinion of the speaker
new information on another topic

replace it with a different city
find it and say which city it is

questions.setup: The lesson moved online because the college building had no heating.

the college building

questions.setup: The article is about a new public garden. It says the gates open at seven each morning.

the name given to the article
a reason the article was written
one specific piece of information

questions.setup: On a map in the geography textbook, blue lines indicate rivers.

show where rivers are

questions.setup: A historian calls the opening of the first public school a significant event in the town's history.

mentioned only in private records

'Significant' in this ordinary historical use means important or meaningful.

questions.setup: Before asking the learners, the tutor plans an online task on the assumption that everyone has home internet.

an idea taken as true without checking
a result established by the task
a rule learners must follow

questions.setup: The group has collected a month's bus arrival times. It will now analyze the data.

questions.setup: You are explaining why adults choose evening courses. A tutor asks for relevant details.

questions.setup: A report claims that its new reading app improves concentration, but gives no supporting results.

questions.setup: For a pronunciation study, researchers collected audio recordings and written comments from learners.

questions.setup: A report has sections called 'Background', 'Method' and 'Results'. Each contains several paragraphs.
questions.prompt: What is a section in this report?
options: a larger part devoted to one aspect
one sentence ending with a full stop
the complete report with its cover
a list of spelling corrections
questions.explanation: A section organizes a report into a major part, which may contain several paragraphs.
feedback: A section organizes a report into a major part, which may contain several paragraphs.

questions.setup: A graph shows weekly participation as 40, 42, 55 and 58. Weekend sessions began after the second week. The tutor asks learners to interpret the graph.

feedback: This reads one value but does not explain what the pattern means.

questions.setup: After comparing the two versions, the tutor concludes that the shorter instructions are easier to follow.

finishes the lesson without giving a view

questions.setup: The guide says, "In this chapter, the term 'habitat' means the natural place where a living thing lives."
questions.prompt: What does 'term' mean here?
options: a period in the teaching year
a word used for a particular idea
a rule agreed in a contract
the final date for an assignment
questions.explanation: A term is a word or expression with a particular meaning in a subject.
feedback: 'Term' can name a teaching period, but here it labels 'habitat' as vocabulary.

'Terms' can be conditions, but this sentence is explaining a word.
The sentence gives no deadline; it defines 'habitat'.

questions.setup: The diagram shows how paper is made, from preparing the fibers to drying the sheets.
questions.prompt: What does 'process' refer to in 'the paper-making process'?
options: the quality rating of the finished paper
the tools listed beside the diagram
the person who drew the diagram
the connected stages of making paper
questions.explanation: A process is a series of actions or changes leading toward a result.
feedback: A rating evaluates the result rather than describes how it is produced.
Tools are used during the process but are not the sequence of actions.
The designer is not the production process shown.
A process is a series of actions or changes leading toward a result.

questions.setup: A tutor likes an essay's ideas but suggests moving the explanation before the examples to improve its structure.
questions.prompt: What is the tutor asking the writer to change?
options: the spelling of individual words
the subject being discussed
the size of the printed letters
the way the parts are arranged
questions.explanation: Structure is the organization of a text; moving explanation and examples changes that organization.
feedback: Spelling concerns word forms; the suggestion changes the order of parts.
The tutor keeps the ideas and changes their arrangement, not the topic.
Print size concerns appearance rather than the order of the reasoning.
Structure is the organization of a text; moving explanation and examples changes that organization.

questions.setup: A questionnaire was sent to 80 learners. Forty respondents returned completed forms.
questions.prompt: Who are the respondents?
options: the people who answered the questionnaire
the people who designed the questions
all the people who received a form
the people who checked the completed forms
questions.explanation: A respondent is someone who responds to questions, especially in a survey.
feedback: A respondent is someone who responds to questions, especially in a survey.
Designers create the questionnaire; respondents supply answers.
Receiving a form does not make someone a respondent if no response is given.
Checking responses is a separate role from providing them.

questions.setup: The project leader selected five photographs because each showed a different stage of construction.
questions.prompt: Which statement preserves what 'selected' means here?
options: She took five new photographs.
She approved every photograph submitted.
She arranged the photographs by date.
She chose five photographs for the project.
questions.explanation: 'Select' means choose from available possibilities; the context gives a reason for the choice.
feedback: Selecting chooses among photographs; it does not say she created them.
Selecting five is not approving the whole collection.
Selection chooses the images; their ordering is a separate step.
'Select' means choose from available possibilities; the context gives a reason for the choice.

questions.setup: Attendance was 60, 65, 63, 70 and 74 over five weeks. The report describes an upward trend.
questions.prompt: What does 'upward trend' mean?
options: an increase in every single week
an overall movement toward higher numbers
the highest number on one particular day
the target set before the course began
questions.explanation: A trend is a general direction; a small fall can occur within an overall rise.
feedback: There was a fall from 65 to 63; a trend need not be uninterrupted.
A trend is a general direction; a small fall can occur within an overall rise.
A trend concerns a pattern across time, not one maximum.
These are observed attendance figures, not an intended target.

questions.setup: The last page of the essay lists the authors, titles and publication dates of the works used.
questions.prompt: What is this reference list mainly for?
options: to help readers identify the works used
to show which books the writer plans to buy
to repeat every sentence from those works
to give the writer's weekly study schedule
questions.explanation: A reference list gives details that identify the sources behind the writing.
feedback: A reference list gives details that identify the sources behind the writing.
The list records works used in the essay, not future purchases.
References identify sources; they do not reproduce their full contents.
Publication details are not the writer's study times.

questions.setup: A study of town travel asked only people at a cycle club. The tutor warns of bias in the sample.
questions.prompt: What is the concern?
options: Cyclists' experiences may be overrepresented.
The answers must have been invented.
The club members could not understand the questions.
The survey must contain too many questions.
questions.explanation: Bias here is an uneven selection that may distort the picture of the wider town.
feedback: Bias here is an uneven selection that may distort the picture of the wider town.
A biased sample can contain honest answers; fabrication is a different problem.
No comprehension problem is described; the concern is who was included.
The number of questions is not the sampling issue described.

questions.setup: Lena explains an author's idea in her own words and gives the author's name and the book details.
questions.prompt: She cites the book but does not quote it. What is the distinction?
options: Citing means agreeing with the author.
Quoting means changing the author's wording.
Citing names a source; quoting reproduces its wording.
Citing means naming a source without using its ideas.
questions.explanation: A citation points to a source, while a quotation reproduces wording from it.
feedback: A writer can cite a source while disagreeing with it.
Quoting reproduces the original words rather than replaces them.
A citation points to a source, while a quotation reproduces wording from it.
A citation can acknowledge ideas used in the text, as Lena's does here.

questions.setup: The sentence says, 'After rowing all morning, we stopped at the bank for lunch.'
questions.prompt: A tutor says to use the context to understand 'bank'. What should the learner use?
options: the surrounding words about the activity
the number of letters in bank
the first meaning in any dictionary entry
the typeface used to print bank
questions.explanation: Context includes nearby language and the situation; rowing helps suggest a river bank here.
feedback: Context includes nearby language and the situation; rowing helps suggest a river bank here.
Word length does not distinguish the place beside a river from a financial bank.
Dictionary order alone does not show which meaning fits this sentence.
Typeface does not explain the sense suggested by the activity.

questions.setup: Before measuring anything, the team proposes that shaded rooms stay cooler than otherwise similar rooms in direct sun. It plans a comparison.
questions.prompt: Why is the proposal a hypothesis in this study?
options: It is the full list of measurements already collected.
It is a conclusion that no longer needs testing.
It is a proposed relationship that can be tested.
It is the procedure for installing the thermometers.
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable proposal or explanation; the room comparison can provide evidence about it.
feedback: Measurements would be data; the proposal comes before collection.
A hypothesis is proposed for investigation, not exempted from testing.
A hypothesis is a testable proposal or explanation; the room comparison can provide evidence about it.
A procedure specifies actions; this proposal states an expected relationship.

questions.setup: A reading study records each participant's age and usual reading time without asking anyone to change either.
questions.prompt: Why can both be called variables?
options: Their values can differ among participants.
The researchers deliberately changed both.
Both are errors in the study design.
They are the study's written instructions.
questions.explanation: A variable can vary across people or observations, even when the researcher does not manipulate it.
feedback: A variable can vary across people or observations, even when the researcher does not manipulate it.
Variables can be observed; manipulation is not required.
A variable is a characteristic that can take different values, not necessarily a flaw.
Instructions tell participants what to do; age and reading time are recorded characteristics.

questions.setup: An assignment asks you to paraphrase a short passage while keeping its full meaning, not reducing it to its main point.
questions.prompt: Which action fulfills that instruction?
options: Reproduce the passage inside quotation marks.
Keep only the central idea and omit the rest.
Correct the writer's argument with your own evidence.
Express the passage's ideas in new wording.
questions.explanation: Paraphrasing restates meaning in different wording; it is not necessarily a shorter summary.
feedback: That is quotation, which preserves the original wording.
That summarizes; the instruction asks you to retain the passage's full meaning.
That critiques or develops the argument rather than restates it.
Paraphrasing restates meaning in different wording; it is not necessarily a shorter summary.

questions.setup: A transport study examines each route through three linked concepts: access, affordability and reliability. These form its analytical framework.
questions.prompt: What role does the framework play?
options: It supplies the raw passenger counts.
It reports the study's final recommendations.
It gives the order in which buses arrive.
It organizes the study's way of examining the routes.
questions.explanation: An analytical framework is a connected set of ideas or categories that guides examination.
feedback: Counts are data; the concepts organize how the data are examined.
Recommendations may follow analysis; the framework guides the analysis itself.
A timetable records service order, not the conceptual organization of the study.
An analytical framework is a connected set of ideas or categories that guides examination.

questions.setup: The regional totals were derived from individual library records by adding the recorded visitor counts.
questions.prompt: Which wording preserves 'derived from' in this context?
options: copied unchanged from a regional report
used to replace the individual records
obtained by working with the individual records
estimated before the individual records were available
questions.explanation: 'Derive from' identifies an origin; here the totals are obtained through calculation using those records.
feedback: The totals were calculated from individual records, not copied as existing regional totals.
Derivation describes how the totals were obtained, not deletion or replacement of records.
'Derive from' identifies an origin; here the totals are obtained through calculation using those records.
The sentence says the records were the basis of the totals, not unavailable at the time.

questions.setup: Only photographs taken before 1900 can enter the historical collection. This date limit is a selection criterion.
questions.prompt: What does 'criterion' mean here?
options: a photograph that has already been selected
a prediction about the collection's popularity
the reason photography was invented
a standard used to decide what qualifies
questions.explanation: A criterion is a standard or condition used in judging or choosing something.
feedback: The criterion is the basis for choosing, not an example chosen.
The date limit governs selection; it does not predict audience interest.
That would be a historical explanation, not the current selection condition.
A criterion is a standard or condition used in judging or choosing something.

questions.setup: The historian knows which three events occurred but is still investigating their sequence.
questions.prompt: Which question concerns their sequence rather than their cause or importance?
options: Which event came before the others?
Which event mattered most to residents?
Which event caused the others?
Which records provide the strongest support?
questions.explanation: Sequence concerns order, such as what happened first, next and last.
feedback: Sequence concerns order, such as what happened first, next and last.
That asks about significance, not chronological order.
Causation concerns why events happened; sequence alone records their order.
That evaluates evidence, not the order being reconstructed.

questions.setup: Twenty of College A's 100 learners cycle to class. Forty of College B's 400 learners do so.
questions.prompt: Which statement correctly uses 'proportion' rather than just 'number'?
options: College B has the higher proportion because forty exceeds twenty.
College A has the higher proportion: 20% compared with 10%.
The proportions are equal because both colleges have cyclists.
The two proportions are 20 and 40, the cyclist counts.
questions.explanation: A proportion relates a part to its whole; 20 of 100 is a larger share than 40 of 400.
feedback: Forty is the larger count, but it comes from a much larger whole.
A proportion relates a part to its whole; 20 of 100 is a larger share than 40 of 400.
Having members of a category does not make their shares equal.
Those are absolute counts; a proportion relates each count to its college's total.

questions.setup: The assignment says to contrast two accounts of the same journey, concentrating on their different descriptions of the travelers.
questions.prompt: Which response carries out that contrast?
options: One portrays the travelers as prepared; the other presents them as reckless.
Both accounts concern the same journey.
The first account was published in a magazine.
The journey took place in the eighteenth century.
questions.explanation: 'To contrast' is to bring out differences, here opposing portrayals of the same people.
feedback: 'To contrast' is to bring out differences, here opposing portrayals of the same people.
That notes a similarity, whereas the instruction focuses on differences in portrayal.
This describes one source alone without relating the portrayals.
That supplies shared background rather than contrasts the accounts.

questions.setup: The study explores how adult learners describe belonging in their own words, examining themes in interviews rather than counting how many choose each answer.
questions.prompt: Which term best describes this emphasis on meanings and experiences?
options: historical
qualitative
numerical
experimental
questions.explanation: Qualitative research examines qualities, meanings or experiences, often through material such as interviews.
feedback: 'Historical' specifies a focus on the past; the interview emphasis alone does not establish that.
Qualitative research examines qualities, meanings or experiences, often through material such as interviews.
Numerical work centers on quantities, unlike the thematic emphasis described.
'Experimental' concerns testing through planned interventions; no such intervention is described.

questions.setup: A report examines access to city parks but excludes how the parks are financed. Its scope is stated in the introduction.
questions.prompt: What does 'scope' describe here?
options: the issues the report covers and leaves outside
the strength of the evidence for each finding
the writer's reason for preferring city life
the total number of words allowed
questions.explanation: Scope sets the range or boundaries of the inquiry, here access but not financing.
feedback: Scope sets the range or boundaries of the inquiry, here access but not financing.
Evidence quality is a separate question from the range of subjects covered.
The scope does not tell us the writer's personal preference.
Length can constrain a report, but 'scope' here describes its subject boundaries.

questions.setup: A letter lists complaints about the food and beds without directly stating the writer's view of the journey. A reader uses these clues to work out that view.
questions.prompt: Who is doing the inferring?
options: The writer, by suggesting more than is stated
The editor, by deleting the writer's complaints
The reader, by reaching a conclusion from clues
The traveler, by copying another person's words
questions.explanation: 'Infer' means reason from evidence or indications to a conclusion.
feedback: That describes implying; 'infer' names drawing the conclusion from clues.
No deletion is described; inference is an act of interpretation.
'Infer' means reason from evidence or indications to a conclusion.
Copying wording is not drawing a conclusion, and it is not described here.

questions.setup: The assignment asks students to assess a travel diary's usefulness for studying working life, considering both what it records and what it leaves out.
questions.prompt: Which activity is assessment rather than description alone?
options: Listing the diary's chapter headings
Copying its publication details
Retelling each journey in date order
Judging how well it answers the research question
questions.explanation: 'Assess' means 'evaluate'; here the judgment is about usefulness for a specified inquiry.
feedback: A list describes organization but does not judge usefulness.
Bibliographic details identify the source without evaluating it.
Retelling describes content but may leave its usefulness unevaluated.
'Assess' means 'evaluate'; here the judgment is about usefulness for a specified inquiry.

questions.setup: The two observers gave different amounts of detail, but their accounts were consistent with each other.
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves 'consistent' here?
options: They used exactly the same sentences.
Their accounts did not contradict each other.
They had checked their accounts together beforehand.
They described events in the same number of words.
questions.explanation: Accounts are consistent with each other when their claims can fit together without conflict.
feedback: Consistency does not require identical wording or detail.
Accounts are consistent with each other when their claims can fit together without conflict.
Agreement does not establish that the observers coordinated their accounts.
The sentence explicitly allows different detail; consistency is not equal length.

questions.setup: The course follows the principle that learners should be able to explain how their work was assessed. Different tutors use different forms to achieve this.
questions.prompt: What is the principle?
options: the particular form every tutor must use
the general idea guiding the different practices
the average grade learners receive
the order in which forms are printed
questions.explanation: A principle is a basic idea or rule that guides action; more than one procedure can put it into practice.
feedback: The tutors use different forms, so the principle is broader than one form.
A principle is a basic idea or rule that guides action; more than one procedure can put it into practice.
The passage concerns guidance for assessment, not a numerical result.
Printing order is an operational detail, not the guiding idea.

questions.setup: A linguist examines 500 messages selected from a collection of 40,000. The 500 messages form the sample.
questions.prompt: What does 'sample' mean in this study?
options: the full collection of 40,000 messages
the conclusions written after the analysis
the selected part examined for the study
the instructions for selecting the messages
questions.explanation: A research sample is a subset studied; it can consist of texts or objects, not just people.
feedback: The full collection is the larger set; the sample is the selected part examined.
Conclusions are produced from analysis, not the material selected for it.
A research sample is a subset studied; it can consist of texts or objects, not just people.
Selection instructions are the procedure, not the selected messages.

questions.setup: A second laboratory follows the published procedure with new materials to see whether it obtains a similar result. It attempts to replicate the study.
questions.prompt: What is it attempting to do?
options: publish the first team's text under new names
translate the original article into another language
repeat the investigation to check its findings
revise the first team's recorded measurements
questions.explanation: 'Replicate a study' means carry it out again to examine whether its findings recur; success is not guaranteed.
feedback: That would concern copying authorship, not repeating the investigation.
Translation changes language rather than repeats the study.
'Replicate a study' means carry it out again to examine whether its findings recur; success is not guaranteed.
The second laboratory gathers its own material rather than edits earlier measurements.

questions.setup: Before the main article, a short section states the study's purpose, method and main findings. It is headed 'Abstract'.
questions.prompt: What does 'abstract' mean as this heading?
options: a brief overview of the research article
an idea that cannot be pictured physically
the complete list of cited publications
an early unfinished version of the article
questions.explanation: An abstract summarizes the study so readers can quickly understand its purpose and main content.
feedback: An abstract summarizes the study so readers can quickly understand its purpose and main content.
That is a different sense of 'abstract'; the heading names a part of an article.
That list supplies references, not an overview of the study.
A draft is a preliminary version; an abstract can accompany the finished article.

questions.setup: The researchers use a simplified computer model of traffic flow, leaving out details that are not needed for their question.
questions.prompt: Which understanding of 'model' fits?
options: a complete copy containing every real-world detail
a prediction that replaces the need for observations
an ideal driver whom other people should imitate
a representation used to study the real system
questions.explanation: A model represents selected features of a system; useful simplification is part of its purpose.
feedback: The model is explicitly simplified, so completeness is not required.
Models can produce predictions, but 'model' does not mean observations become unnecessary.
'Model' can mean an example to follow, but here it is a representation of traffic.
A model represents selected features of a system; useful simplification is part of its purpose.

questions.setup: A study uses voluntary discussion contributions as one indicator of engagement, while also examining written reflections.
questions.prompt: What role do the contributions have as an indicator?
options: They are the rule that defines engagement completely.
They provide observable information about engagement.
They are the researchers' instructions to learners.
They explain the original cause of engagement.
questions.explanation: An indicator is a sign or measure used to learn about something that may not be directly observable.
feedback: One indicator supplies a sign; it is not necessarily a complete definition of the concept.
An indicator is a sign or measure used to learn about something that may not be directly observable.
The contributions are observed behavior, not directions given by the researchers.
An indicator can signal engagement without explaining what caused it.

questions.setup: Under 'Methodology', the author explains why observation suits her question, what assumptions guide it, and how those assumptions shaped the design.
questions.prompt: What does 'methodology' encompass in this particular section?
options: The approach and reasoning behind the research design
The resulting measurements, arranged for inspection
The practical recommendations made after the investigation
The sequence of publication and peer-review events
questions.explanation: Here methodology includes the methods' underlying rationale, not just a list of actions performed.
feedback: Here methodology includes the methods' underlying rationale, not just a list of actions performed.
Those are results or data; this section explains the approach behind gathering them.
Recommendations concern what should follow the findings, not the basis of the design.
Publication history does not explain the research approach described.

questions.setup: Across surveyed neighborhoods, longer commutes were associated with lower course attendance. The report calls this a negative correlation.
questions.prompt: What does 'negative' describe in this expression?
options: The measures tend to move in opposite directions.
The association is undesirable for the researchers.
The recorded values are all below zero.
The evidence contradicts the existence of any relationship.
questions.explanation: 'Negative correlation' describes an inverse association; 'negative' does not mean 'undesirable' or 'statistically worthless'.
feedback: 'Negative correlation' describes an inverse association; 'negative' does not mean 'undesirable' or 'statistically worthless'.
'Negative' describes the direction of the relationship, not the researchers' feelings about it.
Positive values can be negatively correlated; the term concerns their relationship.
A negative correlation is a relationship, not the absence of one.

questions.setup: A college uses a spelling test to decide who can participate effectively in spoken discussions. Reviewers question the validity of that use, even though spelling scores are marked consistently.
questions.prompt: Which concern is about validity here?
options: Whether the scores support the intended speaking decision
Whether different markers assign the same spelling score
Whether a marker scores unchanged work consistently over time
Whether the test's different spelling items produce consistent scores
questions.explanation: Validity concerns the support for a proposed interpretation or use of scores; spelling may not support this speaking judgment.
feedback: Validity concerns the support for a proposed interpretation or use of scores; spelling may not support this speaking judgment.
That concerns scoring reliability; consistent scoring does not establish suitability for this decision.
That concerns consistency within a rater, not evidence that spelling indicates discussion ability.
Internal consistency can describe relationships among items without establishing that the scores support this speaking decision.

questions.setup: The excavation team releases preliminary findings from the first trench while work continues elsewhere on the site.
questions.prompt: Which meaning is carried by 'preliminary' rather than added by assumption?
options: The findings have already been disproved.
The findings were produced without observation.
The findings concern events before written history.
The findings come from an early stage of the work.
questions.explanation: 'Preliminary' identifies an initial, not-yet-final stage; it does not itself measure evidential quality.
feedback: 'Preliminary' does not mean 'false'; later work may confirm or revise the findings.
An early stage can still produce observational evidence.
That would be 'prehistoric'; 'preliminary' concerns the stage of the investigation.
'Preliminary' identifies an initial, not-yet-final stage; it does not itself measure evidential quality.

questions.setup: A study finds that readers miss information placed only in footnotes. Its discussion considers the implications for textbook design, without yet recommending a particular layout.
questions.prompt: What does 'implications' mean in this use?
options: The exact layout changes the authors have prescribed
The unspoken personal criticisms of textbook writers
The original conditions under which readers were recruited
The consequences the finding may have for design choices
questions.explanation: Practical implications are what a finding could mean for subsequent understanding or action.
feedback: The passage explicitly separates implications from specific recommendations.
'Implications' can mean unstated meanings, but here practical consequences for design are intended.
Recruitment conditions concern methods, not what follows from the finding.
Practical implications are what a finding could mean for subsequent understanding or action.

questions.setup: Researchers interview the same adults each year for a decade to follow changes in their reading habits.
questions.prompt: Why is 'longitudinal' an appropriate description of this design?
options: It compares different age groups at one moment.
It follows change in the participants over time.
It combines findings from several published investigations.
It studies participants from widely separated locations.
questions.explanation: Longitudinal research follows a subject or group across time, enabling examination of change.
feedback: That describes a cross-sectional comparison rather than repeated observation of these adults.
Longitudinal research follows a subject or group across time, enabling examination of change.
Combining prior studies is a research synthesis, not what repeated interviews describe.
Geographical spread is not the meaning of 'longitudinal' in research design.

questions.setup: A reviewer wants a synthesis of three studies, not three self-contained summaries placed one after another.
questions.prompt: Which revision best meets that request?
options: Shorten each study's summary without linking the studies
Organize their agreements and tensions into a connected account
Arrange the complete summaries by publication date
Replace the summaries with the studies' abstracts unchanged
questions.explanation: A synthesis integrates material into a whole, showing relationships rather than merely listing sources.
feedback: Brevity alone leaves the three accounts separate.
A synthesis integrates material into a whole, showing relationships rather than merely listing sources.
Chronological ordering can help, but does not by itself integrate the findings.
Reproducing abstracts compiles existing text rather than creates an integrated account.

questions.setup: A study carefully documents winter use of a public square. The author identifies the lack of summer observations as a limitation.
questions.prompt: What is the limitation's role in this account?
options: It identifies an error in the recorded winter counts.
It restricts conclusions about year-round use.
It explains the practical reason the team chose winter.
It supplies a recommendation for the square's summer design.
questions.explanation: A limitation can bound the reach of findings without invalidating the work within that boundary.
feedback: The lack of summer observations does not establish that the winter counts are wrong.
A limitation can bound the reach of findings without invalidating the work within that boundary.
A limitation states a constraint on the account; it does not itself supply the reason for the timing choice.
The omission may motivate future research, but it supplies no specific design recommendation.

questions.setup: Researchers know that a coating slows water loss. They investigate the mechanism: how its layer changes the movement of moisture.
questions.prompt: What does 'mechanism' focus on?
options: The frequency with which the coating is sold
The strength of the statistical association alone
The process through which the effect is produced
The terminology used to name the coating
questions.explanation: A mechanism explains how something happens by identifying the processes connecting cause and effect.
feedback: Sales frequency is not the process producing the effect.
An association describes co-variation; a mechanism concerns how an effect is produced.
A mechanism explains how something happens by identifying the processes connecting cause and effect.
A name does not explain the physical process.

questions.setup: A researcher compares interview accounts with field observations and attendance records to examine the same participation question.
questions.prompt: Why might this be described as triangulation?
options: It repeats one identical measurement exactly three times.
It averages all findings into a single numerical score.
It examines a question through different kinds of evidence.
It ensures that the sources must reach the same conclusion.
questions.explanation: Triangulation brings multiple sources, methods or perspectives to bear on an inquiry; it can reveal disagreement as well as agreement.
feedback: The term is not a rule requiring three repetitions of the same measure.
Comparing different sources does not require reducing them to one number.
Triangulation brings multiple sources, methods or perspectives to bear on an inquiry; it can reveal disagreement as well as agreement.
Triangulation may expose conflicts; it does not guarantee agreement or truth.

questions.setup: Two assessors repeatedly give similar scores to the same set of presentations. The course team describes high inter-rater reliability.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion is specifically about this reliability?
options: The scores are consistent across the assessors.
The presentations test every skill needed in the workplace.
The scores predict future job performance accurately.
The marking process is faster than the previous system.
questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability concerns consistency between raters, not by itself the appropriateness of what is assessed.
feedback: Inter-rater reliability concerns consistency between raters, not by itself the appropriateness of what is assessed.
Coverage of the intended skill domain is not established by agreement between assessors.
Prediction requires further evidence; assessor agreement alone does not establish it.
Speed and reliability are different features; timing information is not provided.

questions.setup: The seminar asks whether the ending is contingent on the narrator's final decision or would occur regardless of what she chooses.
questions.prompt: Which meaning of 'contingent on' fits that contrast?
options: chronologically earlier than
accidentally similar to
dependent on
fully explained before
questions.explanation: 'Contingent on' means 'dependent on a condition'; 'regardless of' presents the contrasting independence.
feedback: Contingency is about dependence, not simply time order.
Similarity does not express the dependence being contrasted with 'regardless'.
'Contingent on' means 'dependent on a condition'; 'regardless of' presents the contrasting independence.
An explanation's timing is not the issue in the seminar question.

questions.setup: Records cover factory output from 1920 to 1940. An author uses that trend to estimate output in 1950, outside the recorded period.
questions.prompt: Which term precisely names extending the pattern beyond the observed range?
options: transcribing
interpolating
classifying
extrapolating
questions.explanation: Extrapolation extends a pattern beyond the observed range; its reliability depends on further assumptions.
feedback: Transcribing reproduces recorded information; the 1950 estimate is not in the records.
Interpolation estimates within an observed range, not beyond its endpoint.
Classification assigns items to categories rather than extends a trend.
Extrapolation extends a pattern beyond the observed range; its reliability depends on further assumptions.

questions.setup: The study treats belonging as a construct and uses several questions to investigate it; no single question is taken to be belonging itself.
questions.prompt: What is the construct here?
options: the abstract concept the study is investigating
the questionnaire used to collect the responses
the total score printed beside each name
the scoring rule used to combine the responses
questions.explanation: A construct is a concept developed for explanation or investigation, distinct from any one instrument used to study it.
feedback: A construct is a concept developed for explanation or investigation, distinct from any one instrument used to study it.
The questionnaire is an instrument for investigating the construct, not the construct itself.
A score is a recorded measure; it does not become the whole abstract concept.
The scoring rule operationalizes part of the investigation; it is not the abstract belonging concept.

questions.setup: A review of research on sleep and learning says, 'The literature is divided on whether the effect lasts.'
questions.prompt: What does the sentence report?
options: Each individual study contradicts itself about the effect.
Published work in the field reaches differing positions.
The review divides a shared conclusion into separate topics.
The field agrees on the effect but disagrees about terminology.
questions.explanation: 'The literature' means the body of relevant writing; 'divided' indicates a lack of agreement within it.
feedback: Disagreement across the literature does not require internal contradiction within each study.
'The literature' means the body of relevant writing; 'divided' indicates a lack of agreement within it.
The phrase 'divided on whether' signals disagreement about the question, not the review's section structure.
The stated disagreement concerns whether the effect lasts, not merely the words used to describe it.

questions.setup: For this study, walkability is operationalized as the number of everyday services reachable within a ten-minute walk.
questions.prompt: What has the researcher done?
options: Established the only legitimate meaning of walkability
Completed the construction of new pedestrian routes
Demonstrated that walking causes access to services
Specified an observable measure for the concept
questions.explanation: Operationalizing connects an abstract concept to defined observations or procedures, here a service count within a time limit.
feedback: An operational definition selects a way to investigate a concept; it need not exhaust the concept's meaning.
'Operationalize' in research does not mean put a building project into operation.
The definition provides a measure, not a causal demonstration.
Operationalizing connects an abstract concept to defined observations or procedures, here a service count within a time limit.

questions.setup: In reviewing a transcript, the analyst identifies repeated references to losing contact with neighbors as especially salient.
questions.prompt: Which meaning does 'salient' add?
options: statistically representative of the wider population
chronologically earlier than the other references
particularly noticeable or important for the analysis
demonstrated to be the cause of the other experiences

feedback: Prominence in a transcript does not establish population representativeness.

Salient features stand out as prominent or relevant in the context being examined.

questions.setup: The aggregate completion rate rose, although several individual courses saw their rates fall.
questions.prompt: How can both parts be true?
options: Aggregate means the rate for the least successful course.
Aggregate describes the combined result, not every component.
Aggregate means a rate predicted for the following year.
Aggregate means the figures have been corrected for errors.
questions.explanation: An aggregate combines data across parts; its direction need not match the direction in each part.
feedback: The term refers to combination, not selection of the lowest-performing component.
An aggregate combines data across parts; its direction need not match the direction in each part.
Aggregation concerns how data are combined, not whether they are forecasts.
Combining figures does not itself mean that errors were detected or corrected.

questions.setup: The essay contrasts a prediction derived from theory with empirical evidence from classroom observations and learner interviews.
questions.prompt: What makes the evidence empirical in this contrast?
options: It consists exclusively of numerical measurements.
It has been accepted as beyond further challenge.
It was obtained without any guiding research ideas.
It comes from observation or experience.
questions.explanation: Empirical evidence is grounded in observation or experience, in contrast to derivation from theory alone.
feedback: Empirical material may include qualitative observations and interviews, not only numbers.

Empirical evidence is grounded in observation or experience, in contrast to derivation from theory alone.

questions.setup: A model treats having a course available and being able to afford it as the same thing. A reviewer calls this a conceptual weakness, even though the calculations are correct.

options: In the numerical operations performed on the data
In the consistency with which observations were recorded
In the way the model distinguishes its underlying ideas
In the size of the sample chosen for the model

questions.setup: A reviewer questions one author's use of the expression 'paradigm shift'.
questions.prompt: Which use of 'paradigm shift' most clearly overstates the development described?
options: A field begins treating readers as makers of meaning rather than passive recipients.
The team puts its existing questionnaire online while retaining the same questions and assumptions.
Researchers redefine what counts as an explanation after abandoning a previously central model.
Previously marginal questions become central as the field rethinks its basic account of learning.
questions.explanation: Changing the delivery tool alone is procedural; it need not alter the assumptions organizing the inquiry.
feedback: This changes the field's conception of its subject, not merely a tool for collecting answers.
Changing the delivery tool alone is procedural; it need not alter the assumptions organizing the inquiry.

questions.setup: An editor checks whether a critic has used 'reify' accurately in an analysis of culture.
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the word in its critical academic sense?

The account reifies culture by using one label while acknowledging diverse local practices.
The account reifies culture by tracing changes in how speakers use the term.

questions.explanation: Reification treats an abstraction as a concrete thing or independent entity, as this account does with culture.
feedback: Keeping rival interpretations open does not itself treat culture as a concrete independent entity.

Tracing a term's changing use examines the concept rather than necessarily treating it as a self-acting thing.
Reification treats an abstraction as a concrete thing or independent entity, as this account does with culture.

questions.setup: The report describes an inscription's purpose as 'underdetermined by the surviving record'.
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the relationship between evidence and explanation?
options: The surviving record permits more than one explanation.
The surviving record contradicts the proposed explanations.
The investigator has not yet formed a personal preference.
The report expresses its preferred explanation in imprecise language.
questions.explanation: Underdetermination means the evidence does not uniquely determine the explanation, not that no explanation is possible.
feedback: Underdetermination means the evidence does not uniquely determine the explanation, not that no explanation is possible.

Personal indecision is not the same as the evidence failing to discriminate among accounts.

questions.setup: A reviewer writes, 'The two evaluation scales may be commensurable without being interchangeable.'
questions.prompt: Which restatement preserves both parts?
options: They yield equal scores but need different names.
They concern the same topic but cannot be compared.
They can replace each other once their units are renamed.
They may share a basis for comparison without being substitutes.
questions.explanation: Commensurability allows comparison on a common basis; it need not make measures interchangeable.
feedback: Equal values do not establish commensurability, and different names do not explain noninterchangeability.

The reviewer explicitly distinguishes comparability from substituting one scale for the other.
Commensurability allows comparison on a common basis; it need not make measures interchangeable.

questions.setup: An account traces dialect innovations to exchanges among the community's speakers rather than to an imposed schooling policy.
questions.prompt: Which adjective most precisely labels the source of the innovations in this account?

endogenous
autonomous
spontaneous

questions.setup: The review says, 'My objection to this conclusion is epistemic, not ethical.'
questions.prompt: Which response addresses the stated objection most directly?

Show how the available evidence warrants accepting the conclusion.

questions.setup: A seminar distinguishes several kinds of questions about a committee.

questions.setup: An editor describes checking unusually long sentences first as a heuristic for finding errors.
questions.prompt: Which follow-up overstates what calling the practice a heuristic establishes?

It establishes that a sentence is faulty because it is long.
Its usefulness can depend on the kind of text being examined.

feedback: A heuristic can direct investigation toward promising places to look.
A heuristic guides a search; calling it one does not turn length into proof of an error.

questions.setup: A review asks the author to replace an unstructured inventory of discussion tasks with a taxonomy.
questions.prompt: Which revision best answers that request?
options: Add publication dates to the task descriptions and arrange them in time order.
Rank the tasks from the most popular to the least popular.
Classify the tasks by function and explain how the classes differ.
Expand each description while retaining the same undifferentiated list.
questions.explanation: A taxonomy supplies a classification system; it does more than enumerate the tasks.
feedback: This creates a chronology, not a function-based or other principled classification.

A taxonomy supplies a classification system; it does more than enumerate the tasks.
A fuller inventory remains a list if it supplies no classification scheme.

questions.setup: An editor separates a policy writer's own normative claims from descriptive reports of other people's positions.
questions.prompt: Which sentence makes a normative claim in the writer's own voice?
options: Most respondents said that universities ought to provide an appeal process.
The handbook describes access to an appeal as essential.
The review records widespread agreement that appeals are desirable.
Universities owe students a fair opportunity to challenge an assessment.
questions.explanation: 'Owe' expresses a normative obligation advocated by the writer, without relying on 'should'.
feedback: This reports respondents' normative views; it does not itself adopt them as the writer's standard.

This reports an observed consensus rather than independently advocates the standard.
'Owe' expresses a normative obligation advocated by the writer, without relying on 'should'.

questions.setup: A reviewer praises an explanation of course participation as 'concise without being reductive'.
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves that distinction?
options: It limits its evidence while making broad claims.
It is brief but preserves the essential complexity.
It selects one cause and leaves other causes unexplored.

feedback: Restricting evidence while broadening claims does not express the praised distinction between brevity and oversimplification.

questions.setup: The town's railway opened in 1880. A historian accepts that date and considers several further research questions.
questions.prompt: Which question proposes a counterfactual analysis?
options: Which earlier plans were considered before the railway was built?

How did merchants describe the railway before it opened?
How might the town have developed if the railway had never been built?

feedback: This investigates plans actually considered in the past; an unbuilt plan can be a factual historical subject.

This explores an unrealized alternative to the accepted past, the basis of counterfactual analysis.

questions.setup: The reviewer calls an account 'falsifiable, though not yet falsified'.
questions.prompt: Which follow-up is inconsistent with that assessment?
options: An appropriately specified observation could count against it.
The proposed test could leave the account standing.
Calling it falsifiable concedes that its conclusion is wrong.

questions.explanation: 'Falsifiable' means open to possible disconfirmation; it does not report that disconfirmation has occurred.
feedback: That is compatible with falsifiability: some possible evidence would challenge the account.

'Falsifiable' means open to possible disconfirmation; it does not report that disconfirmation has occurred.

questions.setup: After reading a study of a specialist choir, a reviewer requests evidence addressing generalizability.
questions.prompt: Which follow-up investigation most directly addresses that request?
options: Examine whether the reported learning pattern also occurs in novice community choirs.
Have new analysts check whether the original recordings were transcribed accurately.
Ask the original analysts to recode the same sessions and compare their decisions.
Check whether the explanation accounts for all the recorded specialist-choir sessions.
questions.explanation: Generalizability concerns the reach of findings beyond the cases or conditions originally studied.
feedback: Generalizability concerns the reach of findings beyond the cases or conditions originally studied.
That checks the original evidence record rather than the findings' applicability beyond it.
That examines consistency within the original material, not extension to other groups.
That tests fit within the studied case; it does not directly investigate reach beyond that case.

questions.setup: A researcher studies a club she once chaired. The reviewer asks for greater reflexivity in her methods discussion.
questions.prompt: Which addition responds to that request?
options: A longer account of her years as chair, separate from the research analysis
A detailed explanation of how members' names were anonymized
An examination of how her former authority shaped interviews and interpretation
A comparison of two analysts' coding decisions, with disagreements reconciled
questions.explanation: Reflexivity analyzes how the researcher's role, assumptions and relationships influence the investigation.
feedback: Biography alone does not examine how her position shapes the inquiry.

Reflexivity analyzes how the researcher's role, assumptions and relationships influence the investigation.

questions.setup: An editor asks for a dialectical development of the philosophy chapter's argument, rather than a catalogue of positions.
questions.prompt: Which revision best meets that request?
options: Use objections to revise the initial claim and examine the revised claim in turn.

Classify the schools by their shared historical origins and terminology.
Trace how each school's vocabulary changed over time in separate historical accounts.

feedback: Dialectical development here advances thought through engagement with opposing reasons and the tensions they reveal.

Classification organizes positions but does not by itself advance an argument through objections.

questions.setup: A linguist plans a synchronic account of verb forms in the language of the mid-fifteenth century.
questions.prompt: Which plan adopts the requested focus?
options: Trace how the forms developed from their earlier medieval equivalents.
Analyze how the verb forms contrast and combine within that period's system.
Compare the frequencies of the forms in fifteenth- and nineteenth-century texts.
Explain how later contact with another language transformed the forms.
questions.explanation: A synchronic account examines a language system at a given stage, including a historical one.
feedback: Tracing development from earlier stages is a diachronic focus.
A synchronic account examines a language system at a given stage, including a historical one.

questions.setup: A journal seeks a metatheoretical contribution to the study of migration.
questions.prompt: Which proposed article most clearly fits that request?

An article estimating how wage differences predict migration across regions
An article combining several regional datasets to refine a model's prediction

questions.explanation: Metatheoretical inquiry examines theories, their assumptions or their explanatory standards.
feedback: Metatheoretical inquiry examines theories, their assumptions or their explanatory standards.

questions.setup: The editor asks the writer to problematize the public/private distinction in an essay on online communication.
questions.prompt: Which revision does that most directly?
options: Examine cases that strain the boundary and ask what the distinction leaves out.
Replace the two familiar labels with more specialized terms but preserve the same boundary.
Add clear examples to each side while leaving the classification's assumptions unexamined.
Compare how often writers use public and private in three online forums.
questions.explanation: Problematizing makes an accepted distinction an object of critical questioning, exposing assumptions or difficulties.
feedback: Problematizing makes an accepted distinction an object of critical questioning, exposing assumptions or difficulties.

Illustrating a distinction takes it as usable; it does not yet problematize it.

questions.setup: A historian distinguishes teleological explanations of state formation from chronological and immediate-cause accounts.

A teleological explanation accounts for development in terms of an end or purpose; this sentence makes the final state the directing endpoint.

questions.setup: Complete the description of the instructions.
