The supplementary relative supplies a completed June recording, adding the very event claim the edit must avoid.

questions.setup: 'The plumber I thought had cancelled arrived at the flat.' A learner proposes adding 'she' after 'thought' because 'had cancelled' otherwise seems to lack a subject.
questions.prompt: Which explanation correctly assesses the original and the proposed addition in standard edited English?
options: The addition is needed because I must be the subject of both thought and had cancelled.
The original is incomplete because a relative marker can never be omitted before I thought.
The original is complete: the relative links plumber to the subject of had cancelled. She would duplicate that role.
The addition makes no structural difference because she is the subject of arrived.
questions.explanation: The relative can be expanded to 'the plumber who I thought had cancelled'. Its subject relationship crosses the intervening 'I thought' clause.
feedback: 'I' is the subject of 'thought', but the relative refers to the plumber as the person thought to have cancelled.
A zero relative is possible here; the embedded subject dependency should not be confused with simply omitting 'who' in 'who had cancelled'.
The relative can be expanded to 'the plumber who I thought had cancelled'. Its subject relationship crosses the intervening 'I thought' clause.
'Arrived' already has the whole noun phrase 'the plumber ...' as its subject; an inserted 'she' after 'thought' would sit inside the relative clause.

questions.setup: Had the road remained open, we would still have walked, cumbersome though our bags were.
questions.prompt: Which expansion preserves both the hypothetical road condition and the concessive role of the heavy bags?
options: If the road had remained open and our bags had been cumbersome, we would have walked.
Because the road remained open, we walked despite the cumbersome bags.
Even if the road had stayed open, we would have walked despite our cumbersome bags.
If our bags had been less cumbersome, we would have walked while the road remained open.
questions.explanation: The inverted condition imagines an open road, still preserves walking under that alternative, and though presents the bags as a concession.
feedback: This makes the bags' cumbersomeness another hypothetical condition instead of a conceded circumstance.
This asserts an open road and actual walking, replacing the hypothetical alternative.
The inverted condition imagines an open road, still preserves walking under that alternative, and though presents the bags as a concession.
This moves the hypothetical condition to the bags and makes the road's openness background to a different decision.

questions.setup: You are introducing your job. Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I am nurse.
I am an nurse.
I am a nurses.
I am a nurse.
questions.explanation: Use a before the singular job noun nurse: I am a nurse. Nurse begins with the consonant sound /n/.
feedback: The singular job noun nurse needs a word such as a before it: I am a nurse.
Nurse starts with the consonant sound /n/, so use a, not an.
A needs a singular noun. Use a nurse, not a nurses.
A nurse correctly names one person's job, with a before the singular noun.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Can I borrow a eraser?
Can I borrow eraser?
Can I borrow an eraser?
Can I borrow an erasers?
questions.explanation: "Eraser" begins with a vowel sound. For one eraser, say "an eraser".
feedback: Use "an" before the vowel sound at the start of "eraser".
"Eraser" names one countable object here, so it cannot stand alone without a determiner.
"An eraser" correctly asks for one countable object beginning with a vowel sound.
"An" is for one object, but "erasers" is plural. Use "an eraser" or simply "erasers".

questions.setup: Choose the words that refer to the door you can both see.
questions.prompt: There is just one door in the room. Please close ___ door.
options: a
the
an
(nothing)
questions.explanation: You can both identify the room's one door. "The door" points to that particular door.
feedback: "A door" means one door without identifying which. Here the speaker means the room's already identified door.
"The" refers to the single door already identified in the room.
"Door" starts with /d/, a consonant sound. "An door" is not grammatical.
A singular countable noun such as "door" needs a determiner in this request.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence about water in general.
questions.prompt: Which sentence says what people need every day?
options: People need a water every day.
People need an water every day.
People need the water every day.
People need water every day.
questions.explanation: "Water" names a substance in general here. We do not put an article before it: "People need water."
feedback: "A water" can mean one serving when ordering a drink. This question is about the substance people need, not a serving.
"An" is not used before the consonant sound /w/. It also does not express water as a substance in general.
"The water" refers to particular water already identified. No such water is meant in this general statement.
No article is needed when "water" means the substance in general.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: That is a my coat.
That is the my coat.
That is an my coat.
That is my coat.
questions.explanation: "My" already shows whose coat it is. Do not add "a", "an", or "the" before "my".
feedback: English does not combine "a" and "my" before the same noun. Say "my coat".
"The" and "my" both identify the noun; they do not go together in "the my coat".
"An" cannot come before the possessive "my". The phrase needs only "my coat".
The possessive "my" supplies the information needed before the singular noun "coat".

questions.setup: You are in your own flat. Choose the usual way to tell a friend where you are.
questions.prompt: I'm ___ now. You can call me.
options: at home
at a home
at an home
at the home
questions.explanation: At home means in the place where you live. This everyday expression has no article before home.
feedback: This is the ordinary expression for being in the place where you live.
A home introduces one home, often a place that provides care. It is not the usual expression for being in your own flat.
Home begins with a pronounced h, so an is wrong. The expression for your location is at home, with no article.
The home points to a particular home already understood, such as a care home. To say you are in your own flat, use at home.

questions.setup: Choose the word for the same bus.
questions.prompt: A bus stops beside us. ___ bus is full.
options: A
An
The
(nothing)
questions.explanation: The first sentence introduces "a bus". The second refers to that same bus, so it says "the bus".
feedback: "A bus" would introduce a bus without clearly linking it to the one in the first sentence.
"Bus" begins with a consonant sound, so "an bus" is not possible.
"The bus" takes the reader back to the bus that has just stopped.
"Bus" is singular and countable; it cannot be used without a determiner here.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence about a general liking.
questions.prompt: You like cats of all kinds. What do you say?
options: I like cats.
I like a cats.
I like an cats.
I like the cats.
questions.explanation: A plural noun with no article can mean the whole kind: "I like cats" means cats in general.
feedback: The plural "cats" without an article expresses the general liking described.
"A" goes with a singular countable noun, not the plural "cats".
"An" cannot introduce a plural noun. It also does not match the initial consonant sound in "cats".
This means a particular group of cats that speaker and listener can identify, not cats of all kinds.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: We have an small kitchen.
We have small kitchen.
We have a small kitchen.
We have a small kitchens.
questions.explanation: Put the article before the adjective: "a small kitchen". "Small" begins with a consonant sound.
feedback: Choose the article using the next sound, which is /s/ in "small". It needs "a".
An adjective does not remove the need for an article before the singular noun "kitchen".
"A" comes before "small" and introduces the one kitchen.
"A" introduces one kitchen; "kitchens" is plural and cannot follow it.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Would you like a apple juice?
Would you like an glass of juice?
Would you like glass of juice?
Would you like a glass of juice?
questions.explanation: The article belongs to "glass", a countable container. We can offer "a glass of juice" even though juice itself is not counted here.
feedback: "Apple" starts with a vowel sound, so an order for one serving would use "an apple juice", not "a apple juice".
"Glass" begins with /g/, so it takes "a", not "an".
One countable container needs a determiner: "a glass of juice".
"A" correctly introduces the container "glass"; no second article is needed before "juice".

questions.setup: Refer to the particular blue cup both people can identify, not just any blue cup.
questions.prompt: There are three cups. Only one is blue. Please use ___ blue cup.
options: an
(nothing)
a
the
questions.explanation: The colour identifies one cup among the three. "The blue cup" tells the listener exactly which cup to use.
feedback: 'Blue' starts with a consonant sound, so 'an blue cup' is not grammatical.
The singular noun 'cup' still needs a determiner even when an adjective comes before it.
'A blue cup' is grammatical and might lead to the same choice here. It does not explicitly present the cup as already identifiable, as this instruction requires.
The definite article presents the blue cup as the particular cup both people can identify.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: We eat breakfast at seven.
We eat a breakfast at a seven.
We eat an breakfast at seven.
We eat breakfast at the seven.
questions.explanation: The ordinary meal name needs no article in "eat breakfast". A clock time is also used without an article: "at seven".
feedback: This uses the usual article-free meal name and clock time.
"A breakfast" can describe one meal, but "at a seven" is not how English gives this clock time.
"An" does not fit the consonant sound /b/. The usual routine expression is simply "eat breakfast".
Do not put "the" before a bare clock time. Say "at seven".

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the price.
questions.prompt: A sign beside the apples says, 'Two euros a kilo.' What does 'a kilo' mean here?
options: For each apple
For each kilo
For half a kilo
For all the apples
questions.explanation: In this price, "a kilo" means "for each kilo". One kilo costs two euros; two kilos cost four euros.
feedback: The unit named is kilo, a weight, not an individual apple.
Here a means for each unit, and the stated unit is one kilo.
The label gives the price for a full kilo. Half a kilo would cost one euro at this rate.
The price applies to each kilo, not to the whole supply of apples.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: This is an old photo of me.
This is a old photo of me.
This is old photo of me.
This is an old photos of me.
questions.explanation: Although "photo" starts with a consonant, the word directly after the article is "old". Its vowel sound requires "an".
feedback: "An" correctly comes before the vowel sound in "old" and introduces one photo.
Use the first sound of "old", not the first sound of "photo", to choose the article.
"Old" describes the photo but cannot replace the article needed with this singular noun.
"An" is singular; it cannot be followed by the plural noun "photos".

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Sun is very bright today.
The sun is very bright today.
An sun is very bright today.
The a sun is very bright today.
questions.explanation: When we talk about the sun in our sky, we normally say "the sun" because we can identify which sun we mean.
feedback: In an ordinary full sentence about our sky, the noun phrase is "the sun", with an article.
"The sun" is the usual way to name the familiar sun in our sky.
"Sun" starts with /s/, so "an sun" is not grammatical.
Do not put "the" and "a" together before the same noun.

questions.setup: Choose the usual sentence for saying where you live.
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the city name correctly?
options: I live in a Tokyo.
I live in the Tokyo.
I live in Tokyo.
I live in an Tokyo.
questions.explanation: The city name "Tokyo" normally stands alone. Do not add an article when you simply say where you live.
feedback: "A Tokyo" is not the usual name of this city in a simple address statement.
The city name does not normally take "the" on its own. Say "in Tokyo".
The proper name "Tokyo" identifies the city without an article.
"An" does not belong before this city name and does not match its initial consonant sound.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I have brother and two sisters.
I have a brother and two sisters.
I have an brother and two sisters.
I have a brother and a two sisters.
questions.explanation: One brother needs "a brother". The number "two" already tells us how many sisters, so no article goes before it here.
feedback: The singular countable noun "brother" needs a determiner such as "a".
This uses "a" for one brother and a number without an article for the sisters.
"Brother" begins with the consonant sound /b/, so use "a".
The singular article "a" cannot introduce the plural number phrase "two sisters".

questions.setup: Choose the usual sentence for introducing yourself.
questions.prompt: Your name is Ana. What do you say?
options: My name is an Ana.
My name Ana.
My name is Ana.
My a name is Ana.
questions.explanation: Use a person's ordinary name without an article: "My name is Ana." A vowel at the start of a name does not mean it needs "an".
feedback: A name does not need an just because it begins with a vowel. In this introduction, say Ana on its own.
A complete statement needs the verb is between my name and Ana. An article cannot replace that verb.
The sentence has the verb is and uses the personal name without an article.
My already identifies whose name you mean. Do not add a between my and name.

questions.setup: Choose the word used with this position.
questions.prompt: Our lesson is on ___ first floor, not the second floor.
options: a
the
an
(nothing)
questions.explanation: Use "the" with the numbered position "first" here: "the first floor", just as we say "the second floor".
feedback: "A first floor" can introduce one in a different description, but this sentence identifies the floor by its position in this building.
"The first floor" identifies a specific floor by its position.
"First" begins with a consonant sound, so "an first floor" is not grammatical.
In this ordinary sentence, the position phrase is "on the first floor", with "the".

questions.setup: Choose the usual sentence about speaking a language.
questions.prompt: Which sentence names the language correctly?
options: We speak English at home.
We speak an English at home.
We speak a English at home.
We speak the English at home.
questions.explanation: Use the language name on its own in "speak English". An article is not needed to name the language you speak.
feedback: "English" names the language directly, without an article.
Although "English" begins with a vowel sound, a language name does not take "an" in this ordinary statement.
"A English" is not the phrase for naming the language. Use "speak English".
"The English" can refer to English people, but the ordinary language phrase here is simply "English".

questions.setup: Choose the words that keep talking about the same car.
questions.prompt: I bought a used car yesterday. ___ car needs two new tyres.
options: An
A
(nothing)
The
questions.explanation: "The car" refers back to the used car just introduced. Repeating "a car" would not clearly maintain that reference.
feedback: "Car" begins with /k/, so "an car" is incorrect.
This would introduce a car without explicitly linking it to the previous sentence. The task asks you to maintain the same reference.
The singular noun "car" needs a determiner; it cannot start this sentence alone.
The reader already knows which car is being discussed: the one bought yesterday.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: My new position begins tomorrow. The company has sent me ___ about my first day.
options: an information
an piece of information
a piece of informations
a piece of information
questions.explanation: "Information" is uncountable. To refer to one detail, use the countable phrase "a piece of information".
feedback: English does not normally count information as "an information". Count a piece or an item of information instead.
"Piece" starts with /p/, so the article must be "a".
The uncountable noun stays "information" after "a piece of"; it does not take plural -s.
"A" introduces the singular countable noun "piece", while "information" stays uncountable.

questions.setup: Choose the correct phrase for this feeling.
questions.prompt: Please turn the music down. I've got ___.
options: headache
an headache
a headache
a headaches
questions.explanation: The usual expression is "have a headache". "Headache" is a singular countable noun and begins with a pronounced /h/.
feedback: This expression normally needs an article: "I've got a headache".
The /h/ in "headache" is pronounced, so use "a".
"A headache" correctly names one instance of this discomfort.
"A" cannot introduce the plural "headaches". Use singular "headache" here.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence about a regular weekly class.
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the day name correctly?
options: We have training every the Monday.
We have training on a Mondays.
We have training on Mondays.
We have training on an Mondays.
questions.explanation: "On Mondays" means regularly on that day of the week. The plural day name does not take an article in this expression.
feedback: Do not combine "every" with "the" here. You can say "every Monday".
The singular article "a" cannot introduce the plural day name "Mondays".
The plural day name without an article expresses the repeated weekly event.
"An" is singular and does not match either the plural form or the initial consonant sound.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: This isn't a language school. It's ___.
options: a university
an university
university
a universities
questions.explanation: "University" starts with the consonant sound /y/, as in "you". The spelling starts with u, but the sound requires "a".
feedback: "A" agrees with the initial sound and introduces one institution of this kind.
The initial sound is /y/, not a vowel sound. Write "a university".
When classifying this institution after "It is", the singular noun needs a determiner.
"A" means one; it cannot be followed by the plural "universities".

questions.setup: No hotel has been mentioned. Choose the phrase for one hotel of the kind wanted, not a particular hotel or an extra one.
questions.prompt: At the tourist office: 'We're looking for ___ near the beach.'
options: the small hotel
another small hotel
that small hotel
a small hotel
questions.explanation: A small hotel describes one place of the kind the travellers want. They can use a before they have found or chosen that place.
feedback: The suggests that the listener can identify which hotel is meant. The travellers are introducing the kind they want.
Another asks for a different or additional hotel. That adds a comparison with a hotel not mentioned in this request.
That points to a particular hotel, perhaps one already discussed. No such hotel has been identified here.
This introduces one hotel of the desired kind without identifying it in advance.

questions.setup: Choose the usual phrase naming the means of travel.
questions.prompt: Flights are expensive, so we're going to Paris ___.
options: by a train
by train
by an train
by the train
questions.explanation: Use "by train" to name the means of travel. In this expression, "by" is followed by the transport word without an article.
feedback: A train counts one vehicle. The usual expression naming this means of travel is by train, without an article.
This names the travel method using the standard by + transport expression.
An cannot come before the consonant sound at the start of train. The method expression also needs no article.
The train identifies a particular vehicle. That can occur in other contexts, but the ordinary phrase for the travel method alone is by train.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: The repair took exactly sixty minutes: ___.
options: an hour
a hour
an hours
hour
questions.explanation: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because its h is silent. One period of sixty minutes is "an hour".
feedback: The article follows the sound, not the silent written h.
The first spoken sound in "hour" is a vowel, so "a" must become "an".
"An" introduces one unit; "hours" is plural.
To name one countable period here, include the article: "an hour".

questions.setup: Choose the phrase for all the details printed on this ticket.
questions.prompt: Check ___ before you travel.
options: the information on your ticket
an information on your ticket
a information on your ticket
the informations on your ticket
questions.explanation: "On your ticket" identifies the information to check. Although "information" is uncountable, it can take "the" when it refers to specific details.
feedback: "The" identifies the particular set of details printed on the ticket.
"Information" is uncountable; "an information" is not a standard singular unit.
The uncountable noun does not take "a", and the following sound is a vowel as well.
"Information" does not normally have a plural -s form in English.

questions.setup: Choose the words for this country name.
questions.prompt: My sister lives in ___ United States.
options: the
a
an
(nothing)
questions.explanation: The conventional country name is "the United States". Some multiword country names use "the", even though names such as Japan do not.
feedback: "The United States" is the established form of this country name.
"A United States" does not name the country in this ordinary location sentence.
The name does not take "an"; "United" also starts with a consonant sound.
The country name normally includes "the" in a full sentence: "in the United States".

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: The map has bus routes and opening times. What ___!
options: an useful guide
a useful guide
useful guide
a useful guides
questions.explanation: The exclamation is "What a useful guide!". "Useful" begins with the consonant sound /y/, so it takes "a".
feedback: The written u in "useful" represents a /y/ sound at the start. Use "a".
This puts "a" before the adjective and uses the correct sound-based choice.
A singular countable noun in this exclamation needs an article: "What a useful guide!".
"A" cannot introduce the plural "guides" in this exclamation.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: At the cafe: "Two coffees, please: ___ and a cappuccino."
options: a espresso
an espressos
an espresso
a espressos
questions.explanation: A drink name can be countable when it means one serving. "An espresso" is one serving, and "espresso" begins with a vowel sound.
feedback: For this vowel sound, the singular article is "an".
"An" is singular, whereas "espressos" is plural.
This correctly names one serving of espresso within the two-drink order.
"A" cannot introduce plural "espressos" and does not match the initial vowel sound.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: Both bags look blue to me. Are they ___ colour?
options: the same
a same
an same
same
questions.explanation: The normal expression is "the same colour". English uses "the" with "same" in this comparison.
feedback: "The same colour" asks whether the colours match.
Do not use "a same" in this expression; say "the same".
"An same" is not the expression and also mismatches the /s/ sound.
In this full question, include "the": "Are they the same colour?".

questions.setup: Choose the ordinary way to name the sport.
questions.prompt: After work, we usually play ___ with our neighbours.
options: a tennis
tennis
an tennis
the tennis
questions.explanation: Sport names normally have no article after "play": "play tennis". The sentence names an activity, not one countable match.
feedback: "Tennis" does not count a single match. You could say "a game of tennis".
"Play tennis" is the standard phrase for taking part in this sport.
"An" neither fits the initial consonant sound nor belongs before this sport name here.
The usual activity phrase is "play tennis". "The tennis" can refer to a particular competition in other constructions.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: We usually eat toast, but yesterday the hotel served us ___.
options: an big breakfast
big breakfast
a big breakfasts
a big breakfast
questions.explanation: An ordinary meal name can become countable when we describe one particular meal: "a big breakfast".
feedback: "Big" begins with /b/, so the article is "a".
The phrase describes one meal with an adjective; it needs a determiner such as "a" here.
"A" introduces one meal and cannot be followed by plural "breakfasts".
"A" introduces one breakfast described as big, rather than the routine activity of eating breakfast.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: At reception, please show ___ with a photo.
options: a ID card
an ID card
an ID cards
ID card
questions.explanation: The letter I is pronounced with a vowel sound. Because ID is read as letter names, the phrase is "an ID card".
feedback: Use the sound of the letter name I. It begins with a vowel sound and needs "an".
"An" matches the spoken beginning of ID and introduces one card.
The article is singular, so the noun must be "card", not "cards".
The singular countable phrase needs a determiner in this request.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that identifies the lowest-priced flat out of all three.
questions.prompt: We saw three flats at different prices. We chose ___.
options: a cheap flat
the cheapest flat
another cheap flat
the cheaper flat
questions.explanation: The cheapest flat identifies the one with the lowest price in the group of three. A cheap flat only says that its price is low; it does not rank it against the other two.
feedback: This describes a flat as low-priced. It does not say it costs less than both of the others.
The + cheapest + flat identifies the lowest-priced member of this group.
Another introduces a different or additional low-priced flat, not the lowest-priced one in the stated group.
Cheaper makes a comparison, normally between two alternatives. It does not explicitly identify the lowest price out of all three as cheapest does.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: My brother gave me an useful advice.
My brother gave me a useful advice.
My brother gave me some useful advice.
My brother gave me some useful advices.
questions.explanation: "Advice" is uncountable, so "some useful advice" works without a or an. An adjective does not make advice countable.
feedback: "Advice" cannot be introduced by "an" here, and "useful" begins with a consonant sound.
An adjective does not turn "advice" into a singular countable noun. Say "some useful advice" or "a useful piece of advice".
"Some" can introduce an unspecified amount of the uncountable noun "advice".
The noun remains "advice", without plural -s, in standard English.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: I take this medicine twice ___: once in the morning and once at night.
options: an day
a days
a day
day
questions.explanation: "Twice a day" means two times each day. Here "a" expresses a repeated rate, not an unidentified calendar day.
feedback: "Day" begins with /d/, so it cannot follow "an".
The article "a" takes the singular unit "day", not plural "days".
"A day" expresses the daily frequency and matches the two times specified.
The frequency expression requires "a day" or "per day" after "twice".

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: The shop assistant offers two sizes: 'Would you like ___?'
options: small or large bag
an small or an large bag
a small or a large bags
a small or a large bag
questions.explanation: A small or a large bag offers two possible sizes of one bag. Repeating a before large is correct; a small or large bag, with one shared article, is also possible.
feedback: The singular noun "bag" needs a determiner in this full question, even when two adjectives are offered.
Both "small" and "large" begin with consonant sounds, so neither can follow "an".
The article "a" cannot introduce the plural noun "bags".
Both alternatives correctly introduce a possible singular bag with "a".

questions.setup: Daria is mentioning an exchange for the first time in a message. Choose the phrase that presents it as one countable event.
questions.prompt: 'After the bookshop event, I had ___ about a first edition.'
options: an interesting conversation
interesting conversation
the interesting conversation
interesting conversations
questions.explanation: An interesting conversation presents one exchange as a countable event and introduces it as new information. Conversation can also be uncountable, and an indefinite singular can sometimes describe a typical activity; this task specifically asks for one newly introduced exchange.
feedback: An introduces one conversation, while interesting begins with a vowel sound. This meets both the counting and first-mention requirements.
This is a possible uncountable use for the activity of talking. It does not explicitly present one countable exchange as requested.
The presents the exchange as identifiable to the recipient. The message is meant to introduce it without assuming that shared identification.
This introduces plural exchanges, not the one event Daria means to present.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: The old recipe is difficult to follow. Could you draw ___ showing when to add each ingredient?
options: an clearer diagram
clearer diagram
a clearer diagrams
a clearer diagram
questions.explanation: Diagram is a singular countable noun here, and clearer describes it. The article comes before the adjective: a clearer diagram. Unlike explanation, diagram does not have an ordinary uncountable reading in this request.
feedback: The next sound is /k/ in clearer, so the article is a, not an.
The singular count noun diagram needs a determiner; the comparative adjective does not replace one.
A introduces one item, so use singular diagram rather than diagrams.
This asks for one diagram whose presentation is clearer than the recipe's current instructions.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase for a second, different message.
questions.prompt: I sent one email this morning. Now I need to send ___ with the missing attachment.
options: a other email
an other email
another email
another an email
questions.explanation: "Another" means one more or a different one. It already contains the indefinite idea, so say "another email" without adding a or an.
feedback: The standard single word is "another", not the separate phrase "a other".
In this ordinary use, "another" is written as one word.
This correctly introduces a further email distinct from the first.
Do not add a second indefinite article after "another".

questions.setup: Choose the phrase for the roof belonging to the rented house.
questions.prompt: We rented a house beside the lake, but ___ leaks whenever it rains.
options: a roof
another roof
one of the roofs
the roof
questions.explanation: The house has introduced an associated roof even though the word "roof" is new. "The roof" means the roof of that house.
feedback: This introduces a roof without identifying it through the rented house. The task asks for the roof associated with that house.
Another introduces an additional or different roof rather than simply identifying the rented house's roof.
This assumes an established set of several roofs and selects one from it. No such set is supplied.
The house makes its associated roof identifiable. A noun can take the on its first literal mention when that relationship supplies the reference.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: The detective cannot solve the case on a guess. She needs ___.
options: an evidence
a convincing evidence
convincing evidence
a pieces of evidence
questions.explanation: "Evidence" is uncountable in this meaning. Say "convincing evidence", or use a unit such as "a piece of evidence".
feedback: English does not normally count a clue as "an evidence"; it can be a piece of evidence.
Adding an adjective does not make "evidence" a singular countable noun.
This correctly uses the uncountable noun without an indefinite article.
The article "a" needs singular "piece", not plural "pieces".

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the sentence.
questions.prompt: "The students in the evening class asked for a later deadline." Who does "the students" identify?
options: Any students who might attend an evening class in future
The particular group belonging to the evening class being discussed
One representative student from any evening class
Students as a general category, including those in morning classes
questions.explanation: "The" and "in the evening class" identify a particular group. The sentence reports what that group did; it is not a general statement about all students.
feedback: The definite group is connected to the class being discussed, and the past-tense request has already happened.
This preserves the definite plural reference and its identifying modifier.
"Students" is plural and identifies a group, not one representative individual.
The phrase restricts reference to the identified evening class.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase in standard written English.
questions.prompt: My passport arrived just before the trip. It was ___ to stop worrying about it.
options: a such relief
such a relief
such the relief
so a relief
questions.explanation: Such comes before a/an when it intensifies a singular countable noun phrase: such a relief. So normally intensifies an adjective or adverb instead, as in so relieved.
feedback: Place such before the indefinite article in this construction: such a relief.
The order is such + a + relief, presenting the news as an instance of relief and intensifying the reaction.
The standard intensifying construction here uses such a relief, not such followed by the definite article.
So does not directly introduce a noun phrase in this order. Use such a relief or an adjective phrase such as so relieved.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: It was a honest mistake, not a deliberate lie.
It was an honest mistake, not a deliberate lie.
It was an honest mistake, not an deliberate lie.
It was honest mistake, not deliberate lie.
questions.explanation: "Honest" begins with a vowel sound because h is silent; "deliberate" begins with /d/. The contrast therefore needs "an honest mistake" and "a deliberate lie".
feedback: The silent h in "honest" requires "an", not "a".
Both articles follow the sounds of their adjectives and introduce singular countable nouns.
"Deliberate" begins with a consonant sound, so the second article must be "a".
Both singular countable nouns need determiners in this full sentence.

questions.setup: Choose the expression for the already identified train.
questions.prompt: My ticket says 8:15, platform four. I'll meet you on ___ from Brighton.
options: the 8:15 train
an 8:15 train
8:15 train
these 8:15 train
questions.explanation: The departure time identifies the booked service. "The 8:15 train" refers to that particular train, rather than naming travel by train in general.
feedback: The time and ticket establish the particular service being referenced.
This can introduce an unspecified service leaving at that time, but the prompt asks for the train already identified by the ticket.
The singular countable noun phrase needs a determiner here.
"These" is plural, while the ticket identifies one train.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase in standard British English.
questions.prompt: Both families need a place to live. The charity helps people find ___ .
options: an accommodation
suitable accommodation
a suitable accommodation
a suitable accommodations
questions.explanation: In the housing sense used here, standard British English treats "accommodation" as uncountable: "suitable accommodation". American English also uses plural "accommodations", but none of the offered indefinite-article forms fits.
feedback: For somewhere to live in this usage, use uncountable "accommodation"; count "a room" or "a flat" instead.
This describes housing without trying to count it as one accommodation.
The housing noun is uncountable in this reading. Other meanings of "an accommodation", such as an adjustment or compromise, are different.
The singular article "a" cannot introduce plural "accommodations", even in varieties that use that plural for lodging.

questions.setup: Choose the words for a new decision, rather than one previously identified.
questions.prompt: After considering several options, the team reached ___ about where to hold the event.
options: decision
an decision
a decision
a decisions
questions.explanation: "Reach a decision" introduces one outcome of discussion. "Decision" is countable and starts with a consonant sound.
feedback: The singular countable noun needs a determiner: "reach a decision".
"Decision" begins with /d/, so "an" is incorrect.
This introduces a newly reached outcome rather than referring to an already identified decision.
The singular article cannot be used before plural "decisions".

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
questions.prompt: "Before the meeting, I read a paper about local water use." What does "a paper" most naturally mean here?
options: Paper as a material for printing
All the documents required for the meeting
One written article or study
A quantity of blank sheets
questions.explanation: With "a" and a topic introduced by "about", "paper" means a countable piece of writing. Article-free "paper" can name the material instead.
feedback: The article and the action of reading a work about a subject support the countable written-work meaning.
"A paper" is singular and does not mean the entire set of documents.
The phrase names one work of writing on the specified subject.
Blank sheets would not be read for information about water use.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase identifying the remaining key.
questions.prompt: There were two keys. I have one; do you have ___?
options: another key
an other key
other key
the other key
questions.explanation: Only two keys are in the stated set. Once one is identified, "the other key" identifies the single remaining key.
feedback: This asks for an additional key without explicitly marking it as the remaining member of the known pair.
The ordinary indefinite form is the single word "another"; it still would not express the definite remaining member as directly.
The singular countable phrase needs a determiner; for this pair, use "the other key".
The two-key context makes the remaining key uniquely identifiable.

questions.setup: Choose the words for the general field of study.
questions.prompt: Her degree is in ___; she studies how people use limited resources.
options: an economics
economics
a economics
the economics
questions.explanation: The name of the field is "economics", without an article in "a degree in economics". Its final -s does not make it a set of countable objects.
feedback: The field name is not a singular countable item that can be introduced with "an".
The article-free subject name matches the stated degree field.
The ordinary name of the subject takes no indefinite article.
"The economics of a project" can refer to a project's financial aspects, but the question names the general field of study.

questions.setup: In a British English conversation about education, a neighbour asks, 'Has your daughter finished secondary school yet?'
questions.prompt: The parent replies, 'No, she's still at school.' What does the article-free phrase express in this exchange?
options: She has stayed on the school premises later than the parent expected.
She works at a school rather than studying there as a pupil.
She is visiting a school without being enrolled as a student.
She is still a pupil rather than having finished that stage of education.
questions.explanation: In this British English exchange, still at school concerns educational status: she has not finished school. The question about finishing education selects that reading rather than a claim about her physical location at this moment.
feedback: At school can describe a location in another context, but the neighbour asks about completing education, not today's departure time.
The negative answer about finishing secondary school concerns continued pupil status, not employment at the institution.
A visit would not answer whether she had finished secondary education. The exchange supports continued attendance as a pupil.
The bare institutional phrase answers the question about whether her school education is complete.

questions.setup: Choose the correct phrase for this building's unique exit of that kind.
questions.prompt: The plan shows just one emergency exit. Staff must keep ___ clear.
options: the emergency exit
an emergency exits
emergency exit
these emergency exit
questions.explanation: The plan establishes one exit of this kind. "The emergency exit" refers back to that identified exit.
feedback: The definite article identifies the exit already established by the plan.
"An" is singular, but "exits" is plural.
The singular countable phrase needs a determiner in this instruction.
"These" cannot introduce the singular noun "exit".

questions.setup: Choose the article used in this river name.
questions.prompt: Their cycling route follows ___ Thames from Oxford towards London.
options: a
an
the
(nothing)
questions.explanation: The conventional river name is "the Thames". English normally uses "the" with named rivers in full sentences.
feedback: "A Thames" does not name the identified river along this route.
The name does not take an indefinite article, and its initial sound is a consonant.
"The Thames" is the established river name in this geographical context.
In an ordinary sentence naming the river, include "the".

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: At the end of each placement, trainees receive ___ about their work.
options: detailed feedback
a detailed feedback
an detailed feedback
detailed feedbacks
questions.explanation: "Feedback" is uncountable in this context. Say "detailed feedback", without a or an and without plural -s.
feedback: This correctly treats the comments as an uncountable body of feedback.
The adjective detailed does not make feedback countable. You can receive "a detailed comment" but not normally "a detailed feedback".
Feedback does not take an indefinite article in this meaning; an also mismatches the /d/ sound in detailed.
Use the uncountable form feedback. To count individual points, use a plural noun such as comments.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that introduces several summaries as new information, without assuming the listener can already identify them.
questions.prompt: The librarian found ___ of the debate, so I could compare different accounts.
options: some useful summaries
a useful summary
the useful summaries
another useful summary
questions.explanation: "Summaries" is plural. "Some useful summaries" introduces an unspecified number; a and an would require a singular noun.
feedback: Some introduces an unspecified plural set as new information, matching the comparison of several accounts.
A introduces one summary, not the several accounts needed for the intended comparison.
The assumes an identifiable set. The task asks for a first introduction without that shared identification.
Another introduces one additional summary and assumes a previous one; it does not introduce the requested plural set.

questions.setup: Two musicians are looking for somewhere to practise. Choose the distinction between the two uses of 'space'.
questions.prompt: 'There's space for the drum kit downstairs, and a rehearsal space upstairs.'
options: The first identifies a booked room; the second names the spare room inside that same booking.
The first counts one rehearsal session; the second counts the musicians who can attend it.
Both count individual rooms, with the article omitted from the first because it is downstairs.
The first concerns available room; the second introduces one area used for rehearsing.
questions.explanation: Bare 'space' describes room available for the drum kit without counting a separate area. 'A rehearsal space' counts one area with a particular use. The same noun can therefore be uncountable or countable with different meanings.
feedback: No booking is mentioned. The two locations are different, and the first use describes capacity rather than identifying a reservation.
Neither use counts sessions or people. The contrast is between available room and one physical area.
'Downstairs' does not determine article use. The first 'space' is uncountable capacity, not a counted room with a missing article.
The drum-kit phrase concerns capacity, while the indefinite noun phrase introduces a rehearsal area.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
questions.prompt: "It was a most enjoyable evening." What does "a most enjoyable evening" mean here?
options: The most enjoyable evening out of every evening compared
An evening enjoyed by most of the guests
A very enjoyable evening, without an explicit ranking
An evening that was enjoyable for most of its duration
questions.explanation: In this formal expression, "a most enjoyable" means "a very enjoyable". "The most enjoyable" would identify the top evening in a comparison.
feedback: That is the normal ranking meaning of "the most enjoyable evening", not the intensifying use with "a".
"Most" modifies enjoyable here; it does not count the guests.
The indefinite article supports the formal intensifier meaning of most.
Nothing in the article phrase divides the evening into enjoyable and unenjoyable periods.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that preserves the writer's emphasis.
questions.prompt: "We still have a few seats, so you can join us." Why does "a few" fit the invitation?
options: It emphasises that almost no seats remain and therefore discourages attendance
It identifies seats already reserved for the listener
It presents the small number of remaining seats positively as available
It says the speaker cannot estimate whether any seats remain
questions.explanation: "A few" means some, though not many. That positive orientation supports "you can join us". Bare "few" would emphasise scarcity instead.
feedback: That interpretation is closer to bare "few" and conflicts with the invitation.
"A few" indicates an unspecified number; it does not identify reserved seats.
The article changes the orientation towards the seats that do remain, which supports the invitation.
The phrase asserts that some seats remain, though it does not give an exact count.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that supports the stated reason for cancelling.
questions.prompt: The guide cancels the climb because the group has almost no experience. Which explanation keeps that emphasis?
options: We have little experience of climbing.
We have a little experience of climbing.
We have a little of the experience of climbing.
We have the little experience of climbing.
questions.explanation: Bare "little" stresses how limited the experience is. "A little" stresses the existence of some experience, which would support a more positive argument.
feedback: Bare little gives the negative orientation needed to explain the cancellation.
This highlights the experience the group does have. It does not preserve the requested emphasis on near-absence.
This awkwardly treats the experience as an identified whole with a small portion; that is not the general lack described.
"The little experience" normally needs a defining continuation such as "we gained last year". It does not express the intended general shortfall here.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the first phrase.
questions.prompt: A website adds an unexpected fee at the final payment step. Its designer calls this 'confusing by design'. What does 'by design' mean?
options: Confusing because the design has not yet been completed
Confusing despite a plan intended to make the process clear
Confusing in its layout rather than in the information it presents
Deliberately confusing as a planned part of the payment process
questions.explanation: By design is an article-free expression meaning intentionally. It says the confusing effect was planned, not that the design was unfinished or that only the visual layout causes difficulty.
feedback: The fixed phrase states intention. It does not attribute the confusion to unfinished work.
Despite the plan would describe an unintended result. By design says the result was intended.
Design here is part of an idiom about intention; it does not limit the problem to visual layout.
By design presents the confusing effect as deliberate, even though the phrase contains no article before design.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the definite noun phrase.
questions.prompt: "The electric car is changing the way cities plan charging networks." In a paragraph about transport trends, what does "the electric car" represent?
options: One electric vehicle being used as the main example throughout the paragraph
The city's first electric vehicle, treated as the beginning of a wider trend
The electric vehicles in one identified fleet, rather than the vehicle type generally
Electric cars as a technological category, rather than a particular physical vehicle
questions.explanation: A definite singular can represent a class or invention. In this general discussion, "the electric car" means the technology or vehicle type, not one physical car.
feedback: An individual-car reading would need an identifiable vehicle. The statement about transport trends instead presents the vehicle type as an influence on cities.
The article does not give the car a first-in-history meaning; that would need wording such as the first electric car.
No fleet is identified. The category reading fits the broad claim about how cities plan their networks.
The definite singular can stand for a class or technological development in a general statement.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the article change.
questions.prompt: Compare "She has experience in emergency nursing" and "She described an experience from her first night on the ward". What does "an" do in the second sentence?
options: It says her practical knowledge is greater than that of other nurses
It presents one event she lived through rather than accumulated practical knowledge
It identifies an event that the listener has already heard about
It says the event was unusual or dangerous
questions.explanation: Uncountable "experience" can mean accumulated knowledge. "An experience" counts one event someone went through. The article itself does not tell us whether that event was unusual, dangerous, or already known.
feedback: The article changes the noun's sense; it does not compare anyone's expertise.
This captures the change from practical knowledge to a countable episode.
The indefinite article does not itself mark a previously identified event.
Those qualities would need additional wording; they do not follow from "an".

questions.setup: A coordinator wants to say that every remaining volunteer stayed, not just an unspecified further group.
questions.prompt: 'Four volunteers left at six. ___ stayed to finish packing.' Which phrase makes the intended reference explicit?
options: Other volunteers
Some other volunteers
The other volunteers
A few other volunteers
questions.explanation: The other volunteers identifies the remainder of the relevant volunteer group after the four who left are excluded. Bare other volunteers introduces further volunteers without explicitly presenting that complete remainder.
feedback: This says that further volunteers stayed. It does not explicitly identify them as the full remainder of the group.
Some presents an unspecified portion or number. It leaves open whether additional volunteers also left.
The definite plural picks out the remaining members of the already established group.
A few adds a small-number claim and does not express that every remaining member stayed.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the force of the article-free expression.
questions.prompt: An old resident says, 'The village has changed beyond recognition.'
options: The village is so different that its former appearance is hard to recognise.
The village has changed in ways that few people have officially acknowledged.
The village has changed, though its old appearance remains easy to recognise.
The village has become better known because people have praised its improvements.
questions.explanation: Beyond recognition means changed so much that the former appearance is hard to recognise. Recognition has no article in this fixed expression; it concerns recognising the place, not acknowledging or praising the changes.
feedback: The paraphrase keeps the strong degree of change expressed by beyond recognition.
This uses recognition in the sense of acknowledgment. The resident is describing how different the village looks, not whether officials acknowledge the changes.
Easy to recognise weakens and reverses the idiom's central point: the changes have made recognition difficult.
This treats recognition as public appreciation. The phrase does not say the changes brought fame or were improvements.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that refers to the people, not their language.
questions.prompt: A travel writer is describing the inhabitants of France as a national group. Which sentence has that reading?
options: French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
The French have influenced the neighbouring regions.
A French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
The French has influenced the neighbouring regions.
questions.explanation: "The French" can name the French people collectively and takes plural agreement. Article-free "French" commonly names the language and takes singular agreement.
feedback: This naturally names the language, while the task specifies the people.
The definite group expression and plural verb identify the people collectively.
To refer to one person, use a countable person noun such as "a French person".
For the national group of people, "the French" takes plural agreement, so use "have".

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that fits the purpose of each visit.
questions.prompt: "During her sentence she was in prison. Years later she returned to the prison to give a talk." What does the added article help signal?
options: It introduces an unfamiliar prison, then identifies a different one for the talk.
It contrasts time spent in prison generally with a return to prisoner status.
It contrasts imprisonment with a later visit to an identified institution.
It describes her earlier circumstances, then leaves the later destination unspecified.
questions.explanation: "In prison" conventionally describes imprisonment. "The prison" identifies a particular institution; the talk establishes that the later visit is not another statement of prisoner status.
feedback: The first phrase expresses imprisonment rather than introducing an unfamiliar institution with a. The wording does not establish a change of prison.
The later purpose is giving a talk. The prison identifies her destination without saying that she is imprisoned again.
Bare in prison expresses prisoner status; the definite phrase identifies the institution she later visits for a talk.
The later definite article presents the destination as identifiable, not unspecified.

questions.setup: A charity tested a new service in one town before expanding it. Choose the interpretation of the indefinite noun phrase.
questions.prompt: "The pilot was a success, although the wider programme still faced difficulties." What does "a success" mean?
options: Success as an abstract quality of every part of the programme
The only successful activity in the organisation's history
A successful person appointed to manage the programme
One undertaking judged to have achieved a good result
questions.explanation: "A success" classifies the pilot as a successful undertaking. It is a countable result use, whereas article-free "success" can name the abstract idea.
feedback: The article makes the pilot a countable example of success; the following clause explicitly limits the wider conclusion.
The indefinite article classifies one case; it does not make an only-ever claim.
The subject is the pilot undertaking, not a person.
This captures the predicative countable use in "was a success".

questions.setup: Choose the explanation of the two article patterns.
questions.prompt: "We need evidence before deciding. The evidence from yesterday's inspection is particularly relevant." Why can the second sentence use "the"?
options: The source phrase identifies a particular body of evidence
Evidence becomes a singular count noun because it comes from one inspection
Repeating evidence requires the even if the second sentence concerns a different source
The article presents the inspection findings as conclusive rather than merely relevant
questions.explanation: The first sentence requests evidence without identifying a body of it. The second points to evidence from a specified inspection. An uncountable noun can take "the" when its reference is identifiable.
feedback: The inspection makes this evidence identifiable; an uncountable noun can take the for that purpose.
Evidence remains uncountable. One identifiable source does not turn it into a count noun.
Word repetition alone does not require the. Here the source phrase identifies which evidence the writer means.
Definiteness identifies the evidence; it does not increase its strength. The sentence describes it as particularly relevant, not conclusive.

questions.setup: Choose the policy wording that covers travel costs as a general category, not a named journey or a fixed allowance.
questions.prompt: Meals are excluded. Which sentence states the intended reimbursement policy?
options: The company reimburses travel, but not meals.
The company reimburses the journey described above, but not meals.
The company pays a travel allowance, but not a meal allowance.
The company reimburses a return journey, but not meals.
questions.explanation: Bare travel names the general expense category, parallel to bare plural meals. A journey counts a trip; the journey identifies one; a travel allowance names a payment arrangement rather than reimbursement of travel costs generally.
feedback: The two article-free nouns name categories of expenses, preserving the intended general policy.
The definite phrase limits reimbursement to an identified journey rather than the general category.
The articles introduce countable allowances. An allowance can be a fixed payment and does not state the intended reimbursement policy.
This counts one return trip and narrows the kind of journey, neither of which is part of the intended general wording.

questions.setup: Choose the explanation that preserves the contrast.
questions.prompt: "An essay can explore a question without answering it; the essay you submitted does neither." How do the articles guide the reader?
options: Both phrases refer to the submitted text, first as new information and then as known information
The first identifies a model essay already written; the second identifies a student's response to it
The first introduces an unidentified text that the writer later discovers to be the submitted essay
A general possibility for essays is contrasted with an assessment of one identifiable submission
questions.explanation: "An essay" supports a general claim through a representative example. "The essay you submitted" then singles out an identifiable text for criticism.
feedback: The first clause describes what essays can do in general. It does not introduce the submitted essay as a particular new referent.
No existing model or response to a model is introduced. The first noun phrase supports a general possibility.
The passage moves from generalisation to assessment, not from ignorance to discovery of a text's identity.
An essay represents a class member in the general statement; the essay you submitted then identifies the particular work being assessed.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite phrase.
questions.prompt: "There is a reason for the delay, but I cannot discuss it yet." What does "a reason" establish?
options: The speaker says the listener already knows the explanation
The speaker presents an explanation as existing without identifying it to the listener
The speaker guarantees that only one contributing factor exists
The speaker says the delay has no explanation that could be expressed
questions.explanation: The indefinite article introduces a reason while withholding its identity. It does not mean the speaker is ignorant of it, nor does it prove there is only one contributing factor.
feedback: The phrase does not mark the reason as already identifiable to the listener.
This separates introducing a referent from revealing which one it is.
"A reason" introduces one reason; it does not exclude further reasons.
The opening explicitly asserts that a reason exists. The speaker is declining to discuss it.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that identifies the previously stated reason.
questions.prompt: The memo cancels the concert because the venue is unsafe. We can dispute ___ without denying that repairs are needed.
options: a further reason given in the memo
some other reasons given in the memo
the reason given in the memo
another reason given in the memo
questions.explanation: The earlier sentence has supplied the reason being discussed: the venue is unsafe. "The reason given in the memo" points back to that identified reason.
feedback: Further adds another reason instead of pointing back to the safety reason just stated.
This introduces several different reasons; the prompt asks for the one already stated.
The definite phrase identifies the safety justification already supplied for cancelling the concert.
Another shifts to a different reason instead of maintaining reference to the safety justification.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the article phrase.
questions.prompt: "After the interview, she felt a confidence she had never felt before." Why is "a confidence" possible?
options: It counts one secret she has told the interviewer
It presents a particular kind or instance of the feeling, described by the following clause
It identifies the feeling as already shared by all the interviewers
It means the noun confidence is always countable after felt
questions.explanation: An abstract feeling can be presented as a particular manifestation when it is characterised: "a confidence she had never felt before". This does not make every use of confidence countable.
feedback: "A confidence" can mean a secret in other contexts, but "felt" and the repeated feeling point to self-assurance.
The following clause characterises the distinctive confidence she experienced.
The sentence concerns her feeling and does not establish a shared state among interviewers.
Compare "She felt confidence in the plan". Countability depends on the chosen interpretation, not a universal rule after felt.

questions.setup: Choose the explanation of the definite reference.
questions.prompt: "The dentist offered an appointment on Friday. Unfortunately, the time clashes with my shift." How does the listener identify "the time"?
options: As the time associated with the offered appointment
As every available appointment time on Friday
As the current clock time during the conversation
As a new unspecified time that the dentist has not offered
questions.explanation: An appointment conventionally has a scheduled time. The offered appointment therefore makes "the time" identifiable without a previous literal mention of the word time.
feedback: The relationship between an appointment and its time supplies the reference.
The singular phrase refers to the offered appointment's time, not all available slots.
The clash is with a shift at the appointment time, not with the moment of speaking.
The definite phrase depends on the appointment just offered; it does not introduce an unrelated time.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence for this meaning.
questions.prompt: The speaker means people who are out of work as a group. Which sentence expresses that?
options: An unemployed needs access to affordable training.
The unemployeds need access to affordable training.
An unemployed people need access to affordable training.
The unemployed need access to affordable training.
questions.explanation: "The unemployed" uses the adjective to refer collectively to unemployed people. It takes plural agreement but does not add a plural -s to the adjective.
feedback: To count one person, say "an unemployed person"; unemployed does not normally stand as that singular count noun.
Do not add plural -s to the adjective in this group construction.
The singular article "an" cannot introduce plural "people".
The definite article plus adjective names the group, with the plural verb "need".

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the repeated noun.
questions.prompt: "The campaign gave the issue publicity, though not the publicity the organisers wanted." What does the second phrase do?
options: It counts one advertisement purchased by the organisers
It identifies a desired kind of public attention and contrasts it with the attention received
It states that the campaign received no public attention
It establishes that all publicity was arranged in advance
questions.explanation: The first article-free use names public attention generally. "The publicity the organisers wanted" then identifies the particular kind or character of attention they had hoped for.
feedback: "Publicity" remains uncountable; the sentence does not identify a purchased advertisement.
This preserves both the existence of publicity and the qualification about its character.
The first clause explicitly says the issue received publicity.
Wanting a kind of attention does not mean the actual attention was planned or controlled.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the two noun phrases.
questions.prompt: "She studies public policy, but the policy she criticised yesterday was her own department's." How do the articles distinguish the references?
options: One established policy is contrasted with a new example of the same policy
Two particular policies are contrasted, with identifying details omitted from the first
A field of study is contrasted with a particular departmental course of action
Two fields of study are contrasted, with the second limited to work in one department
questions.explanation: Article-free "public policy" names a field. "The policy she criticised" identifies one policy through the following clause. Neither article alone tells us whether the policy has legal force or an international scope.
feedback: The first phrase names a field rather than one established policy. The second is definite, not an indefinite introduction of a new example.
Studying public policy describes her subject area; it does not establish a first individual policy whose details have been withheld.
Bare public policy names the academic field. The policy she criticised identifies one adopted policy through the following clause.
The second phrase identifies a policy belonging to a department, not another academic discipline.

questions.setup: Compare the two expressions formed with 'the' plus an adjective.
questions.prompt: A report says, 'The wealthy were protected from the worst of the losses.' How do the two definite expressions differ?
options: Both expressions denote groups of people, distinguished by their financial circumstances.
The first denotes wealth as a resource; the second identifies the people who lost most of it.
The first denotes wealthy people collectively; the second selects the most severe part of the losses.
Both expressions denote abstract conditions, one favourable and the other unfavourable.
questions.explanation: 'The' plus an adjective can denote a human group or an abstract extreme. 'Wealthy' gives the collective people reading; 'worst' is interpreted through the following 'of the losses' phrase.
feedback: 'The wealthy' denotes people, but 'the worst of the losses' selects the most severe part of the losses, not a second human group.
'Wealthy' describes people possessing wealth, not the resource itself. The losses phrase makes 'worst' refer to losses rather than their sufferers.
'The' plus an adjective can denote a human group or an abstract extreme. 'Wealthy' gives the collective people reading; 'worst' is interpreted through the following 'of the losses' phrase.
'The wealthy' has plural human reference, reflected in 'were'. Only the second phrase selects an abstract extent of something in this sentence.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct phrase.
questions.prompt: The proposal attracted ___ than its authors had anticipated.
options: good a many more objections
a good much more objections
a good many more objection
a good many more objections
questions.explanation: "A good many" means quite a large number and takes a plural count noun. Here it modifies the comparison: "a good many more objections".
feedback: The order of the expression is "a good many", not "good a many".
"Objections" is countable and plural; the phrase uses many rather than much.
The meaning involves a number of objections, so the noun must be plural.
The fixed quantity phrase keeps a before good many and agrees with plural objections.

questions.setup: Choose the inference supported by the article-free expression.
questions.prompt: "The board approved the merger in principle, subject to agreement on the financing." What does "in principle" contribute?
options: Support for the merger's general idea, with financing still an outstanding condition
Support for a broad objective but opposition to this particular proposed merger
Approval of the merger without further conditions, apart from routine financial paperwork
Permission to implement the merger immediately while financing is negotiated afterwards
questions.explanation: "In principle" signals assent at the level of the general idea. The financing condition shows that this is not yet unconditional approval of all practical details.
feedback: In principle grants conceptual approval, while subject to keeps agreement on financing as a condition.
The board expresses qualified approval of the merger itself. It does not oppose this proposal while endorsing a different broad objective.
The financing qualification is an unresolved agreement, not merely routine paperwork after unconditional approval.
The sentence does not authorize implementation before the funding condition is met.

questions.setup: Choose the account of the definite reference.
questions.prompt: "A donor offered to fund the restoration. The generosity surprised everyone, but the conditions did not." What identifies "the generosity"?
options: A separate charitable act mentioned before the quoted passage
The donor's general character across all previous donations
The total monetary value of every contribution to the project
The quality inferred from the donor's offer in the preceding sentence
questions.explanation: A noun need not have appeared literally before for definite reference to work. The offer makes a quality of generosity available for reference. The passage does not establish the donor's entire history or the project's total funding.
feedback: The immediately preceding offer supplies the needed connection; no separate act is required.
The passage supports a quality displayed in this offer, not a general biography of the donor.
Generosity names an evaluated quality here, not the sum of all contributions.
The reader derives the quality from the event and can then identify it with the.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the article change.
questions.prompt: "The laboratory performs analysis; this particular procedure is an analysis of trace metals." What does "an analysis" present?
options: Analytical work in general, without presenting an individual procedure
One particular type or instance of an analytical procedure
The specific analysis already identified by the first use of the noun
A laboratory classified by the kind of analytical service it provides
questions.explanation: Article-free analysis can name the general activity. "An analysis of trace metals" presents one analytical procedure or instance. The indefinite article does not certify validity or mark prior familiarity.
feedback: That describes the article-free activity reading in the first clause, not the counted use an analysis of trace metals.
The indefinite article packages the activity as an individual procedure of the specified kind.
The first clause names analysis as an activity; it does not identify an individual procedure for a definite phrase to refer back to.
The second clause classifies the procedure, not the laboratory. Its subject is this particular procedure.

questions.setup: Alex once avoided crowds; now he hosts huge parties. An old friend comments on the change.
questions.prompt: 'This is not the Alex I remember from university.' What does 'the Alex I remember' identify?
options: Another university friend who happened to have the same name
Alex as the person with his former habits and character
Alex as the only person in his university class with that name
Alex as a representative of everyone the speaker knew at university
questions.explanation: The article and following clause select Alex as remembered by the speaker. A personal name can take the when the phrase identifies a particular version, aspect, or namesake; this context favours a remembered version.
feedback: The context explicitly concerns a change in Alex's behaviour, not confusion between two people named Alex.
The article and relative clause select the version of Alex preserved in the speaker's memory.
The definite phrase identifies a remembered version of him; it supplies no information about classmates' names.
The clause identifies the speaker's memory of this individual. It does not make Alex a type representing an entire group.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the article pattern.
questions.prompt: "They elected her chair, but she continued to work as a researcher." Why is the first role bare while the second has "a"?
options: The first is bare because her identity is known; the second is indefinite because her identity is unknown
The first role is uniquely held, so bare chair would also be required after interviewed
The first names an office conferred; the second classifies her continuing professional work
The second article counts a separate research project rather than classifying the person
questions.explanation: After elect, a role complement can be bare: "elected her chair". "As a researcher" classifies her continuing professional activity. The article patterns do not establish pay or permanence.
feedback: The same known person is described in both clauses. The difference is in construction and role, not knowledge of her identity.
Interviewed does not license the same role complement: "They interviewed the chair" normally needs a determiner.
Elect licenses the bare role complement, while as a researcher gives an indefinite professional classification.
The noun researcher denotes a person, so the article classifies her professional role rather than counting projects.

questions.setup: Choose the implication of the introductory phrase.
questions.prompt: "A certain Mr Bell has been asking to see you." What does "a certain Mr Bell" most naturally do?
options: Identifies a visitor the listener is expected to recognise as the only relevant Bell
Presents Bell as an example of a familiar personality type rather than an individual
Introduces a named visitor without assuming shared familiarity with him
Expresses uncertainty about the surname while affirming familiarity with the person
questions.explanation: "A certain" can introduce a person by name while leaving their identity or relevance unsettled for the listener. Certain here does not simply mean confident or reliable.
feedback: The indefinite introduction does not assume that shared identification.
The visitor is an actual person asking for a meeting, not a type defined by the name Bell.
A certain introduces the named individual without treating identification by the listener as settled.
The construction does not itself cast doubt on the name; it marks how the individual is being introduced.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct version in formal prose.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Rarely have we encountered so compelling an argument.
Rarely have we encountered so a compelling argument.
Rarely have we encountered such compelling an argument.
Rarely have we encountered a so compelling argument.
questions.explanation: In the formal pattern "so + adjective + a/an + singular noun", the adjective precedes the article: "so compelling an argument". The article still matches the sound of argument.
feedback: This correctly uses the formal so-adjective-article-noun sequence.
The so-pattern places the adjective before the article: "so compelling an argument".
With such, the normal order is "such a compelling argument"; this mixes the such and so patterns.
The degree word so cannot occupy this position after the article in the standard construction.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct version of the formal expression.
questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Many a promising scheme has failed for lack of maintenance.
Many a promising schemes has failed for lack of maintenance.
Many a promising scheme have failed for lack of maintenance.
A many promising schemes have failed for lack of maintenance.
