questions.explanation: Many a has a plural meaning but uses a singular count noun and singular verb: 'Many a scheme has failed.' Keep this formal construction distinct from ordinary 'many schemes have failed'.
feedback: The formal quantity expression combines the singular scheme with has even though it refers to many cases.
After many a, use the singular noun scheme. The plural meaning does not license schemes in this pattern.
The head noun scheme is grammatically singular in this construction, so its verb is has.
This mixes two patterns. Use either 'many promising schemes have' or 'many a promising scheme has'; a cannot simply precede many here.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that follows from the definite phrase.
questions.prompt: 'We are still searching for a framework. The framework must accommodate exceptions without treating them as errors.' How should the second sentence be understood?
options: It describes a framework already selected, while leaving open whether the framework can meet the requirement
It sets a requirement for the framework being sought, without asserting that one has been found
It refers to an earlier unsuccessful framework and describes the feature that the new one should replace
It announces that the search has ended but that the chosen framework still needs to be tested
questions.explanation: The definite phrase can continue reference to the object of a search. It specifies what the sought framework must be like, without cancelling "still searching" or asserting that one has been found.
feedback: Still searching rules out treating the definite article as an announcement of selection. The phrase continues reference to what is being sought.
Must states the desired property of the sought object. Definite reference can remain within that projected situation.
No earlier failed framework is established. The natural link is back to a framework in the ongoing search.
Changing a to the maintains reference; it does not cancel the statement that the search is continuing.

questions.setup: Choose the account of the fixed phrase.
questions.prompt: "The reform was introduced in the hope that smaller classes would improve participation." Why is "the hope" natural here?
options: The following clause specifies the content of the motivating hope
Hope is countable only when the outcome is guaranteed
Any noun immediately before that must take the
The article proves that all participants shared the same expectation
questions.explanation: "In the hope that" presents a motivating hope and supplies its content in the following clause. It does not promise success or establish that everyone shared the hope.
feedback: This explains the content-linked definite phrase in the established expression.
Having a hope does not guarantee its fulfilment, and countability is not determined by success.
Compare "a claim that surprised us". A following that-clause does not impose the article mechanically.
The phrase states the motivation for the reform, not a unanimous belief among participants.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the indefinite ordinal phrase.
questions.prompt: "The diagnosis was unclear, so she sought a second opinion." Why is "a" possible before "second"?
options: It selects the second opinion from a numbered set already identifiable to the listener
It introduces an additional opinion rather than identifying an established numbered opinion
It introduces another clinician rather than another opinion, regardless of who gives it
It presents the first diagnosis as mistaken and therefore in need of replacement
questions.explanation: Ordinals do not always require the. "A second opinion" introduces another opinion as an additional instance. "The second opinion" would identify an opinion in an established ordered set.
feedback: That would fit the second opinion in an established sequence. A second opinion introduces an additional instance without requiring such a known set.
The indefinite ordinal phrase has the additional-instance reading: another opinion beyond the one already obtained.
The counted noun is opinion. The phrase does not itself identify or count clinicians.
Seeking an additional view does not establish that the original diagnosis is wrong; it may confirm or clarify it.

questions.setup: A museum editor is distinguishing statements about an extinct species from statements about its individual members.
questions.prompt: The editor changes 'A dodo is extinct' to 'The dodo is extinct' but leaves 'A dodo laid eggs' unchanged. Why is the article changed only in the first example?
options: Present-tense general statements require the, whereas past-tense general statements require a
The first statement names a previously identified specimen; the second introduces another specimen
The identifies the only extinct species, while a identifies one of several egg-laying species
Extinction concerns the species as a whole; egg-laying can describe a representative member
questions.explanation: A generic indefinite singular can describe a typical member, as in a dodo laid eggs. In its literal biological sense, extinct applies to a species, not an individual bird that dies. The definite singular can name that kind: the dodo is extinct. The distinction is not a tense rule.
feedback: Article choice is not determined by tense: a dodo has a beak is a possible generic statement, while the dodo became extinct names the species in the past tense.
The museum editor is making general statements, and no individual specimens have been introduced. Extinct does not literally mean that one specimen has died.
The definite article names this species as a kind; it does not claim that no other species is extinct. The indefinite example represents a typical dodo.
The article needs to fit the kind of property being predicated: extinction of a species versus a characteristic of its members.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the fronted expression.
questions.prompt: "For a beginner, the restoration work is remarkably assured." What does "a beginner" contribute?
options: An identified novice whose name the reader already knows
A claim that exactly one beginner contributed to the restoration
A claim that the restorer has never attempted any related task
A comparison standard based on membership of the beginner category
questions.explanation: "For a beginner" frames the evaluation against expectations for someone in that category. The indefinite article classifies; it does not count all contributors or establish the restorer's complete history.
feedback: The phrase supplies a category-based standard, not a name or definite identity.
The article does not state the size or composition of the restoration team.
Beginner status does not imply zero related experience.
This explains how the indefinite phrase qualifies the evaluation of the work.

questions.setup: Choose the account of the contrast.
questions.prompt: "We need research, not a research proposal." What distinction does the article support?
options: An informal conversation versus a published scientific result
A completed investigation versus a document that has already been rejected
Several studies versus several proposals
An activity or body of investigation versus one document proposing it
questions.explanation: Research is uncountable in the first phrase. In the second, the head noun is countable "proposal", so "a" introduces one document; research modifies the kind of proposal.
feedback: The article contrast does not establish informality or publication.
Research need not be complete, and the proposal's rejection is not stated.
The second phrase is explicitly singular; the first does not supply a count.
This identifies the head noun and reference type of each phrase.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the negative article phrase.
questions.prompt: "Not a word of her account was corroborated by the recordings." What does "not a word" convey?
options: One particular word lacked support, while the rest was corroborated
No part of her account received corroboration from those recordings
Her account was conclusively disproved by the recordings
The recordings contained no speech from any participant
questions.explanation: "Not a word" is emphatic: even the smallest part of the account received no corroboration from the specified source. Lack of corroboration is not itself proof that the account is false.
feedback: The emphatic phrase denies support throughout the account; it does not isolate one unsupported word.
This preserves both the force of not a and the limited claim about support from the recordings.
Not being corroborated is weaker than being disproved. The sentence does not assert conclusive falsification.
The sentence concerns whether the recordings support the account, not whether they contain speech.

questions.setup: Consider what is lost when an editor changes the quantity phrase.
questions.prompt: 'She devoted what little free time she had to restoring the archive' becomes 'She devoted a little of her free time to restoring the archive.' Which account preserves the distinction?
options: Both versions say her total free time was scarce; only the revision leaves its use unspecified.
The original presents her available time as plentiful; the revision presents it as scarce.
The original commits her limited supply of free time; the revision states only that she devoted a small amount of it.
The original leaves how much she devoted open; the revision says she devoted her entire small supply.
questions.explanation: What little free time she had refers to the small total available to her. A little of her free time selects a small amount without saying that this exhausted a limited supply.
feedback: A little of her free time specifies a small amount devoted to restoration, but does not say her total supply of free time was small. Its use is still specified.
What little signals that her available time was limited. The revision quantifies the portion used, not the size of her total supply.
What little free time she had refers to the small total available to her. A little of her free time selects a small amount without saying that this exhausted a limited supply.
This reverses the contrast. The totalising reference belongs to what little she had, not to the partitive a little of her free time.

questions.setup: Amira does not practise as an architect, but she sometimes designs useful spaces.
questions.prompt: A critic dismisses her by saying, 'She is no architect.' Choose the revision that states only her occupational status, without judging the quality of her designs.
options: She is not an architect.
She is not much of an architect.
She is not the architect.
She is no great architect.
questions.explanation: Not an architect neutrally denies membership of the professional category. In the critic's dismissive use, no architect suggests that she lacks an architect's competence. The revision removes that evaluation without introducing a particular architect's identity.
feedback: The indefinite noun phrase names the professional category; ordinary negation denies that category membership without rating her design skill.
Not much of evaluates how good she is at the role; it retains the criticism the revision is meant to remove.
The points to a particular architect relevant to a project or conversation. Denying that identity does not deny being an architect professionally.
This denies distinction or excellence, not professional status. It can describe someone who is an architect but not a great one.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation licensed by the articles.
questions.prompt: "Whenever a committee appoints a chair, the chair receives a casting vote." What does "the chair" refer to?
options: The same person appointed to chair every committee
Whoever chairs a committee, whether appointed or acting temporarily
A chair already holding office before the appointment
The particular appointee in each appointment covered by the rule
questions.explanation: "A chair" introduces an appointee inside each situation described by "whenever". "The chair" refers back within that situation; it need not identify one person across all committees.
feedback: The definite phrase is interpreted separately for each appointment. It does not require a single chair shared by all committees.
The sentence establishes its referent through the appointment just mentioned. It does not extend the rule explicitly to acting chairs appointed in no such event.
The antecedent is the appointee introduced by "appoints a chair", not a previously established officeholder.
This preserves the local link from "a chair" to "the chair" under "whenever".

questions.setup: Choose the account of the article change.
questions.prompt: An editor changes "There is little room for doubt" to "There is little room for a doubt of that kind". What does the added article do?
options: It asserts that a particular reservation is already held, despite the limiting phrase
It presents a reservation as one bounded possibility of the specified kind
It identifies a previously discussed reservation rather than introducing a kind
It turns all remaining uncertainty into one objection that the writer accepts
questions.explanation: Without an article, "doubt" names uncertainty as a general state. "A doubt of that kind" packages a reservation as an individual possibility. The negative scope of "little room" still limits it.
feedback: An indefinite within "little room for" does not by itself assert an existing, held reservation.
The indefinite article individuates doubt while the surrounding phrase still limits room for such a reservation.
That would be the identifying function more naturally expressed by "the doubt"; the indefinite phrase characterises a possible instance.
The writer does not assert acceptance of an objection or equate it with all uncertainty.

questions.setup: Choose the account of the two article functions.
questions.prompt: "As the curator of the collection, she approached the purchase with the caution of a curator rather than the enthusiasm of a collector." How do "the curator" and "a curator" function?
options: Both identify her personally; the article change merely avoids repeating an identical noun phrase
The first establishes her occupation; the second leaves whether she is a curator unresolved
The first identifies her role; the second characterises caution by a professional type
The first identifies her position; the second attributes her caution to another curator's influence
questions.explanation: "The curator of the collection" identifies her as the holder of the relevant role. "The caution of a curator" classifies the quality of her approach by reference to a professional type. It does not introduce another curator.
feedback: The second phrase invokes qualities associated with a professional category; it is not simply another identifying reference to her.
The first phrase has already established her role. Using a professional type to describe her manner does not withdraw that information.
The definite role identifies her; the indefinite professional type characterises the caution she displays.
'Of a curator' describes the kind of caution; it does not assert that an adviser influenced her.

questions.setup: Choose the most precise explanation of the contrast.
questions.prompt: Compare "She studies education in coastal communities" with "She studies the education of the three siblings". Why does the second noun phrase use "the"?
options: A postmodifier makes education definite whenever it narrows the range of people being studied
The second identifies the siblings' educational history, while the first can retain a general reading
The second points back to an education mentioned earlier, which the first sentence must introduce
The first refers to education generally, whereas the second must refer to one course shared by the siblings
questions.explanation: The second sentence treats the siblings' education as an identifiable object of study. Postmodification alone does not force "the": "education in coastal communities" remains general in the first sentence.
feedback: The coastal-community modifier also narrows the subject without requiring the. Restricted subject matter is not the same as an identifiable referent.
The siblings' education can be identified through its relation to them. The other sentence treats education as a general subject within a setting.
These are separate examples. An of-phrase can make a referent identifiable without an earlier mention of it.
An identifiable education can cover different schools and many experiences. Definiteness does not turn it into a single course.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the highlighted article use.
questions.prompt: "A new biography promises to reveal a Shakespeare unfamiliar to readers of the school anthologies." What does "a Shakespeare" most naturally mean?
options: A biography whose title is Shakespeare
A writer merely similar in ability to Shakespeare
An aspect or representation of Shakespeare that readers may not know
An unidentified person whose surname happens to be Shakespeare
questions.explanation: The indefinite article allows a proper name to present one version or aspect of the known person. The biography and the reference to school anthologies support this reading of "a Shakespeare".
feedback: The biography promises to reveal Shakespeare; the phrase is not naming the book itself.
"A Shakespeare" can mean a comparable genius elsewhere, but a biography revealing its subject favours a new view of the original person.
The article frames a particular portrayal of the familiar historical person.
That reading is grammatically possible elsewhere, but the biography and anthology context identify the established writer.

questions.setup: Choose the revision that preserves the distinction between an arrangement and consensus.
questions.prompt: Negotiators settled how to share access but still differed over ownership. An editor wants to use 'agreement' for both the settled arrangement and the missing consensus. Which sentence does that?
options: They reached agreement on access, but an agreement on ownership remained unsigned.
They reached the agreement on access, but the agreement on ownership remained unsigned.
They reached an agreement on access, but agreement on ownership remained elusive.
They reached agreements on access, but agreement on ownership remained provisional.
questions.explanation: 'An agreement' packages the access settlement as an arrangement. Bare 'agreement' names consensus, and 'remained elusive' says that consensus had not been reached. This preserves both the noun-sense distinction and the state of the negotiations.
feedback: This reverses the requested noun senses and substitutes an unsigned arrangement for the absence of consensus. Lack of a signature does not establish continued disagreement.
The second definite phrase treats an ownership arrangement as identifiable and awaiting signature, rather than saying consensus is still missing.
The countable arrangement is settled; the uncountable consensus is still missing.
The plural introduces multiple access arrangements, and provisional consensus is tentative consensus, not consensus that remains unreached.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the writer's meaning.
questions.prompt: "He is not the expert on medieval glass, but he is an expert." What distinction is the writer making?
options: His expertise is acknowledged by the writer but denied by other specialists in the field
He has specialist knowledge without being presented as the field's uniquely recognised authority
He is the relevant specialist here, although the writer is unsure about his competence
His expertise is broader than medieval glass, which is why the definite description is rejected
questions.explanation: In this contrast, stressed "the expert" means the person treated as the authority. "An expert" classifies him as a specialist without giving him that uniquely pre-eminent status.
feedback: The contrast concerns category membership and pre-eminence. It does not report a dispute between the writer and other specialists.
The indefinite article grants expertise; the contrastive definite phrase withholds uniquely authoritative status.
The writer positively calls him an expert. The reservation concerns being the outstanding authority, not uncertainty about whether he is competent.
Neither article specifies the breadth of his other knowledge. The contrast does not explain his status by giving him a wider field.

questions.setup: Choose the strongest conclusion the wording supports.
questions.prompt: "The gallery has bought a Hokusai, but it has not said whether the work is a print or a drawing." What does the article permit us to infer?
options: The purchase is one work attributed to Hokusai
The purchase is a portrait depicting Hokusai
The purchase is a copy by an unnamed follower of Hokusai
The purchase is the particular Hokusai work already discussed
questions.explanation: "A Hokusai" uses an artist's name to stand for one work by that artist. The indefinite article introduces a work without identifying its medium or marking it as previously discussed.
feedback: The article counts an artwork through the artist's name, as confirmed by "the work" in the second clause.
The construction normally attributes the work to the artist; it does not say the artist is depicted in it.
A copy or follower attribution would need further wording. The article alone does not supply it.
"A" introduces an unspecified work. "The Hokusai" would more directly identify a previously established work.

questions.setup: An editor queries the article before the plural unit in this sentence. Choose the sound response to the query.
questions.prompt: 'The projectionist waited a further twenty minutes before starting the film.'
options: The article marks an approximation, so twenty minutes must be understood as an imprecise estimate.
The article is licensed because further changes minutes from a countable noun into an uncountable noun.
The article is licensed because the phrase presents one additional duration measured in plural units.
The article is an error here; the plural unit requires either the or no article instead.
questions.explanation: A further twenty minutes is a valid measure expression: the twenty minutes are presented as one additional stretch of time. Minutes remains plural; this construction does not license ordinary phrases such as a minutes or a chairs.
feedback: The duration may be exact or approximate in the real situation. A further does not itself require an approximate reading; it marks an additional amount.
Minutes still counts units of time and retains plural form. The construction groups those units into a duration rather than changing the noun into a mass noun.
The article belongs to the complete measure expression, which packages the plural units as an additional duration.
This applies the elementary a-plus-singular rule too broadly. Modified measure expressions such as a further twenty minutes legitimately contain a plural unit after a.

questions.setup: An editor is checking an old submission file. The editor does not know whether anyone was assigned to review it.
questions.prompt: Which question asks whether a withdrawal occurred without treating either an assigned reviewer or a withdrawal as already established?
options: Has the reviewer withdrawn?
Which reviewer has withdrawn?
When did a reviewer withdraw?
Has a reviewer withdrawn?
questions.explanation: An indefinite inside this yes-no question asks whether there is an instance of a reviewer withdrawing. It does not assert that a reviewer was assigned or that a withdrawal occurred.
feedback: The yes-no question leaves withdrawal open, but the reviewer presents a relevant reviewer as identifiable. That is precisely what the editor does not yet know.
Which reviewer asks for an identity within a withdrawal already treated as having occurred. The editor needs first to establish whether any withdrawal happened.
Although a reviewer is indefinite, when asks for the time of a withdrawal treated as established. Changing the article does not remove that assumption from the question.
An indefinite inside this yes-no question asks whether there is an instance of a reviewer withdrawing. It does not assert that a reviewer was assigned or that a withdrawal occurred.

questions.setup: Read the description as the chair's interpretation, then consider the narrator's correction.
questions.prompt: The chair called the pause 'the silence of agreement'. In fact, nobody had understood the proposal. Why does the definite phrase not establish that the group agreed?
options: The phrase establishes agreement, but leaves its precise content for the reader to identify.
The phrase identifies a previous agreement that the group had reached before the pause.
The phrase denotes a hypothetical silence rather than the pause that actually occurred.
The phrase reports the chair's characterization, which the narrator does not endorse.
questions.explanation: The pause occurred, but the chair's label assigns it an interpretation. The narrator reports that label without endorsing it and immediately explains why it was mistaken. Definiteness inside an attributed description does not turn the described agreement into the narrator's own assertion.
feedback: The narrator disputes the agreement itself, not merely the identification of its content. The is part of the chair's label.
No earlier agreement is established. The description is the chair's interpretation of the present pause.
The pause is real in the narrative. What fails is the interpretation of it as agreement, not its occurrence.
Called attributes the description to the chair, while the following sentence rejects the inference of agreement.

questions.setup: Compare the same indefinite noun phrase in two different kinds of writing.
questions.prompt: A handbook on political fiction says, 'A novel of this kind can outlive the controversy that prompted it.' A security log says, 'A novel of this kind has vanished from the locked display.' How does the reference normally differ?
options: Both phrases introduce particular books; the difference lies only in whether their titles have been supplied.
The handbook identifies the genre's only novel; the log leaves the number of missing books unrestricted.
The handbook presents a representative member of a genre; the log reports an event involving a particular book.
Both phrases identify a shared book because the modifier of this kind makes the indefinite article definite.
questions.explanation: The handbook's statement about what such fiction can do supports a representative, general reading. The log's report of a completed disappearance instead introduces a particular book, even without naming its title. The indefinite article and modifier alone do not decide between those readings; the clause and discourse matter.
feedback: An unnamed particular book is possible in a log, but it misses the handbook's genre-level generalization. A does not always introduce one particular referent.
Representative a does not limit a genre to one member. In the log, the singular phrase reports one book's disappearance, although it does not rule out other losses.
The first clause expresses a characteristic possibility for a kind of fiction; the second locates a disappearance involving one actual display item.
Of this kind narrows the class of novels. It does not by itself establish shared identification of a particular book or change a into a definite article.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the article's effect.
questions.prompt: "It was not merely an inconvenience; it was the inconvenience that finally made her leave." What does the second article contribute?
options: It identifies this inconvenience by its decisive consequence
It turns every inconvenience she had suffered into a single event
It proves that she had never suffered an inconvenience before
It changes inconvenience from an event into an uncountable emotional state
questions.explanation: "An inconvenience" first classifies the event. "The inconvenience that finally made her leave" identifies it through a distinguishing consequence. The definite article does not deny the existence of other inconveniences.
feedback: The following clause specifies what makes this event identifiable in the narrative.
The definite phrase selects the decisive event; it does not merge multiple events.
Other inconveniences may have occurred. "Finally" even makes a sequence of problems plausible.
Both occurrences remain countable event uses; the change concerns reference, not noun class.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that the article contrast supports.
questions.prompt: "She spoke with authority, though she was not an authority on the period." What is contrasted?
options: Her role authorised the speech, though she lacked permission to advise on that period.
Her manner sounded assured, though she was not a recognised specialist in the subject.
Her subject knowledge was authoritative, though her manner failed to convey confidence.
Her expertise was recognised, though she held no official post governing the discussion.
questions.explanation: Article-free "authority" describes the manner or force of her speech. "An authority on" is a countable expression for a recognised expert in a subject.
feedback: This substitutes institutional permission for both senses. The sentence contrasts an assured manner with subject expertise, not two permissions.
With authority describes the force or assurance of her speech; an authority on the period denotes an expert, which the second clause denies.
This reverses the contrast. She sounded authoritative, but the writer denies that she was a recognised expert on the period.
An authority on a period is a specialist, not an official who controls a meeting. The sentence denies specialist status, not an official post.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation licensed by the phrase.
questions.prompt: "The correspondence reveals the Paris of her youth rather than the city the tourist brochures describe." What does "the Paris of her youth" identify?
options: The city as experienced or represented in a particular period of her life
A different city formally named Paris during her youth
An unidentified city sharing some Parisian characteristics
A set of letters whose published title is Paris of Her Youth
questions.explanation: The definite article and modifier select a temporally and personally characterised version of a place. Paris remains the same city; the phrase directs attention to the Paris represented by her youthful experience.
feedback: This captures how the modifier licenses a definite, characterised use of the proper name.
The phrase need not refer to another municipality or a name change; it frames the familiar city through a period of experience.
That would resemble a metaphorical "a Paris" reading, not the identified version of the city described here.
The words identify what the correspondence reveals, not a title assigned to the letters.

questions.setup: Choose the inference warranted by the indefinite phrase.
questions.prompt: "If there is a flaw in the proof, the flaw will lie in the induction step." Which reading is accurate?
options: The writer asserts that the proof contains exactly one flaw
The writer has identified a flaw but is withholding its location
The writer excludes flaws in other proofs because the noun is definite
The second phrase refers back to a flaw under the stated condition, without asserting that one exists
questions.explanation: "A flaw" is introduced inside an if-condition. "The flaw" can refer back inside that hypothetical reasoning without committing the writer to the existence of a flaw.
feedback: The conditional introduction does not assert existence, much less an exact count of actual flaws.
The writer explicitly proposes a location while leaving existence conditional.
The article identifies the locally introduced possibility; it says nothing about other proofs.
This keeps the definite reference within the hypothetical situation introduced by if.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the article phrase.
questions.prompt: "For all his objections, he remained a believer in the project, if not the believer his colleagues had hoped for." What does the final phrase imply?
options: His colleagues wanted another supporter to replace him because they considered him an opponent
His colleagues recognised him as their leading supporter but had not expected his objections
His colleagues doubted his private support because his public commitment exceeded their expectations
His colleagues had envisaged a kind of supporter whose commitment he did not fully display
questions.explanation: "A believer" grants membership in the category of supporters. "The believer his colleagues had hoped for" refers to their envisaged kind of committed supporter. The contrast qualifies his support without cancelling it.
feedback: 'He remained a believer' affirms support. The contrast concerns the kind of supporter he was, not a stated plan to replace an opponent.
The relative clause identifies an envisaged supporter, not an established leading figure. 'If not' withholds the hoped-for characterisation.
The sentence neither divides public from private belief nor says he exceeded their expectations; he falls short of the hoped-for characterisation.
The indefinite phrase grants that he supports the project; the definite description measures him against their unrealised expectation.

questions.setup: A copy editor has a headline but not the accompanying report.
questions.prompt: The headline reads 'Court dismisses claim'. Can the missing article before 'court' be reconstructed as 'a' or 'the' from these words alone?
options: No: headline compression can omit either article; the report must establish how the court is being introduced or identified.
Yes: the completed event requires the because its participants are now definite.
Yes: bare court names the judicial system, so adding either article would change the subject.
No article is missing: capitalisation makes Court a proper name that should remain bare in full prose.
questions.explanation: Headlines commonly omit articles. Bare 'court' here therefore does not settle whether full prose would introduce a court with 'a' or identify the relevant court with 'the'.
feedback: Headlines commonly omit articles. Bare 'court' here therefore does not settle whether full prose would introduce a court with 'a' or identify the relevant court with 'the'.
Completion of an event does not determine article choice. A past event can introduce a participant with 'a' or refer to an identifiable participant with 'the'.
The headline can report a decision by an individual court. Article omission in a headline is not the same as the conventional bare institutional expression in 'go to court'.
The capital occurs at the start of the headline. It does not establish 'Court' as a proper name or license ordinary prose such as 'Court dismissed a claim'.

questions.setup: Choose the explanation of the changed noun phrase.
questions.prompt: A reviewer writes "The chapter offers history, not nostalgia". Another writes "The chapter offers a history, not a memoir". What change accompanies the added articles?
options: The first contrasts approaches to the past; the second classifies an account by genre
Both reviewers describe a single historical account; only the second says whether it is personal
The first judges the account's accuracy; the second establishes that the chapter is a complete book
Both contrast genres; the added articles identify particular accounts already familiar to the reader
questions.explanation: Article-free "history" and "nostalgia" contrast ways of treating the past. "A history" and "a memoir" count kinds of account. Neither article choice establishes accuracy or whether the account is fictional.
feedback: Bare nouns describe modes of treatment; a history and a memoir package accounts as countable genre instances.
The first bare-noun contrast need not count a single account: a chapter can offer historical treatment rather than nostalgic treatment without constituting an individual history.
The first may praise its approach without guaranteeing accuracy. A chapter can offer a history without being a complete book.
The indefinite articles classify accounts without presenting them as already familiar. The first contrast is between historical and nostalgic treatment.

questions.setup: Read the definite phrase in its statistical context; no arithmetic is required.
questions.prompt: 'The average respondent had 1.6 children, although no individual respondent had that number.' Why is 'the average respondent' coherent here?
options: It identifies the actual respondent whose family was closest to the numerical mean.
It denotes an abstract statistical representative rather than an individual person.
It identifies the previously mentioned respondent selected to represent the sample.
It denotes the most frequently occurring family type among the actual respondents.
questions.explanation: The definite phrase presents a statistical abstraction as a representative respondent. It does not require an actual person with exactly the averaged properties. Treating the as a guarantee of one real-world individual would therefore misread the sentence.
feedback: An average representative is not necessarily the nearest actual case. The sentence assigns the averaged value to an abstraction, not a selected person's family.
The definite description names a constructed representative whose properties summarise the sample, so they need not coexist in one person.
No earlier individual is supplied, and the phrase does not perform ordinary backward reference to a survey participant.
The most frequent family type is a different statistical idea. Average respondent here represents an averaged property, not the commonest actual household.

questions.setup: Choose the word that introduces the reason.
questions.prompt: I am leaving work early ___ I have a dentist appointment.
options: but
because
or
before
questions.explanation: Because explains why the speaker is leaving early.
feedback: But would introduce a contrast, not the reason for leaving.
Because explains why the speaker is leaving early.
Or offers a choice; the appointment is a reason, not an alternative.
Before gives a time order without explicitly giving the reason.

questions.setup: Choose the word that introduces the result.
questions.prompt: I forgot my key, ___ I called my flatmate.
options: because
but
or
so
questions.explanation: So introduces what the speaker did as a result of forgetting the key.
feedback: Because would make the call the reason for forgetting the key.
But introduces a contrast, not the requested result.
Or presents alternatives instead of the resulting action.
So introduces what the speaker did as a result of forgetting the key.

questions.setup: Choose the word that shows a good point and a bad point about the flat.
questions.prompt: The flat is cheap, ___ it is very noisy.
options: so
because
or
but
questions.explanation: But contrasts the attractive price with the problem of noise.
feedback: So would present noise as a result of the low price.
Because would give noise as a reason for the price rather than directly contrasting the two points.
Or offers alternatives; both features describe this flat.
But contrasts the attractive price with the problem of noise.

questions.setup: Choose the word that means both things are needed.
questions.prompt: Please buy milk ___ eggs.
options: or
and
but
because
questions.explanation: And adds eggs to milk: buy both.
feedback: Or offers a choice instead of requiring both items.
And adds eggs to milk: buy both.
But introduces a contrast, not a simple shopping list.
Because introduces a reason and cannot join these two list items.

questions.setup: Choose the word that introduces the next step.
questions.prompt: First sign your name. ___ take a visitor badge.
options: Because
Then
But
Or
questions.explanation: Then tells the visitor what to do after signing.
feedback: Because would begin a reason rather than the next instruction.
Then tells the visitor what to do after signing.
But would suggest a contrast between the steps.
Or would make taking a badge an alternative to signing, not the next step.

questions.setup: Choose the word that offers a choice of one drink.
questions.prompt: Would you like juice ___ water?
options: and
or
because
so
questions.explanation: Or presents juice and water as alternatives.
feedback: And asks about the two drinks together, not the requested choice of one.
Or presents juice and water as alternatives.
Because would introduce a reason, not a drink choice.
So introduces a result and cannot connect these alternatives.

questions.setup: Choose the word that means lock the door first.
questions.prompt: Lock the door ___ you leave the building.
options: before
after
because
or
questions.explanation: Before places locking earlier than leaving.
feedback: Before places locking earlier than leaving.
After places locking later than leaving, reversing the instruction.
Because gives a reason without specifying the requested order.
Or presents leaving as an alternative rather than a time reference.

questions.setup: Choose the word that means the call happens later than the end of work.
questions.prompt: I'll call you ___ I finish work.
options: before
because
after
but
questions.explanation: After places the call later than finishing work.
feedback: Before would place the call earlier than finishing.
Because gives finishing as a reason rather than explicitly ordering the events.
After places the call later than finishing work.
But signals contrast, not the requested later time.

questions.setup: Choose the word that tells us the time for the action.
questions.prompt: Press Stop ___ the timer rings.
options: because
or
but
when
questions.explanation: When makes the ringing timer the signal for pressing Stop.
feedback: Because explains a reason, whereas the task asks for the time signal.
Or creates a choice rather than a time link.
But contrasts ideas and does not identify the time to press Stop.
When makes the ringing timer the signal for pressing Stop.

questions.setup: Choose the answer to the why-question.
questions.prompt: 'Why are you wearing a coat?'
options: At the bus stop.
After nine o'clock.
Because it's cold.
The blue one.
questions.explanation: Because introduces the reason for wearing the coat.
feedback: This answers where, not why.
This answers when, not why.
Because introduces the reason for wearing the coat.
This identifies a coat rather than explaining why it is needed.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that gives both facts without making one a reason for the other.
questions.prompt: The room has a desk. It also has a lamp.
options: The room has a desk because it has a lamp.
The room has a desk and a lamp.
The room has a desk or a lamp.
The room has a desk, so it has a lamp.
questions.explanation: And combines the two stated room features without adding a causal link.
feedback: Because makes the lamp a reason for having the desk.
And combines the two stated room features without adding a causal link.
Or makes the two objects alternatives instead of confirming both.
So makes the lamp a result of having the desk.

questions.setup: Choose the word that contrasts wanting to come with being unable to come.
questions.prompt: I'd like to come, ___ I have to work.
options: but
so
because
or
questions.explanation: But introduces the work obligation that prevents accepting the invitation.
feedback: But introduces the work obligation that prevents accepting the invitation.
So presents work as a result of wanting to come.
Because gives work as the reason for wanting to come, which changes the intended relationship.
Or makes these alternatives rather than a wish and an obstacle.

questions.setup: Choose what happens second.
questions.prompt: 'First collect your bag. Then go to the taxi area.'
options: Go to the taxi area.
Collect your bag.
Go back to the plane.
Buy another ticket.
questions.explanation: Then introduces the second step: going to the taxi area.
feedback: Then introduces the second step: going to the taxi area.
First marks collecting the bag as the earlier step.
Returning to the plane is not part of these directions.
The directions do not include buying a ticket.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that keeps the stated order.
questions.prompt: I have breakfast first. I take the bus next.
options: I have breakfast after I take the bus.
I take the bus before I have breakfast.
I have breakfast before I take the bus.
I have breakfast while I am on the bus.
questions.explanation: Before keeps breakfast earlier than the bus journey.
feedback: After reverses the order and puts breakfast later.
This also puts the bus journey before breakfast.
Before keeps breakfast earlier than the bus journey.
While makes the actions happen together instead of one following the other.

questions.setup: Choose the word meaning neither drink is wanted.
questions.prompt: I don't want tea ___ coffee. Water is fine.
options: because
so
but
or
questions.explanation: Under don't want, tea or coffee rejects both alternatives.
feedback: Because cannot join the two unwanted drinks as alternatives.
So would introduce a result rather than another unwanted drink.
But suggests a contrast that the statement rejecting both drinks does not intend.
Under don't want, tea or coffee rejects both alternatives.

questions.setup: Choose the word that simply adds a second action by the same person.
questions.prompt: Eva checked her bag ___ took out her passport.
options: unless
because
and
although
questions.explanation: And connects the two actions sharing the subject Eva.
feedback: Unless would introduce an exception, not simply add the second action.
Because would need a complete reason clause, such as because she needed her passport.
And connects the two actions sharing the subject Eva.
Although would require a contrasting clause rather than directly adding took out here.

questions.setup: Choose the word that adds what another person does.
questions.prompt: I cook dinner, ___ my partner washes the dishes.
options: and
because
unless
or
questions.explanation: And adds a second fact with a different subject.
feedback: And adds a second fact with a different subject.
Because makes the partner's action a reason for cooking, rather than just adding a fact.
Unless makes dishwashing an exception affecting cooking, not an additional fact.
Or offers alternative arrangements instead of describing both people's jobs.

questions.setup: Choose the idea introduced by 'but'.
questions.prompt: 'The bag is small, but it is heavy.'
options: Its color.
Its price.
A choice of bags.
An unexpected feature.
questions.explanation: 'But' presents heaviness as a contrast to what you might expect from a small bag.
feedback: The sentence says nothing about color.
The sentence says nothing about cost.
Both descriptions concern the same bag; no alternative bag is offered.
'But' presents heaviness as a contrast to what you might expect from a small bag.

questions.setup: Choose the reason given in the message.
questions.prompt: 'I'm walking because my bicycle has a flat tire.'
options: The bicycle has a flat tire.
The speaker likes walking.
The road is closed.
The speaker has no bicycle.
questions.explanation: The words after because give the stated reason for walking.
feedback: The words after because give the stated reason for walking.
The message does not state a preference for walking.
No road closure is mentioned.
The speaker has a bicycle, but its tire has a problem.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that makes buying batteries the result of the problem.
questions.prompt: The remote control needed new batteries. I bought some.
options: The remote needed new batteries because I bought some.
I bought some batteries, so the remote needed new ones.
The remote needed new batteries, so I bought some.
I bought some batteries, but the remote didn't need them.
questions.explanation: So puts the purchase after the need as the resulting response.
feedback: Because makes buying batteries the cause of needing them.
This also reverses the intended direction from problem to response.
So puts the purchase after the need as the resulting response.
This denies the stated need instead of keeping both facts.

questions.setup: Choose the connector showing that the visit happened despite the expense.
questions.prompt: ___ the ticket was expensive, I visited my family.
options: Although
Because
Until
So that
questions.explanation: Although presents the expense as an obstacle that did not stop the visit.
feedback: Although presents the expense as an obstacle that did not stop the visit.
Because would make the expense a reason for visiting.
Until gives an endpoint in time, not a contrast with expense.
So that would make the ticket's expense the purpose of the visit.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that correctly introduces the reason in this sentence.
questions.prompt: The outdoor concert stopped ___ a storm.
options: because of
because
although
so that
questions.explanation: Because of introduces the noun phrase a storm as the reason.
feedback: Because of introduces the noun phrase a storm as the reason.
Because needs a clause, such as because a storm began.
Although needs a clause here and would introduce contrast, not the requested reason.
So that needs a clause expressing a purpose or result, not just a storm.

questions.setup: Choose the word showing that the two activities happened at the same time.
questions.prompt: I prepared the salad ___ my friend cooked the rice.
options: after
before
because
while
questions.explanation: While presents the two people's cooking activities as overlapping.
feedback: After puts salad preparation later than cooking the rice.
Before puts salad preparation earlier.
Because gives a reason rather than explicitly showing simultaneous activities.
While presents the two people's cooking activities as overlapping.

questions.setup: Choose the word meaning the waiting continues up to the named time.
questions.prompt: Please wait here ___ the receptionist returns.
options: after
until
because
although
questions.explanation: Until makes the receptionist's return the endpoint of waiting.
feedback: After would place the waiting later than the return.
Until makes the receptionist's return the endpoint of waiting.
Because gives a reason and does not set the end of the wait.
Although would contrast waiting with the return, not mark an endpoint.

questions.setup: Choose the completion expressing the purpose of going to the bank.
questions.prompt: I went to the bank ___ pay in a cheque.
options: because
so that
to
for
questions.explanation: To plus pay gives the purpose of going to the bank.
feedback: Because would need a full clause, such as because I needed to pay in a cheque.
So that needs a subject and verb, such as so that I could pay.
To plus pay gives the purpose of going to the bank.
For does not directly introduce the base verb pay in this purpose phrase.

questions.setup: Choose the connector expressing the purpose of speaking slowly.
questions.prompt: The guide spoke slowly ___ everyone could understand the directions.
options: even though
because of
until
so that
questions.explanation: So that introduces the intended benefit for a different subject, everyone.
feedback: Even though presents understanding as a fact in contrast, not the guide's purpose.
Because of cannot directly introduce the full clause everyone could understand.
Until sets an endpoint rather than stating the intended benefit.
So that introduces the intended benefit for a different subject, everyone.

questions.setup: Choose the connector placing payment later than checking the bill.
questions.prompt: We paid ___ we checked the bill carefully.
options: before
after
because
while
questions.explanation: After places the completed check before payment.
feedback: Before would put payment ahead of checking.
After places the completed check before payment.
Because gives checking as a reason rather than directly stating the requested order.
While would make payment overlap with checking.

questions.setup: Choose the usual verb form for a future event after 'before' in this instruction.
questions.prompt: Check the platform number before the train ___.
options: will arrive
arriving
arrive
arrives
questions.explanation: A future time clause after 'before' normally uses the present simple: the train arrives.
feedback: Use the present simple rather than predictive 'will' in this future time clause.
'Arriving' needs a helping verb to complete the clause.
The singular 'train' takes 'arrives', not 'arrive'.
A future time clause after 'before' normally uses the present simple: the train arrives.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that fits the noun phrase 'the flight'.
questions.prompt: Please keep your phone quiet ___ the flight.
options: while
when
as soon as
during
questions.explanation: 'During' introduces the noun phrase naming the period of time.
feedback: 'While' normally needs a clause here, such as 'while you are on the flight'.
'When' needs a clause or a different reduced structure; 'the flight' alone does not complete it here.
'As soon as' needs an event clause, such as 'as soon as the flight begins'.
'During' introduces the noun phrase naming the period of time.

questions.setup: Choose the connector that means immediately after the named event.
questions.prompt: Send me a message ___ you land, so I know you've arrived safely.
options: long before
as soon as
unless
even though
questions.explanation: As soon as asks for the message immediately after landing.
feedback: Long before would put the message well ahead of landing.
As soon as asks for the message immediately after landing.
Unless makes landing an exception to sending, rather than the trigger.
Even though introduces a contrast and does not specify prompt timing.

questions.setup: Choose the word giving the starting point of a continuing situation.
questions.prompt: I've lived in this building ___ I moved to this city.
options: since
until
during
before
questions.explanation: Since introduces the past event from which the residence continues to now.
feedback: Since introduces the past event from which the residence continues to now.
Until marks an endpoint and would not give the requested beginning of the continuing residence.
During takes a noun phrase, not the full clause I moved to this city.
Before places residence earlier than the move instead of starting with it.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that says the course includes the two skills.
questions.prompt: The course covers both speaking ___ listening.
options: and
or
but
nor
questions.explanation: Both ... and includes the two named skills.
feedback: Both ... and includes the two named skills.
Or offers alternatives and does not complete the both ... and pair.
But introduces a contrast instead of completing this inclusion structure.
Nor belongs in a negative pairing such as neither ... nor, not both ... nor.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that presents two available appointment days.
questions.prompt: You can come either on Tuesday ___ on Thursday.
options: nor
or
and
but
questions.explanation: Either ... or presents Tuesday and Thursday as the available alternatives.
feedback: Nor follows neither in a negative pair, not either in this offer.
Either ... or presents Tuesday and Thursday as the available alternatives.
And adds both days instead of completing the alternative pair either ... or.
But introduces contrast rather than completing the paired choice.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that says both facilities are absent.
questions.prompt: The apartment has neither a lift ___ a balcony.
options: and
but
nor
also
questions.explanation: Neither ... nor excludes both the lift and the balcony.
feedback: And does not complete the standard neither ... nor pairing.
But introduces contrast rather than a second item covered by neither.
Neither ... nor excludes both the lift and the balcony.
Also adds information but does not complete the negative pairing neither ... nor.

questions.setup: Choose the word that signals a contrast between the two sentences.
questions.prompt: The hotel room was small. ___, it had a beautiful view.
options: Therefore
For example
Then
However
questions.explanation: However introduces a positive feature that balances the small room.
feedback: Therefore makes the view a result of the room being small.
For example would make the view an example of small size.
Then orders events in time rather than contrasting two features.
However introduces a positive feature that balances the small room.

questions.setup: Choose the word that adds another service.
questions.prompt: The shop repairs phones. It ___ sells chargers.
options: instead
otherwise
also
therefore
questions.explanation: Also adds charger sales to phone repairs.
feedback: Instead would replace repairing phones with selling chargers.
Otherwise introduces an alternative situation or consequence, not another service.
Also adds charger sales to phone repairs.
Therefore presents sales as a conclusion from repairs, rather than simply adding information.

questions.setup: Choose the word showing that a new plan replaced the old one.
questions.prompt: We didn't go to the cinema. We watched a film at home ___.
options: too
therefore
instead
for example
questions.explanation: Instead identifies watching at home as the substitute for going to the cinema.
feedback: Too would add home viewing to a cinema visit, but the visit did not happen.
Therefore presents a conclusion and is not the natural sentence-final replacement marker here.
Instead identifies watching at home as the substitute for going to the cinema.
For example would introduce an instance of a broader category, not the replacement plan.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase introducing specific examples of tools.
questions.prompt: You can borrow tools here, ___ a hammer or a drill.
options: because of
instead of
such as
as soon as
questions.explanation: Such as introduces a hammer and a drill as examples of tools.
feedback: Because of would make the tools a reason for borrowing rather than examples.
Instead of would present these tools as things replaced, not things included.
Such as introduces a hammer and a drill as examples of tools.
As soon as introduces a time clause, not a list of examples.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that moves the story forward in time.
questions.prompt: I left my wallet on the train. ___, a passenger handed it to the station staff.
options: An hour later
For that reason
In contrast
For example

that
than
questions.explanation: 'No sooner ... than' connects two events occurring in rapid succession, with inversion in the first clause.
feedback: 'When' pairs with 'hardly' or 'scarcely' in the corresponding construction; 'no sooner' takes 'than'.
'Until' marks a duration endpoint and does not complete 'no sooner' here.
'That' introduces other kinds of clauses, not the second event in this conventional pairing.
'No sooner ... than' connects two events occurring in rapid succession, with inversion in the first clause.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the formal purpose clause.
questions.prompt: 'The names were removed lest participants be identified from the quotations.'
options: Removal aimed to prevent identification, without reporting whether identification occurred.
Participants had already been identified, causing removal.
Removal was intended to make identification easier.
Identification was an unexpected fact conceded despite removal.
questions.explanation: Lest introduces the unwanted possibility that motivates the precaution; it does not report its realization.
feedback: Lest introduces the unwanted possibility that motivates the precaution; it does not report its realization.
Lest states a feared outcome to prevent, not an established earlier identification.
This reverses the negative purpose: identification is what removal is meant to prevent.
A lest-clause is preventive, not a concession asserting that the event happened.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the concern introduced by 'for fear that'.
questions.prompt: 'The editor delayed naming the source for fear that disclosure might expose her to pressure.'
options: The source had already faced pressure, and this established event caused the delay.
The delay was intended to put pressure on the source to agree to disclosure.
The editor regarded disclosure as inevitable and delayed only until the pressure ended.
Concern about possible pressure on the source motivated the delay.
questions.explanation: The clause identifies an unconfirmed unwanted consequence as the reason for the editor's caution.
feedback: 'For fear that' with 'might' presents a feared possibility, not a reported event that has already happened.
The feared pressure is an outcome the delay seeks to avoid, not the editor's intended goal.
The sentence does not assert inevitable disclosure or define the delay by the end of actual pressure.
The clause identifies an unconfirmed unwanted consequence as the reason for the editor's caution.

questions.setup: Choose the function of 'granted that' in this argument.
questions.prompt: 'Granted that the service is cheaper, its limited opening hours make it unsuitable for our staff.'
options: It leaves the price comparison entirely unresolved.
It gives low cost as the cause of limited opening hours.
It makes cheapness a guarantee of suitability.
It accepts the price advantage before challenging the overall suitability.
questions.explanation: 'Granted that' concedes the favorable premise while allowing the main argument to reach a different overall judgment.
feedback: The speaker accepts the price advantage for the argument rather than leaving it unresolved.
The connector does not claim that lower cost causes the hours limitation.
The main clause explicitly rejects suitability despite the lower cost.
'Granted that' concedes the favorable premise while allowing the main argument to reach a different overall judgment.

questions.setup: Choose the relationship signaled by 'hence'.
questions.prompt: 'The document refers to an event in 1998; hence, the claim that it was written in 1995 is doubtful.'
options: The reference physically caused the document to be written later.
The date claim caused the document to mention the event.
The reference supplies evidence for questioning the claimed date.
The two dates describe successive stages of publication.
questions.explanation: 'Hence' introduces a conclusion supported by the discrepancy between the reference and the proposed date.
feedback: The sentence draws an inference about dating, not a causal account of the writing process.
This reverses the evidential direction and invents a cause of the reference.
'Hence' introduces a conclusion supported by the discrepancy between the reference and the proposed date.
The writer questions a claim; no two-stage publication history is stated.

questions.setup: Choose the continuation marker that resists the inference suggested by the first sentence.
questions.prompt: The sample is small. ___, the repeated pattern across all three sites deserves investigation.
options: Accordingly
For that reason
Nevertheless
In other words
questions.explanation: Nevertheless acknowledges the limitation while maintaining that the pattern merits attention.
feedback: Accordingly presents the recommendation as following from smallness, rather than resisting its discouraging implication.
For that reason makes small sample size the reason to investigate the pattern.
Nevertheless acknowledges the limitation while maintaining that the pattern merits attention.
In other words would equate the recommendation with small sample size rather than qualify the argument.

questions.setup: Choose the word presenting the action as a response consistent with the assessment, not merely a later event.
questions.prompt: The reviewers judged the evidence insufficient. ___, the editor requested further analysis.
options: Subsequently
Conversely
Accordingly
Meanwhile
questions.explanation: Accordingly connects the editorial action to the assessment that makes it appropriate.
feedback: Subsequently orders the events but does not explicitly show the action following from the judgment.
Conversely introduces a reversed or contrasting relationship, not a response aligned with the judgment.
Accordingly connects the editorial action to the assessment that makes it appropriate.
Meanwhile would emphasize simultaneity rather than a response based on the assessment.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'pending' in this notice.
questions.prompt: 'The estimates remain provisional pending the completion of the independent audit.'
options: The completed audit has already confirmed the estimates.
The estimates retain provisional status while audit completion is awaited.
The estimates are provisional because the audit was cancelled.
Completion of the audit is postponed until the estimates become final.
questions.explanation: 'Pending' marks the period awaiting a specified event; the notice does not say what the audit will conclude.
feedback: Completion is still awaited, and no confirmation is reported.
'Pending' marks the period awaiting a specified event; the notice does not say what the audit will conclude.
The notice does not state cancellation or make it a cause.
This reverses which event is being awaited and which status continues meanwhile.

questions.setup: Choose the connector acknowledging a contrary recommendation while preserving the decision to proceed.
questions.prompt: ___ the consultant's advice to postpone, the organizers confirmed the original date.
options: In accordance with
As a consequence of
For the purpose of
Notwithstanding
questions.explanation: Notwithstanding means despite and highlights that the decision runs against the advice.
feedback: In accordance with would say the decision followed the advice, but the advice was to postpone.
As a consequence of treats the advice as a cause rather than explicitly conceding its contrary direction.
For the purpose of gives an intended goal, not an acknowledged contrary recommendation.
Notwithstanding means despite and highlights that the decision runs against the advice.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation preserving the limited exception.
questions.prompt: 'The two versions are identical, save that the revised one includes a glossary.'
options: The versions differ throughout because a glossary was added.
The glossary is presented as the exception to their identity.
The revised version replaces the original text with a glossary.
The versions will become identical after the glossary is added.
questions.explanation: Save that means except that and isolates the added glossary as the stated difference.
feedback: Save that limits the difference rather than extending it throughout the versions.
Save that means except that and isolates the added glossary as the stated difference.
Includes does not mean replaces; the other text remains identical according to the statement.
The sentence compares existing versions and reports no future step toward identity.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that preserves the degree limitation.
questions.prompt: 'The recommendation is persuasive to the extent that its cost estimates are reliable.'
options: Its persuasive force depends on how reliable the cost estimates are.
The recommendation itself makes the estimates reliable.
The recommendation is persuasive despite unreliable estimates.
Reliability has been established beyond question.
questions.explanation: To the extent that limits persuasive force according to the degree of reliability in its basis.
feedback: To the extent that limits persuasive force according to the degree of reliability in its basis.
This reverses the dependency between supporting estimates and persuasive force.
The sentence ties persuasive force to reliability, rather than conceding unreliability.
The degree clause does not itself establish the estimates' actual reliability.

questions.setup: Choose what the whether-clause does in the sentence.
questions.prompt: 'The panel debated whether the existing evidence justified a second trial.'
options: It states that the evidence justified a second trial.
It gives the cause of holding a second trial.
It identifies an unresolved question that the panel discussed.
It sets a condition that automatically requires another trial.
questions.explanation: The clause supplies the content of the debate as an open yes-or-no issue.
feedback: Whether introduces the issue for debate, not an assertion of the positive answer.
The sentence reports discussion and does not report a second trial being held.
The clause supplies the content of the debate as an open yes-or-no issue.
This is an embedded question, not a rule stating a sufficient condition for a trial.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite reporting an observed consequence without attributing an intention.
questions.prompt: Closing the side entrance made the queue longer. We do not know why the entrance was closed.
options: The side entrance was closed with the result that the queue became longer.
The side entrance was closed in order that the queue would become longer.
The side entrance was closed for fear that the queue would become longer.
The side entrance was closed on condition that the queue became longer.
questions.explanation: With the result that reports the observed effect while leaving the decision-makers' intention unspecified.
feedback: With the result that reports the observed effect while leaving the decision-makers' intention unspecified.
In order that attributes a purpose to the closure, which the evidence does not establish.
For fear that attributes a preventive motive and makes the longer queue an outcome to avoid.
On condition that turns the consequence into a stipulation governing closure.

questions.setup: Choose the conclusion that respects the stated limit on agreement.
questions.prompt: 'I accept the reviewer's criticism insofar as it concerns the missing citations, but not its judgment of the argument itself.'
options: The writer accepts the reviewer's overall judgment.
The writer accepts the citation criticism while rejecting the broader judgment.
The writer denies that citations are missing.
The writer will accept the argument criticism once citations are added.
questions.explanation: The degree/respect clause limits agreement to citations, and the second clause excludes the argument judgment.
feedback: Insofar as and the following but-clause explicitly restrict acceptance to one respect.
The degree/respect clause limits agreement to citations, and the second clause excludes the argument judgment.
The writer accepts criticism of the citations rather than denying its basis.
No future condition for accepting the broader criticism is stated.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase preserving the unwanted outcome in the lest-clause.
questions.prompt: 'The editor retained the qualification lest the conclusion appear stronger than the evidence warranted.'
options: The editor retained it to avoid making the conclusion seem unjustifiably strong.
The editor retained it because the conclusion had already been proved too strong.
The editor retained it to make the conclusion seem more forceful.
The editor retained it despite knowing the conclusion could not seem too strong.
questions.explanation: The unwanted outcome is an impression of excessive strength; retaining the qualification is intended to prevent it.
feedback: The unwanted outcome is an impression of excessive strength; retaining the qualification is intended to prevent it.
Lest expresses prevention of a possible appearance, not a finding already proved.
This promotes the outcome the editor intended to prevent.
This turns a feared risk into a denied possibility and changes prevention into concession.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that preserves the writer's acceptance of a premise while keeping the inference limited.
questions.prompt: 'Given that the archive is incomplete, the absence of a record cannot by itself establish that the transaction never occurred.'
options: The archive's incompleteness proves the transaction occurred.
The writer merely hypothesizes that the archive might be incomplete.
The archive's incompleteness weakens the proposed inference from missing documentation.
The missing record caused the whole archive to become incomplete.
questions.explanation: Given that adopts incompleteness as a premise; the main clause limits what a missing record can establish on its own.
feedback: Failure to prove nonoccurrence does not prove occurrence.
Given that presents incompleteness as accepted for this argument, rather than marking it as a mere possibility.
Given that adopts incompleteness as a premise; the main clause limits what a missing record can establish on its own.
The relationship concerns evidential support, not a claim about how the archive became incomplete.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation preserving the particular basis of the description.
questions.prompt: 'The procedure is participatory inasmuch as members can propose amendments; this says nothing about who makes the final decision.'
options: Members' ability to propose amendments is the stated basis for the limited description.
Members' proposals guarantee that they control the final decision.
The procedure is participatory despite excluding member proposals.
The final decision is participatory only when amendments are rejected.
questions.explanation: Inasmuch as identifies the respect that supports participatory while the final clause blocks a broader inference.
feedback: Inasmuch as identifies the respect that supports participatory while the final clause blocks a broader inference.
The following clause explicitly withholds a claim about final decision-making power.
The sentence states that members can propose amendments and uses that as support, not an obstacle.
No condition about rejecting amendments appears in the statement.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that keeps the concession attached to the forecast, not to the data's existence.
questions.prompt: 'Notwithstanding the revised figures, we remain unconvinced that demand will recover.'
options: The writers acknowledge revised figures but do not accept the recovery forecast.
The writers deny that the figures were revised.
Revising the figures is presented as the cause of a future recovery.
The writers are certain that demand cannot recover.
questions.explanation: The concessive phrase acknowledges evidence that might encourage confidence, while remain unconvinced withholds acceptance of the forecast.
feedback: The concessive phrase acknowledges evidence that might encourage confidence, while remain unconvinced withholds acceptance of the forecast.
Notwithstanding concedes the figures rather than denying that the revision exists.
The sentence concerns belief in a forecast and does not make revision cause an economic change.
Being unconvinced of recovery is weaker than being certain recovery is impossible.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation preserving the limited exception to publication.
questions.prompt: 'The transcript will be published, except insofar as passages disclose confidential personal details.'
options: One confidential detail requires withholding the entire transcript.
The exclusion applies to the passages that disclose the specified details.
Confidential passages must be published as examples.
Publication depends on proving that no passage is confidential.
questions.explanation: The combined phrase restricts the exception to the extent that the specified disclosure occurs.
feedback: Except insofar as limits the exclusion; it does not turn one passage into a reason to withhold the whole transcript.
The combined phrase restricts the exception to the extent that the specified disclosure occurs.
The sensitive passages are the exception to publication, not mandatory examples.
This changes a selective exclusion into an all-or-nothing condition for publication.

questions.setup: Choose the relationship conveyed by 'only to'.
questions.prompt: 'She spent weeks restoring the file, only to discover that a complete copy had been stored elsewhere.'
options: Finding the complete copy was the sole purpose of restoring the damaged file.
The discovery is an unexpected outcome that makes the effort seem unnecessary.
Restoration occurred only after the complete copy was discovered.
The sentence leaves it open whether she discovered the copy.
questions.explanation: 'Only to' introduces a subsequent, often frustrating discovery rather than the intended purpose of the effort.
feedback: This mistakes an ironic result for an exclusive purpose.
'Only to' introduces a subsequent, often frustrating discovery rather than the intended purpose of the effort.
The discovery follows the restoration effort, not the other way round.
The construction reports the discovery as an event, not an unresolved possibility.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'so much so that'.
questions.prompt: 'The terminology puzzled experienced readers, so much so that the journal commissioned a glossary.'
options: The glossary was commissioned before the puzzlement was observed.
Puzzling readers was the journal's purpose in commissioning a glossary.
The glossary is offered as an alternative explanation for the puzzlement.
The extent of the puzzlement is illustrated by the response it prompted.
questions.explanation: 'So much so that' intensifies the preceding claim and gives a consequence demonstrating its degree.
feedback: The glossary is presented as a response to the puzzlement, not an earlier event.
This reverses the remedial relationship and attributes an unsupported purpose.
The sentence states a consequence, not a competing explanation.
'So much so that' intensifies the preceding claim and gives a consequence demonstrating its degree.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation preserving the writer's reframing without making it absolute.
questions.prompt: 'The exchange was not so much a negotiation as an attempt to clarify each side's position.'
options: The writer says no negotiating element could have been present.
The writer gives negotiation and clarification exactly equal weight.
The writer says clarification happened only after negotiations ended.
The writer treats clarification as the more accurate primary description.
questions.explanation: The construction favors the second characterization while allowing the first to have some relevance.
feedback: Not so much ... as shifts emphasis; it need not deny every trace of the first description.
The phrasing explicitly gives greater weight to clarification, not equal weight.
The contrast concerns how to characterize the exchange, not two stages in time.
The construction favors the second characterization while allowing the first to have some relevance.

questions.setup: Choose what remains unresolved in the sentence.
questions.prompt: 'The discussion ended abruptly, whether because time ran out or because the chair wished to avoid the issue.'
options: Whether the discussion ended abruptly.
Which of the suggested explanations accounts for the abrupt ending.
