Receiving them later so they can be checked again
questions.explanation: The sooner, the better means that an earlier action would be preferable.
feedback: The expression favors earlier delivery but gives no fixed time.
The sooner, the better means that an earlier action would be preferable.
Sooner compares timing, not the quantity of information.
Later is the opposite of the timing preference expressed.

questions.setup: A colleague says, 'Today's briefing took longer than usual.'
questions.prompt: Which comparison point is stated?
options: The duration of yesterday's briefing specifically
The time allowed in today's written schedule
The longest briefing the speaker has attended
The normal duration of these briefings
questions.explanation: Than usual compares today's event with the typical duration of events of this kind.
feedback: Yesterday could be typical or unusual; the sentence does not specifically select it.
A scheduled duration can differ from what normally happens; usual names the normal pattern.
Usual is a typical benchmark, not a record maximum.
Than usual compares today's event with the typical duration of events of this kind.

questions.setup: The morning shift handles 40 parcels; the evening shift handles 80.
questions.prompt: Choose the grammatically correct completion: The evening shift handles twice ___ the morning shift.
options: as much parcels as
many parcels than
as many parcels as
as many parcels than
questions.explanation: Twice as many parcels as compares two counts and expresses a two-to-one ratio.
feedback: Parcels are separate countable items, so use many rather than much.
The twice construction here needs as many ... as, not many ... than.
Twice as many parcels as compares two counts and expresses a two-to-one ratio.
The second comparison word must be as in twice as many ... as.

questions.setup: A supplier offers two screens. 'This one is bigger, but the other is brighter.'
questions.prompt: Which summary preserves both comparisons?
options: Neither screen leads on both size and brightness.
The bigger screen is also the brighter one.
The screens are equal in size but differ in brightness.
The screens differ in size but have equal brightness.
questions.explanation: One screen leads on size, while the other leads on brightness; the advantages are split.
feedback: One screen leads on size, while the other leads on brightness; the advantages are split.
The supplier assigns greater brightness to the other screen.
Bigger states a size difference, so equality loses part of the comparison.
The other is brighter explicitly states a brightness difference as well as a size difference.

questions.setup: A visitor says, 'This is the most interesting tour I've ever taken.'
questions.prompt: Which group is the visitor using for the comparison?
options: All tours currently available in the city
All the tours the visitor has taken up to now
Only tours taken during the current holiday
All tours that other visitors have recommended
questions.explanation: I've ever taken defines a personal experience set extending up to the present.
feedback: The relative clause limits the group to tours the visitor has taken, not all available tours.
I've ever taken defines a personal experience set extending up to the present.
Ever includes earlier experience too, unless the context separately restricts it.
Recommendations are not the same as the speaker's own experience.

questions.setup: Three meeting rooms hold 20, 35, and 50 people respectively.
questions.prompt: Which capacity belongs to the second-largest room by seating capacity?
options: 50 people
20 people
35 people
Either 35 or 50 people
questions.explanation: Second-largest means one place below the largest; 35 lies between 50 and 20.
feedback: Fifty is the largest capacity, not the second-largest.
Twenty is the smallest capacity, two places below the largest in this group.
Second-largest means one place below the largest; 35 lies between 50 and 20.
Second-largest names a single rank here; the different capacities leave no tie.

questions.setup: The metal stand costs more but lasts longer than the plastic stand.
questions.prompt: Which sentence preserves both relations while starting with the plastic stand?
options: The plastic stand is cheaper and more durable.
The plastic stand is dearer but less durable.
The plastic stand is cheaper but less durable.
The plastic stand is dearer and more durable.
questions.explanation: Reversing the products makes the plastic one lower in both cost and durability.
feedback: Cheaper preserves the price relation, but more durable reverses the lifetime relation.
Less durable is right, but dearer incorrectly gives plastic the higher price.
Reversing the products makes the plastic one lower in both cost and durability.
Both comparisons are reversed: plastic costs less and lasts less long.

questions.setup: As the course progresses, each task requires more effort than the previous one.
questions.prompt: Choose the standard completion that describes this trend: The tasks are becoming ___.
options: most and most demanding
more demanding and more
more and more demanding
more and demanding
questions.explanation: Repeating more around and expresses a growing degree with a longer adjective.
feedback: Most is a superlative; repeating it does not form this increasing-degree expression.
The repeated degree words belong together before demanding: more and more demanding.
Repeating more around and expresses a growing degree with a longer adjective.
The second comparative marker is missing; and cannot join more directly to demanding this way.

questions.setup: Two notices say 'The new stop is farther from the school' and 'The new stop is further from the school.'
questions.prompt: Which comment on these distance comparisons is accurate in standard English?
options: Both farther and further can compare physical distance.
Only farther can refer to physical distance.
Only further can refer to physical distance.
Farther and further describe equal distances.
questions.explanation: For physical distance, farther and further are both established alternatives; this context does not force one.
feedback: For physical distance, farther and further are both established alternatives; this context does not force one.
Further also commonly compares physical distance; it is not restricted to figurative uses.
Farther is a standard physical-distance comparative too.
Both are comparative forms of far; neither expresses equality here.

questions.setup: A: 'The appendices can wait; only the main report matters.' B: 'The appendices are no less useful than the main report.'
questions.prompt: Which reading of B's comparison is supported?
options: B ranks the appendices as slightly less useful than the report.
B says the appendices are useful only when read after the report.
B rejects placing the appendices below the report in usefulness.
B ranks the appendices above the report by a small amount.
questions.explanation: No less useful denies inferiority on that scale; it counters A's dismissal without requiring that the appendices be superior.
feedback: No negates the lower ranking; it does not merely reduce the size of a disadvantage.
The comparison addresses usefulness, not a required reading order.
No less useful denies inferiority on that scale; it counters A's dismissal without requiring that the appendices be superior.
They may be equally useful; no less does not require a positive lead.

questions.setup: After viewing two charts, a reader says, 'The first isn't nearly as clear as the revised one.'
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase best preserves the strength and direction of the comparison?
options: The revised chart is only slightly clearer than the first.
The revised chart is considerably less clear than the first.
The revised chart is considerably clearer than the first.
The revised chart is almost as clear as the first.
questions.explanation: Not nearly as ... as places the first well below the revised chart in clarity.
feedback: Not nearly as clear marks a substantial gap, not just a slight improvement.
This reverses which chart is clearer.
Not nearly as ... as places the first well below the revised chart in clarity.
Almost as clear places the revised chart slightly below the first, changing both direction and degree.

questions.setup: In an informal conversation about three rooms, one guest says 'This room is cheapest of the three'; another says 'This room is the cheapest of the three.'
questions.prompt: Which editorial comment is accurate?
options: Only the version with the can express a group ranking.
The bare version compares two rooms; the version with the compares three.
The bare version means very cheap without comparing the rooms.
Both can express the same lowest-price ranking in this context.
questions.explanation: After is with no following noun, informal English permits the to be omitted here; both versions rank this room lowest in price.
feedback: A predicative superlative without a following noun can omit the in informal use and still rank the group.
The phrase of the three sets the group in both versions; article choice does not change its size.
Cheapest and of the three still supply a superlative ranking; omitting the does not turn it into very cheap.
After is with no following noun, informal English permits the to be omitted here; both versions rank this room lowest in price.

questions.setup: The organiser writes, 'The instructions are all the easier to follow for having a diagram.'
questions.prompt: What role does the diagram have in this comparison?
options: It contributes to making the instructions easier to follow.
It makes every instruction equally easy to follow.
It compensates for instructions that have become harder overall.
It is compared with the instructions as an alternative set of directions.
questions.explanation: All the plus a comparative, followed by a reason, presents that reason as adding to the degree described.
feedback: All the plus a comparative, followed by a reason, presents that reason as adding to the degree described.
All the easier strengthens an improvement; all does not distribute equal ease across every instruction.
The phrase attributes increased ease to the diagram; it does not report an overall deterioration.
For having a diagram gives a reason for the increased ease, not a second set of instructions being ranked.

questions.setup: An adviser says, 'No other form in this packet is as confusing as the registration form.'
questions.prompt: Which ranking follows in the ordinary degree reading?
options: The registration form is more confusing than every other form in the packet.
The registration form ties with at least one other for most confusing.
At least one form is more confusing than the registration form.
The registration form is the most confusing form the adviser has ever seen.
questions.explanation: No other form reaches its degree of confusion; the sentence gives it the top position without a tie in this packet.
feedback: No other form reaches its degree of confusion; the sentence gives it the top position without a tie in this packet.
A tied form would be as confusing, which no other excludes.
A more confusing form would exceed the level that no other says any form reaches.
The comparison set is this packet, not the adviser's entire experience.

questions.setup: A: 'Was the checklist useful?' B: 'More than useful. It prevented us from sending the wrong files.'
questions.prompt: What does B's reply do?
options: It compares the number of checklists with the number of files.
It contrasts the checklist's usefulness with its accuracy.
It limits the checklist's usefulness to correcting earlier mistakes.
It treats useful as too weak a description of the checklist's value.
questions.explanation: More than useful upgrades A's description; the prevented mistake supplies a reason for the stronger praise.
feedback: More than modifies the assessment useful, not a count of objects.
No separate quality such as accuracy is introduced as the comparison point.
The example concerns preventing a mistake, and the phrase strengthens rather than restricts the praise.
More than useful upgrades A's description; the prevented mistake supplies a reason for the stronger praise.

questions.setup: The technician says, 'The damaged cable is less of a problem than the missing software.'
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the comparison?
options: The cable is damaged to a lesser physical extent than the software.
The missing software presents the greater difficulty.
The cable has fewer individual faults than the software.
The cable is not a problem once the software is installed.
questions.explanation: Less of a problem grades how serious an issue is; the cable is below the missing software on that scale.
feedback: Less of a problem compares difficulty caused, not the physical extent of damage to each item.
Less of a problem grades how serious an issue is; the cable is below the missing software on that scale.
The sentence compares overall difficulty, not counts of faults.
A smaller problem is still compatible with a problem; the sentence gives no condition that removes it.

questions.setup: At a ticket desk, a traveller asks, 'Would it be any cheaper to return on Tuesday?'
questions.prompt: What is the traveller asking about?
options: Which Tuesday service has the lowest price of all services
Whether changing the return day would reduce the price at all
Whether Tuesday's price would be lower by a particular amount
Whether a Tuesday return is cheaper than every other return day
questions.explanation: Any before cheaper asks whether even some reduction is available, without specifying its size.
feedback: The question compares the proposed change with the current plan; it does not request a ranking of every Tuesday service.
Any before cheaper asks whether even some reduction is available, without specifying its size.
Any cheaper leaves the amount open rather than naming a required saving.
No comparison with every other day is stated.

questions.setup: An editor observes, 'The more detail we add, the less readable the guide becomes.'
questions.prompt: Which pattern does the editor describe?
options: Both detail and readability increase together.
Readability falls as the amount of detail rises.
Detail is being removed because readability has already fallen.
The guide becomes less detailed as readers gain experience.
questions.explanation: The paired comparatives move in opposite directions: more detail accompanies less readability.
feedback: Less readable marks a decrease in readability, not an increase.
The paired comparatives move in opposite directions: more detail accompanies less readability.
The sentence describes adding detail and the associated change, not a decision to remove it.
Neither removal of detail nor readers' experience is the stated changing factor.

questions.setup: A profile must give equal weight to Tessa's roles as designer and manager, without claiming how she divides her hours.
questions.prompt: Which sentence achieves that writing goal?
options: Tessa spends as much time managing as designing.
Tessa is as much a manager as she is a designer.
Tessa is more a manager than a designer.
Tessa manages as many designers as the other managers do.
questions.explanation: As much a ... as gives the roles equal standing without measuring time spent on them.
feedback: This compares hours, which the writing goal explicitly leaves unclaimed.
As much a ... as gives the roles equal standing without measuring time spent on them.
More ... than gives the managerial role greater weight rather than equal weight.
This compares staff numbers, not the importance of her two roles.

questions.setup: An organiser writes, 'More people registered than there are seats in the hall.'
questions.prompt: Which relationship is asserted?
options: The hall has more seats than registered people.
The number attending exceeds the number registered.
The registration count exceeds the seating capacity.
The hall needs more seats than any other hall.
questions.explanation: The than-clause supplies the seat count as the standard for the number of people registered.
feedback: That reverses which quantity is greater.
The sentence compares registrations with seats, not attendance with registration.
The than-clause supplies the seat count as the standard for the number of people registered.
No other hall appears in the comparison.

questions.setup: A pass cost $100 last year and costs $80 this year.
questions.prompt: Which statement accurately compares the new price with last year's price?
options: This year's price is 80% lower than last year's.
Last year's price was 20% higher than this year's.
This year's price has fallen to 20% of last year's.
This year's price is 20% lower than last year's.
questions.explanation: The decrease is twenty dollars out of the old hundred-dollar price, so the reduction is 20%.
feedback: Eighty percent lower would leave a twenty-dollar price; eighty dollars is 80% of the old price.
The reverse percentage uses eighty as its base; twenty dollars is 25% of eighty, not 20%.
To 20% describes a twenty-dollar final price rather than the twenty-dollar decrease.
The decrease is twenty dollars out of the old hundred-dollar price, so the reduction is 20%.

questions.setup: A shop advertises, 'Selected desks: up to 30% cheaper than last month.'
questions.prompt: What does this wording allow?
options: Every desk in the shop has a 30% reduction.
Thirty percent is the minimum reduction for selected desks.
Some selected desks may have a reduction smaller than 30%.
The desks now cost 30% of last month's prices.
questions.explanation: Up to sets an upper limit on the advertised reduction; it does not give every selected desk the maximum discount.
feedback: Selected restricts the stock, and up to does not promise the maximum for every selected item.
Up to makes 30% the upper, not the lower, limit.
Up to sets an upper limit on the advertised reduction; it does not give every selected desk the maximum discount.
Thirty percent cheaper means a reduction from the old price, not a final price equal to 30% of it.

questions.setup: A report says the new system processed nearly twice as many requests as the old one under the same test conditions.
questions.prompt: Which count pair best fits that description?
options: Old: 100 requests; new: 105 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 195 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 205 requests
Old: 100 requests; new: 295 requests
questions.explanation: Nearly twice as many places the new count close to, but below, two times the old count.
feedback: That is only slightly more, not close to double.
Nearly twice as many places the new count close to, but below, two times the old count.
This is slightly more than twice as many, not nearly twice in the ordinary below-target reading.
That is nearly three times the old count, not nearly twice.

questions.setup: After a supposed consultation, a resident says, 'It felt more like a sales presentation than a discussion.'
questions.prompt: What is being compared?
options: The number of sales presentations and discussions held
The resident's preference for presentations over discussions
The meeting's resemblance to two kinds of event
The duration of the sales and discussion portions
questions.explanation: More like ... than compares how well two descriptions fit the same experience.
feedback: More modifies like here, not a count of events.
The sentence characterizes what the meeting resembled; it does not say which event the resident prefers.
More like ... than compares how well two descriptions fit the same experience.
The comparison concerns resemblance, not explicitly the time spent on separate portions.

questions.setup: A report calls a design 'the best of the three we tested.' An editor changes this to 'the best possible design.'
questions.prompt: How does the edit change the comparison?
options: It expands the ranking claim beyond the three tested designs.
It limits the claim to designs that passed the test.
It changes the design from best to merely acceptable.
It makes the claim depend only on the most recent test.
questions.explanation: Best of the three is bounded by the tested set; best possible reaches across what could be available or achieved.
feedback: Best of the three is bounded by the tested set; best possible reaches across what could be available or achieved.
Best possible does not retain the explicit group of three or add a pass condition.
Both versions use a highest-rank description; the issue is the comparison set, not a downgrade to acceptable.
The edit says nothing about which test occurred most recently.

questions.setup: After a long absence, a listener says, 'Her playing is as expressive as ever.'
questions.prompt: Which reading best fits this comment?
options: Her playing retains the expressive quality the listener remembers.
Her playing has become more expressive than at any earlier time.
Her playing was never expressive before this performance.
Her playing is less expressive than the listener remembers.
questions.explanation: As expressive as ever presents the familiar degree as continuing, rather than announcing a new improvement or decline.
feedback: As expressive as ever presents the familiar degree as continuing, rather than announcing a new improvement or decline.
That would be more expressive than ever; as ... as does not announce a new peak.
As ... as ever invokes an established quality rather than its first appearance.
The equality comparison does not report a loss of expressiveness.

questions.setup: A: 'Should I buy the cheaper printer?' B: 'You'd be better off keeping the old one; these cartridges cost a fortune.'
questions.prompt: What comparison does B make?
options: The old printer necessarily produces higher-quality pages.
The old printer has a lower purchase price than the new one.
A could sell the new printer for more than the old one.
Keeping the old printer would put A in a more favorable practical position.
questions.explanation: Better off compares the person's likely situation under two choices, here with running costs as the reason.
feedback: Better off evaluates A's situation; the stated reason concerns cartridge costs, not page quality.
A already owns the old printer, and B's reason concerns cartridges rather than a comparison of purchase prices.
The reply recommends retaining the old printer; it does not compare resale values.
Better off compares the person's likely situation under two choices, here with running costs as the reason.

questions.setup: A: 'Is the repaired scanner any more reliable?' B: 'If anything, it's less reliable now.'
questions.prompt: What does B convey?
options: Any change B can identify goes toward lower reliability, not improvement.
B confirms a small but clear improvement in reliability.
B says reliability will improve if another repair is made.
B says the scanner's reliability has remained exactly equal.
questions.explanation: If anything tentatively directs the comparison toward the opposite of the suggested improvement.
feedback: If anything tentatively directs the comparison toward the opposite of the suggested improvement.
Less reliable points toward deterioration, the opposite of improvement.
If anything here is not a condition requiring another repair.
B favors a negative change, though cautiously; exact equality is not the comparison offered.

questions.setup: A city newsletter says, 'The library now stays open three hours later, not three hours longer.'
questions.prompt: Which situation fits that distinction?
options: The opening time stayed fixed and closing moved three hours later.
Closing stayed fixed and opening moved three hours earlier.
Both opening and closing moved three hours earlier.
Both opening and closing times moved three hours later.
questions.explanation: Moving both endpoints equally shifts the closing time later while leaving the number of open hours unchanged.
feedback: That would extend the daily duration by three hours, so longer would also apply.
That would make the day longer, but the library would not close later.
The duration would stay the same, but closing would be earlier rather than later.
Moving both endpoints equally shifts the closing time later while leaving the number of open hours unchanged.

questions.setup: A test summary says, 'The revised model is not more robust than its predecessor.' An editor proposes 'The revised model is less robust.'
questions.prompt: What is the problem with the proposed paraphrase?
options: It replaces a comparison of reliability with a comparison of size.
It makes the predecessor less robust than the revised model.
It excludes equal robustness, which the original still permits.
It weakens a definite decline into an uncertain improvement.
questions.explanation: Not more robust denies a positive advantage; the revised model could be equally robust or less robust. Less robust asserts the lower ranking.
feedback: Both sentences retain robustness as their dimension; the change concerns negation and ordering.
Less robust still assigns the lower position to the revised model, not the predecessor.
Not more robust denies a positive advantage; the revised model could be equally robust or less robust. Less robust asserts the lower ranking.
The original does not assert a definite decline; the edit adds one.

questions.setup: A privacy assessment concludes, 'Proposal B is preferable to A on privacy grounds, though A is cheaper and easier to implement.'
questions.prompt: Which summary preserves the stated basis of preference?
options: B is preferable overall because privacy automatically outweighs the other criteria.
A ranks above B for privacy because it is easier to implement.
B ranks above A for privacy; the sentence leaves the overall choice open.
The proposals are equally preferable once all three criteria are considered.
questions.explanation: On privacy grounds limits the ranking to a criterion, while the other advantages prevent an automatic overall conclusion.
feedback: The assessment states a privacy-based preference, not a rule assigning decisive weight to privacy.
Ease of implementation is assigned to A, but the privacy preference is explicitly assigned to B.
On privacy grounds limits the ranking to a criterion, while the other advantages prevent an automatic overall conclusion.
The sentence supplies no weights or combined score that would establish an overall tie.

questions.setup: A reviewer writes, 'This application is more likely to be deferred than rejected.'
questions.prompt: Which comparison is expressed without adding information?
options: This application is more likely to be deferred than the previous application was.
For this application, deferral is judged more probable than rejection.
Deferral is judged more probable than all the other possible outcomes combined.
The application will probably be deferred rather than approved.
questions.explanation: More likely scopes over two outcomes of the same application: being deferred and being rejected.
feedback: The than phrase compares outcomes for this application, not different applications.
More likely scopes over two outcomes of the same application: being deferred and being rejected.
Only rejection is the stated alternative; approval and other outcomes are not included in the comparison.
The sentence neither compares deferral with approval nor necessarily puts deferral above a 50% probability.

questions.setup: A reviewer says, 'The speech was more confident than convincing; several key objections went unanswered.'
questions.prompt: Which interpretation best fits the review?
options: The speech was more convincing than the speaker's earlier speeches.
Confidence is a better description of the speech than persuasiveness is.
The speaker's confidence caused the audience to accept the argument.
The speech contained a greater number of confident claims than persuasive examples.
questions.explanation: More confident than convincing contrasts characterizations of the same speech; the remaining objections support the distinction.
feedback: No earlier speech is the comparison standard; two qualities of this speech are contrasted.
More confident than convincing contrasts characterizations of the same speech; the remaining objections support the distinction.
The unanswered objections and contrast with convincing do not support successful persuasion.
The phrase grades the fit of two descriptions rather than explicitly counting claims and examples.

questions.setup: Tests show a small robustness advantage for Model B over Model A, but neither has been checked against the required standard.
questions.prompt: Which report sentence preserves both the measured comparison and the limit of the tests?
options: B is marginally more robust than A; compliance with the standard remains untested.
B is robust enough to meet the standard, though only marginally more robust than A.
B is no more robust than A, and compliance with the standard remains untested.
B is substantially more robust than A, although compliance remains untested.
questions.explanation: Marginally states the small relative advantage, while the second clause avoids claiming an untested absolute threshold.
feedback: Marginally states the small relative advantage, while the second clause avoids claiming an untested absolute threshold.
The threshold claim is unsupported because neither model was checked against that standard.
No more removes the measured positive advantage.
Substantially overstates the small advantage established by the tests.

questions.setup: Of 100 residents surveyed in East Ward, 60 support the plan. Of 200 in West Ward, 80 support it.
questions.prompt: Which comparison distinguishes the supporter count from the support rate?
options: East has more supporters in the sample and a higher proportion supporting the plan.
West has fewer supporters in the sample but a higher proportion supporting the plan.
The wards have equal support because both have a majority opposed.
East has fewer supporters in the sample but a higher proportion supporting the plan.
questions.explanation: The raw count is 60 versus 80, while the rates are 60% versus 40%; the two rankings go in opposite directions.
feedback: East has the higher rate, but sixty supporters is fewer than eighty.
Both claims are reversed: West has more supporters but the lower rate.
East has a supporting majority of 60%; neither equal rates nor two opposing majorities follows.
The raw count is 60 versus 80, while the rates are 60% versus 40%; the two rankings go in opposite directions.

questions.setup: A: 'The landlord has offered us one evening with a portable heater.' B: 'Well, it's better than nothing.'
questions.prompt: Which response meaning is best supported?
options: B regards the offer as the best option among the landlord's available solutions.
B acknowledges limited value without presenting the offer as satisfactory.
B considers the offer equivalent to receiving no help.
B rejects the offer as worse than managing without a heater.
questions.explanation: The low comparison point provides qualified acceptance: some help is better than none, but that is restrained praise.
feedback: The benchmark is nothing, not a comparison with all solutions the landlord could offer.
The low comparison point provides qualified acceptance: some help is better than none, but that is restrained praise.
Better than nothing grants some improvement over no help rather than complete equivalence.
That reverses the direction of better than nothing.

questions.setup: The organiser writes, 'As few as six people came to the public session.'
questions.prompt: What stance does 'as few as' communicate here?
options: The attendance is given only as a maximum of six.
Six is described as the minimum attendance required to hold the session.
Six people came in addition to the usual attendees.
The attendance is presented as notably low.
questions.explanation: 'As few as' frames six as a surprisingly or notably small count in context.
feedback: 'As few as' highlights the low figure; 'at most six' would state only an upper bound.
The sentence reports turnout; it does not establish a procedural minimum.
'As few as' modifies the reported total, not an added subgroup.
'As few as' frames six as a surprisingly or notably small count in context.

questions.setup: A museum curator says, 'No fewer than forty volunteers helped to catalogue the collection.'
questions.prompt: Which reading best captures the curator's emphasis?
options: The curator presents the volunteer count as impressively large.
The curator complains that there were fewer than forty volunteers.
The curator sets forty as the maximum number allowed to help.
The curator says exactly forty volunteers were needed before work could start.
questions.explanation: No fewer than highlights the scale of the count, presenting forty as noteworthy rather than merely listing it.
feedback: No fewer than highlights the scale of the count, presenting forty as noteworthy rather than merely listing it.
No fewer than negates a lower count rather than asserting one.
The sentence reports participation; no fewer than is not a maximum restriction.
Participation is reported, but no minimum staffing rule or start condition is stated.

questions.setup: A: 'Does the second draft come close to the first in clarity?' B: 'It's nothing like as clear.'
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase retains B's comparative judgment?
options: The second draft is clearer but written in a different style.
The second draft is almost as clear as the first.
The second draft falls well short of the first in clarity.
The drafts differ in subject, so clarity cannot be compared.
questions.explanation: Nothing like as ... as strongly denies closeness to the comparison standard.
feedback: Nothing like as clear rejects comparable clarity, not merely similarity of style.
Almost as clear understates the large shortfall conveyed by nothing like.
Nothing like as ... as strongly denies closeness to the comparison standard.
B does compare clarity; no difference in subject is stated.

questions.setup: Across the test sample, Method A was faster on average than Method B. An editor writes, 'A was faster for every participant.'
questions.prompt: What does the edit incorrectly add?
options: A comparison with a method that was not tested.
A claim that B has the lower average completion time.
A participant-by-participant advantage that an average comparison does not establish.
A statement that the methods had equal sample sizes.
questions.explanation: An average can be lower even when some individual results favor B; every participant is a stronger, distributive claim.
feedback: Both sentences compare A with B; the edit changes how broadly the advantage applies.
The edit does not reverse the named winner; it overextends that winner's advantage.
An average can be lower even when some individual results favor B; every participant is a stronger, distributive claim.
Every participant does not itself report or compare the sample sizes.

questions.setup: The minutes say, 'Keeping the old timetable would have been no worse than adopting this one.'
questions.prompt: Which assessment is expressed?
options: The rejected option is judged strictly better than the adopted one.
The two timetables are said to have produced identical observed outcomes.
The adopted timetable is judged better because the other was rejected.
The rejected option is judged at least equal to the adopted one, not necessarily better.
questions.explanation: No worse denies that keeping the old timetable would rank below the actual choice, while allowing a tie.
feedback: No worse permits equality; it does not require an advantage.
Would have been evaluates an unrealized alternative, not two observed outcomes.
The comparative judgment points the other way: rejection does not establish inferiority.
No worse denies that keeping the old timetable would rank below the actual choice, while allowing a tie.

questions.setup: A design brief says, 'The registration process should be no more intrusive than necessary for confirming membership.'
questions.prompt: Which requirement does the comparison impose?
options: The process should collect exactly the same data as the current process.
Intrusion should not exceed what the stated membership check requires.
The process should be less intrusive than every available alternative.
Any information that might later be useful should be collected.
questions.explanation: No more ... than caps the degree at a purpose-specific necessity threshold, allowing less if the purpose can still be met.
feedback: Necessary for confirming membership is the benchmark, not the existing process.
No more ... than caps the degree at a purpose-specific necessity threshold, allowing less if the purpose can still be met.
The sentence sets a necessity-based ceiling; it does not rank every design.
Possible future usefulness is broader than what is necessary for the named membership check.

questions.setup: A draft says, 'Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam.' The writer means that Ravi's trust in Lena exceeds Sam's trust in Lena.
questions.prompt: Which revision removes the ambiguity while preserving that meaning?
options: Ravi trusts Lena more than he trusts Sam.
Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam trusts Ravi.
Ravi is trusted by Lena more than Sam is.
Ravi trusts Lena more than Sam does.
questions.explanation: Does restores trusts Lena after Sam, making Sam the second subject rather than a second object of Ravi's trust.
feedback: This compares Ravi's trust in two different people, not two people's trust in Lena.
This changes the recipient of Sam's trust from Lena to Ravi.
This makes Lena the trusting person and compares her trust in Ravi and Sam.
Does restores trusts Lena after Sam, making Sam the second subject rather than a second object of Ravi's trust.

questions.setup: A review says, 'The archive is less accessible than it could be.'
questions.prompt: Which comparison does the review make, without adding a historical claim?
options: Current accessibility is lower than it was before the refurbishment.
Current accessibility is below that of every similar archive.
Current accessibility has fallen even though no improvement is possible.
Current accessibility is below an attainable level.
questions.explanation: Could be supplies a possible improved state as the standard, not a claim about the archive's past.
feedback: No earlier state or refurbishment is named in the sentence.
The comparison is with the archive's own potential, not a complete set of other archives.
The sentence neither asserts a decline over time nor denies possible improvement.
Could be supplies a possible improved state as the standard, not a claim about the archive's past.

questions.setup: A salary report calls Noor 'the highest-paid part-time employee in the department,' using annual earnings before tax.
questions.prompt: Which claim preserves the report's ranking and comparison set?
options: Noor earns more per hour than any employee in the department.
Noor's annual earnings exceed those of all full-time departmental staff.
No other part-time departmental employee has higher annual earnings before tax.
Noor is the department's only part-time employee at that annual earnings level.
questions.explanation: This retains the subgroup and annual measure without inventing an hourly ranking or excluding possible ties.
feedback: Hourly pay is a different measure, and any employee expands the group beyond part-time staff.
Full-time staff are outside the stated comparison group.
This retains the subgroup and annual measure without inventing an hourly ranking or excluding possible ties.
Highest-paid does not by itself exclude another employee tied at the same level.

questions.setup: Approval rose from 40% to 50%. The report must describe the increase in percentage points, not the relative percentage increase.
questions.prompt: Which sentence meets that precise reporting goal?
options: Approval was ten percentage points higher than before.
Approval was ten percent higher than before.
Approval was twenty-five percentage points higher than before.
Approval was fifty percentage points higher than before.
questions.explanation: Percentage points compare the displayed percentages directly: fifty minus forty is ten points.
feedback: Percentage points compare the displayed percentages directly: fifty minus forty is ten points.
A ten-percent relative increase on forty would reach forty-four; the required measure is percentage points.
Twenty-five is the relative percentage increase, not the point difference between forty and fifty.
Fifty is the new rate, not its increase over forty.

questions.setup: A: 'Did the second briefing explain why the venue changed?' B: 'I'm none the wiser.'
questions.prompt: What does B's comparative expression convey?
options: B now understands the reason but disagrees with the decision.
The briefing has not improved B's understanding of the reason.
B knows less about the reason than before the briefing.
B understands less than every other person at the briefing.
questions.explanation: None the wiser means no better informed as a result of the intervening event.
feedback: None the wiser denies a gain in understanding; disagreement is not the stated issue.
None the wiser means no better informed as a result of the intervening event.
The idiom signals no improvement, not necessarily an actual loss of knowledge.
The comparison concerns B's change in understanding, not a ranking of participants.

questions.setup: A: 'Has the extension been approved?' B: 'It's as good as approved; only the routine signature is missing.'
questions.prompt: Which reading best fits B's reply?
options: B treats approval as virtually settled while acknowledging it is not formally complete.
B compares the quality of this approval with that of an earlier approval.
B says approval and rejection remain equally likely.
B confirms that every required approval step has been completed.
questions.explanation: As good as approved means effectively or almost approved here; the missing signature keeps formal completion separate.
feedback: As good as approved means effectively or almost approved here; the missing signature keeps formal completion separate.
As good as before approved has a near-equivalence meaning, not a quality ranking between approvals.
As good as approved expresses strong expectation of approval, not an evenly balanced outcome.
The routine signature is explicitly still missing, so formal completion is not claimed.

questions.setup: An exhibition review says, 'No single photograph is more powerful than the sequence as a whole.'
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the units being compared?
options: The complete sequence is at least as powerful as each individual photograph.
Each photograph is equally powerful when displayed by itself.
The complete sequence is more powerful than all photographs outside the exhibition.
The sequence's power is exactly the sum of the individual photographs' power.
questions.explanation: No individual image exceeds the whole; at least as powerful preserves possible equality as well as superiority of the whole.
feedback: No individual image exceeds the whole; at least as powerful preserves possible equality as well as superiority of the whole.
The sentence compares each photograph with the whole, not individual photographs with one another.
The comparison does not extend to photographs outside this sequence.
A ranking between whole and parts does not establish an additive measurement.

questions.setup: A: 'Khan has spent years challenging this approach, yet she endorses the new trial.' B: 'Her endorsement is all the more persuasive coming from her.'
questions.prompt: What supplies the added force in B's comparison?
options: Khan's endorsement makes the trial's results stronger than their recorded values.
Khan's prior criticism makes her support especially persuasive.
Khan's current endorsement is more persuasive than all her earlier endorsements.
Khan's support shows that the trial has persuaded its previous critics as a group.
questions.explanation: All the more identifies an added reason for persuasiveness; coming from her refers back to Khan's history of challenging the approach.
feedback: The comparison concerns the force of an endorsement, not a change in the underlying measurements.
All the more identifies an added reason for persuasiveness; coming from her refers back to Khan's history of challenging the approach.
The exchange gives her prior criticism as a reason, not a set of earlier endorsements being ranked.
The speakers discuss this source's added credibility, not an endorsement by all critics.

questions.setup: A survey recorded multiple decisions by each editor, then pooled the decision records. Its summary says, 'More often than not, an editor chose the shorter version.'
questions.prompt: Which rewrite avoids turning the frequency comparison into an unsupported claim about editors as individuals?
options: Most recorded decisions favored the shorter version.
A majority of the editors chose the shorter version on every occasion.
Each editor chose the shorter version more often than the longer one.
The shorter version was preferred by the editor who made the most decisions.
questions.explanation: More often than not compares the frequency of decision outcomes; it does not distribute that majority pattern to each editor.
feedback: More often than not compares the frequency of decision outcomes; it does not distribute that majority pattern to each editor.
A majority of decisions need not come from a majority of editors, and every occasion adds consistency the summary does not claim.
The overall pattern does not establish a separate majority for every editor's decisions.
The aggregate frequency does not identify the most active editor or that editor's own preference.

questions.setup: A: 'The summary gives us an independent assessment.' B: 'It's no more an independent assessment than the press release it copies word for word.'
questions.prompt: Which reading of B's response is best supported?
options: B rates the two documents as independent assessments of equal quality.
B rejects the summary's independence by likening it to its source.
B grants the summary independence but regards the press release as more accurate.
B says the summary contains less assessment material because it is shorter.
questions.explanation: In this rebuttal, no more an ... than aligns the disputed category with a source whose claimed independence is being rejected.
feedback: The copied press release is invoked to challenge independence, not to endorse both as independent assessments.
In this rebuttal, no more an ... than aligns the disputed category with a source whose claimed independence is being rejected.
The response targets independence itself and makes no separate accuracy comparison.
The wording compares category membership and provenance, not the quantity of assessment material or document length.

questions.setup: A market report says, 'Demand rose by more than analysts had predicted it would fall.'
questions.prompt: Which comparison does the sentence make?
options: Actual demand exceeds the forecast level by exactly the forecast decrease.
The actual increase exceeds an increase that analysts had forecast.
The forecast decrease is larger than the gap between actual and forecast demand.
The actual increase exceeds the magnitude of the forecast decrease.
questions.explanation: By more than compares amounts of change, while rose and would fall assign those amounts opposite directions.
feedback: The sentence compares two changes, not the exact gap between an actual level and a forecast level.
The forecast direction is fall, so it was a decrease rather than a smaller increase.
No such gap comparison is stated; the actual upward change is compared with the anticipated downward change.
By more than compares amounts of change, while rose and would fall assign those amounts opposite directions.

questions.setup: A: 'The minority report admits that several dates remain uncertain.' B: 'It's none the weaker for acknowledging that.'
questions.prompt: Which assessment does B make about the acknowledgment?
options: The acknowledgment does not diminish the report's strength; B need not be claiming that it improves it.
The acknowledgment makes the minority report as strong as the majority report.
The acknowledgment proves that the disputed dates are accurate despite the uncertainty.
The acknowledgment necessarily strengthens the report by removing the original uncertainty.
questions.explanation: None the weaker for denies a weakening attributable to that acknowledgment. It allows unchanged or increased strength without asserting either alone.
feedback: None the weaker for denies a weakening attributable to that acknowledgment. It allows unchanged or increased strength without asserting either alone.
The comparison concerns the effect of acknowledging uncertainty, not parity with another report.
The reply evaluates argumentative strength; it does not settle the historical dates.
No loss does not entail an improvement, and acknowledging uncertainty does not remove it.

questions.setup: A selection note says, 'Chen is as well qualified as any applicant we actually interviewed.'
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the ranking while avoiding an extra uniqueness claim?
options: Chen is better qualified than every applicant, including those not interviewed.
Chen has the same qualifications as every applicant who was interviewed.
Among those interviewed, no applicant is better qualified than Chen; a tie is possible.
Chen is the uniquely best-qualified interviewee, though someone unexamined may be better.
questions.explanation: As well qualified as any places Chen at the top of the stated set without excluding equal qualifications.
feedback: The relative clause restricts the set to interviewees, and as ... as any does not require strict superiority.
Matching the top level does not require every interviewee to be equal, nor does degree equality mean identical qualifications.
As well qualified as any places Chen at the top of the stated set without excluding equal qualifications.
The external caveat is compatible with the set restriction, but uniquely adds a distinction the original does not establish.

questions.setup: A staffing note says, 'We need more experienced technicians.' The writer means that the current technicians need greater experience, not that the team needs additional members.
questions.prompt: Which revision removes that ambiguity without changing the intended staffing claim?
options: Our existing technicians need greater experience.
We need more technicians with substantial experience.
We need more of the experienced technicians already on the team.
We need the most experienced technicians on a larger team.
questions.explanation: Existing fixes the staff membership, while greater attaches the increase to experience rather than headcount.
feedback: Existing fixes the staff membership, while greater attaches the increase to experience rather than headcount.
This selects the headcount reading and requests additional staff.
More of still selects a greater number of people rather than a higher experience level in the current staff.
This adds a larger team and a highest-rank selection, neither of which is the intended development of the current staff.

questions.setup: A cost review says, 'The revised estimate exceeds the original by more than the original exceeded the budget.'
questions.prompt: Which relation is asserted?
options: The revised estimate is larger than the budget by the original overrun alone.
The revised estimate is more than twice the total original estimate.
The increase between estimates is larger than the original budget overrun.
The budget increase is larger than the increase between the two estimates.
questions.explanation: Each exceed defines a difference: revised minus original is compared with original minus budget.
feedback: The revised estimate includes a further increase that itself exceeds the original overrun; the gap is not merely the original overrun.
The comparison is between two differences, not between the full revised estimate and twice the full original amount.
Each exceed defines a difference: revised minus original is compared with original minus budget.
No increase in the budget is stated; the budget is the reference point for the earlier overrun.

questions.setup: A report says, 'Route A is twice as likely to be delayed as Route B.' An editor changes it to 'Route B is twice as unlikely to be delayed as Route A.'
questions.prompt: Why is the edit not a reliable preservation of the quantitative claim?
options: A reversal is impossible because twice as ... as can compare only physical quantities.
A ratio of delay probabilities does not give the same inverse ratio for their complements.
The first sentence compares expected delay duration, while the second compares delay frequency.
The edit is reliable whenever Route A has the higher delay probability.
questions.explanation: If delay probabilities are 40% and 20%, no-delay probabilities are 60% and 80%, not a two-to-one ratio. Likely and unlikely cannot simply exchange places in a numerical claim.
feedback: Twice as likely is an established way to express a probability ratio; the problem is complementing it.
If delay probabilities are 40% and 20%, no-delay probabilities are 60% and 80%, not a two-to-one ratio. Likely and unlikely cannot simply exchange places in a numerical claim.
The first already concerns the probability of a delay, not how long a delay lasts.
Having the higher probability sets an order, but it does not establish the required ratio for the complementary probabilities.

questions.setup: An observational summary says, 'The more support participants reported receiving, the less isolated they reported feeling.'
questions.prompt: Which rewrite preserves the paired comparison without strengthening it into a demonstrated cause?
options: Increasing support would reduce isolation by the same amount for each participant.
Higher reported support was associated with lower reported isolation.
Lower isolation led participants to obtain more support.
Participants who reported more support felt less isolated at every stage of the study.
questions.explanation: The paired comparatives describe an inverse pattern in reported measures; the observational wording does not itself demonstrate what an intervention would cause.
feedback: This adds a causal intervention, a fixed amount of effect, and a uniform individual response, none established by the paired reports.
The paired comparatives describe an inverse pattern in reported measures; the observational wording does not itself demonstrate what an intervention would cause.
This chooses a causal direction that the observed comparative pattern does not establish.
This distributes the relationship across every stage and shifts from reported feeling to an unqualified state.

questions.setup: A review says, 'Leila is at her most persuasive when she leaves the slides aside and answers questions.'
questions.prompt: Which comparison does the superlative make in this sentence?
options: It ranks Leila above the other speakers specifically during the question period.
It identifies the question period as the only situation in which Leila persuades anyone.
It compares Leila's persuasiveness across situations, not her rank among speakers.
It identifies slide-free answers as the most persuasive format for speakers generally.
questions.explanation: At her most persuasive locates the high point of her own persuasiveness under the stated circumstances.
feedback: Her most persuasive compares Leila's own performances or states; it does not supply an interpersonal ranking.
A personal maximum does not make all lower degrees ineffective.
At her most persuasive locates the high point of her own persuasiveness under the stated circumstances.
The personal possessive confines the judgment to Leila rather than generalizing it to all speakers.

questions.setup: In a three-way vote, Proposal A received 45 first preferences, B received 35, and C received 20. The summary says A received 'the most first preferences.'
questions.prompt: Which edit retains exactly that claim without converting a relative lead into a majority?
options: A received more first preferences than either rival separately.
A received more first preferences than the two rivals combined.
Most voters gave A their first preference.
A received first-preference support from more than half of the electorate.
questions.explanation: The most identifies the largest individual tally; it does not require more than half of all votes.
feedback: The most identifies the largest individual tally; it does not require more than half of all votes.
The rivals together received fifty-five, so a relative lead over each is not a lead over their combined support.
Most voters would mean a majority here, but forty-five of one hundred is below half.
The count establishes neither a majority of the voters nor a majority of the potentially larger electorate.

questions.setup: A: 'Half the catalogue entries name the wrong artist.' B: 'Then calling it less than perfect was rather generous.'
questions.prompt: How does B treat the phrase 'less than perfect' in this exchange?
options: As a precise estimate that nearly all entries are correct
As a comparative ranking of this catalogue below another named catalogue
As an understatement whose weak benchmark understates the seriousness of the faults
As a rejection of all useful content in the catalogue
questions.explanation: 'Less than perfect' literally excludes perfection; the extensive errors make that restrained description seem overly mild to B.
feedback: The phrase does not quantify correctness, and the exchange gives substantial errors rather than near-perfection.
Perfection is the benchmark; no second catalogue is named for comparison.
'Less than perfect' literally excludes perfection; the extensive errors make that restrained description seem overly mild to B.
Neither 'less than perfect' nor B's criticism establishes that every part lacks value.

questions.setup: A report says, 'North's reduction in waiting time was twice South's.' Both districts started from different waiting times.
questions.prompt: Which information would preserve the report's stated comparison without adding a common baseline?
options: North's final wait was twenty minutes and South's was ten.
North's original wait was twice South's original wait.
North's wait fell by twenty percent and South's by ten percent.
North reduced its wait by twenty minutes and South by ten.
questions.explanation: The sentence compares decreases, so twenty minutes versus ten preserves the ratio independently of starting levels.
feedback: Final waiting times do not identify either reduction when the initial times differ.
A ratio of starting levels does not determine the ratio of their reductions.
With different starting times, those percentages do not necessarily give a two-to-one ratio of time reductions.
The sentence compares decreases, so twenty minutes versus ten preserves the ratio independently of starting levels.

questions.setup: An editor writes, 'The unsigned account is scarcely less convincing than the signed one, although neither has been independently corroborated.'
questions.prompt: Which reading preserves the comparative degree and the evidential qualification?
options: The unsigned account is close to the signed one in persuasiveness; that does not establish either account's truth.
The unsigned account is substantially weaker, but independent checking has made both credible.
The accounts are exactly equal in persuasiveness because neither has corroboration.
The unsigned account is more convincing because a signature would imply a conflict of interest.
questions.explanation: Scarcely limits the lower degree to a small difference; the separate corroboration caveat prevents the persuasive comparison from becoming a truth claim.
feedback: Scarcely limits the lower degree to a small difference; the separate corroboration caveat prevents the persuasive comparison from becoming a truth claim.
Scarcely less indicates at most a small shortfall, and the sentence explicitly withholds independent corroboration.
Scarcely less does not require exact equality, and shared lack of corroboration does not establish equal persuasiveness.
Neither an advantage for the unsigned account nor a conflict created by a signature is stated.

questions.setup: A: 'The reporting rules allow that omission.' B: 'Then so much the worse for the reporting rules.'
questions.prompt: What does B's response most naturally imply?
options: The rules have recently changed and now permit more omissions than before.
The rules' allowance becomes a reason to judge the rules adversely, rather than to excuse the omission.
The omission is worse when a rule expressly forbids it than when the rule permits it.
The omission must be excused because the rules are comparatively less important.
questions.explanation: So much the worse for X directs adverse judgment toward X because of the fact just presented.
feedback: The response does not describe a change over time; it evaluates the rules in light of their allowance.
So much the worse for X directs adverse judgment toward X because of the fact just presented.
B does not compare two regulatory conditions; B turns the supposed defense into criticism of the rules.
The expression rejects the rules' adequacy as a defense rather than accepting that defense.

questions.setup: A review says, 'The proposal deserves attention, not least because it addresses the maintenance costs that earlier plans ignored.'
questions.prompt: What role does 'not least' assign to the following reason?
options: It ranks maintenance costs below every other reason for considering the proposal.
It identifies maintenance costs as the sole reason that justifies attention.
It marks that reason as especially important without claiming it is the only reason.
It withdraws the maintenance argument while preserving the other reasons.
questions.explanation: 'Not least' uses a negated lowest-rank expression to give the named reason prominence among possible reasons.
feedback: The phrase gives this reason emphasis rather than placing it at the bottom.
'Not least' highlights a reason without excluding others.
'Not least' uses a negated lowest-rank expression to give the named reason prominence among possible reasons.
The negation does not reject the reason; it denies that the reason should be treated as insignificant.

questions.setup: A panel has not finalized all rankings. Its chair says, 'Even on the most favorable reading of these scores, this design is at best second.'
questions.prompt: Which conclusion preserves the limit without claiming a final exact rank?
options: The design is definitively ranked second, with first place already allocated.
The design is guaranteed at least second place, with first still possible.
The design ranks second under every reasonable reading of the scores.
Second is the best attainable rank; a lower placing remains possible.
questions.explanation: At best second places second as the most favorable attainable rank under the stated scoring interpretation.
feedback: At best supplies an upper limit on its position, not a finalized exact ranking or a named winner.
That treats second as a lower bound on performance; at best makes it the upper bound.
The chair identifies the favorable limit, not an invariant rank across interpretations.
At best second places second as the most favorable attainable rank under the stated scoring interpretation.

questions.setup: A summary says, 'Each team chose a venue more expensive than it had budgeted for.' The teams had different budgets.
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the individual comparison standards?
options: Every chosen venue cost more than the highest of the teams' budgets.
The team with the highest budget chose the most expensive venue.
Every team exceeded the same budget by a different amount.
Every team exceeded its own venue budget; the sentence does not rank the teams' venue prices.
questions.explanation: Each binds it to the relevant team, so the comparative baseline varies from one team to another.
feedback: Each venue is compared with its own team's budget, not the maximum budget across teams.
The per-team overruns establish no ordering of actual venue prices across teams.
The budgets explicitly differ, and the sentence does not establish whether overrun amounts differ.
Each binds it to the relevant team, so the comparative baseline varies from one team to another.

questions.setup: A: 'Did the host help with the access arrangements?' B: 'She couldn't have been more helpful. She checked every entrance with us.'
questions.prompt: Which reading of B's comparative construction is supported by the exchange?
options: B says the host wanted to help but practical constraints prevented useful action.
B says another host would probably have provided greater assistance.
B says the host was forbidden to provide any additional help.
B presents the host's actual helpfulness as effectively maximal.
questions.explanation: In this appreciative reply, the impossibility of a higher degree is rhetorical praise for the assistance actually provided.
feedback: The completed assistance and emphatic comparison praise what she did; they do not describe unsuccessful intentions.
The expression does not compare her with a hypothetical better host; it presents her assistance as exceptionally high.
Couldn't have been more helpful is evaluative here, not a statement of an external prohibition.
In this appreciative reply, the impossibility of a higher degree is rhetorical praise for the assistance actually provided.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If it rains tomorrow, I will ___ at home.
options: stay
staying
stays
to stay
questions.explanation: Will takes the base form stay to describe the plan for tomorrow.
feedback: Will takes the base form stay to describe the plan for tomorrow.
After will, use stay, not the -ing form.
Do not add -s to a verb after will.
Will is followed directly by stay, without to.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: You can sit here if the seat ___ free.
options: is
be
are
am
questions.explanation: The seat is singular, so the condition uses is free.
feedback: The seat is singular, so the condition uses is free.
The seat needs a present-tense verb; use is, not be.
Are goes with plural subjects or you, not the seat.
Am goes with I, not the seat.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If you need help, ___ me.
options: calls
calling
call
to call
questions.explanation: Call is the base verb used to give the instruction after the condition.
feedback: A direct instruction uses call, without -s.
Calling alone cannot give this instruction.
Call is the base verb used to give the instruction after the condition.
An instruction begins with call, not to call.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the message.
questions.prompt: 'If you are hungry, there is bread in the kitchen.' When is the bread useful to you?
options: When you want food.
When you want sleep.
When you want directions.
When you want a shower.
questions.explanation: Hungry means wanting food; the speaker tells you where to find some.
feedback: Hungry means wanting food; the speaker tells you where to find some.
Wanting sleep means being tired, not hungry.
The message offers food, not help finding a place.
A shower is for washing; hungry describes needing food.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If the bus is late, we ___ walk to work.
options: can to
cans
are can
can
questions.explanation: Can walk gives an available choice when the bus is late.
feedback: Can takes walk directly, without to.
Can does not take an -s ending.
Do not put are before can; can is already the helping verb.
Can walk gives an available choice when the bus is late.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If you ___ cold, close the window.
options: is
am
be
are
questions.explanation: You takes are: if you are cold.
feedback: Is does not agree with you.
Am belongs with I, not you.
Use are as the present-tense verb after you.
You takes are: if you are cold.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If the shop is closed, ___ wait outside.
options: not
doesn't
don't
no
questions.explanation: Don't wait is the negative instruction for the situation in the if-clause.
feedback: A negative instruction needs don't before wait.
Doesn't describes a third-person action; it does not form this instruction.
Don't wait is the negative instruction for the situation in the if-clause.
No cannot directly make wait into a negative instruction.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of the condition in this invitation.
questions.prompt: 'If you are free tonight, come for dinner.'
options: Because you are free
When you are not busy
On the days you work
After you eat dinner
questions.explanation: Here being free means not being busy; the invitation depends on that.
feedback: Because gives a reason and treats being free as a fact; if leaves it open.
Here being free means not being busy; the invitation depends on that.
Working is not the condition in this invitation.
Tonight is the time, but eating dinner first is not the condition.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If my phone ___, please answer it.
options: ring
ringing
to ring
rings
questions.explanation: My phone takes rings in this present-tense condition.
feedback: My phone is singular, so add -s in the present simple.
Ringing needs a helping verb; it cannot stand here alone.
To ring is not a complete verb for the subject my phone.
My phone takes rings in this present-tense condition.

questions.setup: Choose the reply that follows the instruction.
questions.prompt: 'If the bag is heavy, ask me for help.' The bag is heavy. What do you say?
options: Where did you buy it?
Is the bag new?
Can you help me?
What color is it?
questions.explanation: The instruction says to ask for help when the bag is heavy.
feedback: Asking where the bag came from does not request help carrying it.
The bag's age is not the condition given.
The instruction says to ask for help when the bag is heavy.
Asking about color does not follow the instruction to request help.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: Take this umbrella if you ___ one.
options: needs
needing
need
to need
questions.explanation: You need completes the condition; one refers to an umbrella.
feedback: After you, the present-simple verb is need, without -s.
Needing alone does not complete the condition.
You need completes the condition; one refers to an umbrella.
To need cannot serve as the complete verb after you.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning that matches the message.
questions.prompt: 'If the light is green, you can enter.' The light is green. What does the message say?
options: You must leave now.
You can turn off the light.
You must wait outside.
You can go in.
questions.explanation: The green-light condition is true, so the message permits entry.
feedback: Enter means go in, not leave.
The message gives permission to enter, not to use the light switch.
Waiting outside does not match the permission to enter when the light is green.
The green-light condition is true, so the message permits entry.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If there ___ two cups, we can have tea together.
options: are
have
am
be
questions.explanation: There are introduces more than one cup.
feedback: There are introduces more than one cup.
There have does not introduce the existence of the cups; use there are.
Am can follow I, not there with two cups.
This condition needs the present-tense form are, not be.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: I'll make coffee if you ___ tea.
options: doesn't want
not want
don't wants
don't want
questions.explanation: You don't want uses don't plus the base verb to make a negative condition.
feedback: With you, use don't, not doesn't.
Add don't before want to form this negative present-tense clause.
After don't, use want without -s.
You don't want uses don't plus the base verb to make a negative condition.

questions.setup: Choose the instruction that matches the situation.
questions.prompt: 'If you are tired, sit down. If you are thirsty, have some water.' You are thirsty.
options: Sit down.
Have some water.
Open the door.
Turn on the light.
questions.explanation: Thirsty means needing a drink, so the water instruction applies.
feedback: Sitting down is the instruction for being tired, not thirsty.
Thirsty means needing a drink, so the water instruction applies.
Opening the door is not an instruction in this message.
The message gives no instruction about a light.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion.
questions.prompt: If Sam ___ at work, call his home number.
options: isn't
not is
doesn't is
aren't
questions.explanation: Isn't means is not and agrees with the singular subject Sam.
feedback: Isn't means is not and agrees with the singular subject Sam.
Put not after is: is not, or isn't.
Do not use doesn't with is; negate is directly.

questions.setup: Choose the words that give the condition.
