questions.prompt: The trip was cancelled. If we'd gone, we ___ through the mountains at noon yesterday.
options: would have driven
would have finished driving
would have started driving
would have been driving
questions.explanation: Would have been driving places an imagined ongoing activity at noon yesterday.
feedback: The simple form presents the drive as an event, without the requested focus on it being in progress at noon.
This places the end of the driving at noon instead of presenting the activity as ongoing then.
This locates the start at noon rather than viewing the drive as already in progress.
Would have been driving places an imagined ongoing activity at noon yesterday.

questions.setup: Choose the completion meaning that somebody should have inspected the bridge before the accident.
questions.prompt: If the bridge ___ earlier, the weakness might have been discovered in time.
options: had inspected
has been inspecting
had been inspecting
had been inspected
questions.explanation: Had been inspected is past-perfect passive: an earlier inspection of the bridge is imagined.
feedback: Had inspected makes the bridge the inspector, not the object of inspection.
Has been inspecting is active and present perfect, so it gives the bridge an ongoing inspecting role.
Had been inspecting is also active; it describes the bridge performing an inspection.
Had been inspected is past-perfect passive: an earlier inspection of the bridge is imagined.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that describes a condition fulfilled before a future result.
questions.prompt: If you ___ the safety course by Friday, you can start on Monday.
options: are completing
have completed
were completing
had been completing
questions.explanation: Have completed can mark completion by a future deadline inside an if-clause.
feedback: Are completing presents work in progress and does not establish completion by Friday.
Have completed can mark completion by a future deadline inside an if-clause.
Were completing presents past or remote ongoing work, not the required completed future prerequisite.
Had been completing describes an earlier ongoing process rather than completion by the specified deadline.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence with the same counterfactual meaning.
questions.prompt: 'But for your warning, I would have signed the wrong document.'
options: Because you warned me, I signed the wrong document.
Even if you had warned me, I would have signed the wrong document.
Unless you had stayed silent, I would have signed the wrong document.
If you hadn't warned me, I would have signed the wrong document.
questions.explanation: But for your warning means without that warning; the if-clause makes the absent-warning alternative explicit.
feedback: This makes the warning cause the mistake, reversing its protective role.
Even if says the warning would not have prevented the mistake.
Unless you had stayed silent applies when there was a warning, reversing the original condition.
But for your warning means without that warning; the if-clause makes the absent-warning alternative explicit.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that presents an unexpected possible need, not a past need or an obligation.
questions.prompt: If you ___ need an extra room during next month's conference, contact reception.
options: did
must
used to
should
questions.explanation: Should in this if-clause means if the need happens to arise.
feedback: Did adds emphasis to a past-form need; it does not itself mark the tentative future contingency requested.
Must introduces necessity or an inference, not a tentative unexpected possibility.
Used to refers to a former recurring need, not an unexpected need at next month's conference.
Should in this if-clause means if the need happens to arise.

questions.setup: Choose the connector that explicitly states a condition of the agreement.
questions.prompt: We will extend the lease ___ the owner repairs the heating before winter.
options: provided that
even though
so that
in case
questions.explanation: Provided that makes the owner's repair a condition of the agreement to extend.
feedback: Provided that makes the owner's repair a condition of the agreement to extend.
Even though introduces a concession, not the requested condition on extending the lease.
So that presents the repair as the purpose of extension rather than a condition of agreement.
In case presents preparation for a possible repair, not a repair requirement.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that matches the sentence.
questions.prompt: 'Even if we had left an hour earlier, we would still have missed the connection because the road was closed.'
options: An earlier departure would have guaranteed the connection.
The speakers actually left an hour earlier.
An earlier departure would not have solved the connection problem.
The road closed because the speakers left early.
questions.explanation: Even if and still show that the result persists under the imagined earlier departure.
feedback: The sentence explicitly says the connection would still have been missed.
Had left here imagines an alternative; it does not report an actual early departure.
Even if and still show that the result persists under the imagined earlier departure.
The road closure explains the missed connection, not a consequence of the speakers' departure.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that describes preparation for a possible problem.
questions.prompt: Before the interview, I printed a copy of my application ___ the interviewer needed one.
options: only if
unless
in case
even though
questions.explanation: In case shows that printing was a precaution against a possible later need.
feedback: Only if makes printing depend on a known need, rather than preparation before the interview.
Unless reverses the relationship, suggesting printing except when a copy was needed.
In case shows that printing was a precaution against a possible later need.
Even though treats the need as a fact in a concession, rather than an uncertain possibility.

questions.setup: Choose the completion emphasizing that the journey will be finished by a future deadline.
questions.prompt: If traffic stays light, we ___ the border by noon tomorrow.
options: had reached
will have reached
will be approaching
would have reached
questions.explanation: Will have reached presents arrival as completed by the specified future time.
feedback: Had reached puts completion before a past point, not tomorrow's noon deadline.
Will have reached presents arrival as completed by the specified future time.
Approaching presents travel towards the border, not arrival completed by the deadline.
This presents completion under a remote or unreal scenario rather than the open future prediction introduced by if traffic stays light.

questions.setup: Choose the completion preserving a possible action that was not taken last night.
questions.prompt: I didn't know you were stranded. If you'd called, I ___ you up, but you chose to walk.
options: have picked
will pick
could have picked
am picking
questions.explanation: Could have picked presents a missed opportunity or available help in the unreal past situation.
feedback: Have picked reports an actual completed pickup, contrary to the account.
Will pick concerns a future pickup, not the missed opportunity last night.
Could have picked presents a missed opportunity or available help in the unreal past situation.
Am picking describes an ongoing or arranged pickup, not the past alternative.

questions.setup: Choose the completion referring to support that exists now.
questions.prompt: My colleague covers my afternoon shifts. If it weren't for her help, I ___ attend this course.
options: wouldn't have been able to
haven't been able to
am not able to
wouldn't be able to
questions.explanation: Wouldn't be able to expresses the imagined present consequence of removing existing support.
feedback: The perfect form places the imagined inability in a completed past period rather than the current situation requested.
Haven't been able to reports actual inability, not the imagined alternative to current support.
This reports actual present inability rather than imagining the loss of ability if support were absent.
Wouldn't be able to expresses the imagined present consequence of removing existing support.

questions.setup: Choose the statement guaranteed by the rule, without adding an extra promise.
questions.prompt: 'We will consider an application only if both references arrive.'
options: Both references arriving guarantees acceptance.
An application without both references will not be considered.
Sending the application guarantees that references will arrive.
Both references arriving guarantees immediate consideration.
questions.explanation: Only if makes both references necessary; without them, consideration is ruled out.
feedback: Consideration is not acceptance, and the rule does not guarantee either outcome when references arrive.
Only if makes both references necessary; without them, consideration is ruled out.
The rule says nothing about whether sending an application causes references to arrive.
A necessary condition is not a promise of immediate action once it is met.

questions.setup: Choose the completion preserving both the unreal past decision and its present consequence.
questions.prompt: We rejected the merger in June and remain independent. ___ it, we would now be part of a larger group.
options: Had we approved
Should we approve
Were we to approve
If we approve
questions.explanation: Had we approved means if we had approved; the inverted past condition can have a present result.
feedback: Had we approved means if we had approved; the inverted past condition can have a present result.
Should we approve introduces an open future contingency, not the rejected June decision.
Were we to approve imagines a prospective decision, not an alternative to June's completed decision.
If we approve leaves approval open and prospective, contrary to the fixed past decision.

questions.setup: Choose the formal rewrite that preserves the hypothetical meaning.
questions.prompt: 'If the supplier were to withdraw, we would need another source.'
options: Had the supplier withdrawn, we would have needed another source.
Since the supplier is withdrawing, we need another source.
Should the supplier have withdrawn, we need another source now.
Were the supplier to withdraw, we would need another source.
questions.explanation: Were + subject + to-infinitive is a formal inverted version of the original future hypothesis.
feedback: This changes a prospective withdrawal into an unreal completed past event.
Since asserts withdrawal as a fact and removes the hypothetical condition.
This asks about a possibly completed withdrawal and introduces a present need instead.
Were + subject + to-infinitive is a formal inverted version of the original future hypothesis.

questions.setup: Choose the formal inverted condition for a possible future failure to agree.
questions.prompt: ___ a settlement, the mediation service will offer a second session.
options: Had the parties not reached
Should the parties not reach
Were the parties not reaching
If the parties should not reach
questions.explanation: Should + subject + not + base verb gives a formal future contingency with the negative after the subject.
feedback: Had ... not reached describes a past condition, not the future contingency requested.
Should + subject + not + base verb gives a formal future contingency with the negative after the subject.
Were ... not reaching presents a hypothetical ongoing process rather than a failure to reach agreement at the next stage.
This has the intended contingency meaning, but it retains if and is not an inverted condition.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that explains 'will' in the if-clause.
questions.prompt: 'If the technicians will share their notes, we can avoid repeating the tests.' The technicians have so far refused to share them.
options: If sharing has already finished, repetition can be avoided.
If the technicians are required to share their notes, repetition can be avoided.
If the technicians used to share their notes, repetition can be avoided.
If the technicians are willing to share their notes, repetition can be avoided.
questions.explanation: 'Will' expresses willingness in this context; the issue is cooperation after a refusal.
feedback: 'Will share' does not mark an already completed action.
The conditional asks for willingness, not an externally imposed duty.
'Will' here does not describe an old habit; the refusal concerns current cooperation.
'Will' expresses willingness in this context; the issue is cooperation after a refusal.

questions.setup: Choose the reading of "won't" supported by the context.
questions.prompt: The witness is able to answer but refuses. 'If she won't answer voluntarily, we'll end the interview for today.'
options: She is physically unable to speak.
She remains unwilling to answer.
She has already answered in writing.
She was not expected to attend.
questions.explanation: "Won't" can express refusal; here the condition concerns unwillingness, not mere future time.
feedback: The context explicitly states that she can answer; inability is not the problem.
"Won't" can express refusal; here the condition concerns unwillingness, not mere future time.
No written answer is reported, and the refusal remains active.
The condition concerns answering during the interview, not expectations about attendance.

questions.setup: Choose the function of the conditional in this exchange.
questions.prompt: An interviewer says, 'If you would take a seat, we can begin.'
options: Predicting where the visitor will sit tomorrow.
Politely requesting an immediate action.
Imagining that the visitor had sat down earlier.
Reporting a rule about habitual seating.
questions.explanation: If you would softens a request for cooperation before the interview begins.
feedback: The invitation is immediate; would is not a prediction about tomorrow.
If you would softens a request for cooperation before the interview begins.
There is no perfect form or past context indicating an earlier missed action.
The utterance addresses this visitor now, not a repeated seating rule.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that fits the information offer.
questions.prompt: 'If you're looking for somewhere quiet, there's a reading room upstairs.' The room is open all day.
options: The listener's needs make the information relevant.
The room will become available when the listener asks for it.
The listener has already requested a quiet room.
The speaker is uncertain whether the upstairs room is quiet.
questions.explanation: The if-clause limits when the information is useful to the listener rather than when the room exists.
feedback: The if-clause limits when the information is useful to the listener rather than when the room exists.
The room is already open; the if-clause does not make availability depend on a request.
If leaves the listener's need open rather than reporting an actual request.
The uncertainty concerns the listener's needs; the speaker presents the room as a suitable suggestion.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that refers to the failure of the first possibility.
questions.prompt: The archive may already hold the original. If so, request a scan; ___, contact the donor.
options: if ever
if anything
if not
if only
questions.explanation: If not stands for if the archive does not already hold the original.
feedback: If ever concerns occurrence at any time; it does not negate the preceding possibility here.
If anything introduces a correction or stronger alternative, not the missing-original condition.
If not stands for if the archive does not already hold the original.
If only usually introduces a wish or a restrictive idea; it does not supply this negative reference.

questions.setup: Choose the conclusion warranted by this exception rule alone.
questions.prompt: 'The hearing will proceed unless the chair adjourns it.' The chair's decision is still unknown.
options: The hearing will proceed whether the chair adjourns it or not.
The chair is expected to adjourn the hearing.
The hearing has already been adjourned.
If the chair does not adjourn it, the hearing will proceed.
questions.explanation: The rule guarantees proceeding in the absence of the specified exception.
feedback: This removes the stated exception involving adjournment.
Unless introduces an exception without forecasting whether it will occur.
The chair's decision is unknown; the rule reports no completed adjournment.
The rule guarantees proceeding in the absence of the specified exception.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence in formal written English.
questions.prompt: Place the necessary condition first for emphasis.
options: Only if the board agrees the director may sign.
Only if the board agrees may the director sign.
Only if agrees the board may the director sign.
Only if the board agrees may sign the director.
questions.explanation: The if-clause keeps normal order, while the main clause inverts may and the director.
feedback: Fronted only if requires inversion in the main clause: may the director sign.
The if-clause keeps normal order, while the main clause inverts may and the director.
The conditional clause needs subject before verb: the board agrees.
The main-clause subject belongs after may and before sign.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that commits to publication in both possible voting outcomes.
questions.prompt: We will publish the minority report ___ the committee approves it or not.
options: unless
provided
whether
only if
questions.explanation: Whether ... or not explicitly covers approval and non-approval.
feedback: Unless would set an exception and does not form the intended two-alternative construction here.
Provided would impose approval as a condition and needs a different construction.
Whether ... or not explicitly covers approval and non-approval.
Only if makes approval necessary, contradicting publication in both outcomes.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the opening phrase.
questions.prompt: 'Supposing the figures were accurate, how would that affect your recommendation?' The analyst has not verified them.
options: The speaker certifies that the figures are accurate.
The speaker reports that the figures used to be accurate.
The speaker asks the analyst to reason from a temporary assumption.
The speaker requires the analyst to change the figures.
questions.explanation: Supposing invites consideration of a premise without verifying or endorsing it.
feedback: The question leaves accuracy unverified rather than certifying it.
Were marks the hypothetical assumption here; it need not describe a past state.
Supposing invites consideration of a premise without verifying or endorsing it.
The requested action is reasoning about a recommendation, not altering data.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'were to' in this scenario exercise.
questions.prompt: 'If the network were to fail during the presentation, how would you continue?'
options: The network failed during an earlier presentation.
The network is currently failing.
A prospective failure is being imagined for planning purposes.
The network is required to fail before the presentation.
questions.explanation: 'Were to' presents a possible future event with hypothetical distance so that a response can be planned.
feedback: 'Were to fail' here is prospective, not a report of an earlier failure.
The question sets up a scenario rather than reporting an ongoing outage.
'Were to' presents a possible future event with hypothetical distance so that a response can be planned.
The construction describes a hypothetical event, not an obligation for the network.

questions.setup: Choose the connector that leaves approval unsettled and makes it a condition for release.
questions.prompt: Approval is still pending. The dataset can be released ___ the review panel authorizes it.
options: given that
now that
provided that
seeing that
questions.explanation: Provided that leaves authorization open and makes release conditional on it.
feedback: Given that treats authorization as an accepted premise, contrary to its pending status.
Now that presents authorization as a newly established fact.
Provided that leaves authorization open and makes release conditional on it.
Seeing that supplies an accepted reason rather than an unresolved condition.

questions.setup: Choose the formal rewrite with the same past counterfactual meaning.
questions.prompt: 'Without the emergency grant, the theatre would have closed last winter.'
options: Were it not for the emergency grant, the theatre would close next winter.
Had it not been for the emergency grant, the theatre would have closed last winter.
Should the emergency grant arrive, the theatre will remain open.
Had the theatre closed, the emergency grant would have arrived.
questions.explanation: Had it not been for expands without into a formal inverted condition about missing past support.
feedback: This shifts the condition and closure to a present/future hypothesis.
Had it not been for expands without into a formal inverted condition about missing past support.
This treats the grant as a future possibility rather than support that prevented a past closure.
This reverses the dependency, making closure a condition for the grant.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that acknowledges a possible loss without asserting that it has occurred.
questions.prompt: The result is not yet known. ___ we lose the contract, we will continue the research.
options: Even if
Even though
Now that
Given that
questions.explanation: Even if treats losing as an unconfirmed possibility that will not change the research plan.
feedback: Even if treats losing as an unconfirmed possibility that will not change the research plan.
Even though normally treats the loss as a conceded fact, which the prompt does not establish.
Now that presents the loss as an established new circumstance.
Given that adopts the loss as an accepted premise rather than leaving it unsettled.

questions.setup: Choose the function of the if-clause.
questions.prompt: 'If I remember correctly, the lease expires in November.'
options: It qualifies the reliability of the speaker's claim.
It postpones giving the date until the speaker has checked the lease.
It asks the listener to confirm the date before the speaker gives it.
It signals that the lease contains two possible expiry dates.
questions.explanation: The clause signals that the assertion depends on the accuracy of the speaker's memory.
feedback: The clause signals that the assertion depends on the accuracy of the speaker's memory.
The speaker gives November immediately, while qualifying confidence in that information.
The phrase limits the speaker's confidence; it does not explicitly request prior confirmation.
The uncertainty belongs to the speaker's memory, not to the lease's contractual provisions.

questions.setup: Choose the explanation of 'will' in the if-clause.
questions.prompt: 'I'll redraw the chart if it will make the results easier to compare.'
options: The redraw depends on the listener's willingness to compare the results.
The speaker promises to redraw it before assessing whether that will help.
The comparison has already become easier.
The anticipated benefit is the condition for deciding to redraw it.
questions.explanation: The speaker bases the decision to act on the expected usefulness of that action.
feedback: The clause concerns the redraw's expected effect, not another person's willingness to cooperate.
The expected benefit determines whether to redraw; the promise is conditional rather than unconditional.
'Will make' points to a prospective effect, not a completed improvement.
The speaker bases the decision to act on the expected usefulness of that action.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that preserves uncertainty about what happened yesterday.
questions.prompt: The engineer has not yet established whether the valve was closed. She wants to state a consequence conditional on it having been closed.
options: If the valve was closed, the leak should have stopped.
If the valve had been closed, the leak would have stopped, but it wasn't.
Since the valve was closed, the leak must have stopped.
The valve was closed, so the leak stopped.
questions.explanation: The open past if-clause leaves closure undecided; should have states its expected consequence.
feedback: The open past if-clause leaves closure undecided; should have states its expected consequence.
But it wasn't explicitly denies closure and removes the required uncertainty.
Since accepts closure as fact rather than leaving it to be established.
This asserts both closure and stopping as actual events.

questions.setup: Choose the completion that describes the ongoing consequence now of an unreal past action.
questions.prompt: We ignored the early complaints, so the dispute is still consuming our time. If we'd responded then, we ___ with it now.
options: wouldn't have dealt
hadn't dealt
haven't dealt
wouldn't be dealing
questions.explanation: Wouldn't be dealing gives an imagined ongoing present result of responding differently in the past.
feedback: The perfect simple presents a completed past response rather than an activity continuing now.
Hadn't dealt describes an earlier past situation, not a modal consequence now.
Haven't dealt asserts actual non-action, conflicting with the ongoing dispute and hypothetical result.
Wouldn't be dealing gives an imagined ongoing present result of responding differently in the past.

questions.setup: Choose what the conditional itself establishes about whether the memo was read.
questions.prompt: 'If the auditors had read the memo, they would have raised precisely the objection we see in their report. We still need to check whether they received it.'
options: It establishes that the auditors did not read the memo.
It establishes that the auditors received but ignored the memo.
It establishes that reading the memo was the only possible source of the objection.
It leaves reading unresolved while assessing its expected consequence.
questions.explanation: The speaker considers what reading would lead to without resolving whether reading occurred.
feedback: A past-perfect conditional often suggests a contrary-to-fact premise, but this context explicitly leaves reading unresolved.
Receipt and neglect are not established; the next sentence calls for checking receipt.
An expected consequence does not establish that its proposed cause was the only possible cause.
The speaker considers what reading would lead to without resolving whether reading occurred.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the exception and its negation exactly.
questions.prompt: 'The permit remains valid unless the holder fails to renew the insurance.'
options: If the holder fails to renew the insurance, the permit remains valid.
If the holder does not fail to renew the insurance, the permit remains valid.
The permit remains valid only if the holder fails to renew the insurance.
Unless the holder renews the insurance, the permit remains valid.
questions.explanation: Unless negates the whole exception, including fails: in the absence of failure to renew, validity continues.
feedback: This turns the stated exception into a condition guaranteeing continued validity.
Unless negates the whole exception, including fails: in the absence of failure to renew, validity continues.
Only if makes failure necessary for validity, reversing the original protection.
This makes renewal, rather than failure to renew, the exception.

questions.setup: Choose the rule that makes approval both necessary and sufficient for release.
questions.prompt: The editor wants to state two commitments: without approval there is no release, and approval guarantees release.
options: The report will be released if approval is granted.
The report will be released if and only if approval is granted.
The report will be released only if approval is granted.
The report may be released if approval is granted.
questions.explanation: If and only if states both directions: approval is required and is enough for release.
feedback: If grants the approval-to-release direction but does not rule out release by another route.
If and only if states both directions: approval is required and is enough for release.
Only if makes approval necessary but does not promise release when approval is granted.
May gives a possibility even after approval, not the requested guarantee.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation supported by the reply.
questions.prompt: 'Would you endorse the plan?' 'Not if it involves compulsory overtime.'
options: Removing compulsory overtime guarantees the speaker's endorsement.
The speaker asserts that the plan already involves compulsory overtime.
Compulsory overtime would rule out the speaker's endorsement.
The speaker endorses compulsory overtime but questions the rest of the plan.
questions.explanation: Not if supplies a condition under which the answer to endorsing is no.
feedback: Ruling out one condition for refusal does not guarantee endorsement for other reasons.
The reply identifies a possible disqualifier without asserting that it is present.
Not if supplies a condition under which the answer to endorsing is no.
The specified objection is to compulsory overtime; no endorsement of it is expressed.

questions.setup: Choose the function of 'if anything' in this response.
questions.prompt: 'The revisions have made the policy harsher.' 'If anything, they've made it more flexible.'
options: The speaker remains neutral between the two assessments.
The speaker cautiously proposes the opposite assessment.
Flexibility depends on whether any revision exists.
The speaker agrees that harshness and flexibility increased equally.
questions.explanation: 'If anything' introduces a tentative correction in the opposite direction: more flexible rather than harsher.
feedback: The hedge is cautious, but the speaker does favor the opposite assessment, more flexible.
'If anything' introduces a tentative correction in the opposite direction: more flexible rather than harsher.
This is an idiomatic corrective phrase, not an ordinary event condition.
The reply challenges the first assessment; it does not endorse both equally.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that unambiguously expresses the intended modest claim.
questions.prompt: The writer means 'The study is useful, but I am not claiming it is indispensable.' The draft says, 'The study is useful, if not indispensable.'
options: The study is useful, though not necessarily indispensable.
The study is indispensable, if not useful.
If the study is indispensable, it is useful.
The study is useful only if it is indispensable.
questions.explanation: Though not necessarily explicitly withholds the stronger claim and avoids the draft's possible 'perhaps even' reading.
feedback: Though not necessarily explicitly withholds the stronger claim and avoids the draft's possible 'perhaps even' reading.
This promotes indispensable to the asserted description, stronger than intended.
This makes usefulness conditional on indispensability rather than asserting usefulness directly.
Only if makes indispensability necessary for usefulness, which the intended modest claim does not require.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that expresses regret about the past, without making a rule about evidence.
questions.prompt: The curator trusted an unreliable account and now wishes she had checked it.
options: Only if I had checked the account would I have trusted it.
If I check the account, I can decide whether to trust it.
If only I had checked the account before trusting it.
If only I check the account, the decision is mine.
questions.explanation: If only plus past perfect expresses a wish that a completed past choice had been different.
feedback: Only if states a necessary condition for trusting; it does not express the curator's regret.
This sets up a current or future checking condition rather than wishing the past were different.
If only plus past perfect expresses a wish that a completed past choice had been different.
Here only restricts the subject I; it does not form the intended past regret.

questions.setup: Choose the statement licensed by the rule without deciding whether the exception occurs.
questions.prompt: 'The files will be opened to researchers unless both the donor objects and the committee upholds the objection.'
options: If either the donor objects or the committee objects, the files must stay closed.
The donor's objection alone prevents the files from being opened.
The committee has already upheld the donor's objection.
If the donor objects but the committee rejects the objection, the files will be opened.
questions.explanation: The exception requires both stated events; rejection by the committee means that combined exception is absent.
feedback: This substitutes either/or for the rule's both/and and changes the committee's action.
The donor's objection alone does not meet the two-part exception.
The rule sets a future condition; it reports no completed committee decision.
The exception requires both stated events; rejection by the committee means that combined exception is absent.

questions.setup: Choose the distinction accurately made by the two versions.
questions.prompt: A: 'Even if the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.' B: 'Even though the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.'
options: A leaves the mistake open; B presents it as a conceded fact.
A asserts the mistake more firmly than B does.
B makes the timestamps depend on the witness being correct.
A and B both deny that the timestamps establish the sequence.
questions.explanation: The difference is factual commitment to the concession, while the claim about the timestamps remains.
feedback: The difference is factual commitment to the concession, while the claim about the timestamps remains.
Even if does not itself assert the mistake; even though normally concedes it as fact.
B says the timestamps establish the sequence despite the mistake, not because the witness is correct.
Both versions assert the evidential role of the timestamps.

questions.setup: Choose the equivalent condition for withholding access.
questions.prompt: 'If either the identity check or the payment check is incomplete, access must be withheld.'
options: Access must be withheld only when both checks are incomplete.
If the two checks are not both complete, access must be withheld.
If either check is complete, access must be withheld.
If neither check is incomplete, access must be withheld.
questions.explanation: Not both complete covers either incomplete check or both incomplete checks, preserving the original trigger.
feedback: The original triggers withholding when even one check is incomplete, not only when both are.
Not both complete covers either incomplete check or both incomplete checks, preserving the original trigger.
A complete check is not itself the reason for withholding; the other check's status matters.
Neither incomplete means both complete, reversing the triggering condition.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that makes only the appendix, not the main report, depend on consent.
questions.prompt: The main report will be published regardless. The appendix will be included only with the interviewees' consent.
options: If the interviewees consent, we will publish both the report and the appendix; otherwise neither will appear.
We will publish the report only if the interviewees consent, and we may include the appendix.
If we publish the report, the interviewees will consent to the appendix.
We will publish the report; we will include the appendix only if the interviewees consent.
questions.explanation: Separate clauses keep the report unconditional and attach the consent requirement specifically to the appendix.
feedback: This makes the main report conditional too, contrary to its unconditional publication.
This attaches consent to the report and leaves the appendix without the intended restriction.
This reverses the dependency and predicts consent from publication.
Separate clauses keep the report unconditional and attach the consent requirement specifically to the appendix.

questions.setup: Choose the formal sentence preserving a present absence and a current hypothetical result.
questions.prompt: There is no independent audit. With one, we could place greater confidence in the figures now.
options: Were there an independent audit, we could place greater confidence in the figures now.
Had there been an independent audit last year, we could have trusted last year's figures.
Should an independent audit arrive next year, we will trust the figures then.
Since there is an independent audit, we can place greater confidence in the figures now.
questions.explanation: Were there imagines reversing the present absence; could preserves a current hypothetical possibility.
feedback: Were there imagines reversing the present absence; could preserves a current hypothetical possibility.
This moves both the condition and the trust judgment to last year.
This changes the present alternative into a future contingency and future judgment.

options: Use sample because insufficient makes the following noun uncountable.

Keep samples: insufficient can modify plural count nouns as well as uncountable nouns.
Replace insufficient with little while keeping samples.
questions.explanation: 'Insufficient samples' means the number or adequacy of the samples was not enough; 'insufficient' is not restricted to mass nouns.
feedback: 'Insufficient' expresses inadequacy; it does not automatically change the noun's countability.
The phrase can concern an inadequate number or coverage of complete samples; individual incompleteness is not required.
'Insufficient samples' means the number or adequacy of the samples was not enough; 'insufficient' is not restricted to mass nouns.
'Little' does not directly quantify plural countable 'samples' in this meaning; 'too few samples' would express a numerical shortage.

questions.setup: Choose the reading that preserves the countable plural 'understandings'.
questions.prompt: The two departments have different understandings of what counts as a completed case.
options: One department understands the criterion better than the other.
They interpret the completion criterion differently.
Neither department understands what a case is.
Both departments have agreed on a single completion criterion.
questions.explanation: 'Understandings' can count interpretations or conceptions of a matter, while 'understanding' without 's' often describes comprehension generally.
feedback: 'Different understandings' identifies differing interpretations, not a ranking of comprehension.
'Understandings' can count interpretations or conceptions of a matter, while 'understanding' without 's' often describes comprehension generally.
Different interpretations do not establish absence of understanding in either department.
The sentence points to a difference between their interpretations, not agreement on one reading.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase of 'an understanding' that fits the negotiation context.
questions.prompt: After discussing the timetable, the two teams reached an understanding about weekend access.
options: They developed a common explanation of why the access system was unreliable.
They recognized each other's objections without agreeing on access.
They each developed a separate interpretation of weekend access.
They came to an agreement about weekend access.
questions.explanation: 'An understanding' can be a countable agreement, distinct from uncountable 'understanding' as comprehension.
feedback: A shared explanation would concern comprehension of a problem; 'reached an understanding' here reports an agreement about access.
Reaching an understanding goes beyond recognizing opposing views: it presents an agreement.
'Reached an understanding' presents a shared agreement, not separate readings that may differ.
'An understanding' can be a countable agreement, distinct from uncountable 'understanding' as comprehension.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'interests' that preserves the disclosure context.
questions.prompt: Before joining the panel, she declared her financial interests in two companies.
options: She disclosed financial stakes or connections in those companies.
She disclosed the interest rates paid by the companies.
She described how curious she was about the companies' finances.
She reported that the companies had identical financial goals.
questions.explanation: 'Financial interests' can be countable stakes or connections that matter in a disclosure; the plural does not simply measure curiosity or interest income.
feedback: 'Financial interests' can be countable stakes or connections that matter in a disclosure; the plural does not simply measure curiosity or interest income.
'Interest rates' would concern charges or returns on money; 'interests' here refers to her financial stakes or connections.
'Interest' as curiosity is not the financial-stake meaning required by 'declared...interests' in this context.
The sentence describes her interests, not a shared objective of the companies.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that retains the distinction between issues raised and the intensity of worry.
questions.prompt: The residents raised several concerns about drainage and access, although the report does not assess how anxious they were.
options: They showed several times as much anxiety as other residents.
They identified several matters of concern; their level of anxiety is unspecified.
Several residents were anxious about one shared issue.
Their lack of anxiety means that the concerns were not serious.
questions.explanation: Concerns counts issues raised, whereas concern as worry can refer to an emotional state; the count does not measure that state's intensity.
feedback: A count of concerns provides no comparison of anxiety levels or a multiplier.
Concerns counts issues raised, whereas concern as worry can refer to an emotional state; the count does not measure that state's intensity.
Several quantifies concerns, not residents, and drainage and access need not reduce to one issue.
The report leaves anxiety unassessed rather than establishing its absence; seriousness is not determined by that omission.

questions.setup: Choose the editorial change that preserves stories of separate events rather than converting them into a claim about expertise.
questions.prompt: The oral-history chapter describes the workers' experiences during the factory's closure.
options: The chapter recounts events the workers lived through during the closure.
The chapter measures the workers' professional experience when the factory closed.
The chapter compares how long each worker had been employed.
The chapter lists the workers' qualifications for finding new jobs.
questions.explanation: Experiences is countable for lived events; recounts events preserves that meaning without treating them as a skill measure.
feedback: Experiences is countable for lived events; recounts events preserves that meaning without treating them as a skill measure.
Professional experience refers to accumulated expertise, not the events described in their life stories.
Experiences does not supply employment durations or establish a comparison of tenure.
Qualifications may relate to expertise, but they are not what the stated lived-experience noun means.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'histories' that fits the contrast between accounts.
questions.prompt: The exhibition presents competing histories of the same town, each written from a different social perspective.
options: Different pasts lived by several unrelated towns.
Different lengths of time for which the town has existed.
Different accounts or interpretations of the town's past.
Separate historical periods that cannot overlap.
questions.explanation: 'A history' can be a written account of past events; 'competing histories' can recount one town from different perspectives.
feedback: The sentence identifies the same town; 'histories' counts accounts of its past, not separate towns.
'Histories' does not give competing durations of existence; it identifies differing narratives.
'A history' can be a written account of past events; 'competing histories' can recount one town from different perspectives.
The accounts may cover overlapping periods; the plural does not establish a division into nonoverlapping eras.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'a literature' that fits this academic usage.
questions.prompt: A substantial literature has developed on how cities reuse industrial buildings.
options: One unusually long book addresses the topic.
An extensive annotated list of publications has been produced.
Researchers have reached a shared conclusion about the topic.
A substantial body of published work addresses the topic.
questions.explanation: 'A literature' is a conventional academic use for a body of writing on a particular topic, even though 'literature' is often uncountable more generally.
feedback: 'A literature' can refer to a body of work; the article does not reduce it to one book.
'A literature' means the body of writing itself, not necessarily a bibliography or annotated list of it.
A substantial literature can include disagreement; the existence of a body of work does not establish consensus.
'A literature' is a conventional academic use for a body of writing on a particular topic, even though 'literature' is often uncountable more generally.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that counts political systems or states rather than referring to democracy as a general principle.
questions.prompt: The comparison needs to identify three separate democratic systems as its units.
options: The study examines democracy in three different ways.
The study examines three arguments in favor of democracy.
The study compares three democracies with different electoral systems.
The study measures support for democracy across three generations.
questions.explanation: Democracies is countable when it refers to states or systems organized as democracies, rather than the general principle.
feedback: This counts approaches to examining a general concept, not three democratic systems.
Three counts arguments, while democracy remains the general principle being discussed.
Democracies is countable when it refers to states or systems organized as democracies, rather than the general principle.
The counted units are generations, not separate political systems.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that retains the plural noun's focus on particular appealing features.
questions.prompt: The essay describes the less obvious beauties of the old industrial landscape.
options: It explains how the landscape was restored to its original beauty.
It judges the landscape beautiful as a whole without identifying particular features.
It identifies particular features of the landscape that the writer finds beautiful.
It compares several industrial landscapes without discussing individual features.
questions.explanation: Beauties can count attractive features or things; beauty without s more often names the quality generally.
feedback: Particular beauties may be described without any claim that restoration occurred.
Plural beauties focuses on identifiable attractive aspects, rather than only a general judgment of the whole landscape.
Beauties can count attractive features or things; beauty without s more often names the quality generally.
The singular landscape and plural beauties place the variety within this one landscape.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that treats 'an injustice' as a particular wrong without limiting its effects to one person.
questions.prompt: The campaign challenged an injustice that affected several neighbourhoods.
options: It challenged one identifiable wrong affecting several neighbourhoods.
It challenged the general existence of unfairness without identifying any particular wrong.
It challenged a wrong affecting exactly one resident.
It challenged several unrelated wrongs, one in each neighbourhood.
questions.explanation: 'An injustice' counts a particular wrong or unfair arrangement; the following clause states that its effects extend across neighbourhoods.
feedback: 'An injustice' counts a particular wrong or unfair arrangement; the following clause states that its effects extend across neighbourhoods.
'An injustice' presents an identifiable instance or form of unfairness, not only the abstract condition.
A singular 'injustice' can affect many people; its grammatical number does not count those affected.
The original uses 'one injustice' and does not distribute separate wrongs across the neighbourhoods.

questions.setup: Choose the statement that does not infer a machine count from an event count.
questions.prompt: The maintenance log records two engine failures, but does not identify the engines involved.
options: Exactly two different engines failed.
Two failure events are recorded; they need not involve two different engines.
One engine certainly failed on two occasions.
Both failures necessarily had different technical causes.
questions.explanation: Failures counts occurrences here, not necessarily different machines or different underlying faults.
feedback: One engine could have failed twice, so the event count does not establish the count of distinct engines.
Failures counts occurrences here, not necessarily different machines or different underlying faults.
That is possible, but the log does not identify the engines, so it is not established.
Separate failure events can share a cause; the plural does not identify causes.

questions.setup: Choose the assessment that identifies what the editor has changed.
questions.prompt: Original: 'Emergency supplies were delivered in two shipments.' Edit: 'Two emergency supply systems were installed.'
options: The edit keeps the same counted objects and merely replaces delivered with a more formal verb.
The edit changes two types of provision into two deliveries of the same type.
The edit preserves the meaning because plural supplies implies separately installed systems.
The edit changes delivered provisions into installed systems and moves the count from shipments to systems.
questions.explanation: Supplies names provisions or equipment. The original counts delivery batches, whereas the rewrite describes the installation of two organized systems.
feedback: A shipment is a delivery batch, not a supply system, and installed is not simply a more formal synonym of delivered.
Two originally modifies shipments, not types; the rewrite does not count deliveries.
Supplies does not imply installation or identify supply systems; it can refer to ordinary stored goods.
Supplies names provisions or equipment. The original counts delivery batches, whereas the rewrite describes the installation of two organized systems.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of 'economy' in this explanation of the editor's cuts.
questions.prompt: Several repeated examples were removed for reasons of economy, not because their content was inaccurate.
options: They were removed because the writer charged a separate fee for every example.
They were removed because repetition made the underlying claims false.
They were removed to narrow the article to one economic theory.
They were removed to use words or space more efficiently.
questions.explanation: 'Economy' can be an uncountable quality of avoiding waste; repeated examples invite a concise-editing interpretation.
feedback: 'Reasons of economy' can concern resources, but the editing context does not establish a fee arrangement.
The sentence explicitly excludes inaccuracy as the reason for the cuts.
'Economy' describes efficiency of expression here, not a named theory or a change in subject matter.
'Economy' can be an uncountable quality of avoiding waste; repeated examples invite a concise-editing interpretation.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves a count of plans without claiming a count of constructed objects.
questions.prompt: The archive holds three designs for the tower; the note does not say which were built.
options: It records three towers that were completed.
It holds three proposed versions of the tower's design.
It contains three physical models of a single design.
It gives three reasons for choosing the completed tower.
questions.explanation: A design can be a countable plan or version; three designs does not establish that three structures were built.
feedback: Designs counts plans or proposed versions, not completed buildings.
A design can be a countable plan or version; three designs does not establish that three structures were built.
Models are representations of designs; the note counts designs themselves and does not specify models.
The note counts plans, not reasons, and leaves construction outcomes unstated.

questions.setup: Choose the reading of 'languages' that fits this comparison of academic disciplines.
questions.prompt: Although both articles are written in English, the editor says that sociology and engineering use different languages to discuss risk.
options: The disciplines have translated the same analysis from different national languages.
The disciplines use the same terminology but disagree only about numerical results.
The disciplines address readers with different levels of English proficiency.
The disciplines use different specialized vocabularies and ways of expressing ideas.
questions.explanation: 'Languages' can count distinct systems or styles of expression within one natural language, especially in this disciplinary comparison.
feedback: Both articles are written in English, and the comment concerns disciplinary expression rather than a stated translation history.
'Different languages' points to different expressive systems or terminology, not merely different numerical conclusions.
Specialized disciplinary language does not by itself establish the readers' general proficiency in English.
'Languages' can count distinct systems or styles of expression within one natural language, especially in this disciplinary comparison.

questions.setup: Choose the concise edit that removes duplicated wording without turning an unspecified amount of research into a counted project or result.
questions.prompt: The committee requested further additional research before revising its recommendation.
options: The committee requested further research before revising its recommendation.
The committee requested another study before revising its recommendation.
The committee requested further findings before revising its recommendation.
The committee requested several research projects before revising its recommendation.
questions.explanation: Further already means additional here. Removing additional preserves research as an unspecified activity or body of investigation.
feedback: Further already means additional here. Removing additional preserves research as an unspecified activity or body of investigation.
Another study specifies an additional countable project, whereas the original leaves the form and number of investigations open.
Findings are results; the original requests investigation, which does not guarantee particular additional results.
Several projects adds a count and a project structure absent from the original.

questions.setup: Choose the accurate assessment of how the edit changes the countable and uncountable nouns.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The essay offers scant examples but ample discussion.' Edit: 'The essay contains numerous discussions, each offering few examples.'
options: The edit preserves the same quantities because ample discussion means numerous discussions.
The edit corrects scant examples, which should have been expressed as few examples.
The edit removes the contrast by claiming that both discussion and examples are abundant.
The edit divides discussion into separate units and assigns few examples to each, neither of which the original specifies.
questions.explanation: Uncountable discussion leaves its segmentation open. The edit introduces countable discussions and a per-discussion claim, while the original evaluates examples across the essay.
feedback: An ample amount of discussion need not consist of numerous separately identifiable discussions.
Scant examples is grammatical. Replacing scant with few does not justify the new discussion units or the distribution of examples.
The edit still says few examples per discussion; it does not straightforwardly describe both as abundant.
Uncountable discussion leaves its segmentation open. The edit introduces countable discussions and a per-discussion claim, while the original evaluates examples across the essay.

questions.setup: Choose the criticism that identifies what the rewrite claims without support.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The laboratory renewed three site licenses for software already in use.' Rewrite: 'The laboratory installed three new software packages.'
options: The rewrite turns a purchase of individual user accounts into a purchase of licenses.
The rewrite turns renewed usage rights into newly installed programs.
The rewrite changes the institution holding the licenses from the laboratory to the software provider.
The rewrite says that the laboratory renewed the same programs for a shorter period.
questions.explanation: Three counts licenses in the original. Renewing those rights for existing software does not establish the installation of three new programs.
feedback: The original already counts site licenses, not individual accounts; the rewrite does not retain that license count.
Three counts licenses in the original. Renewing those rights for existing software does not establish the installation of three new programs.
Neither version transfers ownership or usage rights to the provider.
The rewrite does not specify renewal or a period; installed new packages describes a different action and object.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that retains different assigned importances without inventing numerical values.
questions.prompt: The panel assigned different weights to cost and accessibility, but the report gives no coefficients.
options: The criteria received different relative importance, with the precise values unstated.
Cost received greater weight, although the size of its advantage was not reported.
The panel used different criteria but assigned them the same importance.
The panel reported how often each criterion mattered, but omitted how strongly it mattered.
questions.explanation: Weights can count assigned degrees of importance; different distinguishes them, while the absence of coefficients leaves their numerical values unreported.
feedback: Weights can count assigned degrees of importance; different distinguishes them, while the absence of coefficients leaves their numerical values unreported.
Different weights does not identify which criterion received greater weight; listing cost first supplies no ranking.
Different modifies weights, not merely the names of the criteria, so equal importance is not the reported assignment.
Weights refers to assigned importance, not the frequency with which a criterion mattered.

questions.setup: Choose the editorial response that avoids inferring a collection count from mass-noun grammar.
questions.prompt: The report consistently writes 'the data is reliable.' A reviewer concludes that this wording means the report used only one data set.
options: The inference is valid because singular agreement counts the data sets as one.
The inference is unsupported: mass data can refer to information pooled from several data sets.
The sentence must instead refer to one individual datum.
The mass use proves that the report contains qualitative rather than numerical information.
questions.explanation: Data treated as a mass noun can describe pooled information from one or many collections; data set is the count noun needed to establish collection number.
feedback: Grammatical singular agreement in a mass-noun use does not count the underlying collections.
Data treated as a mass noun can describe pooled information from one or many collections; data set is the count noun needed to establish collection number.
A datum is one observation or fact; the mass use data does not specify an individual observation.
Both qualitative and numerical information can be referred to by mass data; agreement does not determine content type.

questions.setup: Choose the idiomatic summary that preserves distinct fields of competence without changing them into people or their opinions.
questions.prompt: The project combines specialist competence in conservation, translation and digital cataloguing. The summary needs to name those different fields.
options: The project brings together several experts.
The project adopts several expert opinions.
The project brings together several areas of expertise.
The project acquires a greater amount of expertise.
questions.explanation: Areas of expertise names distinct domains while keeping expertise as the general competence noun.
feedback: Experts counts people. One person might contribute competence in several fields, so the personnel count is not established.
Opinions are judgments or outputs, not the fields of competence the task asks to identify.
Areas of expertise names distinct domains while keeping expertise as the general competence noun.
This gives an increase in overall competence without preserving the explicit distinction among fields.

questions.setup: Choose the modern paraphrase that preserves visible manifestations without claiming a conclusive reconstruction.
questions.prompt: An older description notes 'the visible evidences of earlier alterations' in a building. The writer points to filled doorways and different brickwork.
options: The surviving records documenting the earlier alterations.
The separate earlier alterations still visible in their original form.
The visible traces of earlier alterations.
The visible signs of proposed alterations that were never carried out.
questions.explanation: In this marked older use, evidences can mean manifestations or signs. Traces retains those counted features without turning them into conclusive proofs.
feedback: The supplied evidences are physical features of the building, not necessarily documentary records.
Traces such as a filled doorway may reveal an alteration without preserving that alteration in its original form.
In this marked older use, evidences can mean manifestations or signs. Traces retains those counted features without turning them into conclusive proofs.
Earlier alterations refers to past changes; the original does not describe unrealized proposals.

questions.setup: Choose the explanation that makes the two claims compatible.
questions.prompt: The merger produced economies of scale, yet total expenditure increased because output expanded substantially.
options: The savings were forecasts, while the increased expenditure was an observed result.
Economies refers to reduced output, while expenditure refers to increased output.
The merger reduced overall spending, but the same report labels that reduction an increase.
Lower cost per unit can coexist with higher total spending when more is produced.
questions.explanation: Economies of scale refers to efficiencies associated with scale; such savings do not alone imply a lower total when production expands.
feedback: Produced presents the economies as achieved, not merely forecast; a forecast-versus-result contrast is not supplied.
Economies of scale names efficiencies associated with scale, not a reduction in output.
This substitutes overall spending for the efficiency measure and invents a labeling contradiction.
Economies of scale refers to efficiencies associated with scale; such savings do not alone imply a lower total when production expands.

questions.setup: Choose the objection to the edit that is justified by the original sentence.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The reviewer gave no grounds for rejecting the submission.' Edit: 'The reviewer's rejection was groundless.'
options: The edit turns an absence of stated reasons into a claim that no justification existed.
The edit is equivalent because an unreported ground cannot justify a decision.
The edit weakens a judgment about the reasons into a statement about how they were presented.
The edit changes the claim from insufficient reasons to sufficient but unpersuasive reasons.
questions.explanation: No grounds were given does not establish that no grounds existed. Groundless makes the stronger substantive judgment.
feedback: No grounds were given does not establish that no grounds existed. Groundless makes the stronger substantive judgment.
The original establishes only that no grounds were given; it does not rule on whether unreported reasons could justify the decision.
The direction is reversed: the original concerns reasons supplied, while groundless judges the rejection's basis.
Groundless does not describe sufficient reasons, and gave no grounds does not say that some insufficient reasons were offered.

questions.setup: Choose the accurate assessment of the plural 'methods' in the proposed rewrite.
questions.prompt: Original: 'Their means of communication proved reliable.' Edit: 'Their communication methods were reliable.' No other context identifies how many methods were used.
options: The edit preserves an explicit plural because their assigns a separate method to each person.
The edit removes a claim that each person used the same method.
The edit fixes a plural count that the original wording leaves open.
The edit reduces several methods to one shared system of communication.
questions.explanation: 'Means' can be singular or plural, 'their' does not decide its number, and past-tense 'proved' supplies no agreement distinction. 'Methods' explicitly chooses plural.
feedback: 'Their' can refer to a shared method as well as separate ones; a plural possessor does not determine the number of 'means'.
The original allows a shared method but does not assert one; the edit does not remove an established shared-method claim.
'Means' can be singular or plural, 'their' does not decide its number, and past-tense 'proved' supplies no agreement distinction. 'Methods' explicitly chooses plural.
'Methods' is explicitly plural. It does not reduce the count to one system.

questions.setup: Choose the editorial assessment that best accounts for the change from plural to uncountable 'silence'.
questions.prompt: A memoir describes an interview: 'Her silences unsettled me.' An editor proposes 'Her silence unsettled me.' No other sentence describes the pauses.
options: The edit establishes that she said nothing throughout the interview.
The edit preserves the same segmentation because her refers to the same speaker.
The edit no longer explicitly presents separate episodes of silence.
The edit changes deliberate pauses into an involuntary inability to speak.
questions.explanation: 'Silences' presents distinct stretches or occasions. 'Silence' presents the state generally, so the explicit segmentation is lost, even though repeated pauses remain possible.
feedback: Singular 'silence' does not by itself establish an uninterrupted absence of speech throughout the interview.
The possessive identifies whose silence is involved, not whether it is presented as separate episodes.
'Silences' presents distinct stretches or occasions. 'Silence' presents the state generally, so the explicit segmentation is lost, even though repeated pauses remain possible.
Neither countable 'silences' nor uncountable 'silence' by itself establishes intention or an inability to speak.

questions.setup: Choose the neutral revision that retains the separate acts without converting them into a general judgment of character.
questions.prompt: The witness recalled several kindnesses from her former employer, while declining to describe him as a kind person.
options: She acknowledged his kind character but could not recall particular acts.
She recalled several kind acts by him but did not describe his character as kind.
She recalled his acts as kind only because she had already judged his character.
She recalled several acts that she once considered kind but now regarded otherwise.
questions.explanation: Countable kindnesses packages separate acts. It does not oblige the witness to endorse kindness as a general personal quality.
feedback: This reverses the distinction: she recalls particular acts and declines the general character description.
Countable kindnesses packages separate acts. It does not oblige the witness to endorse kindness as a general personal quality.
The proposed cause is absent. The original expressly separates the remembered acts from a character judgment.
Nothing retracts the description of the acts as kindnesses; the reservation concerns the person's character.

questions.setup: Choose the justified criticism of the financial summary; no calculation is needed.
questions.prompt: Source: 'The firm recorded losses on three contracts.' Summary: 'The firm operated at a loss.' The source gives no information about its other work.
options: The summary converts three causes of one loss into three separate accounting periods.
The summary turns losses on particular contracts into a claim about the firm's overall result.
The summary accurately compresses the plural losses into their necessary combined result.
The summary changes a prediction of future losses into a report of completed losses.
questions.explanation: Plural losses are attached to specified contracts. At a loss describes the firm's overall operation here, which cannot be inferred without information about other work.
feedback: Neither version specifies causes or accounting periods. The relevant change is from particular contracts to the firm's overall result.
Plural losses are attached to specified contracts. At a loss describes the firm's overall operation here, which cannot be inferred without information about other work.
Other work could be profitable enough to offset those contract losses, so the overall result is not established.
Recorded already reports losses; the original is not a forecast.

questions.setup: Choose the revision that preserves both separately negotiated arrangements and the absence of a wider concession.
questions.prompt: The parties reached several practical accommodations on access to the archive, without settling their dispute over ownership.
options: They agreed on several practical access arrangements while leaving ownership unresolved.
They resolved the ownership dispute by agreeing to several ways of accessing the archive.
They agreed in principle to seek access arrangements once ownership had been resolved.
They made one comprehensive access settlement that also defined their ownership rights.
questions.explanation: Here accommodations means adjustments or arrangements reached between the parties. Counting those arrangements does not imply settlement of the wider ownership dispute.
feedback: Here accommodations means adjustments or arrangements reached between the parties. Counting those arrangements does not imply settlement of the wider ownership dispute.
This makes the practical arrangements settle the wider dispute, contrary to without settling.
Reached reports completed arrangements, not a future undertaking dependent on resolving ownership.
This collapses several practical accommodations into one comprehensive settlement and adds an ownership decision.

questions.setup: Choose the objection that identifies the change in what the catalogue counts.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The collection includes several editions of each of two works by Neri.' Edit: 'The collection includes several works by Neri in two editions each.'
options: The edit merely moves the same quantities to a more natural position.
The edit changes two jointly authored works into works written by Neri alone.
The edit counts several works rather than several editions of two works.
The edit changes a collection of two complete works into several incomplete editions.
questions.explanation: A work and an edition of that work are different catalogue units. Reassigning the quantities changes the collection being described.
feedback: Moving the quantities changes their heads: two originally counts works, while several counts editions of each work.
The original says by Neri and gives no joint-authorship information; the quantities concern works and editions, not authors.
A work and an edition of that work are different catalogue units. Reassigning the quantities changes the collection being described.
Neither wording says that an edition is incomplete; completeness is not the distinction introduced by moving the quantities.

questions.setup: Choose the neutral paraphrase that preserves the translator's qualified admission without adding an accusation or a claim of permission.
questions.prompt: The translator acknowledged taking a few liberties with the wording, though not with the argument.
options: The translator admitted some departures from the wording while maintaining the argument.
The translator claimed permission to alter the wording but not the argument.
The translator admitted changing the argument through apparently minor wording choices.
The translator admitted that the wording changes misrepresented the author's position.
questions.explanation: Countable liberties here means departures from strict fidelity. The contrast limits them to wording, without establishing permission or dishonesty.
feedback: Countable liberties here means departures from strict fidelity. The contrast limits them to wording, without establishing permission or dishonesty.
Taking liberties reports departures, not necessarily permission granted by anyone.
The original expressly excludes liberties with the argument; this paraphrase undermines that qualification.
That adds an accusation about the argument or position, whereas the original says the liberties did not extend to the argument.

questions.setup: Choose the assessment that respects the distinction between cited sources and an established view.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The essay cites several authorities in support of its dating.' Summary: 'The dating is the authoritative view.'
options: The summary simply replaces a plural noun with its equivalent adjective.
The summary understates the original, which establishes agreement among the field's authorities.
The summary says that the essay is an authority rather than that its dating is authoritative.
Citing several recognized sources does not by itself establish the dating as the authoritative view.
questions.explanation: Countable authorities can be recognized experts or their works. Their citation supplies support, but does not establish a uniquely authoritative position.
feedback: The adjective changes the claim: several supporting authorities become a status assigned to the dating itself.
Several supporting authorities does not say that authorities across the field agree; other views may exist.
The subject of the summary is the dating, not the essay, so this identifies the wrong change.
Countable authorities can be recognized experts or their works. Their citation supplies support, but does not establish a uniquely authoritative position.

questions.setup: Choose the criticism that identifies an unsupported change from pooled savings to separate results.
questions.prompt: Source: 'Taken together, the changes produced savings exceeding their combined cost.' Summary: 'Each change paid for itself.'
options: The summary changes possible future savings into savings already achieved.
The summary loses a claim that the changes each generated the same savings.
The summary preserves the source because plural savings distributes one saving to each change.
The summary assigns cost recovery to every change, which the source establishes only for the changes together.
questions.explanation: Savings is pooled in the source, reinforced by taken together and combined cost. A profitable change could offset another that did not recover its cost.
feedback: Produced already presents achieved savings; the unsupported change concerns their distribution, not their timing.
The source gives a combined result, not equal individual savings.
The plural form does not distribute savings automatically; the source explicitly evaluates them together.
Savings is pooled in the source, reinforced by taken together and combined cost. A profitable change could offset another that did not recover its cost.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves the distinction between document count and independent accounts.
questions.prompt: Six reports reproduce the same witness's account; none includes testimony from anyone else.
options: Six independent accounts corroborate the witness's testimony.
The witness gave six separate accounts, one for each report.
Six reports independently obtained testimony from the same witness.
One witness's account is reproduced in six reports.
questions.explanation: This retains both counting units: six documents carry one witness's account. Repetition does not create independent testimony.
feedback: Six counts reports, not independent accounts; they reproduce the same witness's account.
Reproduction of the same account does not establish six separate occasions on which the witness gave an account.
The source specifies reproduction, not independent collection of testimony by each report's author.
This retains both counting units: six documents carry one witness's account. Repetition does not create independent testimony.

questions.setup: Preserve the spoken quotation exactly, then summarize it in ordinary standard written British English without changing its intended item count.
questions.prompt: Pointing to two new tools, the speaker said, 'We bought two equipments.' Which report meets the editing brief?
options: 'We bought two items of equipment,' she said, referring to two new tools.
'We bought two equipments,' she said, referring to two items of equipment.
