questions.prompt: Almost all of the letters that survive mention at least one supplier.
options: Nearly every supplier appears in a surviving letter.
Nearly every surviving letter mentions a supplier.
Nearly every letter about suppliers has survived.
Nearly every surviving letter mentions most suppliers.
questions.explanation: Nearly every preserves almost all; surviving still restricts the letters, and a supplier preserves the per-letter existence claim.
feedback: This quantifies the suppliers instead of the letters, asserting broad supplier coverage that the original does not establish.
Nearly every preserves almost all; surviving still restricts the letters, and a supplier preserves the per-letter existence claim.
This reverses the restriction: the original describes the contents of surviving letters, not the survival rate of supplier-related letters.
Most suppliers strengthens the per-letter claim far beyond at least one supplier.

questions.setup: Choose the accurate assessment of the proposed edit.
questions.prompt: Original: 'Every witness recognized someone in the photograph.' Proposed summary: 'There was one person in the photograph whom every witness recognized.'
options: The summary is equivalent; its opening merely makes the recognized person easier to refer to.
The summary weakens every to one and no longer includes all the witnesses.
The summary adds a shared recognized person; the original allows witnesses to recognize different people.
The summary contradicts the original, which requires a different person for each witness.
questions.explanation: One witness could recognize only Ana and another only Bo. Each would recognize someone, but no person would be recognized by both, so the summary is not guaranteed.
feedback: The new opening fixes a single person as recognized by everyone. The original can be true when witnesses recognize different people.
One counts the recognized person, not the witnesses; every witness still includes the full witness group.
One witness could recognize only Ana and another only Bo. Each would recognize someone, but no person would be recognized by both, so the summary is not guaranteed.
The original allows different recognized people but does not require them; it also permits everyone to recognize the same person.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves the exception while leaving the exceptional panelist's final position unstated.
questions.prompt: All but one of the panelists declined to endorse the recommendation.
options: Only one panelist endorsed it; the others declined.
One panelist declined; the others did not state their positions.
One panelist has yet to decide; the others declined.
Only one panelist did not decline; their final position is not specified.
questions.explanation: All but one creates a single exception to declining, without telling us whether that person endorsed, deferred or withheld a response.
feedback: Not declining is not itself endorsement: the exceptional panelist might still be undecided.
This makes one the size of the declining group instead of the exception to that group.
Indecision is possible for the exception, but the original does not specifically establish it.
All but one creates a single exception to declining, without telling us whether that person endorsed, deferred or withheld a response.

questions.setup: Choose the defensible comparison. Both journals use 'few' for a low proportion of their own submissions.
questions.prompt: Journal A says, 'Few of our fifty submissions were accepted.' Journal B says, 'Few of our five thousand submissions were accepted.'
options: The journals accepted the same number because both used few.
B must have accepted more manuscripts because it received more.
Each journal accepted at most four manuscripts.
B may have accepted more manuscripts than A, despite both using few.
questions.explanation: A low proportion of a large pool can exceed a low proportion of a small pool in absolute count; 'few' alone does not settle the comparison.
feedback: 'Few' is context-dependent; using the same vague quantifier does not establish equal counts across different-sized groups.
A larger submission pool does not guarantee a larger accepted count without actual acceptance figures.
'Few' does not have a fixed ceiling of four, especially when it describes a proportion of thousands.
A low proportion of a large pool can exceed a low proportion of a small pool in absolute count; 'few' alone does not settle the comparison.

questions.setup: Choose a neutral rewrite that explicitly starts with each report and retains a sizeable count of objections separately for it.
questions.prompt: Each report leaves not a few objections unanswered.
options: Each report leaves a considerable number of objections unanswered.
A considerable number of objections remain unanswered in every report.
Each report leaves most of the objections unanswered.
Some reports leave a considerable number of objections unanswered.
questions.explanation: A considerable number makes not a few direct, while keeping that quantity inside the claim made separately about each report.
feedback: A considerable number makes not a few direct, while keeping that quantity inside the claim made separately about each report.
This foregrounds the objections and allows a shared-set reading. The requested rewrite must explicitly retain each report as the starting point for its own count.
Most adds a majority claim; not a few signals a sizeable number without fixing its proportion of all objections.
Some reports weakens the original each report, so it no longer covers every report individually.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that restricts the quantified group to samples collected before noon.
questions.prompt: The laboratory rechecked all the samples that were collected before noon. Later samples are outside this statement's claim.
options: Every sample was rechecked before noon.
Every sample collected before noon was rechecked.
All the samples were collected before noon and were rechecked.
Every rechecked sample had been collected before noon.
questions.explanation: The collection-time modifier remains inside the group quantified by every, preserving the original restriction.
feedback: This moves before noon from collection time to rechecking time and includes all samples.
The collection-time modifier remains inside the group quantified by every, preserving the original restriction.
This makes the collection-time condition true of the entire sample set rather than restricting the claim.
This reverses the implication: it limits rechecked samples instead of guaranteeing rechecking of early samples.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that retains the defined class and allows reporting a first instance of it.
questions.prompt: A discrepancy affecting the final total must be investigated. If ___ is discovered, record it separately.
options: a discrepancy of another kind
any discrepancy whatsoever
any such discrepancy
the same discrepancy again
questions.explanation: Such preserves the defined property; any allows an instance to trigger the condition without assuming an earlier instance.
feedback: Another kind changes the class rather than referring back to discrepancies affecting the final total.
This removes the restriction to discrepancies affecting the final total, broadening the condition.
Such preserves the defined property; any allows an instance to trigger the condition without assuming an earlier instance.
The same...again introduces recurrence of an identified discrepancy, whereas the instruction must cover a first discovery.

questions.setup: Choose the revision that preserves both exhaustive use and the small number of sources available.
questions.prompt: The historian consulted what few independent sources there were.
options: The historian consulted all the independent sources available, which were few.
The historian consulted a few of the independent sources available.
The historian consulted fewer independent sources than expected.
The historian consulted independent sources whenever any became available.
questions.explanation: What few combines all of the available set with an assessment that the set was small.
feedback: What few combines all of the available set with an assessment that the set was small.
A few of selects a small subset and does not retain consultation of the full available set.
Fewer introduces a comparison with an expectation, not the totality of the available small set.
Whenever adds a repeated timing condition and does not state exhaustive consultation of the small set.

questions.setup: Choose the editorial objection that is justified by the original wording.
questions.prompt: Original: 'Three reviewers each rejected two different proposals.' Summary: 'The reviewers rejected six distinct proposals.'
options: The summary incorrectly assumes that each reviewer rejected more than one proposal.
The summary wrongly changes rejection of a shared pair into rejection of separate pairs.
The summary assumes that the reviewers' pairs did not overlap.
The summary changes an approximate total into an exact total.
questions.explanation: Different separates the two proposals within each reviewer's pair. It does not establish that one reviewer's pair differs from another's.
feedback: Two different proposals explicitly gives each reviewer more than one rejection, so that inference is licensed.
The original does not establish a shared pair either; the problem is assuming disjointness, not contradicting known overlap.
Different separates the two proposals within each reviewer's pair. It does not establish that one reviewer's pair differs from another's.
The original provides exact per-reviewer counts, not an approximate total of distinct proposals; overlap is the missing information.

questions.setup: Choose the accurate assessment of the change from 'any' to 'only'.
questions.prompt: Original: 'Any account supported by two independent sources will be included.' Edit: 'Only accounts supported by two independent sources will be included.'
options: The original guarantees inclusion for qualifying accounts; the edit excludes others without guaranteeing inclusion for the qualifying accounts.
Both versions guarantee inclusion for qualifying accounts; the edit merely expresses the same rule more directly.
The original excludes nonqualifying accounts; the edit guarantees inclusion whenever the source condition is met.
Neither version commits to including qualifying accounts; both merely express a preference for independently supported sources.
questions.explanation: 'Any...will' gives a sufficient condition for inclusion. 'Only' makes that condition necessary, without preserving the guarantee for every qualifying account.
feedback: 'Any...will' gives a sufficient condition for inclusion. 'Only' makes that condition necessary, without preserving the guarantee for every qualifying account.
'Only' restricts what may be included, but does not guarantee inclusion of every account meeting that restriction.
This reverses the functions: 'any' guarantees inclusion on qualification, while 'only' makes qualification necessary.
'Will be included' in the original is a commitment, and 'only' in the edit is a restriction, not a preference.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that unambiguously prohibits every applicant from sharing a login.
questions.prompt: An editor wants to clarify 'Any applicant may not share a login.'
options: Not every applicant is permitted to share a login.
Every applicant may choose not to share a login.
No applicant is permitted to share a login.
Any applicant may share a login only once.
questions.explanation: No applicant places every member of the class outside the permitted group, stating the blanket prohibition clearly.
feedback: This denies universal permission but allows permission for some applicants.
This permits abstaining from sharing; it does not prohibit sharing.
No applicant places every member of the class outside the permitted group, stating the blanket prohibition clearly.
This grants limited sharing permission, contradicting the complete prohibition.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that preserves the tested-to-date restriction and reports failure without asserting impossibility.
questions.prompt: Every solution tested so far has failed.
options: All the solutions tested to date have failed.
Every solution has so far been tested and has failed.
Every solution has failed each test conducted so far.
No solution tested so far could have succeeded.
questions.explanation: Tested to date remains a restriction on the solutions, and have failed preserves an outcome claim rather than a claim of impossibility.
feedback: Tested to date remains a restriction on the solutions, and have failed preserves an outcome claim rather than a claim of impossibility.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that says precisely one consultant recommended the change, without limiting what else that consultant recommended.
questions.prompt: The intended restriction concerns the number of consultants, not the number of recommendations.
options: One consultant recommended only the change.
Only one consultant recommended the change.
One consultant only recommended the change.
The consultant recommended one change only.
questions.explanation: Only one restricts the consultant count to exactly one in this positive report; the consultant may have made other recommendations.
feedback: Only now restricts what was recommended, not how many consultants recommended it.

questions.setup: Choose the concise revision that retains numerical approximation while removing duplicate approximation markers.
questions.prompt: Some sixty or so participants joined the consultation.

Some of the sixty participants joined the consultation.
questions.explanation: Some already means approximately before sixty, so or so can be removed without losing the estimate.
feedback: Removing both markers turns an approximate number into an unqualified count.
Some already means approximately before sixty, so or so can be removed without losing the estimate.

questions.setup: Choose the statement NOT established by the sentence.

options: No manager approved zero plans.
Each manager approved one or more plans.

All managers belong to the group that approved a plan.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves the additional reason for value without ranking the reasons or making scarcity the sole cause.
questions.prompt: These letters are valuable for the detail they contain. The absence of other records makes them all the more valuable.
options: Their contents give them value, which the lack of other records further increases.

feedback: All the more adds a further reason for increased value to the value already attributed to their contents.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that preserves both the exception and the per-person limit.
questions.prompt: All contributors except the editor may submit at most two illustrations each.

questions.setup: A lunch note says, 'Bring a drink. For example, bring some water.'

questions.setup: A receptionist says, 'Your room is on the second floor. It is opposite the lift.'

A reason to use a different room
A request to wait beside the lift

questions.setup: A message says, 'For your first day, bring your ID, your bank details, and a pen.'

options: A list of things to bring

The order for using three things

Correcting the day Ben gave

questions.setup: At a ticket machine, a visitor says, 'Can you show me how to use this?'

Telling the guest where to put the coat

questions.setup: A worker says, 'This printer has no paper.' A colleague replies, 'Use the printer in my office.'

options: It explains why there is no paper.

questions.setup: A feedback guide says, 'Reviewers first read each application without the applicant's name. This is intended to reduce the influence of personal familiarity.'
questions.prompt: What does the second sentence explain?
options: The purpose of a feature of the reviewing method
The measured success of the reviewing procedure
The reason applicants chose not to give their names
The order in which applicants should submit information
questions.explanation: Removing names is the method feature, and reducing familiarity's influence is its stated rationale.
feedback: Removing names is the method feature, and reducing familiarity's influence is its stated rationale.
'Intended to' states an aim, not a result that has been measured.
The reviewers' procedure removes names; no applicant choice is described.
The guide describes review and its purpose, not submission steps.

questions.setup: A report says, 'Satisfaction rose in both branches. The increase was greater in the branch that extended its opening hours.'
questions.prompt: What does the second sentence add to the first?
options: A correction showing satisfaction fell in one branch
A comparison of the size of the two increases
A definition of satisfaction for the survey
A claim that opening hours were the sole cause of both increases
questions.explanation: The first sentence gives a shared direction of change; the second differentiates the branches by the amount of change.
feedback: Both increases remain accepted; one is described as larger.
The first sentence gives a shared direction of change; the second differentiates the branches by the amount of change.
No measurement definition is supplied.
The sentence compares changes and identifies a branch; it does not establish that causal explanation.

questions.setup: An article asks whether a town needs another bridge. After discussing traffic, maintenance, and alternatives, it ends, 'The case for a second bridge therefore remains weak.'
questions.prompt: What is the final sentence doing in the article as a whole?
options: Introducing the topic for the first time
Answering the opening question through an overall assessment
Providing another example of bridge maintenance
Explaining the historical cause of current traffic
questions.explanation: The writer returns to whether the bridge is needed and evaluates the case after the intervening discussion.
feedback: The opening question has already introduced the bridge issue.
The writer returns to whether the bridge is needed and evaluates the case after the intervening discussion.
The conclusion evaluates the case; it adds no maintenance example.
The sentence judges the proposal rather than explaining how the traffic developed.

questions.setup: A staff memo says, 'Previously, requests needed a manager's signature. From Monday, an email from the team leader will be sufficient.'
questions.prompt: Why are the two sentences placed together?
options: To show that both approval methods are still required
To explain why managers prefer email
To make a change in the approval procedure clear
To compare how quickly two managers answer requests
questions.explanation: The old requirement establishes a reference point; the second sentence explains what replaces it from Monday.
feedback: The second method is sufficient from Monday, so the old signature is not also stated as required.
No preference or reason for it is reported.
The old requirement establishes a reference point; the second sentence explains what replaces it from Monday.
The memo compares requirements over time, not individual response speed.

questions.setup: A draft says the attendance estimate comes from interviews. An editor writes, 'The figure comes from entry records, not interviews.'
questions.prompt: What does the editor's sentence do?
options: It argues that interviews are generally unreliable.
It revises the numerical estimate of attendance.
It corrects the stated source of a particular figure.
It gives a reason people entered the venue.
questions.explanation: The positive source followed by 'not interviews' replaces the draft's mistaken attribution.
feedback: The editor corrects the source of this figure without judging interviews in general.
No new number is supplied; the correction concerns where the figure came from.
The positive source followed by 'not interviews' replaces the draft's mistaken attribution.
Records are the source of the estimate, not a motivation for attendance.

questions.setup: A reviewer writes, 'Please include the response rate; without it, readers cannot judge how much of the invited group is represented.'
questions.prompt: What function does the part after the semicolon have?
options: It gives the missing response rate in another form.
It concludes that the invited group was represented well.
It retracts the request because the information is unavailable.
It justifies the requested addition by explaining its value to readers.
questions.explanation: The second part explains why the response rate is needed, supporting the instruction to include it.
feedback: No numerical rate or count is supplied.
The reviewer says representation cannot yet be judged.
The request remains active; the reviewer does not say the rate is unavailable.
The second part explains why the response rate is needed, supporting the instruction to include it.

questions.setup: A writer says, 'The survey asks how satisfied passengers feel. It does not measure whether trains actually arrive on time.'
questions.prompt: What is the role of the second sentence?
options: It prevents one measure from being mistaken for another.
It disputes the reported passengers' feelings.
It explains why trains are delayed.
It recommends replacing passengers' answers with train times.
questions.explanation: The negative sentence separates subjective satisfaction from punctuality, clarifying what the survey result can describe.
feedback: The negative sentence separates subjective satisfaction from punctuality, clarifying what the survey result can describe.
The writer distinguishes two measures without saying the feelings are false.
The sentence gives no cause of late arrival.
A distinction between measures does not itself recommend replacing one with the other.

questions.setup: An editorial argues, 'The critics are right that the current scheme is costly. The issue, however, is whether their alternative can deliver the same coverage at a lower cost.'
questions.prompt: How does the second sentence develop the acknowledgment in the first?
options: It withdraws the acknowledgment by showing that the current scheme is inexpensive.
It recasts the disagreement around a test the proposed alternative must meet.
It accepts the critics' alternative because cost is the decisive criterion.
It explains how the current scheme originally became expensive.
questions.explanation: After conceding the cost problem, the writer redirects attention to the alternative's ability to preserve coverage while costing less.
feedback: The cost acknowledgment remains; the second sentence does not reverse it.
After conceding the cost problem, the writer redirects attention to the alternative's ability to preserve coverage while costing less.
The alternative is posed as a question for evaluation, and coverage matters as well as cost.
The writer changes the evaluative focus rather than offering a history of the cost.

questions.setup: A chapter states, 'Whether the policy is affordable will be considered in the final section. For now, the question is whether it can be implemented with the available staff.'
questions.prompt: What is the writer doing with the affordability question?
options: Deferring it while identifying the current line of inquiry
Treating it as settled by the staffing discussion
Dismissing it as irrelevant to the chapter's argument
Using it as the premise from which the staffing conclusion follows
questions.explanation: The first sentence postpones one issue; 'for now' establishes implementation with current staff as the immediate focus.
feedback: The first sentence postpones one issue; 'for now' establishes implementation with current staff as the immediate focus.
The writer reserves affordability for later rather than deriving an answer from staffing.
A later section is explicitly assigned to the question, so it is not dismissed.
No affordability finding is supplied as a premise.

questions.setup: A critic responds, 'The question is not whether the painting is popular, but whether popularity is a useful measure of artistic achievement.'
questions.prompt: What does the sentence do to the discussion?
options: It disputes the evidence that the painting is popular.
It recommends a different method of measuring the painting's popularity.
It defines artistic achievement as a high level of public approval.
It shifts attention from a reported fact to the criterion used to evaluate it.
questions.explanation: The critic moves from whether popularity exists to whether it should count as evidence of artistic achievement.
feedback: Popularity itself is not the point being challenged.
The critic questions the relevance of popularity, not the method used to count it.
The sentence raises doubt about using approval as that measure rather than defining achievement by it.
The critic moves from whether popularity exists to whether it should count as evidence of artistic achievement.

questions.setup: An essay introduces urban transport, then states, 'This essay addresses access within cities; travel between cities is outside its scope.'
questions.prompt: What role does the second statement play in the introduction?
options: It provides the main finding about intercity travel.
It argues that travel between cities is less important.
It explains why city travel causes intercity problems.
It establishes the boundary of the discussion.
questions.explanation: The statement specifies the included subject and names the related subject the essay will not address.
feedback: The writer excludes intercity travel from the inquiry and offers no finding about it.
Exclusion from scope is not a judgment of relative importance.
No causal connection between the two kinds of travel is proposed.
The statement specifies the included subject and names the related subject the essay will not address.

questions.setup: A report says, 'The interviews described difficulties navigating the website. The recorded user sessions reveal the same difficulties, particularly at the payment screen.'
questions.prompt: How does the second sentence support the report?
options: It converts the interview statements into instructions for using the website.
It corroborates one source using a different kind of evidence.
It corrects the interviews by showing that users had no navigation difficulties.
It establishes that the interviews caused the difficulties in the sessions.
questions.explanation: Observed sessions independently show the difficulties reported in interviews, providing converging support for the account.
feedback: The sessions are evidence of user behavior, not a set of instructions.
Observed sessions independently show the difficulties reported in interviews, providing converging support for the account.
The second source agrees about difficulties rather than contradicting them.
Agreement across sources does not introduce that causal relationship.

questions.setup: A news analysis quotes the developer: 'The project will benefit the whole district.' It then reports that the planned footbridge will serve only the western side.
questions.prompt: What does the footbridge detail do immediately after the quotation?
options: It places the developer's broad claim under scrutiny.
It supplies a definition of what the developer means by project.
It endorses the developer's district-wide benefit claim.
It explains why the developer chose to give a quotation.
questions.explanation: The specific service area gives readers a concrete reason to question how well the quoted claim describes the project's reach.
feedback: The specific service area gives readers a concrete reason to question how well the quoted claim describes the project's reach.
The detail identifies a limitation in the claimed reach, not a definition of project.
Serving only the western side complicates rather than supports the claim of district-wide benefit.
The writer supplies project information, not the developer's motivation for speaking.

questions.setup: A response states, 'Let us accept, for the moment, that the scheme will save money. That still leaves the question of whether the savings justify the loss of service.'
questions.prompt: What does the temporary acceptance achieve?
options: It grants one point so that a separate evaluative question can be examined.
It establishes the saving as a verified finding of the response.
It makes loss of service the stated cause of every saving.
It withdraws concern about whether the scheme is worthwhile.
questions.explanation: The writer provisionally accepts the saving while showing that this alone does not settle whether the scheme is justified.
feedback: The writer provisionally accepts the saving while showing that this alone does not settle whether the scheme is justified.
'For the moment' grants the point for discussion rather than verifying it.
The response weighs savings against a loss; it does not assert an exhaustive causal explanation.
The second sentence explicitly maintains a question about justification.

questions.setup: An essay compares an archive to a filter: 'It preserves some voices and screens out others. Unlike a simple filter, however, it can be reshaped by later decisions about what to collect.'
questions.prompt: What does the second sentence do to the analogy?
options: It replaces the analogy with an unrelated historical example.
It treats the archive as a literal physical filter.
It limits the comparison while retaining its initial usefulness.
It dismisses selection as irrelevant to how archives work.
questions.explanation: The writer keeps selective preservation as the shared feature but identifies a respect in which an archive differs from a simple filter.
feedback: The archive-filter comparison remains the subject; a difference is identified within it.
The phrase 'unlike a simple filter' distinguishes the archive from the object used in the comparison.
The writer keeps selective preservation as the shared feature but identifies a respect in which an archive differs from a simple filter.
Selection remains central; the second sentence adds that selection practices can change.

questions.setup: A commentator writes, 'Consultation gives residents an opportunity to express a view. It should not be confused with giving them the final decision.'
questions.prompt: What does the second sentence contribute?
options: It recommends ending the consultation process.
It explains why residents declined to express their views.
It separates participation in discussion from decision-making authority.
It establishes that consultation gives residents no influence of any kind.
questions.explanation: The writer distinguishes the opportunity to speak from the power to determine the outcome, preventing the concepts from being treated as equivalent.
feedback: The sentence clarifies what consultation means without recommending its removal.
No refusal to participate is reported or explained.
The writer distinguishes the opportunity to speak from the power to determine the outcome, preventing the concepts from being treated as equivalent.
Lacking the final decision is not the same as having no influence.

questions.setup: A proposal states, 'One objection is that weekend opening will increase staffing costs. The additional ticket revenue, however, is expected to cover those costs.'
questions.prompt: How do the two sentences function together?
options: They anticipate an objection and offer a response to it.
They supply two independent objections to weekend opening.
They retract a previous claim that staffing costs will rise.
They explain the procedure for collecting weekend tickets.
questions.explanation: The first sentence voices a likely concern, and the second argues that another effect may offset that concern.
feedback: The first sentence voices a likely concern, and the second argues that another effect may offset that concern.
The revenue point answers the cost objection rather than adding another objection.
The increase in staffing costs is accepted; the writer proposes how it will be covered.
Revenue is part of the argument about costs, not a ticketing procedure.

questions.setup: A report moves from describing interview recruitment to presenting themes. Between those sections it states, 'The account that follows reflects the experiences of those who agreed to be interviewed.'
questions.prompt: Why place this sentence at that point?
options: To explain the chronological order in which interviews occurred
To state that nonparticipants had the same experiences
To announce a new recruitment method after the interviews ended
To frame how readers should understand the following findings
questions.explanation: At the transition into findings, the writer identifies the participants whose accounts form the basis of the themes.
feedback: The sentence identifies whose experience is represented, not when interviews happened.
It says nothing about whether nonparticipants' experiences match.
The sentence looks forward to the account, not a new recruitment procedure.
At the transition into findings, the writer identifies the participants whose accounts form the basis of the themes.

questions.setup: An author writes, 'I use "resilience" here to mean the ability to restore basic services after disruption. I do not use it as a synonym for "economic growth".'
questions.prompt: What is accomplished by adding the second sentence?
options: The author demonstrates that economic growth is undesirable.
The author prevents a related but unintended reading of the key term.
The author withdraws the definition in the first sentence.
The author gives an example of restoring a basic service.
questions.explanation: The negative clarification rules out a plausible alternative interpretation after the intended meaning has been supplied.
feedback: Excluding a meaning does not evaluate the desirability of growth.
The negative clarification rules out a plausible alternative interpretation after the intended meaning has been supplied.
The first definition remains; the second sentence protects it from confusion.
No restoration event is described; an alternative meaning is excluded.

questions.setup: An essay claims that speed is the best measure of a service. The next paragraph begins, 'Imagine a clinic that sees patients quickly but repeatedly loses their records.'
questions.prompt: What is the imagined clinic intended to do in the argument?
options: Report an observed problem at a named clinic
Explain why clinics lose records when they are slow
Test the adequacy of speed as the sole measure of service quality
Define the average speed of a clinic appointment
questions.explanation: The imagined case combines speed with a serious failure, inviting readers to question whether speed alone is a sufficient measure.
feedback: 'Imagine' introduces a hypothetical case, not a documented report about a clinic.
The case describes a quick clinic and does not establish a causal account of record loss.
The imagined case combines speed with a serious failure, inviting readers to question whether speed alone is a sufficient measure.
No duration or average is provided; the example probes a criterion.

questions.setup: A review says, 'The pilot shows that the booking procedure can be run by existing staff. It leaves open whether customers actually prefer it.'
questions.prompt: What is the role of the second sentence?
options: It explains why existing staff prefer the booking procedure.
It distinguishes an unanswered evaluative question from the demonstrated practical result.
It claims that the pilot failed to run successfully.
It treats customer preference as the reason the pilot was not conducted.
questions.explanation: The writer separates the ability to operate the procedure from evidence that customers favor it.
feedback: The sentence concerns customers' preferences, which remain unestablished.
The writer separates the ability to operate the procedure from evidence that customers favor it.
The first sentence's feasibility result is left intact.
The pilot occurred; no reason for failing to conduct it is supplied.

questions.setup: A methods section describes two people independently sorting the same comments. The author wants the next sentence to explain the reason for this design, without reporting a result.
questions.prompt: Which sentence serves that function?
options: This arrangement was intended to reveal differences in how the comments were interpreted.
The reviewers agreed on 86% of the comments.
The comments were collected during the spring term.
A table of the final categories appears below.
questions.explanation: 'Was intended to' explains the purpose of using two independent reviewers without claiming that the design achieved a particular result.
feedback: 'Was intended to' explains the purpose of using two independent reviewers without claiming that the design achieved a particular result.
This reports an outcome of the procedure rather than its intended purpose.
This adds collection background, not the reason for independent sorting.
This signposts where results are displayed rather than explaining the design.

questions.setup: A reply states, 'Even if the new system is faster, that does not answer the concern about accessibility.'
questions.prompt: What does the opening clause do in the reply?
options: It establishes speed as the only relevant basis for the reply.
It denies that the new system could be faster.
It identifies lack of accessibility as the cause of greater speed.
It allows the speed claim for argument without letting it settle the other issue.
questions.explanation: 'Even if' grants the possible speed advantage while maintaining that it is insufficient to answer an accessibility objection.
feedback: The reply argues that accessibility remains a separate concern.
The opening entertains the claim; it does not deny it.
The relationship is argumentative relevance, not a stated causal connection.
'Even if' grants the possible speed advantage while maintaining that it is insufficient to answer an accessibility objection.

questions.setup: An essay recounts how one remote worker arranged childcare around meetings. It then says, 'The example illustrates a wider point: flexibility is useful only when workers can exercise it in practice.'
questions.prompt: What shift occurs in the second sentence?
options: From an established principle to a chronological account of its origin
From praise of one worker to criticism of that worker's choices
From a factual anecdote to instructions for repeating the same childcare arrangement
From a particular experience to a general principle it illustrates
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly uses the individual case to articulate a broader point about meaningful flexibility.
feedback: The anecdote precedes the principle; no history of the principle is given.
The broader point concerns conditions of flexibility, not a personal judgment about the worker.
The writer generalizes the lesson rather than prescribing the person's arrangement.
The writer explicitly uses the individual case to articulate a broader point about meaningful flexibility.

questions.setup: A guide introduces a complex filing system by saying, 'Think of it as a library: broad subjects are like shelves, and individual records are like books.'
questions.prompt: Why introduce the library comparison?
options: To argue that the filing system should be used only by librarians
To report that the filing system was originally designed for books
To explain an unfamiliar structure through a familiar one
To show that physical shelves are required to use the system
questions.explanation: The analogy maps broad subjects and records onto shelves and books, making the organization easier to understand.
feedback: The library is a familiar comparison, not a restriction on users.
No historical origin is given.
The analogy maps broad subjects and records onto shelves and books, making the organization easier to understand.
The comparison explains relationships; it does not specify physical equipment.

questions.setup: After presenting the case for expanding a museum, an essay says, 'So far, the discussion has assumed that growth is the objective. That assumption itself now needs examination.'
questions.prompt: What does this passage signal?
options: A summary confirming that expansion is the settled conclusion
A turn from assessing means to questioning the underlying goal
A change from argument to a list of construction instructions
A correction of the dates on which the museum grew
questions.explanation: The writer identifies growth as the previously accepted objective and makes that objective the next issue for scrutiny.
feedback: The writer reopens an underlying assumption rather than settling the conclusion.
The writer identifies growth as the previously accepted objective and makes that objective the next issue for scrutiny.
No procedural instructions are introduced.
The passage concerns a premise of the discussion, not historical dates.

questions.setup: A review discusses faster service in busy branches and higher costs in quiet ones. It concludes, 'The policy's value depends less on a single national verdict than on where it is applied.'
questions.prompt: How does the conclusion relate to the mixed findings?
options: It rejects the favorable findings because other branches had costs.
It averages the measured costs into one numerical result.
It integrates the contrasting findings into a context-dependent assessment.
It attributes the conflicting findings to mistakes in the review.
questions.explanation: The writer draws the two patterns together by arguing that application context matters more than one overall judgment.
feedback: The conclusion does not discard either pattern; it locates their relevance in different settings.
No average or other numerical synthesis is given.
The writer draws the two patterns together by arguing that application context matters more than one overall judgment.
The conclusion treats the differences as meaningful context effects, not identified errors.

questions.setup: A response states, 'Calling the review "hostile" tells us how it was received. The relevant question is whether its specific objections survive scrutiny.'
questions.prompt: What argumentative move does the second sentence make?
options: It infers the reviewer's intention from readers' reactions.
It treats the objections as sound because they provoked hostility.
It distinguishes evaluation of the objections from reactions to the review.
It rejects scrutiny of the objections until the reviewer's tone improves.
questions.explanation: The writer shifts the basis of judgment from how the review felt to whether its reasons withstand examination.
feedback: The writer redirects attention away from reception rather than inferring a hostile intention.
The objections are proposed for scrutiny, not validated by their reception.
The writer shifts the basis of judgment from how the review felt to whether its reasons withstand examination.
The sentence prioritizes scrutiny now; it does not make it dependent on a change of tone.

questions.setup: A historian writes, 'The account explains why the committee believed the rumor. It does not establish that the rumor was true.'
questions.prompt: What distinction structures the two sentences?
options: A distinction between explaining belief and justifying its content
A distinction between an early rumor and a later rumor
A distinction between a mistaken belief and a belief already disproved
A distinction between the committee's public and private statements
questions.explanation: A cause or explanation of the committee's belief does not by itself provide evidence that what they believed was true.
feedback: A cause or explanation of the committee's belief does not by itself provide evidence that what they believed was true.
The same rumor is discussed at two explanatory levels, not two stages.
The passage withholds a truth judgment; it does not establish either error or disproof.
The context supplies no public-private comparison.

questions.setup: A researcher writes, 'Granted, the participants were unusually experienced. Nevertheless, their accounts identify questions worth putting to newcomers; they do not supply newcomers' answers.'
questions.prompt: How does the passage respond to the limitation?
options: It treats the limitation as a reason to generalize the participants' answers.
It replaces the experienced participants' accounts with evidence from newcomers.
It preserves a role for the evidence while changing what that role can support.
It accepts the limitation only provisionally until the questions are answered.
questions.explanation: The experience bias is conceded, but the accounts remain useful for generating questions rather than answering them for a different group.
feedback: The final clause expressly distinguishes useful questions from transferable answers.
Newcomers are a proposed next audience for inquiry; their evidence has not been supplied.
The experience bias is conceded, but the accounts remain useful for generating questions rather than answering them for a different group.
The limitation is granted, not made contingent on later answers.

questions.setup: A critique notes, 'The introduction uses "participation" to mean attending meetings. The conclusion uses it to mean shaping decisions. The apparent improvement depends on this shift.'
questions.prompt: What is the final sentence diagnosing?
options: A disagreement among participants about when meetings occurred
A successful refinement that makes the earlier and later measures equivalent
A change in the sequence of events that explains the improvement
A change in meaning that makes the conclusion appear better supported than it is
questions.explanation: The author moves between attendance and influence, and the critique identifies that shift as doing the work of the improvement claim.
feedback: The critique concerns the author's shifting use of a term, not participants' memories.
The two meanings are distinguished, not shown to be interchangeable measures.
The shift is semantic within the argument, not a reported historical event.
The author moves between attendance and influence, and the critique identifies that shift as doing the work of the improvement claim.

questions.setup: An author responds, 'The counterexample defeats the claim that the method works in every setting. It does not defeat the narrower claim that it works when the specified conditions hold.'
questions.prompt: What is the response's main argumentative function?
options: To deny that the counterexample is a genuine case
To redefine the method so that it cannot be tested
To use the counterexample as direct evidence that the narrower thesis is true
To preserve a restricted thesis while conceding the failure of a broader one
questions.explanation: The author acknowledges the counterexample's target and explains why its force does not automatically extend to a conditional version.
feedback: The first sentence accepts its force against the unrestricted claim.
The response distinguishes two claims; it does not say the conditions are untestable.
Showing that an objection misses a thesis is not itself positive evidence proving that thesis.
The author acknowledges the counterexample's target and explains why its force does not automatically extend to a conditional version.

questions.setup: A recommendation states, 'Even setting aside the projected savings, the change is justified by the need to replace unsupported software.'
questions.prompt: What does 'even setting aside' accomplish?
options: It concedes that the projected savings have been disproved.
It claims an independent justification that does not rely on the disputed benefit.
It makes replacement conditional on the savings later materializing.
It identifies projected savings as the explanation for the software losing support.
questions.explanation: By removing savings from consideration, the writer argues that the need for replacement is sufficient to sustain the recommendation.
feedback: Setting a point aside for the argument does not reject its truth.
By removing savings from consideration, the writer argues that the need for replacement is sufficient to sustain the recommendation.
The recommendation is presented as supportable without relying on savings.
The sentence offers a separate justification, not that causal account.

questions.setup: An exhibition review says, 'The curator reads the empty room as an invitation to reflect; several visitors read the same emptiness as an absence of content.'
questions.prompt: What does the sentence set against each other?
options: Two factual accounts of whether the room was occupied
An artist's intention and proof that visitors misunderstood it
Two interpretations of a shared feature
A sequence in which reflection gradually became dissatisfaction
questions.explanation: The empty room is the common object; the contrast lies in the significance assigned to it by different observers.
feedback: Neither side disputes the emptiness; they evaluate what it means differently.
The curator's interpretation is not established as the artist's intention or as a standard proving visitor error.
The empty room is the common object; the contrast lies in the significance assigned to it by different observers.
The sentence juxtaposes perspectives rather than describing one person's changing response over time.

questions.setup: A debate frames the choice as either closing a museum or retaining its current structure. A response says, 'That overlooks the possibility of keeping the collection open while transferring administration.'
questions.prompt: What role does the response play?
options: It challenges the framing by identifying an excluded alternative.
It supplies a reason for preferring closure within the original two options.
It accepts the existing structure but changes the name used for it.
It shows that closure and unchanged administration have identical effects.
questions.explanation: The proposed combination separates public access from administration, showing that the original either-or choice is incomplete.
feedback: The proposed combination separates public access from administration, showing that the original either-or choice is incomplete.
The response adds a different option rather than choosing closure.
Transferring administration is a substantive alternative, not a renamed unchanged structure.
The response questions the completeness of the option set, not the equality of the two outcomes.

questions.setup: A report recounts one resident's difficulty appealing a decision, then states, 'This case shows how the procedure can fail, not how frequently it does so.'
questions.prompt: What does the qualification specify about the case's role?
options: That the resident's account is too doubtful to contribute to the report
That it illustrates a possible failure mechanism without estimating prevalence
That the case establishes the usual outcome of appeals
That the case proves the procedure should be abandoned rather than repaired
questions.explanation: 'How' concerns the way failure can occur; 'how frequently' is a separate question the single case is not used to answer.
feedback: The case is assigned a useful explanatory role rather than dismissed as unreliable.
'How' concerns the way failure can occur; 'how frequently' is a separate question the single case is not used to answer.
The sentence explicitly withholds an inference about frequency.
The case's evidential role is clarified without making that policy recommendation.

questions.setup: A critic calls consultation an obstacle to reform. A reply says, 'Consultation does not merely slow reform down; it helps determine what would count as a successful reform.'
questions.prompt: What is the reply doing beyond denying that consultation is an obstacle?
options: It redefines consultation as part of establishing the goal of reform.
It concedes the critic's definition of success and disputes only the timetable.
It argues that slower procedures are necessarily more successful.
It treats consultation as evidence that reform has already succeeded.
questions.explanation: The reply shifts consultation from an external delay to a process that helps specify the standard by which reform should be judged.
feedback: The reply shifts consultation from an external delay to a process that helps specify the standard by which reform should be judged.
The reply questions how success is defined, not merely when it is reached.
No general rule connecting slowness with success is offered.
The reply describes a role in defining success, not a completed successful outcome.

questions.setup: A response argues, 'Suppose the attendance figures are accurate. The recommendation still requires the additional premise that attendance is the right measure of success.'
questions.prompt: What argumentative gap does the response identify?
options: A missing evaluative premise between accepted figures and the recommendation
A missing calculation needed to establish whether the figures are accurate
A contradiction showing that attendance cannot be counted
A conflict between two recommendations already supported by the same premise
questions.explanation: The figures are granted for discussion, but the recommendation also needs justification for treating attendance as the relevant standard.
feedback: The figures are granted for discussion, but the recommendation also needs justification for treating attendance as the relevant standard.
Accuracy is temporarily assumed rather than examined in the response.
The response does not question the possibility of counting attendance.
Only one recommendation and its missing support are discussed.

questions.setup: A reviewer writes, 'The label "community" is carrying more weight than the analysis supports: it turns a set of neighboring households into a group with supposedly shared priorities.'
questions.prompt: What is the criticism directed at?
options: The author's decision to study households rather than public organizations
The unsupported inference imported through the chosen label
The use of an unfamiliar word that readers cannot understand
The claim that neighboring households have disagreed about priorities
questions.explanation: The reviewer argues that naming neighbors 'a community' makes shared priorities seem established without supplying evidence for them.
feedback: The objection concerns an inference from the label, not the choice of population itself.
The reviewer argues that naming neighbors 'a community' makes shared priorities seem established without supplying evidence for them.
The issue is the word's argumentative implications, not its unfamiliarity.
The passage criticizes presumed agreement; it does not identify a documented disagreement.

questions.setup: A commentary states, 'The policy grants applicants the right to be considered. Treating that right as a right to be selected makes the subsequent criticism miss its target.'
questions.prompt: Why does the writer distinguish the two rights?
options: To argue that applicants should have neither right
To show that being considered normally causes selection
To explain the chronological order of two guaranteed outcomes
To expose a criticism based on attributing a stronger promise to the policy
questions.explanation: A guarantee of consideration is being misread as a guarantee of selection, so the criticism addresses a promise the policy does not make.
feedback: The first right is accepted; neither is rejected as a policy recommendation.
No frequency or causal connection is asserted.
Selection is not established as guaranteed, so the point is conceptual rather than merely temporal.
A guarantee of consideration is being misread as a guarantee of selection, so the criticism addresses a promise the policy does not make.

questions.setup: An essay compares a digital platform to a public square, then adds, 'The analogy makes exclusion visible, but it cannot tell us which access rules are justified. For that, we need an argument about rights and responsibilities.'
questions.prompt: What does the final sentence do after the limit on the analogy?
options: It abandons the problem of exclusion because the analogy is imperfect.
It supplies a second analogy intended to settle the access rules.
It treats the visibility of exclusion as sufficient justification for any access rule.
It identifies the further kind of argument needed to answer the unresolved question.
questions.explanation: The writer moves from what the analogy reveals to the rights-and-responsibilities reasoning required to justify rules.
feedback: The essay keeps the problem and identifies a different kind of reasoning needed to address it.
No new analogy is offered; a normative argument is requested.
The preceding sentence explicitly denies that the analogy settles justification.
The writer moves from what the analogy reveals to the rights-and-responsibilities reasoning required to justify rules.

questions.setup: An essay opens with a librarian placing a book on a shelf, apparently a routine act. After examining how classification reflects institutional choices, it returns to that scene: 'The shelving decision now looks less like neutral storage than an act of interpretation.'
questions.prompt: What does the return to the opening scene accomplish?
options: It adds an independent observation that corroborates the opening anecdote.
It summarizes the chronological history of library shelving practices.
It reinterprets the initial example through the argument developed since its introduction.
It withdraws the opening account by claiming that the librarian did not actually shelve the book.
questions.explanation: Returning to the same action lets readers apply the essay's account of classification and revise the initially neutral interpretation.
feedback: The essay revisits the same scene; it does not provide a second independent observation.
The passage changes how one action is understood, not its place in a historical sequence.
Returning to the same action lets readers apply the essay's account of classification and revise the initially neutral interpretation.
The action remains the same; its significance is reassessed rather than its occurrence denied.

questions.setup: A reply says, 'The dispute turns not on whether the files were accessible, but on whether access without notice counts as meaningful access.'
questions.prompt: What does this formulation redirect?
options: Attention from access to the technical cause of the missing notice
Attention from the dispute to an unrelated definition of a file
Attention from notice to proof that the files did not exist
Attention from the existence of access to the adequacy of that access
questions.explanation: The writer sets aside the binary factual question and focuses on the criterion for treating access as meaningful.
feedback: The sentence asks what should count as meaningful access, not why notice was missing.
The reformulation remains within the central access dispute.
File existence is not challenged; the quality of access is the issue.
The writer sets aside the binary factual question and focuses on the criterion for treating access as meaningful.

questions.setup: An essay states, 'The footnote looks incidental. Yet removing it would turn a claim about one institution into a claim about institutions generally.'
questions.prompt: What is the writer doing by contrasting appearance and consequence?
options: Arguing that the footnote is irrelevant because of its placement
Replacing the footnote with a general claim the author prefers
Showing that an apparently minor element performs essential limiting work
Explaining why the author placed the footnote at the end of the essay
questions.explanation: The footnote's visual or structural modesty contrasts with its role in keeping the claim tied to one institution.
feedback: The consequential change from removing it is evidence of importance, not irrelevance.
The passage warns about the change, without endorsing it.
The footnote's visual or structural modesty contrasts with its role in keeping the claim tied to one institution.
No account of the author's placement decision is supplied.

questions.setup: A reviewer argues, 'The objection rejects a distinction between public and private action, yet relies on that very distinction to classify the examples it cites.'
questions.prompt: What problem does the reviewer identify?
options: The objection depends on a distinction it seeks to discredit.
The objection cites examples in the wrong chronological order.
The objection offers too few examples to estimate the frequency of private action.
The objection gives a neutral definition of the distinction before rejecting it.
questions.explanation: The classification of its own examples uses the very conceptual division the objection rejects, creating a self-undermining dependence.
feedback: The classification of its own examples uses the very conceptual division the objection rejects, creating a self-undermining dependence.
The issue concerns the basis for classification, not the timing of examples.
No frequency estimate or sample-size issue is raised.
The reviewer says the distinction is relied on in the objection's reasoning, not merely defined for discussion.

questions.setup: A reviewer writes, 'I am not claiming that the interpretation is false. I am claiming that the passage equally supports a competing interpretation.'
questions.prompt: What does the second sentence do to the reviewer's criticism?
options: It withdraws the criticism by accepting both readings as true.
It specifies a challenge to uniqueness of support rather than a claim of falsity.
It supplies evidence that the competing reading is better supported.
It changes the disagreement from interpretation to the authenticity of the passage.
questions.explanation: The reviewer argues that the evidence does not select this reading over a rival, while withholding a verdict that the reading is false.
feedback: Equal textual support does not amount to asserting that both interpretations are true.
The reviewer argues that the evidence does not select this reading over a rival, while withholding a verdict that the reading is false.
The reviewer explicitly says the support is equal, not stronger for the rival.
The passage's authenticity is not challenged; its capacity to distinguish readings is.

questions.setup: A review concludes, 'By explaining departure solely through individual ambition, the account makes workplace exclusion disappear from view.'
questions.prompt: What does this conclusion criticize?
options: The account's failure to describe any individual's ambitions

The account's proof that workplace exclusion does not occur
The decision to study departure before studying arrival
questions.explanation: The review argues that an exclusively individual explanation sidelines an institutional factor that also deserves attention.
feedback: Individual ambition is central to the account, not absent from it.
The review argues that an exclusively individual explanation sidelines an institutional factor that also deserves attention.
The review describes exclusion becoming invisible in the explanation, not being disproved.
The criticism concerns explanatory framing rather than chronological research order.

questions.setup: This suitcase is too big for the small locker.
questions.prompt: What does 'big' describe?

its weight
its price
its age

A big suitcase can be light; 'big' describes size.
A high price makes something expensive, not big.

questions.setup: The room is small, but it has a large window and lots of light.
questions.prompt: What does 'small' tell us about the room?

It has little noise.

A small room has little space; it can still be bright.
Little noise makes a room quiet, not small.

questions.setup: I take the fast train because the journey takes less time.

'Fast' describes speed; the train covers the journey in less time.

questions.setup: The film will begin at eight. Please be in your seat before then.

'Begin' and 'start' both describe the first point of an activity.

questions.setup: Eva is happy about her new job. She smiles as she tells her family.

questions.setup: Rui feels sad when his sister moves far away. He will miss her.

questions.setup: I have washed the plates. They are clean, but they are still wet.

questions.setup: This house is old. My grandparents lived here sixty years ago, and it is still in good condition.

questions.setup: The route is easy to follow: go straight and turn left at the bridge.

Easy directions can be understood and followed without much difficulty.

questions.setup: The fresh bread has a hard crust and a soft middle.

Full means there is no space or capacity for more; the next sentence makes that limit clear.

questions.setup: Lena wants to buy a used bicycle from her neighbor.

Borrowing gives temporary use, with an expectation of return; it does not transfer ownership.

questions.setup: Nadia invited her neighbor to dinner, but he has not replied yet.

questions.setup: We are moving next month. Our new flat is on the other side of town.

questions.setup: The concert was expected to finish at ten, but it finished at nine thirty. It ended early.
