questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the agreed arrangement.
questions.prompt: 'The courier is supposed to collect the parcel at three.'
options: The courier collected the parcel before three.
The arrangement says collection should happen at three.
The courier is able to lift the parcel at three.
The courier would prefer a three o'clock collection.
questions.explanation: Be supposed to can refer to an agreed plan or an expected duty; it does not confirm performance.
feedback: Is supposed to describes the arrangement, not a completed collection.
Be supposed to can refer to an agreed plan or an expected duty; it does not confirm performance.
Ability to lift is different from an arrangement to collect.
The sentence reports what is arranged, not the courier's preference.

questions.setup: Choose the words that say the necessary permission was missing, not that the action was physically impossible.
questions.prompt: I ___ access the archive yesterday because the manager had not approved my request.
options: wasn't allowed to
wasn't able to
didn't need to
wasn't willing to
questions.explanation: Wasn't allowed to directly identifies permission as the missing condition.
feedback: Wasn't allowed to directly identifies permission as the missing condition.
This describes inability more broadly; it does not explicitly identify lack of permission as requested.
This removes a need to access the archive, not permission.
This would mean you refused or did not want to enter, not that approval was missing.

questions.setup: The technician expects the repair to last about an hour. Choose the words expressing that expectation, not necessity or mere possibility.
questions.prompt: The printer ___ be ready by four.
options: might
should
must not
has to
questions.explanation: Should can express an expected result based on what normally happens or on current information.
feedback: Might leaves readiness as a possibility without expressing the technician's expectation.
Should can express an expected result based on what normally happens or on current information.
Must not gives a negative rule or conclusion, not the expected completion time.
Has to would make four a necessary deadline, which is not what the technician is estimating.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence meaning that early starts now feel normal to the speaker.
questions.prompt: The speaker has worked morning shifts for a year.
options: I used to get up at five.
I ought to get up at five.
I'm used to getting up at five.
I'd rather get up at five.
questions.explanation: Be used to + -ing means an activity is familiar or normal to you.
feedback: Used to + basic verb describes a former habit rather than present familiarity.
Ought to recommends the action, not how familiar it feels.
Be used to + -ing means an activity is familiar or normal to you.
Would rather expresses a preference, not being accustomed to the routine.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence expressing a personal preference for walking instead of taking a taxi.
questions.prompt: Both options are available and allowed.
options: I ought to walk rather than take a taxi.
I have to walk rather than take a taxi.
I might walk rather than take a taxi.
I'd rather walk than take a taxi.
questions.explanation: Would rather + verb + than states a preference between two available actions.
feedback: Ought to says walking is advisable, not simply what the speaker prefers.
Have to makes walking necessary, contrary to both options being available.
Might describes a possible choice without directly stating a preference.
Would rather + verb + than states a preference between two available actions.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of 'can' in this general description.
questions.prompt: 'This coastal road can be very busy in summer.'
options: Drivers have permission to make the road busy.
The road needs heavy traffic in summer.
Heavy traffic occurs on this road at some times in summer.
The speaker is predicting heavy traffic this afternoon.
questions.explanation: 'Can' can describe an occasional or typical possibility, such as summer traffic.
feedback: This is not permission; 'can' describes a feature that sometimes occurs.
'Can' does not express a need for traffic.
'Can' can describe an occasional or typical possibility, such as summer traffic.
The sentence is a general description of summer conditions, not a forecast for a specific afternoon.

questions.setup: The manager says a printed copy is unnecessary. Choose a sentence with the same meaning.
questions.prompt: 'The electronic signature is enough.'
options: You needn't print the form.
You mustn't print the form.
You shouldn't print the form.
You can't print the form.
questions.explanation: Needn't means there is no necessity to print; printing is not thereby forbidden.
feedback: Needn't means there is no necessity to print; printing is not thereby forbidden.
Mustn't prohibits printing; the manager has only said it is unnecessary.
Shouldn't advises against printing, which goes beyond saying it is not needed.
Can't states an inability or prohibition instead of removing a requirement.

questions.setup: Choose the negative form that preserves this strong advice.
questions.prompt: 'You'd better ___ the warning light.'
options: not ignore
don't ignore
not to ignore
not ignoring
questions.explanation: The usual negative is had better not + basic verb: you'd better not ignore.
feedback: The usual negative is had better not + basic verb: you'd better not ignore.
Do not add don't after had better. Put not before ignore.
Had better takes the basic verb without to, including after not.
Had better not is followed by ignore rather than ignoring.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of 'would' in this memory.
questions.prompt: 'During our first year in business, we would meet every Friday to compare sales.'
options: The meetings were a future plan that had not begun.
The speaker is making a polite request for a meeting.
Meeting on Fridays was a repeated past activity.
The meetings were possible only under an unstated condition.
questions.explanation: 'Would' can describe repeated actions within an established past period.
feedback: The opening time phrase and 'every Friday' frame a remembered routine, not an unstarted plan.
This statement recounts what happened; it is not a request addressed to someone.
'Would' can describe repeated actions within an established past period.
No hypothetical condition is needed here because 'would' describes an actual past routine.

questions.setup: Leo has refused several offers to discuss the problem. Choose the meaning of "won't" here.
questions.prompt: 'He won't talk to us about it.'
options: He is unable to speak our language.
He refuses to discuss it with us.
He is not permitted to speak to us.
He does not need to discuss it with us.
questions.explanation: "Won't" can express unwillingness, as Leo's repeated refusals show.
feedback: The stated problem is refusal, not a lack of language ability.
"Won't" can express unwillingness, as Leo's repeated refusals show.
Nothing indicates a ban; Leo has chosen to reject the invitations.
Lack of necessity does not explain the unwillingness highlighted in the context.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that explicitly asks for permission in a formal interview.
questions.prompt: You want the interviewer to allow you to consult your notes.
options: Must I consult my notes?
May I consult my notes?
Should I consult my notes?
Will I consult my notes?
questions.explanation: May I...? is a conventional formal way to request permission for your own action.
feedback: Must I asks whether using notes is required, not permitted.
May I...? is a conventional formal way to request permission for your own action.
Should I asks for advice about whether notes would be useful.
Will I asks about a future action rather than requesting permission.

questions.setup: The rule now requires online submission. Choose the words describing a possible future change to that requirement.
questions.prompt: If the website stays offline, we ___ submit the appeal by post instead.
options: used to
might have to
would rather
must not
questions.explanation: Might makes the future necessity uncertain: postal submission may become necessary.
feedback: Used to describes a past habit, not a possible future requirement.
Might makes the future necessity uncertain: postal submission may become necessary.
Would rather states a preference, not a change that may be required.
Must not would forbid postal submission, the opposite of the possible requirement.

questions.setup: Complete the sentence with the correct grammar to express a possibility about the past.
questions.prompt: Mina cannot find the file. She may ___ it on the train yesterday.
options: has left
have leave
have left
had left
questions.explanation: May have + past participle expresses a possible past event: may have left.
feedback: After may, use the basic form have, not has.
The perfect phrase needs the past participle left after have.
May have + past participle expresses a possible past event: may have left.
A modal takes the basic form have, not had, even when the event is in the past.

questions.setup: Express the speaker's strong conclusion from the evidence, without presenting it as an obligation or an uncertain guess.
questions.prompt: The office is locked and its closing alarm is set. The staff ___ have left for the day.
options: should
must
might
ought to
questions.explanation: Must have left expresses a confident conclusion about a past event from present evidence.
feedback: Should have left would express an expectation or judgment about what was appropriate, rather than the strong inference requested.
Must have left expresses a confident conclusion about a past event from present evidence.
Might have left presents departure as only a possibility.
Ought to have left concerns what was advisable or expected, not the specified strong inference.

questions.setup: The security camera proves that Elena remained in another city all evening. Rule out her presence at yesterday's meeting.
questions.prompt: Elena ___ at the meeting.
options: should have been
might have been
can't have been
must have been
questions.explanation: Can't have been rules out a past situation because it conflicts with the evidence.
feedback: This says attendance was expected or advisable, not that it was impossible.
This leaves attendance possible despite the evidence ruling it out.
Can't have been rules out a past situation because it conflicts with the evidence.
This strongly concludes that she attended, contradicting the evidence.

questions.setup: Nora paid to print the report, then learned that a digital copy was enough. Choose the sentence that states that the completed printing was unnecessary.
questions.prompt: What can you say to Nora?
options: You mustn't have printed it.
You couldn't have printed it.
You might not have printed it.
You needn't have printed it.
questions.explanation: Needn't have + past participle says an action occurred but was not necessary.
feedback: This does not express lack of necessity; depending on context it can convey a negative conclusion about whether printing happened.
This denies the possibility or ability to print, contrary to the completed printing.
This makes non-printing a possibility, although the context confirms that Nora printed it.
Needn't have + past participle says an action occurred but was not necessary.

questions.setup: A discount was available, but the team did not use it. Describe the missed opportunity.
questions.prompt: We ___ money by booking earlier, but we paid the full price.
options: must have saved
will have saved
could have saved
had to save
questions.explanation: Could have saved describes an available past opportunity that the following clause shows was missed.
feedback: This concludes that a saving actually occurred, contradicting payment of the full price.
This expresses a confident conclusion or future completion, not the unrealized opportunity described.
Could have saved describes an available past opportunity that the following clause shows was missed.
This states a necessity to save money without expressing the missed opportunity.

questions.setup: The message is missing, and you do not know whether the server delivered it. Express the possibility that it was not delivered.
questions.prompt: The message ___ reached the client.
options: might not have
cannot have
should not have
must have
questions.explanation: Might not have reached means non-delivery is possible, while delivery remains possible too.
feedback: Might not have reached means non-delivery is possible, while delivery remains possible too.
Cannot have rules out delivery more strongly than the stated uncertainty allows.
Should not have judges delivery as inappropriate or unexpected rather than merely uncertain.
Must have reached strongly concludes that delivery occurred, reversing the intended uncertainty.

questions.setup: You know the team sent the wrong price list. Express criticism of that completed action.
questions.prompt: They ___ the figures before sending the list.
options: should have checked
may have checked
must have checked
would have checked
questions.explanation: Should have checked says checking was the appropriate past action and implies it was omitted here.
feedback: Should have checked says checking was the appropriate past action and implies it was omitted here.
This speculates that checking happened, instead of criticizing its omission.
This infers that checking occurred, which is not the judgment requested.
This describes an imagined outcome under a condition rather than directly criticizing what happened.

questions.setup: The speaker is confident about the result of an imagined past condition. Choose the modal that expresses that expected result, not merely a possible one.
questions.prompt: If I had seen your message in time, I ___ have joined the call.
options: might
would
must
may
questions.explanation: Would have joined presents joining as the expected result of the unreal past condition.
feedback: Might have joined leaves the imagined result uncertain, weaker than the confidence specified.
Would have joined presents joining as the expected result of the unreal past condition.
Must have joined normally makes a strong inference about an actual past event, not this unreal result.
May have joined leaves the event possible rather than presenting the confident imagined result requested.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that preserves the original advice while putting the documents first.
questions.prompt: 'You should store these documents securely.'
options: These documents should store securely.
These documents should have stored securely.
These documents should been stored securely.
These documents should be stored securely.
questions.explanation: Should be + past participle keeps the advice while making the documents the recipients of the action.
feedback: This active form does not express someone storing the documents; the intended passive needs be stored.
Have stored is active and perfect; it does not preserve the present advice in the passive.
Been cannot directly follow should. Use should be stored.
Should be + past participle keeps the advice while making the documents the recipients of the action.

questions.setup: Read only what the sentence states. Choose the supported conclusion.
questions.prompt: 'I didn't need to attend the briefing.'
options: I attended, and attendance was unnecessary.
Attendance was unnecessary; the sentence alone does not tell us whether I attended.
I was forbidden to attend the briefing.
I stayed away because I was unable to attend.
questions.explanation: Didn't need to states lack of necessity. Further context establishes whether the action happened.
feedback: That can fit a context, but didn't need to does not itself state that attendance occurred.
Didn't need to states lack of necessity. Further context establishes whether the action happened.
Lack of need is not a prohibition.
The sentence reports no necessity; it does not state inability or establish non-attendance.

questions.setup: The parcel was sent by a reliable overnight service yesterday. Express an expectation about its arrival by now, without criticizing anyone.
questions.prompt: The parcel ___ arrived by now.
options: should have
must not have
ought not to have
could not have
questions.explanation: Should have can express an expected completed event; here the delivery schedule supports expected arrival.
feedback: Should have can express an expected completed event; here the delivery schedule supports expected arrival.
This would suggest a strong negative conclusion about arrival, not the positive expectation given.
This expresses an expectation or judgment against arrival, the opposite of the intended meaning.
This rules out arrival rather than expecting it.

questions.setup: Complete the sentence with the correct grammar for an ongoing action inferred in the past.
questions.prompt: No one answered during the shift. The operators must ___ a break when I called.
options: have taking
be took
had been taking
have been taking
questions.explanation: Must have been + -ing infers an action that was in progress at the past time.
feedback: The ongoing perfect phrase needs been between have and taking.
An ongoing action needs taking, and the past inference requires have been.
After must, use have rather than had: must have been taking.
Must have been + -ing infers an action that was in progress at the past time.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct completion for a possible past action done to the attachment.
questions.prompt: The attachment might ___ by the email filter.
options: have removed
have been remove
been removed
have been removed
questions.explanation: Might have been + past participle combines past possibility with a passive action.
feedback: This active form would make the attachment do the removing, not receive it.
Use the past participle removed after been in this passive phrase.
The modal perfect requires have before been: might have been removed.
Might have been + past participle combines past possibility with a passive action.

questions.setup: It is ten o'clock, and staff training is scheduled from nine until eleven. Express the activity expected to be in progress now.
questions.prompt: The staff ___ in the training room now.
options: should have worked
should have been working
should be working
should have to work
questions.explanation: Should be + -ing expresses an activity expected to be happening at the present moment.
feedback: This looks back at completed work instead of describing expected activity in progress now.
This looks back at an expected ongoing activity; it does not directly locate the expected work in progress now.
Should be + -ing expresses an activity expected to be happening at the present moment.
This introduces expected necessity, not simply an activity expected to be underway.

questions.setup: The repair failed. A different tool offered a chance of success, but success was not certain. Preserve that uncertainty in the imagined past result.
questions.prompt: With a longer cable, we ___ have reached the socket.
options: might
would
must
will
questions.explanation: Might have reached presents success as possible under the unreal condition, without guaranteeing it.
feedback: Might have reached presents success as possible under the unreal condition, without guaranteeing it.
Would have reached presents reaching as the expected result, stronger than the chance specified.
Must have reached makes a strong inference about a past result, not this uncertain alternative.
Will have reached expresses a confident completion or inference, not the uncertain unreal result.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence expressing regret about not asking for a written quotation before the repair.
questions.prompt: The bill is much higher than you expected.
options: I must have asked for a quotation.
I ought to have asked for a quotation.
I may have asked for a quotation.
I used to ask for a quotation.
questions.explanation: Ought to have + past participle expresses what would have been advisable before the past event.
feedback: This concludes that you did ask, contrary to the stated omission.
Ought to have + past participle expresses what would have been advisable before the past event.
This leaves whether you asked uncertain, rather than evaluating the known omission.
This describes a former habit rather than regret about this repair.

questions.setup: The technician is reasonably optimistic but has not guaranteed success. Choose the meaning of the combined modal phrase.
questions.prompt: 'With the replacement part, we should be able to restore the signal.'
options: The technician says that using the part is a compulsory repair step.
The technician concludes that the signal has already been restored.
The technician expects the part to make restoring the signal possible.
The technician gives the team permission to restore the signal.
questions.explanation: Should expresses an expectation, while be able to concerns capability; together they predict that restoration will be possible.
feedback: The comment expresses expected capability, not an instruction making a particular step compulsory.
Be able to restore concerns capability for a coming action, not completed restoration.
Should expresses an expectation, while be able to concerns capability; together they predict that restoration will be possible.
The technician is estimating what the repair can achieve, not granting authorization.

questions.setup: The speaker is confident that packing will finish before the collection time. Choose the completion expressing this future completion.
questions.prompt: By the time the van arrives tomorrow, we ___ all the boxes.
options: would have packed
must have packed
might have packed
will have packed
questions.explanation: Will have + past participle locates completion before a specified future point.
feedback: Would have packed suggests an unreal or reported perspective, not this direct confident future prediction.
Must have packed normally draws an inference about completed packing rather than locating a future completion as requested.
Might have packed leaves completion uncertain, weaker than the stated confidence.
Will have + past participle locates completion before a specified future point.

questions.setup: The assistant did disclose the password. You want to criticize that action, not guess whether it happened.
questions.prompt: She ___ the password in a public chat.
options: shouldn't have posted
can't have posted
might not have posted
didn't have to post
questions.explanation: Shouldn't have posted evaluates the completed action as inappropriate.
feedback: Shouldn't have posted evaluates the completed action as inappropriate.
This denies the possibility of the posting, but the context confirms it happened.
This expresses uncertainty about non-posting, not criticism of the known action.
This says posting was unnecessary, which does not directly express the requested criticism.

questions.setup: The deadline requires the report to be finished before Monday's meeting. Choose the completion that explicitly expresses completion by that point.
questions.prompt: We need ___ the report by the time the meeting begins.
options: to have finishing
to have finished
have finished
to having finished
questions.explanation: Need to have + past participle makes completion before the stated point explicit.
feedback: The perfect construction takes finished, not finishing, after have.
Need to have + past participle makes completion before the stated point explicit.
Ordinary positive need requires to before the following verb phrase.
After need to, use the basic form have, not having.

questions.setup: The editor expresses a preference about the researcher's future action. Choose the completion that preserves that future reference and uses the standard would-rather pattern.
questions.prompt: I'd rather you ___ the results until we have checked the calculations.
options: hadn't announced
didn't announced
didn't announce
not to announce
questions.explanation: With a different subject after would rather, a past form can express a present or future preference.
feedback: The past perfect would express a preference about an earlier announcement, not the future action specified.
Did already carries the past form; use announce, not announced, after didn't.
With a different subject after would rather, a past form can express a present or future preference.
After I'd rather you, use a finite clause such as you didn't announce, not a to-infinitive.

questions.setup: Asked what the sponsors' withdrawal means for next month's festival, an analyst gives this response. Choose the closest meaning of 'may well'.
questions.prompt: 'With two major sponsors withdrawing, the festival may well be cancelled.'
options: Cancellation is the action the analyst recommends.
Cancellation has been formally authorized by the sponsors.
Cancellation is a credible, perhaps likely outcome.
Cancellation is an established fact that the analyst concedes.
questions.explanation: 'May well' presents an outcome as quite possible or unsurprising given the circumstances, without making it certain.
feedback: The context is prediction; 'may well' does not state what organizers ought to do.
This sentence does not use 'may' to grant permission or report authorization.
'May well' presents an outcome as quite possible or unsurprising given the circumstances, without making it certain.
The analyst is estimating what may happen, not acknowledging a known cancellation.

questions.setup: Read the cautious planning statement. Choose what is and is not settled.
questions.prompt: 'If the venue loses its licence, we might have to relocate the conference.'
options: The licence will be lost, making relocation necessary.
The organizers prefer relocation if the licence is lost.
Relocation could become necessary if the licence is lost.
The organizers are permitted to relocate only if the licence is lost.
questions.explanation: Might makes the necessity expressed by have to uncertain within the stated condition.
feedback: The if-clause does not predict loss of the licence, and might leaves the resulting necessity open.
Have to concerns necessity rather than their preference.
Might makes the necessity expressed by have to uncertain within the stated condition.
Might have to does not express permission or make licence loss the only condition for it.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that preserves this formal instruction's conditional meaning.
questions.prompt: 'Should any names remain in the report, remove them before circulation.'
options: If any names remain, remove them before circulation.
Because names ought to remain, remove them before circulation.
Names are expected to remain, so remove them before circulation.
Names should have remained until circulation.
questions.explanation: Initial should + subject is a formal conditional pattern meaning if this happens to be the case.
feedback: Initial should + subject is a formal conditional pattern meaning if this happens to be the case.
Conditional should does not recommend retaining names; it introduces a possible circumstance.
The original does not predict that names will remain; it tells you what to do if they do.
This changes a conditional instruction into a judgment about an earlier action.

questions.setup: The inspector infers that cleaning was in progress when the first visitor arrived. Choose the phrase that preserves past time, ongoing action, and the room as receiver of that action.
questions.prompt: The room must ___ when the visitor arrived.
options: have been cleaning
be being cleaned
have been being cleaned
have been cleaned
questions.explanation: Must have been being cleaned combines a past inference with an ongoing passive action.
feedback: This is active and makes the room do the cleaning, rather than receive it.
This expresses an ongoing passive action but lacks the perfect form needed for the specified past inference.
Must have been being cleaned combines a past inference with an ongoing passive action.
This suggests completed cleaning rather than cleaning still in progress at the arrival time.

questions.setup: The interview is over. The speaker wishes that the interviewer had not raised salary so early. Complete the retrospective preference.
questions.prompt: I'd rather the interviewer ___ salary until the end.
options: hadn't mentioned
didn't mention
won't mention
hasn't mentioned
questions.explanation: Would rather + another subject + past perfect expresses a preference about an unreal alternative to a past action.
feedback: Would rather + another subject + past perfect expresses a preference about an unreal alternative to a past action.
A past-simple clause after would rather normally expresses a present or future preference, not this earlier completed interview.
Will not does not form the retrospective preference clause needed here.
The present perfect does not express the unreal past alternative after would rather.

questions.setup: A colleague says, 'This is her first management job.' Another replies as below. Choose the role of 'may' in the reply.
questions.prompt: 'She may be inexperienced, but she has already resolved the staffing problem.'
options: It asks whether the director is permitted to be inexperienced.
It acknowledges a drawback before introducing a counterbalancing point.
It treats the director's inexperience as an unresolved factual question.
It recommends that the director gain more experience.
questions.explanation: 'May ..., but ...' can concede an accepted point while limiting its force with a contrasting consideration.
feedback: The statement does not request permission; it accepts a known characteristic.
'May ..., but ...' can concede an accepted point while limiting its force with a contrasting consideration.
The context establishes that inexperience is known; 'may' introduces a concession here.
No recommendation is made; the speaker weighs a drawback against an achievement.

questions.setup: The exemption rules have not been finalized. Choose the interpretation of the layered modal phrase.
questions.prompt: 'Existing members may not have to submit fresh references.'
options: Existing members will be forbidden to submit fresh references.
Existing members are certain to be exempt from providing fresh references.
Existing members will probably fail to submit required fresh references.
Existing members might be exempt from providing fresh references.
questions.explanation: May expresses uncertainty about the absence of a requirement: perhaps members will not have to submit references.
feedback: Not applies to have to, removing necessity; it does not create a ban on submission.
May leaves the exemption uncertain; it does not establish it as definite.
The sentence concerns whether submission is required, not whether members will comply.
May expresses uncertainty about the absence of a requirement: perhaps members will not have to submit references.

questions.setup: Choose the claim made by the analyst, without strengthening it.
questions.prompt: 'An increase in complaints need not indicate a decline in service quality.'
options: More complaints show that service quality has stayed the same.
Service quality is required to improve when complaints increase.
A decline in service quality makes increased complaints impossible.
More complaints do not necessarily mean that service quality has declined.
questions.explanation: Need not can deny that an inference is necessary while leaving that inference possible.
feedback: Need not rejects a necessary connection; it does not establish unchanged quality.
This imposes a duty that the analyst's statement does not express.
This reverses the relationship and replaces lack of necessity with impossibility.
Need not can deny that an inference is necessary while leaving that inference possible.

questions.setup: 'Did the reviewer read the supplementary file?' 'There's no way to tell from her comments.' A colleague then says the following. Choose its meaning.
questions.prompt: 'She could have overlooked the appendix.'
options: She may actually have missed the appendix when reading.
She had an opportunity to overlook it but deliberately read it.
She ought to have ignored the appendix when reviewing the paper.
She was unable to read the appendix because access was blocked.
questions.explanation: With the event unknown, could have can speculate that overlooking it may actually have happened.
feedback: With the event unknown, could have can speculate that overlooking it may actually have happened.
An unused opportunity reading is not supported here; the context concerns an unknown past event.
Could have does not recommend ignoring material or judge that she should have done so.
The comment does not state an access problem or inability.

questions.setup: The speaker has just heard a plan to publish unverified figures. Choose the conversational purpose of this reply.
questions.prompt: 'I would have thought we should check the figures first.'
options: It confirms that the speaker checked the figures before hearing the plan.
It predicts that checking will be unnecessary if the plan changes.
It reports a past belief that the speaker now accepts was mistaken.
It softens a challenge to publishing before checking.
questions.explanation: I would have thought can soften disagreement by framing an objection as an expectation.
feedback: Thought concerns an expectation; it does not report that checking was completed.
The speaker favors checking first, not removing that step.
In this context the phrase softens a current challenge; the speaker has not withdrawn the belief.
I would have thought can soften disagreement by framing an objection as an expectation.

questions.setup: The next train is delayed by an hour, and the cafe is the only comfortable place nearby. Choose the meaning of the suggestion.
questions.prompt: 'We may as well get a coffee while we wait.'
options: Coffee is probably available, although the cafe may have run out.
Getting coffee seems a reasonable use of the unavoidable wait.
Buying coffee is a condition for being allowed to wait for the train.
The speaker strongly prefers coffee to other ways of passing the time.
questions.explanation: May as well suggests an acceptable action when there is no clearly better alternative in the circumstances.
feedback: The phrase recommends an action; it is not chiefly a guess about stock.
May as well suggests an acceptable action when there is no clearly better alternative in the circumstances.
May as well does not express a rule or a requirement for permission.
May as well presents coffee as a reasonable available option; it does not express a strong personal preference.

questions.setup: Before discussing candidates, the chair reads this line from the panel's procedure. Choose the interpretation of 'are to'.
questions.prompt: 'Panel members are to declare any personal connection with an applicant before discussion begins.'
options: Panel members are instructed to make the declaration before discussion.
Panel members are likely to make the declaration of their own accord.
Panel members would prefer to declare connections after discussion.
Panel members were expected to declare connections at an earlier meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Be to' + verb can give a formal instruction or establish an official requirement.
feedback: 'Be to' + verb can give a formal instruction or establish an official requirement.
The context identifies an instruction, not a prediction about voluntary behavior.
The statement gives neither a preference nor permission to delay the declaration.
'Are to' applies to the current instruction and does not locate it at an earlier meeting.

questions.setup: Read this invented committee procedure as a formal rule. Choose the function of 'shall'.
questions.prompt: 'The secretary shall record any declared conflict in the minutes.'
options: It offers to let the secretary decide whether recording is useful.
It imposes a duty on the secretary to record the conflict.
It predicts what the secretary will probably do based on past habits.
It invites the secretary and speaker to write the minutes together.
questions.explanation: 'Shall' can express a requirement in formal procedures; here it assigns the recording duty.
feedback: This rule assigns a duty; it does not present recording as optional.
'Shall' can express a requirement in formal procedures; here it assigns the recording duty.
In the explicitly formal rule, 'shall' is directive rather than a forecast.
The offer or suggestion use of 'Shall we...?' does not fit this third-person rule.

questions.setup: 'Have you read the revision?' 'Not yet. I sent the author a checklist covering every objection.' The reviewer then adds the statement below. Choose the reading of 'should have'.
questions.prompt: 'The author should have dealt with that objection in the revision.'
options: The reviewer knows it was omitted and is criticizing the author.
The reviewer expects a response in the unread revision.
The reviewer concludes that addressing the objection was unnecessary.
The reviewer is granting permission to address the objection later.
questions.explanation: Here 'should have' expresses expected completion based on the checklist, rather than known failure.
feedback: That reading is possible elsewhere, but this reviewer has not inspected the revision.
Here 'should have' expresses expected completion based on the checklist, rather than known failure.
'Should have' does not remove the need to address the objection.
The phrase concerns expected completion in the existing revision, not future permission.

questions.setup: The speaker travelled overnight and regretted it. Choose the sentence expressing a preference for a different completed journey, without saying the alternative actually happened.
questions.prompt: A daytime journey was also available.
options: I would rather travel during the day.
I would have to travel during the day.
I must have travelled during the day.
I would rather have travelled during the day.
questions.explanation: Would rather have + past participle expresses a preferred alternative to a past action.
feedback: This states a present or future preference rather than explicitly looking back at the completed trip.
Would have to introduces a conditional necessity, not a preference about the past journey.
This infers an actual daytime journey, contradicting the stated overnight trip.
Would rather have + past participle expresses a preferred alternative to a past action.

questions.setup: Read the speaker's words with stress on 'WILL'. Choose the meaning it conveys in this exchange.
questions.prompt: 'I've asked him to wait for the agenda, but he WILL interrupt before I've finished.'
options: The speaker is announcing a newly scheduled interruption.
The speaker is allowing him to interrupt before the agenda ends.
The speaker is irritated by his persistent tendency to interrupt.
The speaker believes he is physically unable to remain silent.
questions.explanation: Stressed 'will' can criticize a characteristic or persistent behavior, especially when earlier requests have failed.
feedback: The repeated requests and stressed 'will' point to recurring behavior, not an arranged future event.
The complaint and requests to wait show that permission is not being granted.
Stressed 'will' can criticize a characteristic or persistent behavior, especially when earlier requests have failed.
The complaint concerns persistent behavior, not an established inability.

questions.setup: The launch was cancelled yesterday. Choose the meaning of the earlier arrangement.
questions.prompt: 'The new service was to have been launched this morning.'
options: The launch happened this morning, as the earlier arrangement required.
A launch this morning had been arranged, but the cancellation prevented it.
The speaker strongly infers that the launch happened earlier than planned.
The service is now expected to launch tomorrow instead of this morning.
questions.explanation: Was to have + past participle can look back on an intended event; the cancellation establishes that it did not happen.
feedback: The cancellation rules out this actual-completion reading.
Was to have + past participle can look back on an intended event; the cancellation establishes that it did not happen.
Was to have been states a prior arrangement, not an evidence-based inference.
No replacement date is supplied by the phrase or the context.

questions.setup: The team used a loaned scanner and completed the survey. Choose the statement saying that the scanner was necessary for their ability to finish.
questions.prompt: What does the team conclude about the alternative without it?
options: Without the scanner, we wouldn't have had to finish.
Without the scanner, we shouldn't have finished.
Without the scanner, we might not have finished.
Without the scanner, we wouldn't have been able to finish.
questions.explanation: Wouldn't have been able to denies ability under the unreal past condition while remaining compatible with actual success.
feedback: This removes an obligation to finish rather than removing the ability to do so.
This evaluates or predicts finishing without explicitly denying ability.
This allows possible failure but does not state that finishing would have been beyond their ability.
Wouldn't have been able to denies ability under the unreal past condition while remaining compatible with actual success.

questions.setup: The speaker infers from the new safety system that the owners faced a requirement to replace the wiring. Choose the phrase preserving both the inference and the past necessity.
questions.prompt: To obtain approval for that system, they ___ replace the wiring.
options: must have had to
must not have to
should have been able to
might have preferred to
questions.explanation: Must expresses the present inference; have had to places the inferred necessity in the past.
feedback: Must expresses the present inference; have had to places the inferred necessity in the past.
This concerns an inferred absence of present necessity, not a past requirement.
This expresses expected past ability instead of a strong inference about necessity.
This expresses uncertain past preference, not the inferred requirement.

questions.setup: A colleague says, 'I knew they planned to question you about the missing figures, but I didn't think to mention it.' Choose the function of 'might have' in the reply below.
questions.prompt: 'You might have warned me before I walked into that meeting.'
options: It tentatively suggests that the colleague did give a warning.
It reproaches the colleague for failing to give an expected warning.
It expresses uncertainty about whether the speaker attended the meeting.
It grants retrospective permission to issue a warning.
questions.explanation: With a known omission and irritated tone, 'might have' can criticize a failure to take a considerate action.
feedback: The admitted omission rules out a speculative reading about whether a warning occurred.
With a known omission and irritated tone, 'might have' can criticize a failure to take a considerate action.
The uncertainty reading concerns neither the stated attendance nor the admitted omission in this context.
The speaker is criticizing the omission, not deciding whether warning was permitted.

questions.setup: The board decided in April. The report remained sealed until June. At a later review of the decision, an observer makes the statement below. Choose the intended claim.
questions.prompt: 'The board could not have known what the unpublished report would later reveal.'
options: The board had the evidence but was forbidden to refer to it.
The board may have read the evidence but failed to understand it.
The board was not required to discover whether any report existed.
The later evidence was unavailable at the decision time.
questions.explanation: Could not have known denies knowledge available under the circumstances at the decision time; would later reveal looks forward from that past point.
feedback: The context establishes lack of access, not merely a restriction on using known information.
The report was unavailable then; the defense concerns what the board could know, not poor comprehension.
The claim concerns unavailable knowledge, not an exemption from investigative duties.
Could not have known denies knowledge available under the circumstances at the decision time; would later reveal looks forward from that past point.

questions.setup: An editor must remove an ambiguity. The intended rule forbids disclosure; it is not a prediction about what the researcher might do. Choose the clearest replacement.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The researcher may not disclose the source.'
options: The researcher might not disclose the source.
The researcher need not disclose the source.
The researcher must keep the source confidential.
The researcher is unlikely to disclose the source.
questions.explanation: Must keep the source confidential explicitly requires non-disclosure, removing may not's possible uncertainty reading.
feedback: This selects the uncertain non-disclosure reading, not the intended prohibition.
Need not removes a requirement but still permits disclosure.
Must keep the source confidential explicitly requires non-disclosure, removing may not's possible uncertainty reading.
Unlikely predicts behavior without forbidding it.

questions.setup: The museum rejected the donation. The speaker is considering an unreal alternative without guaranteeing that more funds would have secured acceptance. Choose the closest interpretation.
questions.prompt: 'Even if storage funds had been provided, the museum might still have refused the donation.'
options: Providing the funds would have made refusal the expected outcome.
The museum actually received the funds and then refused the donation.
Providing the funds would not have ruled out refusal.
The museum's refusal proves that the funds were insufficient.
questions.explanation: Even if treats funding as a potentially favorable unreal condition; might still leaves refusal possible despite it.
feedback: Might allows refusal but does not identify it as the expected result of funding.
The unreal condition does not assert that funds were provided.
Even if treats funding as a potentially favorable unreal condition; might still leaves refusal possible despite it.
The statement neither establishes funding nor claims insufficiency as the cause.

questions.setup: A reviewer knows that the records were disclosed. Choose the sentence that criticizes disclosure without disputing that it occurred or merely calling it unnecessary.
questions.prompt: The reviewer is judging the agency's completed conduct.
options: The agency cannot have disclosed the records.
The agency need not have disclosed the records.
The agency might not have disclosed the records.
The agency ought not to have disclosed the records.
questions.explanation: Ought not to have expresses a retrospective judgment against the known action, leaving its occurrence intact.
feedback: This challenges the possibility of disclosure, contrary to the known event.
This says the disclosure was unnecessary; it does not by itself evaluate it as improper.
This entertains non-disclosure as possible instead of evaluating the established disclosure.
Ought not to have expresses a retrospective judgment against the known action, leaving its occurrence intact.

questions.setup: After sending the report, its author writes, 'I still need to compare the mailing list with the full register,' followed by the sentence below. Interpret 'should' in that sentence.
questions.prompt: 'If I should have omitted anyone from the list, please accept my apologies.'
options: The sender says omitting someone would have been the proper action.
The sender admits a known omission and apologizes for it.
The sender promises to omit someone if an apology is accepted.
The sender apologizes conditionally for a possible earlier omission.
questions.explanation: 'If ... should have ...' can frame a tentative condition about a completed event; it need not express obligation or regret about a known failure.
feedback: 'Should' belongs to a tentative condition here; it does not evaluate omission as appropriate.
The if-clause leaves the omission unconfirmed.
This reverses the relation: the possible omission is the condition for the apology, not its future consequence.
'If ... should have ...' can frame a tentative condition about a completed event; it need not express obligation or regret about a known failure.

questions.setup: On Monday, the analyst promised a completed review by Friday. It is now Wednesday, and the work is on schedule. Choose the reading of 'would have'.
questions.prompt: 'She said she would have reviewed the figures by Friday.'
options: It presents the review as an unreal alternative to a known failure.
It reports future completion viewed from the earlier promise.
It infers that she had finished before making the promise.
It says she was required to finish but refused to do so.
questions.explanation: 'Would have reviewed' is the reported counterpart of 'will have reviewed' here; it does not inherently mean the action is unrealized.
feedback: There is no failed condition or known failure; the work remains on schedule.
'Would have reviewed' is the reported counterpart of 'will have reviewed' here; it does not inherently mean the action is unrealized.
'By Friday' places the completion after Monday's promise, not before it.
'Would have reviewed' reports anticipated completion, not necessity or refusal.

questions.setup: A committee member says, 'The contractor completed six comparable projects last year.' The chair replies as below. Choose the force of the first clause.
questions.prompt: 'The contractor may well have the experience, but that does not establish that this bid offers good value.'
options: It treats the contractor's experience as doubtful and therefore rejects the bid.
It authorizes the contractor to acquire experience before revising the bid.
It predicts that relevant experience will make the bid the best value.
It grants the experience but challenges what that establishes.
questions.explanation: In this accepted-fact context, may well ... but ... grants a point while limiting the conclusion that can be drawn from it.
feedback: The context establishes acceptance of the experience; the objection concerns what that fact proves.
This is a concession about an existing qualification, not permission for a future action.
The second clause explicitly resists that inference.
In this accepted-fact context, may well ... but ... grants a point while limiting the conclusion that can be drawn from it.

questions.setup: An interviewer asks, 'You have never met her former manager, so why expect him to question her claim?' The speaker replies as below. Choose the modal's role.
questions.prompt: 'Any careful manager would ask for evidence before accepting that claim.'
options: It describes a hypothetical careful manager's expected response.
It reports what the candidate's actual manager repeatedly did.
It expresses the speaker's preference to become the candidate's manager.
It guarantees that the candidate's manager will request evidence tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Would can characterize an expected response in an imagined situation without referring to past time.
feedback: Would can characterize an expected response in an imagined situation without referring to past time.
The indefinite any and the stated lack of contact make this a general hypothetical judgment, not a past memory.
The subject is any careful manager; no personal preference about employment is stated.
A general hypothetical judgment does not establish a particular person's future action.

questions.setup: The speaker reasons from the notice's prominent placement. Choose the closest paraphrase of the nested negatives.
questions.prompt: 'The visitors cannot have failed to notice the warning.'
options: The speaker is strongly convinced that the visitors missed the warning.
The visitors were forbidden to overlook the warning.
The speaker is strongly convinced that the visitors noticed the warning.
The speaker considers noticing and missing the warning equally possible.
questions.explanation: Cannot have rules out failure to notice, yielding a strong positive inference that they noticed it.
feedback: Failed to notice means missed; cannot have rejects that possibility rather than asserting it.
The phrase makes a deduction about a past event, not a rule governing their conduct.
Cannot have rules out failure to notice, yielding a strong positive inference that they noticed it.
The modal rules out one alternative in the speaker's judgment; it does not leave the two alternatives equally open.

questions.setup: An omission is established, but its cause is unknown. Choose what the historian's comment allows.
questions.prompt: 'The omission need not have been deliberate.'
options: The omission was deliberate but making it was unnecessary.
Both accidental and deliberate omission remain possible.
The historian has established that the omission was accidental.
The historian doubts that any omission occurred.
questions.explanation: Need not have been deliberate leaves intention open: deliberate action is not the only possible account.
feedback: That reads need not have as unnecessary performance; here it denies that deliberate intention is a necessary explanation.
Need not have been deliberate leaves intention open: deliberate action is not the only possible account.
Need not rejects necessity, not the possibility of deliberate intent.
The existence of the omission is established; its intention is what remains uncertain.

questions.setup: The policy makes attendance compulsory for some applicants but exempts others. Choose the sentence that preserves this scope without forbidding anyone to attend.
questions.prompt: How should the editor summarize the policy?
options: Some applicants must attend; others need not.
Some applicants need not attend; the others must not.
All applicants must attend, though some are exempt from attendance.
No applicant has to attend, though some may choose to.
questions.explanation: This assigns a requirement to one group and removes it for the other without creating a ban.
feedback: This assigns a requirement to one group and removes it for the other without creating a ban.
Must not prohibits the second group rather than requiring their attendance.
All conflicts with the stated exemptions; the two clauses cannot preserve the policy together.
This removes the requirement from everyone, including those for whom it is compulsory.

questions.setup: This invented interview protocol protects participants' choice. Choose what the nested modal phrase requires.
questions.prompt: 'Participants must be allowed to decline any question.'
options: Participants must refuse questions unless the interviewer permits an answer.
Participants may refuse only when they can prove answering is impossible.
The interviewer must permit refusal; participants are not required to refuse.
The interviewer may decide whether participants are allowed to refuse.
questions.explanation: Must applies to making refusal permissible. It does not impose an obligation on participants to exercise that permission.
feedback: This reverses both the protected action and the source of the requirement.
No inability condition is attached to the permission in the protocol.
Must applies to making refusal permissible. It does not impose an obligation on participants to exercise that permission.
Must makes provision of that permission a duty, not a discretionary choice.

questions.setup: The admissions rule is still under discussion. Choose the interpretation preserving uncertainty, requirement, and completion before applying.
questions.prompt: 'Applicants may have to have completed the placement before submitting an application.'
options: Applicants probably completed the placement because they submitted applications.
A rule may require completion of the placement before an application is submitted.
Applicants are already required to finish the placement after applying.
Applicants are allowed to submit an application without completing the placement.
questions.explanation: May marks an uncertain requirement; have to expresses that requirement; have completed locates completion before applying.
feedback: This turns an uncertain rule into an inference about actual applicants; the sentence establishes neither event.
May marks an uncertain requirement; have to expresses that requirement; have completed locates completion before applying.
May leaves the rule unsettled, and before places completion earlier than submission.
The phrase considers a possible completion requirement rather than granting an exemption.

questions.setup: A critic ends a review with this sentence. Choose the recommendation it conveys.
questions.prompt: 'I cannot recommend this performance too highly.'
options: The critic gives the performance an exceptionally strong recommendation.
The critic recommends it, but only with substantial reservations.
The critic cannot judge the performance because evidence is missing.
The critic advises readers against attending the performance.
questions.explanation: Cannot ... too highly means that even very high praise would not be excessive, so the recommendation is emphatic.
feedback: Cannot ... too highly means that even very high praise would not be excessive, so the recommendation is emphatic.
The too highly idiom intensifies the recommendation here rather than limiting it.
In cannot recommend too highly, the negative intensifies the recommendation; it does not signal a lack of evidence.
This mistakes the negative wording for a negative recommendation; the idiom has positive force.

questions.setup: After the team agrees on a spending limit, a colleague selects the premium option. Read the response below with stress on 'WOULD'. Choose its implication.
questions.prompt: 'You WOULD choose the one option that exceeds the budget.'
options: The speaker is unsure whether the colleague has made any choice yet.
The choice is presented as irritatingly typical of the colleague.
The speaker is offering permission to exceed the budget next time.
The colleague would choose that option only if an unstated condition occurred.
questions.explanation: Stressed 'would' can react to a known event as characteristic and exasperating; it need not place the event in an unreal condition.
feedback: The context establishes that the choice has just been made.
Stressed 'would' can react to a known event as characteristic and exasperating; it need not place the event in an unreal condition.
The comment criticizes a known choice rather than granting future permission.
The utterance reacts to an actual choice; its force is characteristic disapproval, not an incomplete hypothetical result.

questions.setup: A says, 'I know the client asked us to wait until tomorrow, but I'm calling him tonight.' B replies as below. Choose the interpretation best supported by their exchange.
questions.prompt: 'If you must call tonight, at least keep it brief.'
options: B recognizes an external obligation to make the call tonight.
B authorizes the call because A has satisfied a stated condition.
B yields to A's insistence but asks A to limit the disruption.
B doubts that A intends to call and challenges the claim.
questions.explanation: A insists despite the client's request to wait. If you must accommodates that insistence; at least keep it brief limits the action rather than endorsing it.
feedback: The only external request is to wait until tomorrow. The pressure to call tonight comes from A's insistence.
No permission condition has been met. B responds to A's determination and adds a request about how the call is handled.
A insists despite the client's request to wait. If you must accommodates that insistence; at least keep it brief limits the action rather than endorsing it.
Keep it brief treats the intended call as something to manage; B does not challenge whether A intends to make it.

questions.setup: After checking the attendance record, the secretary makes the remark below. Choose the role of 'should have' in that remark.
questions.prompt: 'It is extraordinary that the chair should have missed the one briefing devoted to this issue.'
options: It presents an established event as striking or surprising.
It identifies missing the briefing as the chair's unfulfilled duty.
It leaves open whether the chair missed the briefing at all.
It predicts a missed briefing later than the present discussion.
questions.explanation: After an evaluative expression such as 'it is extraordinary', 'should' can highlight a reaction to a fact without expressing obligation.
feedback: After an evaluative expression such as 'it is extraordinary', 'should' can highlight a reaction to a fact without expressing obligation.
The sentence treats missing it as an established event, not as an action the chair ought to have performed.
The context establishes the absence; 'should' is evaluative here rather than a marker of factual uncertainty.
'Should have missed' refers to the completed event under evaluation, not a later briefing.

questions.setup: A supplier says, 'We'll bill your firm for correcting the error in our installation.' The customer replies as below. Choose the force of the question.
questions.prompt: 'Why should we have to pay to correct their mistake?'
options: It asks how the payment can be processed efficiently.
It expresses doubt about whether the supplier made any mistake.
It concludes that the speaker's group already paid the charge.
It challenges why this group should bear the cost.
questions.explanation: Rhetorical why should challenges justification; have to identifies the obligation being challenged.
feedback: The question challenges who should bear the duty rather than how payment works.
Their mistake is treated as the basis of the objection, not an uncertain event.
Have to pay describes a requirement, not a completed payment.
Rhetorical why should challenges justification; have to identifies the obligation being challenged.

questions.setup: During discussion of a proposed compulsory evening timetable, the manager says the following to an employee. Choose the interpretation of the preference.
questions.prompt: 'I'd rather you didn't have to attend every evening session.'
options: The manager prefers the employee to be free of the requirement to attend them all.
The manager prefers the employee to be prohibited from attending any evening session.
The manager states that the employee has already missed all evening sessions.
The manager prefers compulsory attendance at fewer sessions but rules out voluntary attendance at others.
questions.explanation: Would rather introduces a preference; didn't have to removes the duty, not the option of attending voluntarily.
feedback: Would rather introduces a preference; didn't have to removes the duty, not the option of attending voluntarily.
Absence of obligation does not create a prohibition, and every is not equivalent to any in this rewrite.
The past form after would rather expresses a current preference, not a report of past absence.
The sentence does not impose a new smaller quota or rule out additional voluntary attendance.

questions.setup: Compare 'Sit here' and 'Please sit here.'
questions.prompt: What does 'please' add?
options: A different place to sit
A reason for sitting
A later time to sit
A more polite way to ask
questions.explanation: Please makes the request more polite; it does not change the seat or action.
feedback: Here points to the same place in both requests.
Please marks politeness, not a reason.
Neither request names a later time.
Please makes the request more polite; it does not change the seat or action.

questions.setup: Ana says, 'I like this song.' Ben says, 'I love this song.'
questions.prompt: Whose words show a stronger positive feeling?
options: Ana's
Both show dislike
Ben's
Both show the same strength
questions.explanation: Love is stronger than like when describing enjoyment of a song.
feedback: Like is positive, but love expresses a stronger positive feeling here.
Both like and love are positive in these statements.
Love is stronger than like when describing enjoyment of a song.
The choice between like and love changes the strength of the feeling.

questions.setup: A host offers you more coffee. You do not want any.
questions.prompt: Choose a clear, polite answer that thanks the host.
options: Yes, please.
No more coffee!
Thank you. I want some.
No, thank you.
questions.explanation: No declines the offer, and thank you shows appreciation.
feedback: This politely accepts coffee rather than refusing it.
This refuses coffee but does not thank the host.
The second sentence asks for coffee, which changes your meaning.
No declines the offer, and thank you shows appreciation.

questions.setup: You ask, 'Can we leave?' Your friend says, 'I'm almost ready.'
questions.prompt: What does your friend mean?
options: I am ready now.
I am starting to get ready.
I do not want to go.
I need a little more time.
questions.explanation: Almost ready means close to ready, with something still left to do.
feedback: Almost ready stops short of being ready.
Almost suggests being near the end, not just starting.
Readiness and willingness are different; no refusal is expressed.
Almost ready means close to ready, with something still left to do.

questions.setup: Jo sees a price and says, 'Only five dollars!'
questions.prompt: How does 'only' present the price?
options: As a large amount
As a small amount
As an unknown amount
As an amount paid yesterday
questions.explanation: Only presents five dollars as little in this reaction; it adds the speaker's view of the price.
feedback: Only lowers the apparent size of the amount rather than emphasizing a high price.
Only presents five dollars as little in this reaction; it adds the speaker's view of the price.
Five dollars states the amount; only is not an uncertainty word here.
Only does not tell us when payment happened.

questions.setup: Compare 'The shop is busy today' and 'The shop is always busy.'
questions.prompt: How does the second sentence change the time reference?
options: It describes an earlier part of today.
It describes a pattern across occasions.
It describes how long one visit lasted.
It describes a change expected tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Always extends the description across occasions; today limits it to the present day.
feedback: Always describes a pattern across occasions, not an earlier hour.
Always extends the description across occasions; today limits it to the present day.
Always concerns the repeated state of the shop, not one visit's duration.
The sentence gives a general pattern, not a future change.

questions.setup: Tom says, 'I never eat fish.'
questions.prompt: Which gives Tom's stated habit without adding a reason or limiting it to one meal?
options: Eating fish is not part of Tom's habits.
Tom does not like fish.
Tom cannot cook fish.
Tom does not eat fish at breakfast.
questions.explanation: Never means on no occasions in this description of Tom's habits; it does not supply a reason.
feedback: Never means on no occasions in this description of Tom's habits; it does not supply a reason.
He may have another reason; never describes what he does, not why.
The statement says nothing about his cooking skills.
Never is not limited to breakfast; this answer narrows the statement.

questions.setup: Lena says, 'I sometimes walk to work.'
questions.prompt: Which reply adds a detail Lena did NOT give?
options: Walking is one way you get to work.
You walk to work every Monday.
You walk to work on some days.
You do walk to work.
questions.explanation: Sometimes gives no fixed day; every Monday adds a schedule Lena did not state.
feedback: Sometimes walking makes it one of her ways of travelling.
Sometimes gives no fixed day; every Monday adds a schedule Lena did not state.
On some days gives the ordinary meaning of sometimes here.
Sometimes confirms that walking happens.

questions.setup: At the cafe, a server says, 'Your food will be ready soon.'
questions.prompt: Which response matches the message?
options: I can take the food now.
I will wait a little longer.
I need to return tomorrow.
My food was ready earlier.
questions.explanation: Soon places readiness a short time ahead, so a little more waiting fits.
feedback: Will be ready soon does not say it is ready now.
Soon places readiness a short time ahead, so a little more waiting fits.
Soon does not suggest a wait until another day in this cafe exchange.
Will be points forward, not to earlier readiness.

questions.setup: Nora writes, 'The printer is working again.'
questions.prompt: What does 'again' suggest about the printer?
options: It is working for the first time.
It will start working tomorrow.
It works now after not working.
It works faster than before.
questions.explanation: Working again presents a return to an earlier working state after an interruption.
feedback: Again points to an earlier working state, not a first use.
Is working describes the present, not tomorrow.
Working again presents a return to an earlier working state after an interruption.
Again signals a return, not an increase in speed.

questions.setup: At seven, Ali says, 'I'm at work.' At eight, he says, 'I'm still at work.'
questions.prompt: What does 'still' show?
options: Ali has not left work yet.
Ali arrived at eight.
Ali works at a different place.
Ali is going back to work.
questions.explanation: Still shows that being at work continues from seven to eight.
feedback: Still shows that being at work continues from seven to eight.
Still links the later message to the earlier state, not a new arrival.
Still concerns continuation; no change of workplace is stated.
Going back would mean a return; still presents an uninterrupted state.

questions.setup: I expected Mia home at six. At five she says, 'I'm already home.'
questions.prompt: What does 'already' add here?
options: Mia wants to go home.
Mia is late getting home.
Mia is leaving home soon.
Mia is home earlier than I expected.
questions.explanation: Already highlights that the state has been reached by now; five is before the expected arrival.
feedback: She says she is home, not that she wants to go there.
Five is earlier than the expected six.
Already says nothing about her next departure.
Already highlights that the state has been reached by now; five is before the expected arrival.

questions.setup: A cashier asks, 'One bag or two?' You answer, 'Just one bag, please.'
questions.prompt: What does 'just' emphasize here?
options: One bag bought a moment ago
One bag at a lower price
One bag for each person
One bag, not more
questions.explanation: Before one bag, just limits the quantity; it does not describe when the bag was bought.
feedback: Just can concern recent time elsewhere, but here it modifies one bag.
No discount is requested.
The reply limits the total requested; it does not distribute bags among people.
Before one bag, just limits the quantity; it does not describe when the bag was bought.

questions.setup: Compare 'The soup is very hot' and 'The soup is too hot to eat.'
questions.prompt: Which sentence says the heat is a problem for eating it?
options: The soup is very hot.
The soup is too hot to eat.
Both sentences say this.
Neither sentence says this.
questions.explanation: Too ... to marks excess for an action: the heat prevents eating it as it is.
feedback: Very marks a high temperature without itself saying it prevents eating.
Too ... to marks excess for an action: the heat prevents eating it as it is.
Very hot gives a high degree but does not explicitly say eating is prevented.
Too hot to eat explicitly links the heat to the problem with eating.

questions.setup: A guest changes 'The meal was good' to 'The meal was very good.'
questions.prompt: What changes in the message?
options: The praise gives more detail about the food.
The guest becomes less sure of the opinion.
The praise becomes stronger.
The guest changes the praise into a request.
questions.explanation: Very increases the degree of good, making the praise stronger.
feedback: Very increases degree but does not identify particular dishes or qualities.
Very strengthens the positive description rather than making it uncertain.
Very increases the degree of good, making the praise stronger.
Both sentences evaluate the meal; neither asks for an action.

questions.setup: A friend asks about your new flat. You say, 'It's not bad. I like it.'
questions.prompt: How should your friend understand 'not bad' here?
options: You are unhappy with it.
You have not seen it yet.
You think it is okay or good.
You think it is perfect.
questions.explanation: Not bad can give a modest positive judgment; I like it confirms that reading here.
feedback: I like it rules out this negative reading in this exchange.
The answer gives a view of the flat, not a statement about visiting it.
Not bad can give a modest positive judgment; I like it confirms that reading here.
Not bad is a modest positive comment, not a claim of perfection.

questions.setup: 'The tickets are free.' 'Really? I thought they were twenty dollars.'
questions.prompt: What does 'Really?' show in this reply?
options: Surprise at the new information
Certainty that the first speaker is wrong
Thanks for an offer of free tickets
Agreement that the tickets still cost twenty dollars
questions.explanation: The old expectation of twenty dollars makes Really? a surprised check of the new claim.
feedback: The old expectation of twenty dollars makes Really? a surprised check of the new claim.
