questions.prompt: There is no space on the tour because all twenty places ___.
options: have reserved
are reserving
have been reserved
were reserving
questions.explanation: Have been reserved is present perfect passive; completed reservations explain the lack of space now.
feedback: Have reserved is active and would make the places perform reservations.
Are reserving also makes the places the actors and presents activity rather than completed reservations.
Have been reserved is present perfect passive; completed reservations explain the lack of space now.
Were reserving is active past continuous, not a completed passive result.

questions.setup: Choose the form showing that planting was already in progress when the rain started.
questions.prompt: The young trees ___ when heavy rain forced the volunteers to stop.
options: were being planted
had planted
have been planted
were planting
questions.explanation: Were being planted places the trees as receivers of an activity underway at the past interruption.
feedback: Were being planted places the trees as receivers of an activity underway at the past interruption.
Had planted is active and makes the trees the planters; it also looks back at prior completion.
Have been planted reports a result up to now rather than an activity underway at that past moment.
Were planting is active and makes the trees perform the planting.

questions.setup: Choose the passive form explicitly placing the booking before my call.
questions.prompt: When I phoned the campsite, the last cabin ___, so I booked a tent space instead.
options: has booked
was booking
has been booking
had been booked
questions.explanation: Had been booked places a completed booking before the past call and keeps the cabin as its receiver.
feedback: Has booked is active and would make the cabin the booking agent.
Was booking is active continuous; it neither places the cabin as receiver nor marks the earlier completed booking.
Has been booking is active perfect continuous and gives the cabin an ongoing booking role.
Had been booked places a completed booking before the past call and keeps the cabin as its receiver.

questions.setup: Choose the form giving advice about what people should do with the paint.
questions.prompt: The paint should ___ away from direct sunlight.
options: store it
being stored
have stored
be stored
questions.explanation: Should be stored is a passive recommendation: someone should keep the paint in the stated conditions.
feedback: Store it is active and repeats the paint as an object while making it the storing agent.
Should requires the base form be, not being, before stored.
Should have stored is active perfect and makes the paint the actor; it does not give the intended advice about what people should do with it.
Should be stored is a passive recommendation: someone should keep the paint in the stated conditions.

questions.setup: Choose the form stating a requirement for passengers.
questions.prompt: Travel passes ___ to the inspector on request.
options: have to show
has to be shown
have to be shown
have to showing
questions.explanation: Have to be shown expresses a requirement while making the passes the things shown to the inspector.
feedback: Have to show is active and makes the passes the people showing something.
Has does not agree with the plural subject travel passes.
Have to be shown expresses a requirement while making the passes the things shown to the inspector.
After have to, the passive uses be shown, not showing.

questions.setup: Choose the passive sentence keeping 'us' as the people receiving the offer.
questions.prompt: The host offered us a quieter table.
options: We offered the host a quieter table.
The host was offered our quieter table.
We were offered a quieter table.
We were offering a quieter table.
questions.explanation: 'We' becomes the passive subject as the recipient of the host's offer; the offered table stays in the sentence.
feedback: This makes us the people offering something and the host its recipient.
This makes the host receive an offer of our table, reversing the original offer to us.
'We' becomes the passive subject as the recipient of the host's offer; the offered table stays in the sentence.
'Were offering' is active continuous and makes us the offerers rather than recipients.

questions.setup: Choose the passive version beginning with 'the replacement battery' and preserving the recipient.
questions.prompt: The supplier sent the customer a replacement battery.
options: A replacement battery was sent to the customer.
A replacement battery was sent by the customer.
A replacement battery sent the customer to the supplier.
A replacement battery was sending the customer.
questions.explanation: When the battery is the passive subject, 'to the customer' preserves the recipient of the supplier's sending.
feedback: When the battery is the passive subject, 'to the customer' preserves the recipient of the supplier's sending.
'By the customer' makes the customer the sender, reversing the original recipient role.
This makes the battery act and turns the supplier into a destination.
'Was sending' is active continuous and makes the battery the sender.

questions.setup: Choose the passive phrase meaning the council will investigate the complaint.
questions.prompt: The noise complaint will ___ next week.
options: be looked
look into
be looking into
be looked into
questions.explanation: Be looked into is the passive of look into. Keep into because it is part of the investigation expression.
feedback: Looked needs into to retain the investigate meaning of look into.
Look into is active and would make the complaint investigate something.
Be looking into is active continuous rather than passive.
Be looked into is the passive of look into. Keep into because it is part of the investigation expression.

questions.setup: Choose the concise notice preserving the collection rule without inventing a collector.
questions.prompt: Someone collects recycling from these bins every Wednesday. The notice is about the collection schedule.
options: Recycling is collected from these bins every Wednesday.
The caretaker collects these bins every Wednesday.
These bins collect recycling from Wednesday.
Recycling is collected only when the bins are full.
questions.explanation: The passive keeps the recycling and schedule prominent while leaving the unspecified collector unnamed.
feedback: The passive keeps the recycling and schedule prominent while leaving the unspecified collector unnamed.
The source does not identify the caretaker and says recycling, not the bins themselves, is collected.
This changes collection into a function of the bins and replaces a weekly schedule with a starting point.
This replaces the stated weekly schedule with a fullness condition that was not supplied.

questions.setup: Choose the form meaning other people interrupt me.
questions.prompt: I don't enjoy ___ while I am explaining a problem.
options: interrupting someone
having interrupted
being interrupted
be interrupted
questions.explanation: Being interrupted is a passive -ing form; I receive the interruption from someone else.
feedback: Interrupting someone makes me the person who interrupts, reversing the intended role.
Having interrupted describes my earlier action as the interrupter, not an interruption I receive.
Being interrupted is a passive -ing form; I receive the interruption from someone else.
Enjoy takes an -ing form here, so the passive must be being interrupted.

questions.setup: Choose the form meaning the company may promote me.
questions.prompt: After completing the training, I hope ___ to team leader.
options: promoting
to be promoted
to promote
being promote
questions.explanation: To be promoted is a passive infinitive, placing me as the person receiving the hoped-for promotion.
feedback: Hope normally takes a to-infinitive here, and promoting would make me the actor.
To be promoted is a passive infinitive, placing me as the person receiving the hoped-for promotion.
To promote makes me the person promoting someone else; the intended meaning is that I receive promotion.
Being promote combines being with a base form and does not fit after hope.

questions.setup: Choose the standard British English passive preserving what was explained and to whom.
questions.prompt: The instructor explained the safety rule to us.
options: The safety rule was explained to us.
We were explained the safety rule.
The safety rule was explained by us.
We were explaining the safety rule.
questions.explanation: The rule becomes the passive subject, and to us keeps the people who received the explanation.
feedback: The rule becomes the passive subject, and to us keeps the people who received the explanation.
In standard British English, explain takes the content as its direct object; make the rule the passive subject and retain to us.
By us makes us the explainers rather than the people receiving the explanation.
Were explaining is active continuous and makes us the instructors.

questions.setup: Choose the correct arrival statement in contemporary standard British English.
questions.prompt: Describe the guests reaching the venue just after six.
options: The guests were arrived just after six.
The guests arrived just after six.
The guests were arrive just after six.
The guests did arrived just after six.
questions.explanation: Arrived is active and intransitive: the guests reach the venue without receiving an action from a separate agent.
feedback: In contemporary standard British English, arrive does not form an ordinary passive with were arrived in this meaning.
Arrived is active and intransitive: the guests reach the venue without receiving an action from a separate agent.
Were cannot directly combine with the base form arrive in this statement.
Did requires the base form arrive, not arrived.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of 'got promoted' in this informal account.
questions.prompt: My colleague got promoted after leading the successful launch.
options: The colleague promoted another worker.
The colleague received a promotion.
The colleague arranged a launch for a promoted worker.
The colleague lost a promotion after the launch.
questions.explanation: 'Got promoted' is an informal get-passive: someone promoted the colleague.
feedback: 'Got promoted' makes the colleague the recipient, not the person promoting others.
'Got promoted' is an informal get-passive: someone promoted the colleague.
The phrase describes the colleague's promotion, not the status of another worker.
'Got promoted' states a successful promotion, not its loss; get-passives need not describe bad events.

questions.setup: Choose the statement saying a tailor did the alteration for me.
questions.prompt: I paid a tailor to shorten these trousers.
options: I shortened these trousers myself.
I had shortened these trousers before paying.
I had these trousers to shorten.
I had these trousers shortened.
questions.explanation: Had these trousers shortened uses have plus object plus participle to describe arranging work by someone else.
feedback: Myself says I performed the alteration, contrary to the tailor doing it.
Had shortened is active past perfect and makes me the person who completed the shortening.
Had these trousers to shorten gives me a task to perform, not an alteration performed for me.
Had these trousers shortened uses have plus object plus participle to describe arranging work by someone else.

questions.setup: Choose the passive prohibition that says users must keep this exit clear.
questions.prompt: Bags ___ in front of the emergency exit.
options: must not be left
must not leave them
must not be leaving
must be not leaving
questions.explanation: Must not be left prohibits people from placing or leaving bags in that location.
feedback: Must not be left prohibits people from placing or leaving bags in that location.
This active phrase makes bags the people leaving something and repeats them as an object.
Be leaving is active continuous, not a passive about bags placed by people.
Be not leaving remains active continuous and does not form the required prohibition about bags.

questions.setup: Choose the passive question asking whether the weighing is complete.
questions.prompt: At the airport desk, ask about your suitcase.
options: Has the suitcase been weighing?
Has the suitcase being weighed?
Have the suitcase been weighed?
Has the suitcase been weighed?
questions.explanation: Has ... been weighed is present perfect passive and asks whether the weighing has occurred.
feedback: Been weighing forms an active progressive and does not place the suitcase as the thing weighed.
After has, the passive perfect requires been, not being.
The singular suitcase requires has, not have.
Has ... been weighed is present perfect passive and asks whether the weighing has occurred.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that does not turn the cause into an unidentified person.
questions.prompt: The footpath was blocked by fallen branches after the storm.
options: A person deliberately used the branches to block the path.
The footpath caused the branches to fall.
Fallen branches caused the blockage; no person's action is stated.
The storm was blocked by the footpath.
questions.explanation: A passive by phrase can identify a nonhuman cause. The sentence does not establish a person acting deliberately.
feedback: The by phrase names a cause, but it does not state deliberate action by a person.
This reverses the relation: the branches block the path, not the path causing their fall.
A passive by phrase can identify a nonhuman cause. The sentence does not establish a person acting deliberately.
The storm supplies the setting, not the thing blocked in the passive sentence.

questions.setup: Choose the pair keeping workers as inspectors and damaged goods as receivers of removal.
questions.prompt: Workers ___ each delivery, and damaged goods ___ immediately.
options: are inspected / remove
inspect / are removed
inspect / are removing
are inspecting / have removed
questions.explanation: Inspect is active because workers do the checking; are removed is passive because the goods receive the removal action.
feedback: Are inspected makes workers the receivers, while remove makes damaged goods the actors; both roles are reversed.
Inspect is active because workers do the checking; are removed is passive because the goods receive the removal action.
Are removing makes the damaged goods remove something rather than be removed.
Have removed makes the goods the active removers and changes the routine result into an active completed action.

questions.setup: Choose the continuation keeping the pool as grammatical subject and retaining the named builders.
questions.prompt: The old swimming pool has become a community center. Local apprentices converted it last year.
options: It was converted by local apprentices last year.
The pool was converted last year.
Local apprentices converted the pool last year.
Local apprentices were trained during last year's conversion.
questions.explanation: It keeps the pool as the topic; by local apprentices preserves the supplied agent. Passive voice need not hide who acted.
feedback: It keeps the pool as the topic; by local apprentices preserves the supplied agent. Passive voice need not hide who acted.
This keeps the pool as subject but drops the builders, which the task requires you to retain.
This preserves the event but makes the apprentices, not the pool, the grammatical subject.
This adds a training event that the source does not state and makes the apprentices the subject.

questions.setup: Choose the pair reporting collection at a finished past time and completed testing relevant now.
questions.prompt: The water samples ___ on Tuesday and ___ for contamination, so the results are ready.
options: have collected / tested
were collected / have been tested
were collecting / have tested
have been collected / were testing
questions.explanation: Were collected dates the past sampling; have been tested reports completed testing with results now. Both keep samples as receivers.
feedback: Have collected makes the samples collect something, and tested without an auxiliary remains active in this coordination.
Were collected dates the past sampling; have been tested reports completed testing with results now. Both keep samples as receivers.
Both active forms give samples the role of workers rather than things collected and tested.
Have been collected does not fit the dated event in this ordinary report, and were testing makes the samples active testers.

questions.setup: Choose the form expressing a missed obligation before the event.
questions.prompt: The temporary seating collapsed during rehearsal. It ___ before anyone used it.
options: should inspect
should be inspecting
should have inspected
should have been inspected
questions.explanation: Should have been inspected says the seating ought to have received inspection before use; the criticism concerns an earlier unmet obligation.
feedback: Should inspect makes the seating the inspector and gives a current recommendation rather than a missed earlier obligation.
Should be inspecting is active progressive and makes the seating the inspecting agent.
Should have inspected is active perfect and assigns the inspection to the seating rather than to people checking it.
Should have been inspected says the seating ought to have received inspection before use; the criticism concerns an earlier unmet obligation.

questions.setup: Choose the statement preserving uncertainty about an earlier accidental deletion.
questions.prompt: The shared calendar is empty. Accidental deletion is one possible explanation, but it has not been confirmed.
options: The entries may have been deleted accidentally.
The entries must have been deleted accidentally.
The entries were deleted accidentally.
The entries cannot have been deleted accidentally.
questions.explanation: May have been deleted combines possibility, earlier time, and passive voice without claiming the explanation is verified.
feedback: May have been deleted combines possibility, earlier time, and passive voice without claiming the explanation is verified.
Must have presents a strong conclusion rather than the stated unconfirmed possibility among explanations.
The simple past passive asserts the deletion as a fact, exceeding the evidence.
Cannot have rules deletion out, reversing its status as a possible explanation.

questions.setup: Choose the rule that makes disclosure forbidden rather than optional.
questions.prompt: Temporary access codes are confidential. Staff are prohibited from including them in public notices.
options: The codes need not be included in public notices.
The codes must not be included in public notices.
The codes may be included in public notices.
The codes should have been included in public notices.
questions.explanation: Must not be included expresses the prohibition while keeping the confidential codes as the topic.
feedback: Need not removes an obligation but does not prohibit inclusion.
Must not be included expresses the prohibition while keeping the confidential codes as the topic.
May be included gives permission, contrary to the rule.
Should have been included recommends an earlier action rather than forbidding disclosure.

questions.setup: Choose the statement reporting a belief without upgrading it to proof.
questions.prompt: Several historians think the tunnel once connected the two houses. No one has verified the connection.
options: The tunnel is known to have connected the two houses.
The tunnel is proved to have connected the two houses.
The tunnel has been shown to have connected the two houses.
The tunnel is believed to have connected the two houses.
questions.explanation: Is believed to attributes the connection to a belief; the perfect infinitive places the supposed connection earlier.
feedback: Is known to presents the connection as established knowledge, beyond the source.
Is proved to claims proof, which the source explicitly lacks.
Has been shown to claims that evidence has demonstrated the connection, not merely that historians think it existed.
Is believed to attributes the connection to a belief; the perfect infinitive places the supposed connection earlier.

questions.setup: Choose the impersonal passive report that preserves a current general claim.
questions.prompt: People say that the mineral spring is unusually warm.
options: It is said the mineral spring to be unusually warm.
The mineral spring is said that it is unusually warm.
It is said that the mineral spring is unusually warm.
It says that the mineral spring is unusually warm.
questions.explanation: It is said that provides an impersonal reporting passive while retaining the original claim about the spring.
feedback: This mixes the impersonal it construction with the infinitive pattern; use it is said that plus a finite clause.
With the spring as subject, use is said to be; the impersonal that-clause pattern instead begins it is said.
It is said that provides an impersonal reporting passive while retaining the original claim about the spring.
It says is active and would require it to refer to a source, such as a guidebook; it is not the requested impersonal passive.

questions.setup: Choose the current reporting passive with the medal as grammatical subject and the theft explicitly earlier than the belief.
questions.prompt: The newspaper currently reports an unverified belief that someone stole the medal before the exhibition opened.
options: Someone is believed to have stolen the medal.
The medal is believed to be stolen.
The medal is believed to have been stolen.
The medal was believed to have been stolen.
questions.explanation: Is believed gives the current reporting frame, and to have been stolen explicitly places the medal's theft before that belief.
feedback: This reports the same kind of earlier event but makes someone, not the medal, the grammatical subject.
To be stolen can describe an expected event or a supposed current state; it does not explicitly mark the theft as earlier than the current belief.
Is believed gives the current reporting frame, and to have been stolen explicitly places the medal's theft before that belief.
Was believed locates the reporting belief in the past rather than the current belief requested.

questions.setup: Choose what the get-passive establishes without assigning blame.
questions.prompt: The trainee got dismissed during the restructuring. The account gives no reason for choosing that employee.
options: The trainee deliberately arranged to be dismissed.
The trainee dismissed the person leading the restructuring.
The trainee's misconduct was the reason for the dismissal.
The trainee was dismissed; got does not by itself establish fault or intention.
questions.explanation: Got dismissed presents the trainee as undergoing dismissal; responsibility, intention, and the reason require additional evidence.
feedback: A get-passive does not by itself mean the subject planned or arranged the event.
This reverses the trainee's role from dismissed employee to dismissing agent.
No misconduct is stated, and the get-passive alone cannot supply it.
Got dismissed presents the trainee as undergoing dismissal; responsibility, intention, and the reason require additional evidence.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that explicitly presents a locking action rather than just a continuing state.
questions.prompt: The account must identify a guard performing the locking.
options: The storeroom was locked by the guard at midnight.
The storeroom remained locked overnight.
The storeroom was still locked at dawn.
The storeroom seemed securely locked.
questions.explanation: By the guard identifies an agent and at midnight locates the locking event, giving the requested action reading.
feedback: By the guard identifies an agent and at midnight locates the locking event, giving the requested action reading.
Remained locked describes a continuing state without reporting the guard's action.
Still locked describes the state at dawn, not who performed the locking.
Seemed securely locked reports an apparent state rather than a locking event by a guard.

questions.setup: Choose the passive completion preserving the meaning someone slept in the bed.
questions.prompt: The bed looks freshly made, but it has clearly ___.
options: been slept
being slept in
been sleeping
been slept in
questions.explanation: Been slept in retains in from sleep in and makes the bed the location affected by someone's use.
feedback: Dropping in loses the required relation between sleeping and the bed.
After has, the passive perfect needs been rather than being.
Been sleeping is active perfect continuous; it makes the bed the sleeper.
Been slept in retains in from sleep in and makes the bed the location affected by someone's use.

questions.setup: Choose the passive paraphrase preserving the traveler as beneficiary and the agency as actor.
questions.prompt: The agency reserved a seat for the traveler.
options: A seat was reserved by the traveler for the agency.
A seat was reserved for the traveler by the agency.
The agency was reserved a seat by the traveler.
The traveler was reserved for a seat by the agency.
questions.explanation: For the traveler preserves the beneficiary; by the agency preserves the agent, with the seat as passive subject.
feedback: This exchanges the beneficiary and the reserving agent.
For the traveler preserves the beneficiary; by the agency preserves the agent, with the seat as passive subject.
This also makes the agency receive the reservation and the traveler perform it.
This makes the traveler the thing reserved rather than the person benefiting from the seat reservation.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence preserving 'chair' as the role the members elected the candidate to fill.
questions.prompt: The members elected Dr. Bell chair of the association.
options: Dr. Bell elected the chair of the association.
Dr. Bell was elected by the chair of the association.
Dr. Bell was elected chair of the association.
The chair elected Dr. Bell to the association.
questions.explanation: 'Was elected' is passive, and 'chair' remains the complement naming the role Dr. Bell receives.
feedback: This makes Dr. Bell the voter instead of the person elected.
'By the chair' turns 'chair' into the electing agent rather than the role awarded.
'Was elected' is passive, and 'chair' remains the complement naming the role Dr. Bell receives.
This changes both the electing agent and the role into mere association membership.

questions.setup: Choose the full clause matching the reduced description.
questions.prompt: Goods manufactured locally usually arrive within two days.
options: Goods that manufacture local products
Goods that are manufactured locally
Goods that are manufacturing locally
Goods that have manufactured locally
questions.explanation: Manufactured locally is a reduced passive relative clause meaning goods that are manufactured locally.
feedback: This makes the goods manufacture other products and changes the description.
Manufactured locally is a reduced passive relative clause meaning goods that are manufactured locally.
Are manufacturing is active progressive and gives goods the role of manufacturers.
Have manufactured is active perfect, again making goods the producers rather than their products.

questions.setup: Choose the revision making the sample, not the technician, the thing heated.
questions.prompt: Revise: 'After being heated for ten minutes, the technician weighed the sample.'
options: After being heated for ten minutes, the technician was weighed with the sample.
After heating for ten minutes, the sample weighed the technician.
After being heated for ten minutes, the sample was weighed by the technician.
After being heated for ten minutes, the technician weighed more carefully.
questions.explanation: The subject the sample now matches the understood receiver of being heated, and the technician remains the person weighing it.
feedback: The technician is still the subject understood as heated and is now also made the receiver of weighing.
This makes the sample an active weigher and reverses the measurement relationship.
The subject the sample now matches the understood receiver of being heated, and the technician remains the person weighing it.
The added adverb does not fix the attachment: the opening still points to the technician as the heated subject.

questions.setup: Choose the analysis of this product description.
questions.prompt: This fabric washes well, even in cold water.
options: The active form describes how readily people can wash the fabric.
The fabric is described as actively washing other materials.
The sentence reports a particular wash that has already finished.
The fabric is being washed at the moment of speaking.
questions.explanation: This middle construction uses an active form to describe a property of something people act on; it is not morphologically a be-passive.
feedback: This middle construction uses an active form to describe a property of something people act on; it is not morphologically a be-passive.
In this use, the fabric is understood as the thing washed, not as a washing agent.
The present statement describes a general property, not a dated completed wash.
It is a property statement, not a present continuous passive reporting an action underway.

questions.setup: Choose the reading licensed by the accidental-event context.
questions.prompt: During the storm, our neighbors had their fence damaged by falling debris.
options: The neighbors arranged for workers to damage the fence.
The neighbors experienced damage to their fence.
The neighbors damaged someone else's fence.
The neighbors finished repairing the fence before the storm.
questions.explanation: Had their fence damaged presents an event affecting their property, with falling debris as the stated cause.
feedback: Have an object damaged can describe an unwanted experience; this storm context does not support a commissioned service.
Had their fence damaged presents an event affecting their property, with falling debris as the stated cause.
The fence belongs to the neighbors, and they are not identified as the damaging agents.
The clause concerns damage during the storm, not a completed earlier repair.

questions.setup: Choose the standard passive preserving the officer's observation of the visitor entering.
questions.prompt: An officer saw the visitor enter the courtyard.
options: The visitor was seen enter the courtyard.
The visitor was seen to entering the courtyard.
The visitor was seeing the officer enter the courtyard.
The visitor was seen to enter the courtyard.
questions.explanation: Was seen to enter preserves the visitor as the observed person; the passive restores to before the infinitive.
feedback: The passive counterpart of saw the visitor enter uses to enter in standard English.
After to here, use the base form enter, not entering.
This makes the visitor the observer and the officer the person entering, reversing the original roles.
Was seen to enter preserves the visitor as the observed person; the passive restores to before the infinitive.

questions.setup: Choose the passive sentence preserving the idea that management compelled the staff to wait.
questions.prompt: Management made the staff wait outside.
options: The staff were made to wait outside.
The staff were made wait outside.
The staff were made waiting outside.
The staff made management wait outside.
questions.explanation: In the passive of make someone do something, use be made to do it; the staff remain the people compelled to wait.
feedback: In the passive of make someone do something, use be made to do it; the staff remain the people compelled to wait.
The passive needs to before wait, unlike the active made the staff wait.
Waiting does not form the required complement of were made in this compulsion meaning.
This exchanges the compelling agent and the people who wait.

questions.setup: Choose the inference justified by the omission of the contractor's name.
questions.prompt: A traffic update says, 'The eastbound lane is being resurfaced.' The road authority knows which contractor is working there.
options: The writer has proved that no contractor is involved.
The writer cannot know who is carrying out the work.
The update can foreground the affected lane without naming a known contractor.
The passive implies that the road authority is concealing misconduct.
questions.explanation: Agent omission can serve the update's focus on traffic conditions even when the agent is known.
feedback: Omitting the contractor does not deny that someone is performing the work.
The context explicitly says the authority knows the contractor; a passive need not indicate ignorance.
Agent omission can serve the update's focus on traffic conditions even when the agent is known.
Passive form alone provides no evidence of concealment or misconduct.

questions.setup: Choose the formulation that itself presents scanning as already performed but unnecessary.
questions.prompt: The originals were acceptable. Scanning every receipt added no benefit.
options: The receipts did not need to be scanned.
The receipts should have been scanned.
The receipts must not have been scanned.
The receipts needn't have been scanned.
questions.explanation: Needn't have been scanned normally presents an action that was performed although unnecessary, matching the stated wasted effort.
feedback: Did not need to removes a requirement but does not itself say whether scanning happened.
Should have been scanned presents scanning as desirable or required, reversing the judgment of unnecessary work.
Must not have been scanned suggests a deduction that scanning did not occur, not that it occurred unnecessarily.
Needn't have been scanned normally presents an action that was performed although unnecessary, matching the stated wasted effort.

questions.setup: Choose the cautious statement preserving lack of knowledge rather than asserting non-disclosure.
questions.prompt: The investigation has not established whether the access code was shared.
options: The code is known not to have been shared.
The code is known to have been kept private.
The code is not known to have been shared.
The code is believed to have remained private.
questions.explanation: Not known to have been shared withholds knowledge of sharing while leaving open whether sharing occurred.
feedback: Known not to asserts established non-sharing, which the investigation has not established.
Known to have been kept private also claims knowledge of non-disclosure.
Not known to have been shared withholds knowledge of sharing while leaving open whether sharing occurred.
This substitutes a positive belief in privacy for the stated absence of an established outcome.

questions.setup: Choose the continuation saying the committee had overruled the adviser, which she resented.
questions.prompt: The adviser resented ___.
options: having overruled the committee
not having overruled the committee
not having been overruled by the committee
having been overruled by the committee
questions.explanation: Having been overruled gives the adviser the receiver role and places the committee's earlier action inside the object of her resentment.
feedback: The active perfect gerund makes the adviser the person who overruled the committee.
This makes her resent failing to overrule the committee, changing both role and polarity.
This makes her resent the absence of an overruling, whereas she resents the overruling that occurred.
Having been overruled gives the adviser the receiver role and places the committee's earlier action inside the object of her resentment.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that keeps the reported belief separate from verified work.
questions.prompt: When the observatory reopened, the dome was thought to have been reinforced.
options: People then believed earlier reinforcement had occurred; the sentence does not verify it.
People now believe reinforcement had occurred before an earlier, unspecified belief.
The sentence verifies earlier reinforcement but attributes its purpose to the reopening.
People then considered earlier reinforcement necessary; the sentence leaves its occurrence open.
questions.explanation: Was thought anchors the belief at the past reopening, while to have been reinforced places the supposed work earlier without verifying it.
feedback: Was thought anchors the belief at the past reopening, while to have been reinforced places the supposed work earlier without verifying it.
The finite was thought locates the belief in the past; it does not report a belief held now.
The content of thought is the supposed reinforcement itself, not just its purpose.
Thought to have been reinforced reports a belief about occurrence, not a judgment that reinforcement was necessary.

questions.setup: Choose the passive paraphrase preserving the scope of 'only' over the workers employed.
questions.prompt: The firm employed only local workers for the restoration.
options: Only local workers were employed by the firm for the restoration.
Local workers were employed only by the firm for the restoration.
Local workers were employed by the firm only for the restoration.
Only the firm employed local workers for the restoration.
questions.explanation: 'Only local workers' keeps the restriction on which workers the firm employed.
feedback: 'Only local workers' keeps the restriction on which workers the firm employed.
'Only by the firm' excludes other employers, not nonlocal workers.
'Only for the restoration' limits the work's purpose or occasion rather than the workers' locality.
'Only the firm' restricts the employer and is active, changing the original scope.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation assigning the inspecting role correctly in both clauses.
questions.prompt: The pumps need inspecting, and the engineers insist on inspecting them personally.
options: The pumps perform the first inspection, and the engineers perform the second.
The pumps are to receive inspection, and the engineers intend to perform it.
Both -ing forms make their preceding subjects the receivers of inspection.
The first clause describes inspection already completed; the second describes inspection still required.
questions.explanation: Need inspecting means need to be inspected, whereas the active complement of insist assigns the inspecting to the engineers.
feedback: Need inspecting has a passive meaning here: the pumps need someone to inspect them.
Need inspecting means need to be inspected, whereas the active complement of insist assigns the inspecting to the engineers.
After insist on, inspecting is active and the engineers are its understood actors.
Need expresses a requirement, not a completed inspection; neither -ing ending alone determines completion.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation preserving the uncertainty expressed by the passive idiom.
questions.prompt: It remains to be seen whether the new timetable will reduce crowding.
options: The effect on crowding has not yet been established.
The effect has been established but has not yet been announced.
The timetable has already been observed reducing crowding.
An observer must watch every journey before the timetable can be introduced.
questions.explanation: Remains to be seen presents the outcome as still unresolved, rather than reporting an observation already made.
feedback: Remains to be seen presents the outcome as still unresolved, rather than reporting an observation already made.
The idiom concerns unresolved knowledge, not merely delayed publication of known results.
This asserts an observed benefit that the sentence leaves open.
The expression does not impose a literal observation procedure or a condition for introducing the timetable.

questions.setup: Choose the comparison that does not invent a different interviewer.
questions.prompt: A: 'I have three candidates to interview.' B: 'I have three candidates to be interviewed.'
options: B requires someone other than the speaker to conduct the interviews.
B leaves the interviewer unexpressed; the speaker may still conduct them.
A says the interviews are complete, while B says they are pending.
B makes the candidates the people who will interview the speaker.
questions.explanation: To be interviewed places the candidates as receivers and leaves the interviewer unspecified, which does not rule the speaker out.
feedback: The passive leaves the actor unexpressed; it does not require the actor to differ from the speaker.
To be interviewed places the candidates as receivers and leaves the interviewer unspecified, which does not rule the speaker out.
The infinitives in both versions can refer to pending interviews, not completed ones.
The candidates receive interviewing in B; they do not become the interviewers.

questions.setup: Choose the report explicitly presenting the observed activity from within, without presenting the crossing as a whole or an inference.
questions.prompt: A witness watched the visitor for a few seconds midway across the courtyard.
options: The visitor was seen crossing the courtyard.
The visitor was seen to have crossed the courtyard.
The visitor was seen to cross the courtyard.
The visitor was understood to have been crossing the courtyard.
questions.explanation: Was seen crossing places the directly observed visitor within the unfolding activity without claiming observation of the whole crossing.
feedback: Was seen crossing places the directly observed visitor within the unfolding activity without claiming observation of the whole crossing.
To have crossed presents a crossing as anterior to the perception or evidential judgment, not as the activity directly observed from within.
Was seen to cross presents the crossing as an observed whole event, stronger than the limited view described.
Was understood to have been crossing reports an understanding about an earlier activity, not the witness's direct visual observation.

questions.setup: Choose the comparison appropriate to a context in which a family hired roofers.
questions.prompt: A: 'We had our roof repaired.' B: 'We had repaired our roof.'
options: A and B both identify the family as the people who physically carried out the repairs.
A describes arranging a service; B makes we the repairers in an active past-perfect clause.
A reports an earlier completed repair by the family, while B reports hiring roofers.
A is past perfect, while B is an ordinary past passive.
questions.explanation: The position of our roof distinguishes the service construction from the active perfect; the given context selects the arranged-service reading for A.
feedback: In the supplied hiring context, A presents the family as arranging the service, not physically carrying out the repair.
The position of our roof distinguishes the service construction from the active perfect; the given context selects the arranged-service reading for A.
This reverses the causative-service reading of A and the active perfect structure of B.
A has causative had plus object plus participle; B has the perfect auxiliary had immediately before repaired.

questions.setup: Choose the role assignment that preserves attribution without verifying the attributed event.
questions.prompt: The manuscript was said by its donor to have been translated by a local scholar.
options: The donor is the translator; the scholar supplies the claim.
Both donor and scholar are identified as sources making the same claim.
The donor supplies the claim, and the sentence independently verifies the scholar's translation.
The donor supplies the claim; the scholar is its alleged translator.
questions.explanation: By its donor attaches to was said; by a local scholar attaches to translated inside the reported claim.
feedback: This reverses the two by phrases' attachments to different passive verbs.
The scholar is described as performing translation, not as making a statement.
Was said attributes the translation claim to the donor; it does not independently verify its content.
By its donor attaches to was said; by a local scholar attaches to translated inside the reported claim.

questions.setup: Choose the comparison that respects the status of a reported assessment.
questions.prompt: A: 'The route was considered safe.' B: 'The route was considered to be safe.'
options: A states proven safety; B reports only an assessment.
A describes past safety; B predicts safety after the assessment.
To be makes B an instruction to make the route safe rather than an assessment.
Both report an assessment of safety, without independently verifying safety.
questions.explanation: Both complements are available after was considered here. Neither construction by itself makes the reported judgment an independently established fact.
feedback: Omitting to be does not turn considered into an assertion of proven safety.
To be need not place safety later; both can describe the assessment of a state at the same time.
To be is part of the complement describing the assessed state, not an instruction to change the route.
Both complements are available after was considered here. Neither construction by itself makes the reported judgment an independently established fact.

questions.setup: Choose the statement unambiguously preserving that some passengers were screened and some were not.
questions.prompt: The records show a mixture of screened and unscreened passengers.
options: All the passengers were not screened before boarding.
None of the passengers were screened before boarding.
Some, but not all, passengers were screened before boarding.
No passengers were left unscreened before boarding.
questions.explanation: Some, but not all explicitly preserves both a screened group and an unscreened group.
feedback: All ... not can be read with different scope in usage; it does not unambiguously state the required mixture.
None denies screening for the whole group, losing the screened passengers.
Some, but not all explicitly preserves both a screened group and an unscreened group.
No passengers left unscreened says everyone was screened, losing the unscreened group.

questions.setup: Choose the analysis explaining why this passive is possible without treating all uses of 'arrive' as transitive.
questions.prompt: No agreement was arrived at during mediation.
options: The preposition at is an optional location phrase, so agreement is a direct object promoted to subject.
The unit arrive at means reach a conclusion; agreement is promoted from its prepositional complement.
The passive construction adds an agreement as an object to the otherwise unchanged physical-arrival sense.
The preposition supplies the omitted agent, so no agreement identifies the people who failed to arrive.
questions.explanation: The figurative prepositional construction licenses 'agreement' as a passive subject. This does not make ordinary intransitive physical 'arrive' generally passivizable.
feedback: 'At' is part of the figurative 'arrive at' construction here, not an optional location phrase after a direct object.
The figurative prepositional construction licenses 'agreement' as a passive subject. This does not make ordinary intransitive physical 'arrive' generally passivizable.
The acceptability depends on the figurative prepositional construction, not on passivization creating a direct object for physical 'arrive'.
'At' does not introduce an agent here; agreement identifies the outcome that was not reached.

questions.setup: Choose the comparison matching the stated sources of the two sentences.
questions.prompt: A manual says, 'The hatch is supposed to be sealed during testing.' An unverified recollection says, 'The hatch is supposed to have been sealed before the trial.'
options: Both sentences independently confirm that the hatch was sealed as required.
A attributes an earlier belief; B gives an instruction for a future trial.
A gives a requirement; B attributes an unverified belief about earlier sealing.
Both sentences describe an action currently being performed on the hatch.
questions.explanation: The manual context selects an obligation reading; the recollection context and perfect infinitive select an attributed earlier-event reading.
feedback: Neither an instruction nor an unverified recollection independently establishes that sealing occurred.
This reverses the contexts and overlooks the perfect infinitive in the recollection.
The manual context selects an obligation reading; the recollection context and perfect infinitive select an attributed earlier-event reading.
Neither be sealed nor have been sealed is the progressive being sealed, and the sources concern a rule and an earlier event.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence explicitly making weighing passive and subsequent natural drying active.
questions.prompt: Staff weighed the samples. The samples then dried on their own.
options: The samples were weighed and were dried afterward.
The samples were weighed; they then dried naturally.
The samples were weighed and dried afterward.
Staff weighed the samples and dried them afterward.
questions.explanation: Were weighed makes the measurement passive, while they dried is an active intransitive clause describing the natural change.
feedback: Repeating were marks drying as passive rather than the explicitly active natural process requested.
Were weighed makes the measurement passive, while they dried is an active intransitive clause describing the natural change.
The shared were allows dried to be read as a coordinated passive; it does not make the natural active reading explicit.
This keeps weighing active and makes staff the agents of drying, rather than preserving the requested voice contrast.

questions.setup: Choose the analysis preserving the two affected parties without assuming that demolition has already occurred.
questions.prompt: The residents objected to the bridge being demolished without their being consulted.
options: The objection concerns demolition of the bridge without consultation of the residents; it may concern a proposed action.
The residents oppose being made responsible for demolition without first approving the plan.
The residents object to a completed demolition, and both passive gerunds independently establish completed events.
The residents oppose consultation about the bridge unless demolition has first been completed.
questions.explanation: The bridge is the subject of being demolished, and their refers to the residents as potential consultees; the gerunds do not by themselves establish completed events.
feedback: The bridge is the subject of being demolished, and their refers to the residents as potential consultees; the gerunds do not by themselves establish completed events.
The residents are the potential recipients of consultation, not the stated demolition workers.
Neither passive gerund contains a perfect marking, and an objection can concern a proposal rather than something already done.
Without places the absence of consultation within the objection; it does not make completed demolition a condition for consultation.

questions.setup: Choose the passive recast preserving successful prevention, not merely an attempt or a rule.
questions.prompt: The customs inspection prevented the artifacts from being exported.
options: The artifacts were subjected to an inspection intended to prevent their export.
The artifacts were not permitted to be exported following the customs inspection.
The artifacts were prevented by the customs inspection from being exported.
The artifacts were inspected to determine whether their export could be prevented.
questions.explanation: The inspection remains the preventing cause, and export remains the event stopped from occurring.
feedback: An inspection intended to prevent export states a purpose but does not establish that prevention succeeded.
A prohibition does not itself establish that export was prevented in practice.
The inspection remains the preventing cause, and export remains the event stopped from occurring.
This substitutes an assessment of possible prevention for the stated successful prevention.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'shown to' in this research statement.
questions.prompt: Participants were shown to recognize familiar melodies more quickly than unfamiliar ones.
options: Participants were shown pictures telling them which melodies were familiar.
Researchers instructed participants to recognize familiar melodies more quickly.
Evidence demonstrated a difference in participants' recognition speed.
Participants demonstrated the melodies to the researchers.
questions.explanation: 'Were shown to' introduces a finding established by evidence about the participants' behavior.
feedback: 'Shown to recognize' is not the double-object construction in which people are shown pictures or other objects.
The sentence reports a demonstrated result, not an instruction to perform differently.
'Were shown to' introduces a finding established by evidence about the participants' behavior.
Participants are the subjects of 'recognize', not the people showing melodies to researchers.

questions.setup: Choose the active recast preserving the continuing process, accumulated duration, and named workers without adding a completion claim.
questions.prompt: The stadium has been being renovated by local contractors for months.
options: Local contractors have had the stadium renovated for months.
Local contractors have had months in which to renovate the stadium.
Local contractors have renovated the stadium over a period of months.
Local contractors have been renovating the stadium for months.
questions.explanation: The active perfect progressive preserves the ongoing duration and named actor while avoiding the cumbersome passive auxiliary sequence.
feedback: Have had the stadium renovated presents a causative arrangement or resulting condition; it does not retain the contractors as the grammatical performers of an ongoing process.
Having time available does not assert that the contractors have actually been carrying out the work.
The simple perfect presents the renovation as an accomplished whole rather than retaining the original process viewpoint.
The active perfect progressive preserves the ongoing duration and named actor while avoiding the cumbersome passive auxiliary sequence.

questions.setup: Choose the passive wording that explicitly allows different certificates for different inspectors while retaining coverage of every inspector.
questions.prompt: Every inspector signed at least one certificate; the certificates need not have been the same.
options: At least one certificate was signed by every inspector.
Every certificate was signed by at least one inspector.
For each inspector, at least one certificate was signed by that inspector.
There was a certificate bearing the signature of every inspector.
questions.explanation: For each inspector gives every inspector a certificate-signing requirement while allowing the certificate to vary with the inspector.
feedback: This can place one certificate within the scope of all the inspectors and does not explicitly preserve the allowed inspector-by-inspector variation.
This requires coverage of every certificate, not coverage of every inspector, and leaves some inspectors potentially without a signature.
For each inspector gives every inspector a certificate-signing requirement while allowing the certificate to vary with the inspector.
There was a certificate selects a single certificate bearing all the signatures, which is stronger than the source.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence keeping both levels of attribution without independently confirming either sealing or the assistant's statement.
questions.prompt: An anonymous caller alleges that the assistant said the deposit box had been sealed. Neither claim has been checked.
options: The deposit box is said by the assistant to have been sealed, as the caller has established.
The assistant is alleged by the caller to have said that the deposit box had been sealed.
The assistant is alleged to have sealed the deposit box before making a statement.
The deposit box had been sealed, as the assistant is alleged by the caller to have said.
questions.explanation: The caller remains the source of the allegation about what the assistant said, and sealing stays inside that attributed statement.
feedback: As the caller has established upgrades the unverified allegation about the statement into established evidence.
The caller remains the source of the allegation about what the assistant said, and sealing stays inside that attributed statement.
This moves the allegation from the assistant's speech to the assistant's physical act of sealing.
The opening independent clause asserts sealing as fact; the final attribution does not withdraw that assertion.

questions.setup: Choose the reading that limits unanimity to the layer actually modified.
questions.prompt: The candidate was unanimously expected to be elected, but the ballot was secret.
options: The sentence reports an expectation of a unanimous election result.
The sentence confirms election while leaving the voters' agreement unknown.
The unanimity concerns the prediction, not the ballot or its result.
The sentence reports unanimous support for electing the candidate rather than a prediction.
questions.explanation: Unanimously belongs to the reporting layer: the expectation is shared, while the election result remains unasserted.
feedback: Unanimously modifies expected, not elected; agreement among predictors does not establish a unanimous ballot.
Expected to be elected does not independently confirm that election occurred.
Unanimously belongs to the reporting layer: the expectation is shared, while the election result remains unasserted.
An expectation about a result need not be approval of that result; people can agree on an unwelcome prediction.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation preserving who was persuaded and what that person was to arrange.
questions.prompt: The deputy was persuaded by the chair to have the sealed files released to the archivist.
options: The chair persuaded the deputy to arrange release; the physical handler is unnamed.
The chair persuaded the deputy to release the files personally; the archivist was to arrange their release.
The chair arranged release after being persuaded by the deputy; the physical handler remains unnamed.
The archivist was persuaded to release the files, with the deputy arranging the chair's involvement.
questions.explanation: The deputy receives persuasion and is the understood subject of causative have; the participle released leaves the physical handler unexpressed.
feedback: The deputy receives persuasion and is the understood subject of causative have; the participle released leaves the physical handler unexpressed.
Causative have does not require the deputy to do the physical releasing, and to the archivist marks a recipient rather than an arranger.
By the chair identifies the persuader, not the person receiving persuasion; the deputy controls have.
The archivist is the destination recipient of the files, not the subject of was persuaded or the controller of have.

questions.setup: Choose the wording expressing the analyst's strong inference about prior authorization, not a procedural requirement or an independently verified fact.
questions.prompt: The analyst reasons from the valid access token: 'The transfer ___ before it could use this token.'
options: must have been authorized
had to be authorized under the procedure
was confirmed to have been authorized
was to have been authorized
questions.explanation: Must have been authorized expresses a strong inference about an earlier passive event, supported here by the token evidence.
feedback: Must have been authorized expresses a strong inference about an earlier passive event, supported here by the token evidence.
Had to be authorized under the procedure states a procedural necessity, not the analyst's present inference from the token.
Was confirmed reports verification, which is stronger than the stated reasoning from indirect evidence.
Was to have been authorized describes a prior arrangement or expectation and does not itself express the analyst's deduction.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence preserving established damage but an unresolved claim about its cause.
questions.prompt: The survey confirms damage to the mosaic. It does not establish whether drilling caused that damage.
options: The mosaic was confirmed to have been damaged, but not proved to have been damaged by drilling.
The mosaic was proved not to have been damaged by drilling.
The mosaic was not proved to have been damaged, although drilling was established as the cause.
The mosaic was confirmed to have been damaged by a cause other than drilling.
questions.explanation: The first clause confirms damage; the second withholds proof only of the more specific drilling-caused damage claim.
feedback: The first clause confirms damage; the second withholds proof only of the more specific drilling-caused damage claim.
Proved not to have been damaged by drilling establishes a negative causal conclusion that the survey leaves unresolved.
This withholds confirmation of damage itself while affirming its cause, reversing the two evidential commitments.
A cause other than drilling excludes drilling, whereas the survey has not resolved whether drilling was responsible.

questions.setup: Choose the analysis of the curator's role in these two grammatical sentences.
questions.prompt: A: 'The curator is easy to deceive.' B: 'The curator is eager to be deceived.'
options: The curator receives deception in A but performs it in B because eager expresses intention.
The curator is the potential object of deception in both; only B attributes eagerness to the curator.
Both infinitives are grammatically passive, and both attribute a wish for deception to the curator.
A describes the curator's skill at deception; B describes other people's willingness to deceive the curator.
questions.explanation: A links the curator to the missing object of active deceive; B makes the curator the subject of a passive infinitive and attributes eagerness.
feedback: Eagerness does not make the curator the deceiver in B: to be deceived is passive.
A links the curator to the missing object of active deceive; B makes the curator the subject of a passive infinitive and attributes eagerness.
To deceive in A is active in form with an understood object linked to the curator; easy expresses ease, not a wish.
A evaluates how easily someone could deceive the curator, while B attributes eagerness to the curator, not to other people.

questions.setup: Choose the inference warranted by the ordinary get-passive, without treating a possible implication as part of its meaning.
questions.prompt: The volunteer got excluded from the planning group despite trying to remain involved.
options: Using got makes the volunteer's attempt to remain involved inconsistent with the exclusion.
The get-passive says the volunteer brought about exclusion, even if that result was unwanted.
The get-passive makes the exclusion accidental, regardless of the planners' intentions.
Exclusion affected the volunteer; the sentence does not assign responsibility for causing it to the volunteer.
questions.explanation: Got excluded presents the volunteer as affected by the event; it does not entail self-causation or willingness.
feedback: An unwanted outcome is compatible with the get-passive, so despite introduces a coherent contrast.
The construction can occur where the subject bears responsibility, but it does not encode that responsibility as a requirement.
Got does not determine whether the excluding group acted deliberately or accidentally.
Got excluded presents the volunteer as affected by the event; it does not entail self-causation or willingness.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that locates the deliberate act and preserves the difference between an appearance and an established omission.
questions.prompt: The understudy was deliberately made to appear to have been overlooked when the casting list was circulated.
options: The creation of an appearance was intentional; an actual omission is not established.
The understudy deliberately arranged to be overlooked; the circulation merely exposed the omission.
The understudy was genuinely overlooked, but the people circulating the list did not intend that omission.
The omission was accidental, although the understudy deliberately made it appear intentional.
questions.explanation: Deliberately modifies made to appear; the alleged overlooking remains within appear and is not independently asserted as fact.
feedback: Deliberately modifies made to appear; the alleged overlooking remains within appear and is not independently asserted as fact.
The understudy is the affected subject of made to appear, not an identified arranger of the appearance or of the supposed omission.
An actual omission is not established by made to appear to have been overlooked, and the circulating people are not identified as the makers of that appearance.
This moves intention to the understudy and treats an accidental omission as established; neither follows from the passive layering.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that retains an attempted action without asserting that the vault was opened or that the attempt occurred inside it.
questions.prompt: The locksmith attempted to open the vault, but the account gives no outcome.
options: The vault was opened following an attempt by the locksmith.
The locksmith's attempt to open the vault was unsuccessful.
An attempt was made by the locksmith to open the vault.
The attempt to open the vault was made possible by the locksmith.
questions.explanation: The passive subject is an attempt, so the sentence asserts the effort while leaving the embedded opening unconfirmed.
feedback: Was opened asserts the intended result as an actual event, which the source does not confirm.
Unsuccessful asserts failure, whereas the source leaves the outcome open.
The passive subject is an attempt, so the sentence asserts the effort while leaving the embedded opening unconfirmed.
Making an attempt possible identifies an enabler, not necessarily the person who made the attempt.

questions.setup: Choose the conclusion supported by the restriction, without turning a necessary condition into a guarantee.
questions.prompt: Only parcels that had been weighed were dispatched from the depot.
options: Every parcel weighed at the depot was subsequently dispatched.
Dispatch entails prior weighing, but the converse does not follow.
A parcel's having been weighed guaranteed its dispatch from the depot.
The depot dispatched a parcel if and only if it had been weighed.
questions.explanation: The restrictive relative clause defines the eligible group; the sentence does not assert dispatch of every member of that group.
feedback: Only restricts dispatched parcels to the weighed group; it does not say that the whole weighed group was dispatched.
The restrictive relative clause defines the eligible group; the sentence does not assert dispatch of every member of that group.
The sentence makes weighing necessary for dispatch, not sufficient to guarantee it.
If and only if asserts both directions, whereas the source gives only dispatch implying prior weighing.

questions.setup: Choose the policy wording retaining sponsorship as necessary but not sufficient for admission.
questions.prompt: Applicants need a sponsor to be admitted. Even sponsored applicants may be refused.
options: Admission is conditional on sponsorship, which does not guarantee that an applicant will be admitted.
Sponsored applicants are to be admitted, although applicants without sponsors may be refused.
Applicants may be admitted without sponsorship only when sponsored applicants have been refused.
Admission is guaranteed unless an applicant has been refused sponsorship.
questions.explanation: Conditional on preserves the prerequisite, and the second clause explicitly withholds a guarantee of admission.
feedback: Conditional on preserves the prerequisite, and the second clause explicitly withholds a guarantee of admission.
Are to be admitted gives sponsored applicants an admission entitlement that the source withholds; may be refused also weakens the rule for others.
This creates an exception permitting unsponsored applicants to enter, which the source does not provide.
This makes absence of a refused sponsorship sufficient for guaranteed admission, rather than requiring sponsorship and a separate admission decision.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that keeps theft inside the rumor rather than presenting theft as independently established.
questions.prompt: The violin may or may not have been stolen. A rumor says it was stolen from the rehearsal room.
options: The stolen violin is rumored to have been taken from the rehearsal room.
The violin, which was stolen, is rumored to have come from the rehearsal room.
The theft of the violin is rumored to have occurred in the rehearsal room.
The violin is rumored to have been stolen from the rehearsal room.
questions.explanation: Both theft and its source location remain within the content of is rumored, leaving the event unverified.
feedback: Calling it the stolen violin treats theft as part of the identifying description, outside the rumor about where it was taken from.
The supplementary clause which was stolen asserts theft separately from the rumor about origin.
The theft of the violin treats theft as given and places only its location under the rumor.
Both theft and its source location remain within the content of is rumored, leaving the event unverified.

questions.setup: Choose the statement that removes an obligation to translate without prohibiting translation or asserting that no translation occurred.
questions.prompt: The publisher waived the translation requirement; authors remained free to supply translations.
options: The articles were required not to be translated.
The articles were not required to be translated.
The articles were not translated because the requirement had been waived.
The articles were to be left untranslated under the waiver.
questions.explanation: Not required places negation over the requirement, leaving both voluntary translation and non-translation possible.
feedback: Required not to imposes a negative obligation: it prohibits translation rather than making it optional.
Not required places negation over the requirement, leaving both voluntary translation and non-translation possible.
This asserts non-translation as an actual outcome, which a waiver alone does not establish.
Were to be left untranslated prescribes an untranslated outcome instead of permitting authors to choose.

questions.setup: Choose the comparison preserving what is qualified as wrong in each sentence.
questions.prompt: A: 'The sailor was allegedly wrongly detained.' B: 'The sailor was wrongly alleged to have been detained.'
options: Both say detention occurred and independently condemn it as wrongful.
A rejects the allegation of detention; B attributes an allegation of wrongful detention.
Both withhold judgment about whether the allegation itself was mistaken.
A attributes a claim of wrongful detention; B judges the allegation of detention to be mistaken.
questions.explanation: The placement of wrongly changes its target from the embedded detention to the act or content of alleging detention.
feedback: In A the claim of wrongful detention is attributed; in B wrong qualifies the allegation rather than establishing an actual wrongful detention.
This exchanges the scope of wrongly: it modifies detained in A but alleged in B.
B explicitly evaluates the allegation as wrong, so it does not withhold that judgment.
The placement of wrongly changes its target from the embedded detention to the act or content of alleging detention.

questions.setup: Choose the passive report that keeps the belief attached to the two identified paintings, without asserting that either actually is a forgery.
questions.prompt: The conservator believes that these two paintings are forgeries.
options: There are believed by the conservator to be two forgeries in the collection.
The two forgeries are believed by the conservator to be these paintings.
These two paintings are believed by the conservator to be forgeries.
These two paintings are the forgeries believed by the conservator to be in the collection.
questions.explanation: These two paintings remains the identified subject, while their being forgeries stays within the conservator's belief.
feedback: The existential report supplies a number but need not identify the forgeries as the two paintings singled out in the source.
The two forgeries treats the existence of an identifiable pair of forgeries as given and reports a belief about their identity.
These two paintings remains the identified subject, while their being forgeries stays within the conservator's belief.
The main clause identifies these paintings as the forgeries, placing that classification outside the relative clause's belief report.

questions.setup: Choose the comparison that avoids inventing intention in an inanimate subject or certainty about an unnamed agent.
questions.prompt: A: 'The hatch won't open.' B: 'The hatch won't be opened.' No further context is supplied.
options: A and B both attribute refusal to the hatch itself.
A says opening is physically impossible; B says a named operator has refused to open it.
A asserts a deliberate human refusal; B asserts a mechanical fault.
A can describe a resistant hatch; B leaves the agent and reason unexpressed.
questions.explanation: The active intransitive construction can describe failure to open, while the passive concerns an opening event without specifying who would perform it or why it will not occur.
feedback: An inanimate hatch need not have an intention in either construction; won't can express disposition or prediction.
A need not assert absolute physical impossibility, and B neither names an operator nor necessarily reports a refusal.
This assigns fixed explanations that the two forms do not encode: A can concern a fault and B can express a decision, but neither requires those causes.
The active intransitive construction can describe failure to open, while the passive concerns an opening event without specifying who would perform it or why it will not occur.

questions.setup: Choose the instruction that blocks an inference of permission while leaving the actual permission status unresolved.
questions.prompt: The absence of a reply must not be treated as evidence that permission has been granted.
options: Permission is to be assumed not to have been granted when there is no reply.
It is not to be assumed from silence that permission has been granted.
Permission is known not to have been granted if no reply has been received.
Permission is not granted unless a reply is received.
questions.explanation: Negation applies to the permitted inference from silence, not to the truth of the embedded permission claim.
feedback: This instructs the reader to assume non-permission, whereas the source only blocks an inference of permission.
Negation applies to the permitted inference from silence, not to the truth of the embedded permission claim.
Known not to asserts established non-permission, which the instruction does not establish.
This creates a substantive condition for permission itself rather than a limit on what silence can be taken to show.

questions.setup: Choose the formulation retaining approval conditional on later testing, without claiming either completed testing or unconditional approval.
questions.prompt: The board approved the recommendations on condition that they would be tested before implementation.
options: The recommendations were approved after having been tested before implementation.
The recommendations were approved for implementation, having been selected for testing.
The recommendations were approved because they were to be tested before implementation.
The recommendations were approved subject to being tested before implementation.
questions.explanation: Subject to preserves the condition, and being tested leaves the testing prospective in relation to the approval.
feedback: After having been tested makes completed testing anterior to approval, whereas the source imposes a later condition.
Selection for testing does not state that testing is a condition that must be met before implementation.
Because supplies a reason for approval; it does not explicitly retain testing as a binding condition on that approval.
Subject to preserves the condition, and being tested leaves the testing prospective in relation to the approval.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation consistent with the speaker's denial of commissioning, followed by confirmation that retouching nevertheless happened.
questions.prompt: 'I didn't have my portrait retouched; the photographer did it without asking me.'
options: The first clause denies any retouching, so the second necessarily contradicts it.
The first clause says retouching was incomplete when the photographer intervened.
The speaker denies arranging the retouching, not the occurrence of retouching itself.
The speaker accepts responsibility for arranging the work but denies personally performing it.
questions.explanation: In this context, not scopes over causative have: the speaker did not commission the work, although the photographer performed it.
feedback: The second clause selects the denial-of-commissioning reading of the first; the wording need not deny the resulting event.
Neither didn't have nor retouched provides a progressive or incomplete-stage claim.
In this context, not scopes over causative have: the speaker did not commission the work, although the photographer performed it.
The speaker denies the arrangement itself, not merely the identity of the person who physically retouched the portrait.
