questions.explanation: 'Set up a business' means create and organise it so that it can operate. It need not involve building new premises.
feedback: 'Set up a business' means create and organise it so that it can operate. It need not involve building new premises.
Selling transfers an existing business; setting one up establishes it.
'Set up' does not mean suspend operations or repair a building.
Joining as an employee is different from establishing the business.

questions.setup: Two housemates describe living together.
questions.prompt: 'We get along well, although we have different interests.' Which interpretation fits?
options: They agree about which hobbies are best.
They are progressing at the same speed in their work.
They have a good relationship.
They spend their free time in the same places.
questions.explanation: Get along well means have a friendly or comfortable relationship. People can get along without sharing the same interests.
feedback: Getting along does not require agreement about hobbies; their interests are explicitly different.
Get along can concern progress elsewhere, but we and the housemate context support the relationship sense here.
Get along well means have a friendly or comfortable relationship. People can get along without sharing the same interests.
The phrase describes their relationship, not where they spend their time.

questions.setup: A community centre explains its staff responsibilities.
questions.prompt: 'Nora deals with room-booking enquiries.' Which paraphrase preserves this responsibility without adding a result?
options: Nora approves every room-booking request.
Nora sends all room-booking enquiries elsewhere.
Nora creates the rules for booking rooms.
Nora handles questions about booking rooms.
questions.explanation: Deal with means attend to or handle a matter. It states responsibility here, not that every problem is solved or request granted.
feedback: Dealing with enquiries does not guarantee that each request is approved.
Referral can be part of handling an enquiry, but deals with does not say she forwards them all.
Handling questions about a process does not mean writing its rules.
Deal with means attend to or handle a matter. It states responsibility here, not that every problem is solved or request granted.

questions.setup: Completed expense forms must be submitted to the accounts office.
questions.prompt: Use 'them' for the forms. Which instruction requests submission?
options: Hand them out by Friday.
Fill them in by Friday.
Look them over by Friday.
Hand them in by Friday.
questions.explanation: 'Hand in' means submit something to the person or office that should receive it. With 'them', the object goes before 'in'.
feedback: 'Hand out' means distribute the forms to people, not submit the completed forms for processing.
'Fill in' asks for completion of the information. These forms are already completed and must now be submitted.
Looking them over means checking them; submission is a separate step.
'Hand in' means submit something to the person or office that should receive it. With 'them', the object goes before 'in'.

questions.setup: Read the organiser's brief account of a workshop.
questions.prompt: 'Twelve people signed up, but only eight showed up.' What does the contrast tell us?
options: Eight people gave presentations, although twelve attended.
Twelve registered, but eight attended.
Eight people arrived late, while four arrived on time.
Eight registered before four others did.
questions.explanation: Sign up means register to take part; show up means arrive or be present. Showing up does not itself say whether someone was late or unexpected.
feedback: Showed up means arrived or attended, not performed or presented something.
Sign up means register to take part; show up means arrive or be present. Showing up does not itself say whether someone was late or unexpected.
Show up does not itself mean arrive late, and the sentence does not report twelve arrivals.
The sentence contrasts registration with attendance, not two stages of registration.

questions.setup: Read about passengers waiting after a train cancellation.
questions.prompt: 'The clear announcement calmed them down.' Who became less anxious?
options: The person reading the announcement.
The waiting passengers.
The staff who cancelled the train.
The people writing a later announcement.
questions.explanation: Calm someone down means make that person less upset, anxious, or excited. Them identifies the passengers affected by the announcement.
feedback: Them refers to the passengers, not the announcer.
Calm someone down means make that person less upset, anxious, or excited. Them identifies the passengers affected by the announcement.
The sentence does not name the cancelling staff as the people being calmed.
No later announcement or its writers are introduced; them refers to the waiting passengers.

questions.setup: Maya is preparing for a budget meeting.
questions.prompt: She asks her accountant, 'Could you go over these figures with me?' What does she request?
options: Round all the figures upwards.
Replace the figures with last year's totals.
Examine the figures together.
Send the figures to everyone at the meeting.
questions.explanation: Go over something means review or examine it. With me makes the requested review a shared activity.
feedback: Go over does not instruct the accountant to increase or round the amounts.
Reviewing figures does not itself mean replacing them with another set.
Go over something means review or examine it. With me makes the requested review a shared activity.
Go over concerns examining the figures, not distributing them.

questions.setup: Two friends are checking a restaurant booking.
questions.prompt: 'Hold on, that's the old address.' What is the speaker doing with 'Hold on'?
options: Telling the friend to grip the booking paper tightly.
Asking the friend to keep the old address unchanged.
Pausing the discussion to point out a problem.
Promising to keep the table reserved.
questions.explanation: 'Hold on' can interrupt the current course of a conversation. The comment about the old address explains why the speaker pauses it.
feedback: There is no object to hold. Here 'hold on' pauses the discussion so the speaker can flag a problem.
The phrase does not request preserving the address; the following words question its use.
'Hold on' can interrupt the current course of a conversation. The comment about the old address explains why the speaker pauses it.
'Hold on' is not a promise to hold a reservation in this exchange.

questions.setup: You want to buy takeaway meals less often but not stop buying them.
questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses that plan?
options: I'm going to give up takeaway meals.
I'm going to cut out takeaway meals.
I'm going to cut down on takeaway meals.
I'm going to put off ordering tonight's takeaway.
questions.explanation: Cut down on means reduce the amount or frequency of something. It does not require stopping it altogether.
feedback: Give up means stop the habit, which is stronger than the requested reduction.
Cut out means eliminate them from the routine, not merely have them less often.
Cut down on means reduce the amount or frequency of something. It does not require stopping it altogether.
Put off postpones one order here; it does not state a plan to reduce the wider habit.

questions.setup: Read a comment made outside a bakery.
questions.prompt: 'That smell brings back memories of my grandmother's kitchen.' What effect does the smell have?
options: It encourages the speaker to rebuild the kitchen.
It makes the speaker forget the kitchen's present condition.
It proves the bakery uses the grandmother's recipes.
It makes the speaker remember the kitchen.
questions.explanation: Bring back memories means cause past experiences to return to someone's mind. The kitchen itself does not physically return.
feedback: Remembering a place does not mean deciding to reconstruct it.
The phrase states renewed memories, not forgetting current information.
A smell can remind someone of a place without establishing which recipes the bakery uses.
Bring back memories means cause past experiences to return to someone's mind. The kitchen itself does not physically return.

questions.setup: An old photograph shows a large group at a wedding.
questions.prompt: 'I can just pick out my sister in the back row.' What can the speaker do?
options: Choose the sister as the next photographer.
Remove the sister's image from the photograph.
Persuade the sister to move to another row.
Recognise the sister among the people pictured.
questions.explanation: Pick out can mean distinguish or recognise someone among others. The group photograph and back row support that sense.
feedback: Pick out can mean choose, but here the object is a person being located in an existing picture.
Pick out does not mean edit the person out of the image.
The photograph records a past arrangement; the phrase does not ask the sister to move.
Pick out can mean distinguish or recognise someone among others. The group photograph and back row support that sense.

questions.setup: Read a note about a revised newsletter.
questions.prompt: 'The editor left out the final paragraph.' Which statement preserves the meaning without adding a reason?
options: The editor moved the paragraph to the front.
The editor shortened the final paragraph.
The editor delayed publication of the paragraph until next month.
The editor did not include the final paragraph.
questions.explanation: Leave out means omit or exclude. The phrase alone does not tell us whether that happened deliberately or by mistake.
feedback: Moving it within the newsletter would retain it, whereas left out says it was omitted.
Shortening changes its length; leaving it out excludes it from the version.
A later publication plan is not stated. Left out concerns omission from this version.
Leave out means omit or exclude. The phrase alone does not tell us whether that happened deliberately or by mistake.

questions.setup: Read a meeting summary.
questions.prompt: 'A question about parking came up during the discussion.' What does 'came up' report?
options: The group agreed on an answer about parking.
The question arose in the discussion.
The question was sent to a more senior committee.
The group withdrew the parking question.
questions.explanation: 'Come up' can mean arise or become a topic. The phrase does not name who introduced the question or say that it was answered.
feedback: A question coming up means it entered the discussion, not that agreement followed.
'Come up' can mean arise or become a topic. The phrase does not name who introduced the question or say that it was answered.
'Up' does not identify a higher level of authority in this expression.
Withdrawal removes a question from consideration; 'came up' introduces it into the discussion.

questions.setup: Read an explanation for a late delivery.
questions.prompt: 'The van broke down on the way.' Which event is reported?
options: A fault stopped the van from operating normally.
The driver switched the engine off for a planned stop.
The van was involved in a collision.
The driver unloaded the van beside the road.
questions.explanation: A vehicle breaks down when a mechanical or similar fault prevents normal operation. The phrase does not itself report a collision.
feedback: A vehicle breaks down when a mechanical or similar fault prevents normal operation. The phrase does not itself report a collision.
A planned switch-off is not a breakdown; broke down indicates a failure.
A collision can cause damage, but broke down does not say a collision occurred.
Unloading concerns removing goods, not the vehicle's failure to operate.

questions.setup: A visitor reports a recurring fault in the booking system. You promise an investigation, not a search for a listed definition.
questions.prompt: Use 'it' for the fault. Which reply expresses that promise with correct word order?
options: I'll look it into.
I'll look it up.
I'll look into it.
I'll look out for it.
questions.explanation: 'Look into' means investigate a matter. Its pronoun object follows 'into': 'look into it'.
feedback: In the 'investigate' sense, 'look into' keeps its object after 'into'. It is not separated like 'look it up'.
'Look up' means consult a source for information. It does not specifically promise to investigate the reported fault.
'Look into' means investigate a matter. Its pronoun object follows 'into': 'look into it'.
'Look out for' means watch for something's appearance. That is not the same commitment as investigating the existing report.

questions.setup: Read an announcement about a community theatre.
questions.prompt: 'During Joel's leave, Amina will take over the day-to-day running of the theatre.' What is being transferred?
options: Ownership of the theatre building.
Responsibility for recruiting Joel's replacement permanently.
The theatre's activities to a different building.
Responsibility for its daily operation.
questions.explanation: Take over means assume control or responsibility previously held by someone else. Day-to-day running specifies the responsibility; the leave context makes this an interim arrangement.
feedback: Taking over day-to-day running transfers operational responsibility, not necessarily ownership.
The object is running the theatre. The announcement does not give Amina a recruitment assignment.
Take over does not mean move the activities elsewhere.
Take over means assume control or responsibility previously held by someone else. Day-to-day running specifies the responsibility; the leave context makes this an interim arrangement.

questions.setup: You want to introduce an issue for discussion at a meeting.
questions.prompt: Use 'it' for the issue. Which sentence expresses introducing it with correct word order?
options: I'd like to bring up it at the meeting.
I'd like to bring it up at the meeting.
I'd like to bring it about at the meeting.
I'd like to put it off until after the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Bring up an issue' means introduce it into a discussion. A pronoun object belongs between 'bring' and 'up': 'bring it up'.
feedback: With a pronoun, the object cannot follow 'up' in this sense. Use 'bring it up'.
'Bring up an issue' means introduce it into a discussion. A pronoun object belongs between 'bring' and 'up': 'bring it up'.
'Bring about' means cause something to happen, not introduce an existing issue for discussion.
'Put off' postpones dealing with it; the task calls for introducing it during the meeting.

questions.setup: A manager reflects on a new staff rota.
questions.prompt: 'We worked out a rota, but it didn't work out.' How do the two uses differ?
options: They implemented a rota, but could not calculate its total cost.
They devised the rota, but it was not successful in practice.
They exercised together, but could not agree when to meet.
They solved the rota's problems, but then lost the written copy.
questions.explanation: Work out a rota means devise or determine an arrangement. In it didn't work out, the arrangement is the subject and work out means turn out successfully.
feedback: The first use says they devised the rota, not necessarily implemented it. The second concerns how the arrangement turned out, not a missing calculation.
Work out a rota means devise or determine an arrangement. In it didn't work out, the arrangement is the subject and work out means turn out successfully.
A rota as object rules out physical exercise as the first work-out meaning.
Losing a document is not a meaning of didn't work out; the second clause evaluates the arrangement's success.

questions.setup: A tenant describes the flat above hers.
questions.prompt: 'I can put up with footsteps, but not music after midnight.' What does 'put up with' express?
options: Taking responsibility for stopping a disturbance.
Arranging for the disturbance to happen later.
Agreeing that the disturbance is beneficial.
Tolerating a disturbance.
questions.explanation: 'Put up with' means tolerate something unpleasant. The contrast distinguishes what she can endure from what she considers unacceptable.
feedback: Tolerance does not mean accepting a duty to eliminate the noise.
That would concern postponement. 'Put up with' expresses endurance, not scheduling.
People can put up with something they dislike. Tolerance is not a positive evaluation of it.
'Put up with' means tolerate something unpleasant. The contrast distinguishes what she can endure from what she considers unacceptable.

questions.setup: Read a description of contact with a supplier.
questions.prompt: 'Rina followed up her enquiry with a phone call.' Which sequence does this wording express?
options: She added a phone call after making the enquiry.
A phone call prompted the supplier to send her an enquiry.
She recorded an enquiry while answering the supplier's call.
She replaced her enquiry with a request not to be contacted.
questions.explanation: Follow up an action with another means take that additional action afterwards. The object names the earlier enquiry; with introduces the later call.
feedback: Follow up an action with another means take that additional action afterwards. The object names the earlier enquiry; with introduces the later call.
Her enquiry is the earlier action being followed up, not a later response from the supplier.
The construction does not describe simultaneous note-taking during an incoming call.
Following up continues contact about the matter; it does not cancel the enquiry or prohibit a reply.

questions.setup: Read an update about a festival sponsor.
questions.prompt: 'The company backed out of the sponsorship arrangement.' Which paraphrase best preserves the commitment change?
options: The company reduced the amount while keeping its commitment.
The company completed its part of the arrangement.
The company withdrew from the arrangement.
The company persuaded another sponsor to join it.
questions.explanation: Back out of means decide not to continue with an agreement or planned commitment. It contrasts with simply refusing a new proposal before becoming involved.
feedback: Reducing the contribution is a modification; backing out means withdrawing from the arrangement.
Completion fulfils a commitment rather than withdrawing from it.
Back out of means decide not to continue with an agreement or planned commitment. It contrasts with simply refusing a new proposal before becoming involved.
Recruiting support is not expressed by back out of.

questions.setup: Read a comment about an interview podcast.
questions.prompt: 'I came across Dev's podcast yesterday. In the interview, he came across as impatient.' What do the two expressions mean?
options: I searched for his podcast; he described himself as impatient.
I crossed to his studio; he became impatient during the interview.
I encountered the podcast; he gave an impatient impression.
I recommended his podcast; he persuaded me that patience was unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Come across something means encounter or find it, often by chance. Come across as describes how someone appears to an audience, which need not reveal their actual disposition.
feedback: Come across does not specifically describe a planned search, and come across as concerns the impression given, not self-description.
The first object is a podcast encountered, not a place crossed to. The second describes an impression, not necessarily a change in feeling.
Come across something means encounter or find it, often by chance. Come across as describes how someone appears to an audience, which need not reveal their actual disposition.
Neither recommendation nor persuasion is expressed by these come-across constructions.

questions.setup: Read a participant's assessment of a pottery course.
questions.prompt: 'The excellent teaching made up for the cramped room.' What relationship is expressed?
options: The teaching caused the room to feel physically larger.
The teaching was designed to explain why the room was cramped.
The cramped room helped produce the excellent teaching.
The benefit of the teaching compensated for the room's drawback.
questions.explanation: Make up for means compensate for a disadvantage or loss. The teaching offsets the drawback in the participant's assessment without removing the cramped conditions.
feedback: Compensation is evaluative here. The sentence does not claim the room's size or perception changed.
Make up for does not mean explain or justify the cause of the small space.
This reverses the relationship and adds causation: the teaching is the compensating benefit, not an effect of the room.
Make up for means compensate for a disadvantage or loss. The teaching offsets the drawback in the participant's assessment without removing the cramped conditions.

questions.setup: A coordinator is choosing between two updates about a booking problem.
questions.prompt: How does "We've sorted it out" differ from "We're looking into it"?
options: The first reports a physical rearrangement; the second reports reading instructions.
Both report resolution, but the first says the solution took longer.
Both report investigation, but the first identifies who caused the problem.
The first reports resolution; the second reports investigation in progress.
questions.explanation: 'Sort out a problem' means resolve it. 'Looking into it' describes investigation, which can still leave the outcome open.
feedback: With the booking problem as 'it', 'sorted out' concerns resolution, not sorting objects into groups.
Looking into a problem does not report a solution, and neither expression compares duration.
'Sorted it out' goes beyond investigation to resolution; it does not itself identify the person responsible.
'Sort out a problem' means resolve it. 'Looking into it' describes investigation, which can still leave the outcome open.

questions.setup: Read a review of the final scene in a play.
questions.prompt: 'After the letter is opened, their earlier conversation takes on a different meaning.' What changes?
options: The actors repeat the conversation using different words.
The earlier conversation acquires a new significance.
The conversation becomes somebody else's responsibility.
The letter replaces the earlier conversation in the script.
questions.explanation: Take on can mean acquire a quality or character. Here the letter changes how the audience understands the earlier conversation.
feedback: Taking on a meaning changes how the conversation is interpreted, not necessarily the dialogue performed.
Take on can mean acquire a quality or character. Here the letter changes how the audience understands the earlier conversation.
Take on can concern responsibilities, but meaning as object selects the acquire-a-quality sense.
The earlier conversation remains relevant; the new information changes its significance rather than removing it.

questions.setup: Read an update about flexible opening hours.
questions.prompt: 'The staff group has put forward a proposal.' What stage does 'put forward' itself establish?
options: The proposal has been offered for consideration.
The director has adopted the proposed hours.
The centre has begun using the proposed hours.
The proposal has been withdrawn from discussion.
questions.explanation: 'Put forward' means present an idea or proposal for consideration. The expression does not itself report a decision to adopt or implement it.
feedback: 'Put forward' means present an idea or proposal for consideration. The expression does not itself report a decision to adopt or implement it.
Putting a proposal forward offers it for consideration. It does not establish the director's acceptance.
Implementation is an additional action, not part of putting forward the proposal.
Withdrawal removes a proposal from consideration; putting it forward presents it for consideration.

questions.setup: Read a breakdown of a theatre's annual spending.
questions.prompt: 'Building repairs account for forty percent of expenditure.' How is 'account for' used?
options: To explain why the expenditure was incorrectly recorded.
To say what proportion the repairs make up.
To justify the decision to spend money on repairs.
To predict how much spending will rise next year.
questions.explanation: 'Account for' can mean constitute a stated share of a total. The percentage selects that sense, rather than 'explain why an event occurred'.
feedback: The sentence assigns a share of spending; it does not report an accounting error or its cause.
'Account for' can mean constitute a stated share of a total. The percentage selects that sense, rather than 'explain why an event occurred'.
Stating a proportion does not provide a justification for the spending.
Forty percent is a share of the stated expenditure, not a forecast increase.

questions.setup: A speaker opens a discussion about extending a cycle route.
questions.prompt: 'I'll set out the alternatives before we debate them.' What does the speaker promise?
options: To choose one alternative for everyone.
To put the alternatives into practice before discussion.
To describe the alternatives clearly and systematically.
To remove the alternatives that are difficult to explain.
questions.explanation: Set out information means present or explain it in an organised way. It can be done orally as well as in writing.
feedback: Setting out alternatives presents them; it does not decide which should be adopted.
Implementation is different from explaining options for debate.
Set out information means present or explain it in an organised way. It can be done orally as well as in writing.
Setting out the alternatives does not mean filtering or rejecting some of them.

questions.setup: A language centre explains its lesson-credit policy.
questions.prompt: 'Unused credits can be carried over into the following month.' What does 'carried over' mean here?
options: Converted into a cash refund.
Transferred to another student's account.
Kept available for use in the next month.
Replaced with a fresh allocation unrelated to the unused balance.
questions.explanation: 'Carry over' means transfer or continue something into a later period. The credits remain usable rather than disappearing at the current month's end.
feedback: Carrying credits over preserves them for later use; it does not itself promise a refund.
The following month is a later period, not another recipient.
'Carry over' means transfer or continue something into a later period. The credits remain usable rather than disappearing at the current month's end.
'Carry over' keeps the unused credits available; it does not discard and replace that balance.

questions.setup: Read a description of a documentary.
questions.prompt: 'The film draws on interviews with former factory workers.' What is the relationship between film and interviews?
options: The interviews supply material used in the film.
The film establishes that every interview account is accurate.
The film consists entirely of unedited interview recordings.
The film instructs viewers how to conduct similar interviews.
questions.explanation: Draw on means use something as a source or resource. The filmmakers may select and reshape material rather than reproduce it all.
feedback: Draw on means use something as a source or resource. The filmmakers may select and reshape material rather than reproduce it all.
Using interviews as a source does not certify the truth of each account.
Draw on does not require exclusive use or verbatim reproduction of a source.
Source use does not imply that the film teaches the interview method.

questions.setup: A colleague edits 'Please look over the draft' to 'Please overlook the draft.'
questions.prompt: Why does that edit fail to preserve the request?
options: It changes examination into failing to notice or disregarding the draft.
It changes a required quick check into a required detailed check.
It changes a request for editing into a request for spoken feedback only.
It changes the draft into a completed version ready for publication.
questions.explanation: Look over means examine or review. Overlook normally means fail to notice or choose to disregard, so joining these words does not create an equivalent request.
feedback: Look over means examine or review. Overlook normally means fail to notice or choose to disregard, so joining these words does not create an equivalent request.
The contrast is not a fixed quick-versus-detailed scale. Look over can involve careful examination.
Neither expression sets that written-versus-spoken distinction; the error concerns examine versus overlook.
The noun draft has not changed, and overlook does not confer completed status.

questions.setup: Read a staff member's reflection on a company merger.
questions.prompt: 'The team went through a difficult reorganisation.' Which sense of 'went through' fits?
options: Examined a written proposal for reorganisation.
Formally approved the reorganisation.
Designed the reorganisation for another team.
Experienced the difficult process.
questions.explanation: 'Go through an experience or period' means undergo it. The phrase does not say the team approved it or benefited from it.
feedback: 'Go through' can mean examine material, but here the object is the difficult process experienced, not a document.
Approval is not part of the experience sense. A team may go through a process it did not choose.
The team is presented as experiencing the process, not designing it for others.
'Go through an experience or period' means undergo it. The phrase does not say the team approved it or benefited from it.

questions.setup: Read a report about changes at a public garden.
questions.prompt: 'The change in opening hours was brought about by residents' complaints.' Which active version preserves the relationship?
options: Residents' complaints brought about the change in opening hours.
The change in opening hours brought about residents' complaints.
Residents' complaints described the change in opening hours.
Residents' complaints prevented a change in opening hours.
questions.explanation: Bring about means cause a change or event. In the passive original, the by-phrase names the cause; it becomes the subject of this active version.
feedback: Bring about means cause a change or event. In the passive original, the by-phrase names the cause; it becomes the subject of this active version.
This reverses the reported cause and result: the complaints preceded and caused the change in the original.
Description is not causation. The original credits the complaints with producing the change.
Preventing would stop the change; brought about says the complaints caused it.

questions.setup: A team leader sets a boundary for discussion.
questions.prompt: "We won't stand for personal insults." What does "won't stand for" mean?
options: Will not represent the people who were insulted.
Will not tolerate personal insults.
Will not explain what the insults mean.
Will not discuss whether the insults were accurate.
questions.explanation: 'Stand for' can mean tolerate or accept unpleasant behaviour, especially in negative statements. The leader says such behaviour will not be accepted.
feedback: 'Stand for' can mean represent, but 'personal insults' as the object of this boundary selects 'tolerate'.
'Stand for' can mean tolerate or accept unpleasant behaviour, especially in negative statements. The leader says such behaviour will not be accepted.
The leader is refusing to tolerate conduct, not declining to define expressions.
The statement concerns allowing the behaviour, not debating the accuracy of particular remarks.

questions.setup: Compare two versions of a progress report.
questions.prompt: 'By June, the agency had phased out paper permits' becomes 'In June, the agency was phasing out paper permits.' What claim is no longer made?
options: That the agency had decided to reduce paper use.
That the transition involved stages rather than one immediate switch.
That the removal had been completed by the stated time.
That the agency intended the change to be permanent.
questions.explanation: Phase out means discontinue gradually. Had phased out presents the process as completed by June; was phasing out presents it as ongoing without asserting its completion then.
feedback: The ongoing phasing-out process still presents a move towards ending paper permits.
Phase out retains its gradual-removal meaning in both versions.
Phase out means discontinue gradually. Had phased out presents the process as completed by June; was phasing out presents it as ongoing without asserting its completion then.
Changing the aspect does not replace discontinuation with a temporary suspension; the lost claim concerns completion.

questions.setup: A curator reports on efforts to retain a concert hall.
questions.prompt: 'Lea failed to talk the board out of selling the hall.' Which conclusion follows from the persuasion phrase?
options: The board sold the hall despite Lea's advice.
Lea abandoned her own plan to sell the hall.
The board persuaded Lea that selling was preferable.
Her persuasion did not secure the board's abandonment of the sale plan.
questions.explanation: Talk someone out of doing something means persuade them not to do it. Failed to negates that persuasive success, not the possibility that the plan ended for some other reason.
feedback: Failure to persuade does not establish that a sale subsequently occurred; another event could still have prevented it.
The board is the party she tried to persuade. The sentence does not make the sale Lea's own plan.
This reverses the direction of persuasion and adds a change in Lea's view.
Talk someone out of doing something means persuade them not to do it. Failed to negates that persuasive success, not the possibility that the plan ended for some other reason.

questions.setup: Read a project leader's account of a difficult decision.
questions.prompt: 'We set aside a small budget for the trial and set aside our reservations about its design.' What distinction does the repeated phrase carry?
options: Money was spent; the reservations were answered with evidence.
Money was reserved; the reservations were put to one side in proceeding.
Money was withheld from the trial; the reservations were kept for later publication.
Money and reservations were both rejected as unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Set aside funds means reserve them for a purpose. Set aside reservations means stop allowing those concerns to govern the immediate decision; it need not establish that the concerns were disproved.
feedback: Reserving a budget does not itself spend it, and putting concerns aside does not necessarily answer them.
Set aside funds means reserve them for a purpose. Set aside reservations means stop allowing those concerns to govern the immediate decision; it need not establish that the concerns were disproved.
For the trial specifies the purpose of the reserved money. Nothing in set aside our reservations says they were saved for publication.
The financial use allocates a resource rather than rejecting it. The same phrase has different relations to its two objects.

questions.setup: Compare two statements about a performance.
questions.prompt: 'The timestamps rule out a late start. The organisers rule out repeating the performance.' Why does the second statement not establish that repetition is physically impossible?
options: Rule out is uncertain with a human subject but certain with an inanimate subject.
The second merely postpones consideration until the evidence has been checked.
The second predicts that a repeat would start late, as the first performance did.
The second excludes a course of action from consideration, rather than disproving its physical possibility.
questions.explanation: Rule out can exclude an explanation on evidential grounds or exclude an option from a decision. The timestamps support the first use; the organisers' decision selects the second.
feedback: The distinction is not a mechanical subject rule. People can rule out an explanation using evidence, and circumstances can rule out an option.
Rule out is stronger than put off: it excludes the option from the decision being reported.
Neither statement predicts a later start, and the first actually excludes a late start for the recorded event.
Rule out can exclude an explanation on evidential grounds or exclude an option from a decision. The timestamps support the first use; the organisers' decision selects the second.

questions.setup: A project manager gives two instructions about records.
questions.prompt: 'Back up the files, then use them to back up your account of the delay.' What do the two uses require?
options: Make recovery copies of the files, then use the records as support for the account.
Move the original files elsewhere, then retell the account in reverse order.
Publish the files, then obtain permission to publish the account.
Make several copies, then treat each copy as independent confirmation of the account.
questions.explanation: Back up files means create copies for recovery. Back up an account means substantiate it; the records must actually support the account, since copying alone adds no evidence.
feedback: Back up files means create copies for recovery. Back up an account means substantiate it; the records must actually support the account, since copying alone adds no evidence.
A backup preserves recoverable copies; back up an account means support it, not reverse its chronology.
Neither back-up use inherently involves public release or permission.
Copies preserve the same source; they do not become independent corroborating sources merely because they are duplicated.

questions.setup: An exhibition organiser reflects on vendors who repeatedly broke a display rule.
questions.prompt: 'Their conduct was widely noticed, yet they got away with it.' Why is this not contradictory?
options: Get away with it requires only that the vendors later left the building.
They could escape consequences even though others knew about the conduct.
Being noticed proves that the conduct was permitted under the rule.
Get away with it means they persuaded everyone that the conduct never occurred.
questions.explanation: Get away with something means avoid the punishment or adverse consequences one might expect. Lack of detection can enable that, but is not necessary to the meaning.
feedback: The phrase concerns escaping consequences for conduct, not physically leaving the venue.
Get away with something means avoid the punishment or adverse consequences one might expect. Lack of detection can enable that, but is not necessary to the meaning.
Awareness does not confer permission; the sentence can describe a known breach that went unpunished.
Denial accepted by everyone would conflict with widely noticed. Escaping consequences does not require such a denial.

questions.setup: A volunteer offered to help catalogue a collection.
questions.prompt: 'The trustees followed up the offer, but failed to follow through on their own promise of training.' What contrast is made?
options: They fulfilled the volunteer's offer but declined to make a training promise.
They acted further on the offer but did not carry their training commitment into effect.
They trained the volunteer but did not publicise the training afterwards.
They ignored the offer but continued training other volunteers.
questions.explanation: Follow up means take subsequent action on a matter. Follow through on a promise means act on it through to fulfilment; the negative clause withholds that fulfilment here.
feedback: The offer belongs to the volunteer, not to the trustees to fulfil. Their own promise is already presented as having been made.
Follow up means take subsequent action on a matter. Follow through on a promise means act on it through to fulfilment; the negative clause withholds that fulfilment here.
Failure to follow through concerns carrying out the commitment, not publicising a completed action.
Followed up says they took further action on the offer. The sentence says nothing about other volunteers.

questions.setup: A journal describes a museum reorganisation.
questions.prompt: 'The collection came under the new department, and the arrangement soon came under criticism.' How does 'under' function in the two expressions?
options: Both uses locate something below another object in the building.
The first reports criticism by the department; the second reports a transfer to another department.
The first marks oversight by a department; the second marks being subjected to criticism.
Both uses mean that the collection was being examined for possible transfer.
questions.explanation: 'Come under' can mean enter someone's authority or become subject to an influence or response. The complement selects oversight in the first clause and criticism in the second.
feedback: The 'department' denotes administrative responsibility, and 'criticism' denotes an adverse response; neither is a physical location.
This swaps the relations selected by the complements: 'department' supplies authority, while 'criticism' supplies the response.
'Come under' can mean enter someone's authority or become subject to an influence or response. The complement selects oversight in the first clause and criticism in the second.
The first states that it came under the department, not merely that a transfer was considered. Criticism does not necessarily involve transfer.

questions.setup: An editor replaces 'These observations bear on the hypothesis' with 'These observations bear out the hypothesis.'
questions.prompt: What extra claim does the replacement normally make?
options: That the observations were made before the hypothesis was proposed.
That the observations contradict the hypothesis rather than concern it.
That the observations support the hypothesis, not merely relate to it.
That the hypothesis caused the observations to be recorded.
questions.explanation: Bear on means be relevant to or have a bearing on. Bear out means support or confirm, so the replacement adds a favourable evidential relation.
feedback: Neither expression determines when the observations were made.
Bear out gives support or confirmation, not contradiction.
Bear on means be relevant to or have a bearing on. Bear out means support or confirm, so the replacement adds a favourable evidential relation.
The expressions concern relevance and support, not a causal account of data collection.

questions.setup: A reviewer objects to the conditions attached to an archive request.
questions.prompt: 'Demanding a separate approval for every page amounts to refusing access.' What kind of claim is the reviewer making with 'amounts to'?
options: That the archive has issued an explicit written refusal.
That approval requirements will probably cause a later refusal.
That the requirement is effectively equivalent to a refusal.
That the number of approvals can be calculated from a refusal.
questions.explanation: 'Amount to' can mean be equivalent in effect or significance. The reviewer treats the conditions as a practical refusal without claiming that the archive has used those words.
feedback: The reviewer equates practical effects; the phrase does not require a formal refusal document.
'Amounts to' classifies the present requirement by its effect, rather than predicting a later event.
'Amount to' can mean be equivalent in effect or significance. The reviewer treats the conditions as a practical refusal without claiming that the archive has used those words.
This is not the numerical-total sense of 'amount to'; 'refusing access' names the practical equivalent.

questions.setup: Read a research review.
questions.prompt: 'The new study builds on Rao's sampling method while challenging Rao's conclusion.' Why can both parts be true?
options: Building on a method means merely mentioning it before rejecting it.
Challenging the conclusion guarantees that the new method is unrelated to Rao's.
The new study must use a different meaning of conclusion to avoid contradiction.
It can develop from one part of Rao's work without accepting every conclusion.
questions.explanation: Build on means use something as a basis for further development. The object is the sampling method, so this dependence does not require agreement with Rao's separate conclusion.
feedback: Build on indicates using the method as a basis, not just a passing reference before rejection.
Disagreement about a conclusion does not erase the stated methodological dependence.
There is no need to change the word's meaning: the two clauses concern different parts of the earlier work.
Build on means use something as a basis for further development. The object is the sampling method, so this dependence does not require agreement with Rao's separate conclusion.

questions.setup: A neutral review should say that a book gives brief attention to transport history, without accusing it of evasion or claiming detailed coverage.
questions.prompt: Which sentence meets that description?
options: The book dwells on transport history.
The book delves into transport history.
The book glosses over transport history.
The book touches on transport history.
questions.explanation: Touch on means mention or deal briefly with a topic. It can describe limited coverage without the criticism often conveyed by gloss over.
feedback: Dwell on presents sustained attention, often more than seems necessary, rather than brief neutral coverage.
Delve into suggests detailed examination, which goes beyond the requested brief attention.
Gloss over suggests treating something too lightly or avoiding its difficulties. That adds the criticism the reviewer wishes to avoid.
Touch on means mention or deal briefly with a topic. It can describe limited coverage without the criticism often conveyed by gloss over.

questions.setup: A film crew describes working on location.
questions.prompt: 'We could have done with better lighting, but had to make do with what was available.' What contrast do the two expressions create?
options: Better lighting would have helped, but the crew managed with the available alternative.
The crew rejected poor equipment and obtained the better lights it requested.
The crew could have repaired its lights but chose to replace them.
Better lighting was available, but the crew preferred the existing equipment.
questions.explanation: Could have done with means would have benefited from having. Make do with means manage using what is available despite its limitations; it does not promise an ideal result.
feedback: Could have done with means would have benefited from having. Make do with means manage using what is available despite its limitations; it does not promise an ideal result.
Make do with states that the crew managed with what was available, not that it obtained the preferred equipment.
Could have done with expresses a useful unmet need, not an unrealised repair action.
The first expression presents better lighting as something wanted; make do suggests accepting a less satisfactory available option, not preferring it.

questions.setup: A report says, 'Four participants were excluded from the follow-up interviews.' An editor proposes 'Four participants opted out of the follow-up interviews.'
questions.prompt: What must be verified before accepting that change?
options: That those participants themselves chose not to take part.
That the interviews occurred later than the original sessions.
That exactly four invitations were sent.
That the interviewer used a written rather than a spoken invitation.
questions.explanation: Opt out of attributes nonparticipation to the person's choice. Were excluded leaves open removal by the researchers or another cause, so the edit adds voluntary agency.
feedback: Opt out of attributes nonparticipation to the person's choice. Were excluded leaves open removal by the researchers or another cause, so the edit adds voluntary agency.
Follow-up already identifies a later stage. The edit changes agency, not the sequence.
The number of invitations is not what distinguishes exclusion from opting out.
The medium of invitation does not determine whether participants chose nonparticipation.

questions.setup: An editor inserts 'for' into a sentence about negotiations.
questions.prompt: 'The negotiators held out an improved deal' becomes 'The negotiators held out for an improved deal.' What changes?
options: They change from guaranteeing acceptance to predicting acceptance.
They change from agreeing immediate terms to agreeing terms after a fixed delay.
They change from withdrawing an offer to renewing the same offer.
They change from offering a deal to persisting in pursuit of one.
questions.explanation: 'Hold out a deal' means offer or present it. 'Hold out for a deal' means continue seeking acceptable terms rather than settle for what is available; 'for' changes the negotiators' role from offering to seeking.
feedback: Neither phrase guarantees or predicts the other side's acceptance. The edit changes what the negotiators are doing.
Neither construction establishes agreement or a fixed delay. Holding out for something describes persistence in seeking it.
'Hold out a deal' presents it rather than withdraws it; 'hold out for' does not mean renew an offer.

'Hold out a deal' means offer or present it. 'Hold out for a deal' means continue seeking acceptable terms rather than settle for what is available; 'for' changes the negotiators' role from offering to seeking.

questions.setup: A records manager replaces 'The review identified duplicate entries' with 'The review weeded out duplicate entries.'
questions.prompt: What action does the new verb add to identification?
options: Combining each duplicate with the original to make a longer entry.
Correcting the information inside the duplicate entries.
Removing the duplicates from the relevant set.
Ranking the duplicates by how recently they were created.
questions.explanation: Weed out means identify and remove unwanted members of a set. It adds exclusion from that set, but does not itself say every physical or backup copy was destroyed.
feedback: Weed out means remove selected unwanted items, not merge their content.
Correction keeps and amends an entry; weeding out removes it from the set being processed.
Weed out means identify and remove unwanted members of a set. It adds exclusion from that set, but does not itself say every physical or backup copy was destroyed.
A review might rank entries, but weed out does not specify that ordering operation.

questions.setup: Investigators progressively focused their attention on the scheduling software, without yet identifying it as the cause.
questions.prompt: Which summary preserves that focus without adding a causal conclusion?
options: They pinned the failure on the scheduling software.
They homed in on the scheduling software.
They traced the failure to the scheduling software.
They ruled out the scheduling software.
questions.explanation: Home in on means move towards a precise target or focus attention increasingly on it. The phrase does not itself establish that the target caused the failure.
feedback: Pin a failure on something assigns blame or responsibility; the stated focus has not reached that conclusion.
Home in on means move towards a precise target or focus attention increasingly on it. The phrase does not itself establish that the target caused the failure.
Trace a failure to a source presents that source as identified, which goes beyond the stated investigative focus.
Rule out excludes the software as a candidate rather than focusing investigation on it.

questions.setup: Read the conclusion of a discussion about lending a fragile object.
questions.prompt: 'In the end, the decision comes down to whether it can travel safely.' What role does the 'whether'-clause have?
options: It describes a consequence expected after the decision has been made.
It identifies the question on which the decision ultimately depends.
It names a minor detail left over after the important questions were settled.
It states that safe travel has already been demonstrated.
questions.explanation: 'Come down to' means reduce ultimately to a key factor or question. The 'whether'-clause identifies that question without answering it.
feedback: The clause gives the deciding issue, not a later consequence of the decision.
'Come down to' means reduce ultimately to a key factor or question. The 'whether'-clause identifies that question without answering it.
'Come down to' presents this as the central determining issue, not a minor remainder.
'Whether' leaves the answer open; it does not assert that the condition is satisfied.

questions.setup: A biographer describes an interview with a retired composer.
questions.prompt: 'She opened up to me about her private papers, but she has not opened the papers up to researchers.' What is the distinction?
options: She spoke more freely about them without granting researchers access to them.
She showed the papers to the biographer but refused to describe their contents.
She published the papers but limited discussion of their personal significance.
She let researchers inspect the papers while concealing her own involvement.
questions.explanation: Open up to someone about a subject means disclose thoughts or feelings more freely. Open something up to a group means make it accessible; the second clause withholds that access.
feedback: Open up to someone about a subject means disclose thoughts or feelings more freely. Open something up to a group means make it accessible; the second clause withholds that access.
The first clause concerns speaking openly, not necessarily showing documents; it does not report a refusal to describe them.
Neither publication nor a limit on personal discussion is asserted by opened up to me.
The second clause explicitly withholds opening the papers to researchers, while the first reports personal openness.

questions.setup: An editor changes 'Staff pushed back against the deadline' to 'Staff pushed back the deadline.'
questions.prompt: Why should the editor verify what happened before making that change?
options: The second adds an actual postponement where the first reports resistance.
The second says staff accepted the deadline after initially opposing it.
The second says the deadline was brought forward rather than delayed.
The second changes the staff from opponents into the people affected by someone else's decision.
questions.explanation: Push back against something means oppose or challenge it. Push back a deadline means move it later; resistance alone does not establish that the date changed.
feedback: Push back against something means oppose or challenge it. Push back a deadline means move it later; resistance alone does not establish that the date changed.
Push back a deadline means postpone it, not accept it after resistance.
Pushing a date back moves it later, not earlier.
Staff remains the grammatical subject. The important change is from opposition to causing a later deadline.

questions.setup: A colleague reflects on an unusually guarded briefing.
questions.prompt: 'Nadia knew more than she let on, though less than the team read into her answers.' Which relationship is described?
options: Her disclosure fell below her knowledge, and the team's interpretation exceeded it.
Nadia's disclosure exceeded her knowledge, while the team underestimated both.
The team correctly understood her knowledge but underestimated how much she disclosed.
Her knowledge grew after she spoke, allowing her later answers to correct the team.
questions.explanation: Let on means reveal or disclose. She disclosed less than she knew; read into describes the meaning the team attributed to her answers, here more knowledge than she actually had.
feedback: Let on means reveal or disclose. She disclosed less than she knew; read into describes the meaning the team attributed to her answers, here more knowledge than she actually had.
More than she let on places her knowledge above her disclosure; the team's interpretation goes above her knowledge, not below it.
Less than the team read into says the team's interpretation exceeded her actual knowledge, so it was not an accurate measure of it.
The comparison concerns knowledge, disclosure, and interpretation at the briefing. It does not report later learning or correction.

questions.setup: After a team wins a tournament, a commentator says, 'I wasn't putting them down; I merely put their success down to luck.'
questions.prompt: Which analysis preserves the two verb meanings while allowing that listeners might still feel the remark was disparaging?
options: The first denies a causal explanation; the second provides a negative description of the players.
The speaker denies disparagement but attributes success to luck.
Both expressions deny that the team's success really occurred.
The first admits a criticism that the second then retracts.
questions.explanation: Put someone down means belittle them. Put success down to luck attributes it to a cause; that attribution can still sound belittling even though the expressions have different meanings.
feedback: Put someone down concerns disparagement, while put something down to a cause concerns attribution. This option reverses those functions.
Put someone down means belittle them. Put success down to luck attributes it to a cause; that attribution can still sound belittling even though the expressions have different meanings.
Neither expression denies the result. The dispute concerns how the players and the cause of success are characterised.
I wasn't denies putting the team down. Attributing success to luck does not itself retract the potentially disparaging assessment.

questions.setup: An analyst produces a total delivery-cost estimate and a separate comparison of warehouse efficiency.
questions.prompt: 'Transport costs are factored into the estimate but factored out of the efficiency comparison.' Which reading is warranted?
options: The costs are paid from the estimated budget and refunded after the comparison.
The costs enter one calculation and are excluded from the other, without the actual charges being removed.
The costs are considered in both calculations, with factored out specifying a smaller numerical weight.
The costs are included initially, so excluding them later establishes that the original estimate was wrong.
questions.explanation: Factor into means include as a consideration or calculation component. Factor out means exclude from the assessment at issue; neither operation removes the real-world charges.
feedback: These verbs describe treatment within calculations, not payments or refunds.
Factor into means include as a consideration or calculation component. Factor out means exclude from the assessment at issue; neither operation removes the real-world charges.
Factored out excludes the costs from that comparison; it does not merely assign an unspecified smaller weight.
The calculations answer different questions. Including a cost in a total and excluding it from a narrower comparison need not be inconsistent.

questions.setup: A choir member comments on an apparently successful committee meeting.
questions.prompt: 'We papered over our differences rather than ironing them out.' What is the criticism?
options: The committee resolved the differences but failed to record the resolution.
The committee exaggerated minor differences to make the meeting seem important.
The committee postponed discussing the differences until it could collect written evidence.
The committee concealed the differences instead of resolving them.
questions.explanation: Paper over differences means mask them or give an appearance of agreement. Iron them out means work through and resolve them; the contrast questions the substance of the apparent success.
feedback: Ironing differences out would resolve them. The speaker contrasts that with merely covering them over.
Paper over means conceal or mask difficulties, not magnify them.
Neither the need for evidence nor a definite later discussion is stated. The criticism concerns apparent harmony without resolution.
Paper over differences means mask them or give an appearance of agreement. Iron them out means work through and resolve them; the contrast questions the substance of the apparent success.

questions.setup: A committee member comments on a possible leak of the agenda.
questions.prompt: 'I wouldn't put it past Mara to leak it.' What does the speaker commit to?
options: Mara has already leaked it, but the speaker intends to forgive her.
Mara is unlikely to leak it because the speaker trusts her discretion.
The speaker regards such conduct as within Mara's capabilities or character.
The speaker has evidence of an earlier leak by Mara, but none about this agenda.
questions.explanation: Wouldn't put it past someone to do something means one would not be surprised if they did that, usually something discreditable. It does not assert that Mara actually leaked the agenda.
feedback: Put it past someone is not about forgiving a past act. The conditional expression assesses what Mara might be capable of doing.
This reverses the idiom's negative assessment: the speaker does not exclude Mara as capable of the act.
Wouldn't put it past someone to do something means one would not be surprised if they did that, usually something discreditable. It does not assert that Mara actually leaked the agenda.
A prior incident may inform such a judgment, but the expression does not establish that one occurred.

questions.setup: A translator says, 'I promise to try to finish by Friday.' The client replies, 'I'll hold you to that.'
questions.prompt: Reading 'that' as exactly the commitment offered, what can the client hold the translator to?
options: Delivering the finished translation by Friday regardless of circumstances.
Giving an explanation on Friday instead of attempting the work.
Accepting a deadline the client is free to move earlier.
Making the promised attempt to finish by Friday.
questions.explanation: 'Hold someone to a commitment' means require them to keep it. The translator promised an attempt, so the phrase does not turn that into a guarantee of a completed translation by Friday.
feedback: This removes 'try' from the promise and makes the commitment stronger than the translator stated.
An explanation is not the promised action. The promise concerns trying to meet the deadline.
'Hold to' preserves the stated commitment; it does not grant the client authority to replace it with an earlier one.
'Hold someone to a commitment' means require them to keep it. The translator promised an attempt, so the phrase does not turn that into a guarantee of a completed translation by Friday.

questions.setup: A neighbour describes a disagreement about a shared courtyard.
questions.prompt: 'I had it out with Ravi, but I don't have it in for him.' What distinction is the speaker drawing?
options: The dispute is fully resolved, although the speaker still intends to retaliate.
The speaker concealed the complaint but arranged for someone else to raise it.
The speaker confronted Ravi but denies an ongoing hostile attitude towards him.
Ravi was removed from the courtyard arrangement, but the speaker regrets excluding him.
questions.explanation: Have it out with someone means discuss or confront a grievance frankly. Have it in for someone means hold a hostile intention towards them; one confrontation does not necessarily establish that continuing hostility.
feedback: Having it out describes a frank confrontation, not a guarantee of resolution. Don't have it in for denies hostile intent rather than affirming retaliation.
Had it out with reports directly confronting Ravi, not concealing the complaint or using an intermediary.

Have it out with someone means discuss or confront a grievance frankly. Have it in for someone means hold a hostile intention towards them; one confrontation does not necessarily establish that continuing hostility.
Neither expression says Ravi was expelled or that the speaker regrets an exclusion.

questions.setup: A club member says, 'I can't abide this rule, but I will abide by it.'
questions.prompt: Which interpretation accounts for the apparent tension?
options: The member strongly dislikes the rule but intends to comply with it.
The member cannot understand the rule but will ask others to explain it.
The member initially refused compliance but now approves of the rule.
The member will tolerate breaches of the rule while defending its purpose.
questions.explanation: Can't abide means cannot bear or strongly dislikes. Abide by means comply with; the added by separates obedience in conduct from approval in attitude.
feedback: Can't abide means cannot bear or strongly dislikes. Abide by means comply with; the added by separates obedience in conduct from approval in attitude.
Can't abide expresses strong dislike or intolerance, not failure to understand.
The two clauses contrast current attitude with intended conduct. No change to approval is stated.
Abide by commits the speaker to following the rule, not tolerating other people's breaches.

questions.setup: An editor adds 'with' to a sentence about a workshop's printed instructions.
questions.prompt: 'The organisers dispensed printed instructions' becomes 'The organisers dispensed with printed instructions.' What is the consequence?
options: The organisers distribute the instructions more widely than before.
Distribution of the instructions becomes proceeding without them.
The instructions change from compulsory reading to optional reading, but are still supplied.
The organisers change who distributes the instructions while keeping the same procedure.
questions.explanation: 'Dispense something' means supply or distribute it. 'Dispense with something' means do without it or remove it as a requirement; adding 'with' reverses its role in the organisers' procedure.
feedback: 'With' does not intensify distribution. It creates the different expression 'dispense with'.
'Dispense something' means supply or distribute it. 'Dispense with something' means do without it or remove it as a requirement; adding 'with' reverses its role in the organisers' procedure.
'Dispensed with' does not itself preserve supply while merely changing how recipients should read them.
The organisers remain the subject. The edit changes the action, not its agent.

questions.setup: A passenger describes the railway company's response to a complaint.
questions.prompt: 'We were fobbed off with a promise of a later review.' What criticism is conveyed by 'fobbed off with'?
options: An unsatisfactory response was used to put the complainants off.
The company transferred the complaint to a more competent investigator.
The passenger has proof that the company knowingly made an impossible promise.
The company obtained the passengers' informed agreement that the problem was resolved.
questions.explanation: 'Fob someone off with something' means use an inadequate answer or substitute to satisfy or deflect them. The phrase criticises how the promise functions; it does not by itself prove that no review will ever occur.
feedback: 'Fob someone off with something' means use an inadequate answer or substitute to satisfy or deflect them. The phrase criticises how the promise functions; it does not by itself prove that no review will ever occur.
A transfer of responsibility is not part of this expression. The passenger criticises the adequacy of the response given.
A false promise could be used this way, but proof of impossibility and knowledge goes beyond the expression.
'Fobbed off' is a negative assessment of inadequate treatment, not an account of an informed, satisfactory resolution.

questions.setup: A reviewer describes an improvised theatre performance.
questions.prompt: 'The elaborate stage effect didn't come off, but the performer came off looking resourceful.' What does the repeated expression do?
options: It reports that the effect remained attached to the stage while the performer removed part of the scenery.
It reports that the performer intended the failure in order to appear resourceful.
It reports that both the effect and the performer succeeded, but by different technical methods.
It denies the effect's success while describing the performer's resulting impression favourably.
questions.explanation: Come off can mean succeed or achieve the intended result. Come off looking a certain way describes how someone emerges from a situation in others' eyes, not necessarily how skilful they actually are.
feedback: Neither use concerns physical detachment. The first evaluates the effect's success; the second describes the impression the performer made.
The contrasting outcomes do not establish that the failure was planned.
Didn't come off gives a negative assessment of the effect. A favourable impression of the performer does not change that outcome.
Come off can mean succeed or achieve the intended result. Come off looking a certain way describes how someone emerges from a situation in others' eyes, not necessarily how skilful they actually are.

questions.setup: At a public meeting, the chair responds to an awkward question: 'Who put you up to asking that?'
questions.prompt: How does the phrasal verb frame the questioner's action?
options: As an action prompted by someone else, whose identity the chair asks for.
As a question the chair authorised the person to ask.
As a question made possible by accommodation provided by another person.
As a question whose factual answer must come from an expert.
questions.explanation: Put someone up to doing something means encourage or instigate it, often something troublesome. Who frames an instigator as the assumed source, but the question itself does not prove anyone actually prompted it.
feedback: Put someone up to doing something means encourage or instigate it, often something troublesome. Who frames an instigator as the assumed source, but the question itself does not prove anyone actually prompted it.
Put someone up to doing something concerns prompting or instigating the action, not necessarily giving legitimate permission.
Put someone up can mean provide lodging, but up to asking selects instigation rather than accommodation.
The chair asks about who prompted the question, not who can supply its answer.

questions.setup: An employee describes a private conversation with a factory manager.
questions.prompt: 'She let me in on the relocation plan.' What new position does this place the employee in?
options: Having authority to approve or reject the relocation.
Becoming responsible for drafting the relocation plan.
Agreeing to participate in the relocation as a condition of employment.
Knowing information about the plan that was not openly shared.
questions.explanation: Let someone in on something means share previously private or restricted information with them. It grants knowledge, not necessarily a planning role, decision power, or approval.
feedback: Being informed about a plan is not the same as receiving decision-making authority.
The phrase gives access to information, not an assignment to create the plan.
Let in on does not report the employee's agreement or impose a participation condition.
Let someone in on something means share previously private or restricted information with them. It grants knowledge, not necessarily a planning role, decision power, or approval.

questions.setup: A manager comments on a colleague whose first product launch went badly.
questions.prompt: 'I'm not prepared to write her off as a project leader yet.' What judgment is withheld?
options: That the failed launch should be included in the colleague's record.
That the colleague performed well on the first launch.
That the colleague should be dismissed as having no worthwhile leadership prospects.
That the colleague must receive another project immediately.
questions.explanation: Here, write her off as a project leader means dismiss her prospects in that role as not worth further consideration. Refusing to do so yet leaves those prospects open without endorsing her performance.
feedback: Write someone off is an evaluative expression, not a statement about removing an event from a written record.
The speaker withholds a dismissive negative conclusion; this is not the same as withholding praise for a successful launch.

Here, write her off as a project leader means dismiss her prospects in that role as not worth further consideration. Refusing to do so yet leaves those prospects open without endorsing her performance.
Not dismissing her prospects does not commit the manager to an immediate assignment.

questions.setup: Read an employee's account of a promotion round.
questions.prompt: 'I was passed over for team leader in favour of a less experienced colleague.' What does 'passed over' establish?
options: The employee was never considered as a candidate.
The employee was selected but declined the appointment.
The employee's appointment was confirmed but postponed.
Someone else was selected rather than this employee.
questions.explanation: 'Pass someone over for a position' means not choose them, typically choosing someone else. The expression can convey disappointment without proving that the employee was never considered or that the choice was unjustified.
feedback: 'Passed over' can describe not being chosen even after consideration; it does not establish exclusion from the candidate pool.
That would be a refusal after selection, not being passed over in favour of another candidate.
A postponed appointment still selects the employee. 'In favour of a colleague' instead identifies another successful candidate.

'Pass someone over for a position' means not choose them, typically choosing someone else. The expression can convey disappointment without proving that the employee was never considered or that the choice was unjustified.

questions.setup: A project group receives a short reply to its announcement.
questions.prompt: 'Please don't read an endorsement into our silence.' What interpretation does the writer reject?
options: That the group has already issued an explicit rejection.
That the silence should be taken as approval.
That an endorsement was removed from the written announcement.
That the recipient has read the announcement more than once.
questions.explanation: Read something into something means attribute a meaning or implication to it. The writer rejects treating silence as endorsement, without thereby declaring opposition to the project.
feedback: The writer rejects an endorsement inference from silence, not an earlier explicit rejection.
Read something into something means attribute a meaning or implication to it. The writer rejects treating silence as endorsement, without thereby declaring opposition to the project.
Read into concerns interpretation of a source, not editing words out of a document.
The expression concerns meaning attributed to silence, not the number of readings.

questions.setup: A historian comments on a quotation used in a documentary.
questions.prompt: 'Stripped of its historical context, the quotation appears hostile.' Which paraphrase preserves the relation?
options: The historical context has been removed because it proves the quotation was hostile.
The quotation seems hostile when presented without its historical context.
Removing the historical context also removes the quotation's hostile content.
The historian has established the speaker's hostile intention independently of the context.
questions.explanation: Strip something of a feature means deprive it of that feature. The reduced passive clause describes the quotation without its context; appears reports the resulting impression, not an unconditional judgment of hostility.
feedback: The sentence does not state why the context was removed or claim that it proves hostility.

Strip something of a feature means deprive it of that feature. The reduced passive clause describes the quotation without its context; appears reports the resulting impression, not an unconditional judgment of hostility.
The sentence says the decontextualised quotation appears hostile, not that hostility has been stripped away.
An appearance created by loss of context does not establish the original speaker's intention.
