'With the guests' could mean joining them in apologizing, not addressing them.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that identifies the person who lent the charger.
questions.prompt: I borrowed a charger ___.
options: for my colleague
from my colleague
with my colleague
before my colleague
questions.explanation: 'Borrow from' identifies the person or place supplying the borrowed item.
feedback: This makes the colleague the intended beneficiary, not necessarily the lender.
'Borrow from' identifies the person or place supplying the borrowed item.
This can mean the colleague joined in borrowing; it does not identify the source.
This compares the order of borrowing, not who lent the charger.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that says one person makes the payment while another receives the ticket.
questions.prompt: Ravi buys a ticket for his mother to use.
options: His mother pays Ravi for the ticket.
Ravi pays for the ticket; his mother is its intended user.
Ravi buys the ticket from his mother.
Ravi and his mother each buy a ticket.
questions.explanation: 'For his mother' identifies the beneficiary of the purchase, not its source.
feedback: This reverses who makes the purchase and adds a payment to Ravi.
'For his mother' identifies the beneficiary of the purchase, not its source.
'From' would make his mother the seller, not the intended user.
The sentence mentions one purchase by Ravi, not separate purchases by both people.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that reports the subject discussed, not an argument with a person.
questions.prompt: The neighbours discussed where to put the shared bins.
options: They argued with the person who moved the bins.
They talked to the person who collects the bins.
They spoke for the neighbours who use the bins.
They talked about the position of the bins.
questions.explanation: 'Talk about' introduces the subject of a conversation.
feedback: This adds a disagreement and identifies another participant, not just the topic.
'To' names the listener; this sentence changes the participants and omits the stated topic.
'For' here means representing other people, not discussing a subject.
'Talk about' introduces the subject of a conversation.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that names the hazard the cover guards against, not its method, time, or purpose.
questions.prompt: The cover protects the paintings ___.
options: with a special filter
during transport
for display in the gallery
from sunlight
questions.explanation: 'Protect something from' introduces the potential source of harm: here, sunlight.
feedback: This names the means of protection, not the hazard.
This identifies when protection is provided, not what might harm the paintings.
This gives a purpose for preserving the paintings, not a threat to them.
'Protect something from' introduces the potential source of harm: here, sunlight.

questions.setup: Choose the words that show the ingredients make up the whole salad.
questions.prompt: The salad ___ tomatoes, cucumber, and olives.
options: comes with
is served before
consists of
is covered with
questions.explanation: 'Consists of' introduces the components that make up something.
feedback: This names accompaniments; it does not say what makes up the salad itself.
This describes serving order, not ingredients.
'Consists of' introduces the components that make up something.
This identifies a covering or topping, not necessarily the full composition.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that places the start in 2021 and says the work continues now.
questions.prompt: Eva started working here in 2021 and still works here.
options: Eva worked here until 2021.
Eva has worked here since 2021.
Eva worked here before 2021.
Eva will work here from 2021.
questions.explanation: 'Since' names the starting point of a period continuing to the present in this sentence.
feedback: This makes 2021 the end of her employment, not its beginning.
'Since' names the starting point of a period continuing to the present in this sentence.
This places her work earlier and does not say it continues now.
This uses a future prediction instead of reporting her ongoing employment.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that says preparation finished early enough for the call.
questions.prompt: The screen worked again before the video call began.
options: The screen was repaired in time for the call.
The screen was repaired during the call.
The screen was repaired on time for its service appointment.
The screen was repaired after the call.
questions.explanation: 'In time for' means early enough for a particular event or purpose.
feedback: 'In time for' means early enough for a particular event or purpose.
This places the repair within the call, not before it began.
'On time' refers to a schedule; this adds an appointment and does not express readiness for the call.
This is too late for the screen to be ready when the call began.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that says Jo received the wrong item because someone made a mistake.
questions.prompt: Jo ordered black shoes but received brown ones.
options: The shop sent brown shoes on purpose.
The shop sent brown shoes on request.
The shop sent brown shoes by mistake.
The shop sent brown shoes for comparison.
questions.explanation: 'By mistake' means an action happened unintentionally because of an error.
feedback: This says the choice was deliberate rather than a mistake.
This would say someone asked for brown shoes, contrary to the stated order.
'By mistake' means an action happened unintentionally because of an error.
This adds a purpose for sending brown shoes rather than identifying an error.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence meaning that the team used the new room in place of the old one.
questions.prompt: Which sentence describes replacement, not an additional room?
options: We met in the new room instead of the old one.
We met in the new room as well as the old one.
We met in the new room next to the old one.
We met in the new room after leaving the old one.
questions.explanation: 'Instead of' marks the alternative used in place of something else.
feedback: 'Instead of' marks the alternative used in place of something else.
'As well as' includes both rooms; it does not replace one with the other.
'Next to' locates the room but does not itself express replacement.
This describes an order of locations and can involve meeting in both, not just replacement.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that identifies a reason, not a contrast.
questions.prompt: The path was flooded, so the walkers turned back.
options: They turned back despite the flooding.
They turned back before the flooding.
They turned back because of the flooding.
They turned back without the flooding.
questions.explanation: 'Because of' plus a noun phrase introduces the cause of an event.
feedback: 'Despite' presents something as a difficulty overcome or a contrast, not as the stated cause.
This puts their return earlier than the flooding rather than caused by it.
'Because of' plus a noun phrase introduces the cause of an event.
This removes the flooding from the situation instead of naming it as the cause.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that identifies what increased, without supplying a numerical size for the increase.
questions.prompt: The monthly review notes an increase ___ requests for flexible hours.
options: to
in
by
from
questions.explanation: 'An increase in requests' identifies the thing becoming more numerous.
feedback: 'An increase to' normally introduces a new level or target; requests here are what increased.
'An increase in requests' identifies the thing becoming more numerous.
'An increase by' introduces the size of a change, not the category changing.
'An increase from' introduces a starting level or source rather than the thing increasing.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves the relationship without adding a cause.
questions.prompt: The complaint relates to the new booking system.
options: The complaint concerns the new booking system.
The complaint caused the new booking system to fail.
The new booking system was introduced because of the complaint.
The complaint confirms that the new booking system is faulty.
questions.explanation: 'Relates to' identifies a connection or subject; it does not itself explain causation.
feedback: 'Relates to' identifies a connection or subject; it does not itself explain causation.
A relation to the system does not establish that the complaint caused a failure.
This adds a causal history that 'relates to' does not provide.
A complaint about a system does not by itself confirm a fault.

questions.setup: Choose the edit preserving who recognizes what.
questions.prompt: The warning symbol is familiar to most staff.
options: The warning symbol makes most staff familiar with the danger.
Most staff have become familiar to the warning's designer.
Most staff are familiar with the warning symbol.
Most staff are familiar with designing warning symbols.
questions.explanation: A thing can be familiar to people; those people are familiar with the thing.
feedback: Recognizing the symbol does not establish that it teaches staff about the danger.
This makes the staff recognizable to a different person.
A thing can be familiar to people; those people are familiar with the thing.
This changes recognition of a symbol into knowledge of designing symbols.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that says the manager opposed postponement, not that the manager proposed it.
questions.prompt: The manager objected to postponing the inspection.
options: The manager raised a request for postponement.
The manager raised an objection during the postponed inspection.
The manager objected on behalf of those seeking postponement.
The manager raised an objection to the postponement.
questions.explanation: Both 'object to' and 'an objection to' identify what is opposed.
feedback: A request for postponement seeks it; an objection opposes it.
This changes the opposed action into the time of a different objection.
This identifies represented people but does not preserve opposition to postponement itself.
Both 'object to' and 'an objection to' identify what is opposed.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation supported by this reply, without assuming the records will be complete.
questions.prompt: 'Will we approve the application?' 'That depends on whether the missing records arrive.'
options: The records will arrive once the application is approved.
Approval has already been granted subject to a delivery date.
The application will be approved as soon as any record arrives.
The arrival of the records affects the approval decision.
questions.explanation: 'Depends on whether' makes arrival relevant to the decision without settling the outcome.
feedback: This reverses the direction of dependence and adds a promised arrival.
The reply leaves the decision open; it does not announce approval or a date.
This turns an unspecified dependence into a definite automatic trigger.
'Depends on whether' makes arrival relevant to the decision without settling the outcome.

questions.setup: Choose the statement that preserves the direction of influence.
questions.prompt: The report examines the effect of night shifts on sleep.
options: It examines how night shifts affect sleep.
It examines how sleep affects the allocation of night shifts.
It examines the effect of sleep on working at night.
It examines whether night shifts and sleep have the same causes.
questions.explanation: 'The effect of X on Y' makes X the influence and Y the affected thing.
feedback: 'The effect of X on Y' makes X the influence and Y the affected thing.
This reverses the influence and adds a scheduling decision.
This makes sleep the influence rather than the outcome being affected.
Shared causes are a different relationship from the effect of one on the other.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that says Mira accepted responsibility for the project, not merely membership of its team.
questions.prompt: Which description assigns leadership?
options: Mira took part in the project.
Mira took charge of the project.
Mira took an interest in the project.
Mira took advice on the project.
questions.explanation: 'Take charge of' means assume control or responsibility.
feedback: 'Take part in' describes participation without assigning leadership.
'Take charge of' means assume control or responsibility.
Interest does not establish that Mira leads or manages the work.
Receiving advice does not assign Mira authority over the project.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that preserves the residents' exemption from an admission charge.
questions.prompt: Admission was free of charge for the residents.
options: The residents did not have to pay to enter.
The residents were free to set the admission charge.
The residents were paid for entering the building.
The residents could charge other visitors for admission.
questions.explanation: 'Free of charge' means no payment is required; 'for the residents' limits who receives that benefit.
feedback: 'Free of charge' means no payment is required; 'for the residents' limits who receives that benefit.
This turns exemption from payment into authority to choose a price.
No charge is not the same as receiving payment.
The sentence grants residents no permission to collect fees.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that gives a maximum waiting time, allowing an earlier reply.
questions.prompt: The office promises a reply no later than two working days after receiving your message.
options: We will reply after two working days of receiving your message.
We will reply for two working days after receiving your message.
We will reply in exactly two working days after receiving your message.
We will reply within two working days of receiving your message.
questions.explanation: 'Within' gives an outer time limit measured from the specified starting event.
feedback: 'After' places the reply beyond the stated waiting period rather than within it.
'For' makes two days the duration of replying, not a response deadline.
'Exactly' rules out an earlier reply that the promise permits.
'Within' gives an outer time limit measured from the specified starting event.

questions.setup: The technician performed the action, and the key was the tool. Choose the active sentence preserving those roles.
questions.prompt: The lock was opened with a special key by a technician.
options: A technician made a special key after the lock was opened.
A technician used a special key to open the lock.
A special key was made by the technician who opened the lock.
A technician opened the lock for the owner of a special key.
questions.explanation: In this passive sentence, 'by' names the agent and 'with' names the instrument.
feedback: This adds key-making and changes the order; the key was the opening instrument.
In this passive sentence, 'by' names the agent and 'with' names the instrument.
The original says nothing about who made the key.
This changes the key's role from instrument to something owned by an added beneficiary.

questions.setup: Choose the version stating that study is the purpose of the room, not that study is currently taking place.
questions.prompt: Which description names the room's intended use?
options: This room is for quiet study.
Quiet study is taking place in this room.
This room is beside the quiet study area.
This room was occupied during quiet study.
questions.explanation: 'For' introduces intended use; the room need not be occupied at this moment.
feedback: 'For' introduces intended use; the room need not be occupied at this moment.
This describes current activity, not the room's designated purpose.
This locates the room near a study area rather than assigning its use.
This reports a past occasion, not the room's purpose.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that reports a disagreement about money, without claiming the people dislike each other.
questions.prompt: The partners cannot agree how to divide the costs.
options: They are hostile towards each other.
They compete for control of the partnership.
They have withdrawn from the partnership.
They disagree over the division of costs.
questions.explanation: 'Over' introduces the issue in dispute; it does not itself describe personal animosity.
feedback: This adds personal hostility beyond disagreement over one issue.
This changes a cost dispute into a struggle for control.
The disagreement does not establish that either person has left.
'Over' introduces the issue in dispute; it does not itself describe personal animosity.

questions.setup: Choose the completion meaning that one remaining problem is excluded from a generally positive assessment.
questions.prompt: The flat is ready to rent ___ a faulty kitchen light.
options: because of
in addition to
in exchange for
apart from
questions.explanation: Here 'apart from' marks an exception: the light remains a problem despite general readiness.
feedback: This makes the faulty light a reason the flat is ready, not an exception to readiness.
This adds the faulty light without expressing the intended exception to the assessment.
This describes a trade, not a qualification to the flat's condition.
Here 'apart from' marks an exception: the light remains a problem despite general readiness.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that presents the rain as an obstacle the event continued through, not the reason for continuing.
questions.prompt: The outdoor market stayed open ___ the heavy rain.
options: despite
because of
in preparation for
in the absence of
questions.explanation: 'Despite' marks a contrast between the difficult weather and the market staying open.
feedback: 'Despite' marks a contrast between the difficult weather and the market staying open.
This presents the rain as the cause of staying open.
This makes staying open preparation for rain, rather than continuation through an obstacle.
This says the rain was not present, contrary to the stated situation.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that means the drawing is useful to the designer, without identifying who made it.
questions.prompt: The drawing is ___ the designer.
options: the work of
under review by
of use to
on loan from
questions.explanation: 'Of use to someone' means useful to that person and does not assign authorship.
feedback: This attributes authorship to the designer instead of describing usefulness.
This says the designer is examining it, not that it is useful.
'Of use to someone' means useful to that person and does not assign authorship.
This makes the designer the source of a loan, not necessarily the beneficiary.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that preserves duration, not a deadline for finishing.
questions.prompt: The volunteers continued answering calls until eight.
options: The volunteers had answered the calls by eight.
The volunteers kept answering calls up to eight.
The volunteers began answering calls at eight.
The volunteers agreed before eight to answer calls.
questions.explanation: 'Until' and 'up to' here give the endpoint of a continuing activity.
feedback: 'By eight' reports completion no later than eight, not continued activity up to that time.
'Until' and 'up to' here give the endpoint of a continuing activity.
This changes the endpoint into a starting time.
This places an agreement earlier than eight and no longer reports the actual answering period.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that accurately reports the named source without claiming independent confirmation.
questions.prompt: According to the building manager, the lift will reopen tomorrow.
options: The lift's reopening tomorrow has been independently confirmed.
The building manager says the lift will reopen tomorrow.
The building manager has been told to reopen the lift tomorrow.
The lift will reopen tomorrow in agreement with the building manager.
questions.explanation: 'According to' names the source of the information while leaving its independent accuracy open.
feedback: 'According to' attributes a claim; it does not report independent verification.
'According to' names the source of the information while leaving its independent accuracy open.
This turns a sourced prediction into an instruction to the manager.
Agreement or consent is a different relationship from being the source of a report.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that identifies the explanation offered for the delay, not its duration.
questions.prompt: The airline attributed the delay ___ a staffing problem.
options: for
with
to
from
questions.explanation: 'Attribute X to Y' identifies Y as the explanation offered for X.
feedback: 'For' can introduce a duration after delay, but 'attribute something for a cause' is not this verb's pattern.
'With' can express accompaniment; attribution takes 'to' before the proposed cause.
'Attribute X to Y' identifies Y as the explanation offered for X.
Although 'a delay resulting from a problem' is possible, the verb attribute requires 'to' in this construction.

questions.setup: Choose the concise rewrite that preserves both the person and the thing the speaker is relying on.
questions.prompt: I am relying on Kim to check the figures before publication.
options: I am checking the figures for Kim before publication.
I am checking with Kim whether the figures have been published.
I am counting on Kim to check the figures before publication.
I am accounting for Kim's figures before publication.
questions.explanation: 'Count on someone to do something' expresses reliance on that person's action.
feedback: This makes the speaker the checker and Kim the beneficiary.
This asks Kim for information about publication rather than relying on Kim's checking.
'Count on someone to do something' expresses reliance on that person's action.
'Account for' means explain or justify here; it does not express reliance on Kim.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that means the subject is being examined now, without saying a decision has been made.
questions.prompt: The proposal is under consideration.
options: The proposal has been accepted with conditions.
The proposal has been removed from consideration.
The proposal is being considered.
The proposal will be submitted for consideration.
questions.explanation: 'Under consideration' describes a current process, not its eventual outcome.
feedback: Conditional acceptance is a decision; consideration alone does not establish acceptance.
'Removed from' means it is no longer being considered, reversing the statement.
'Under consideration' describes a current process, not its eventual outcome.
This places submission in the future rather than saying examination is happening now.

questions.setup: Choose the editorial assessment that preserves the distinction between responding to advice and following it.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The procedure was revised in response to the panel's advice.' Edit: 'The procedure was revised in accordance with the panel's advice.'
options: The edit removes the panel's connection with the revision.
The edit adds that the revision followed the advice, not merely that the advice prompted it.
The edit says the panel itself revised the procedure.
The edit changes completed revision into a proposal for revision.
questions.explanation: 'In response to' identifies a stimulus; 'in accordance with' additionally presents conformity with the advice.
feedback: Both versions retain a relationship to the panel's advice; the kind of relationship changes.
'In response to' identifies a stimulus; 'in accordance with' additionally presents conformity with the advice.
Neither prepositional phrase identifies the person who carried out the revision.
Both clauses still report that the procedure was revised; the change concerns conformity, not completion.

questions.setup: Choose the sound editorial judgment about the preposition, without changing the stated relationship.
questions.prompt: 'The agreement sets out the responsibilities shared between the publisher, the printer, and the distributor.' An editor objects that 'between' cannot refer to three parties.
options: Among is required because between becomes ungrammatical whenever a third party is named.
Between proves that each responsibility belongs jointly to exactly two of the parties.
Among would prove that all three parties have identical responsibilities.
Between is possible because the parties are individually identified; three parties do not make it ungrammatical.
questions.explanation: 'Between' can express relationships among separately identified parties. It is not restricted to exactly two.
feedback: The number alone does not prohibit 'between'; it can relate three or more distinct parties.
The preposition does not impose a pair-by-pair allocation of responsibilities.
'Among' would not by itself establish identical duties for everyone.
'Between' can express relationships among separately identified parties. It is not restricted to exactly two.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves emphasis without upgrading it to an exclusive priority.
questions.prompt: The committee placed renewed emphasis on privacy in its review of the software.
options: Privacy replaced usability as the review's sole concern.
The software review was conducted on behalf of privacy campaigners.
Privacy received fresh emphasis during the software review.
The committee's review resulted in stronger privacy protections.
questions.explanation: 'Emphasis on' marks a focus of attention; renewed emphasis does not exclude other priorities or specify its comparative amount.
feedback: An emphasis on privacy does not establish replacement of other concerns or exclusivity.
'On privacy' names the focus of emphasis, not a group represented by the reviewers.
'Emphasis on' marks a focus of attention; renewed emphasis does not exclude other priorities or specify its comparative amount.
Attention to privacy does not itself establish that protections were changed.

questions.setup: An editor wants to distinguish permission to consult letters from possession of the originals. Choose the faithful summary.
questions.prompt: The agreement gives researchers access to the archive's letters, but the originals remain in the archive.
options: Researchers receive the original letters for their own collections.
Researchers acquire ownership of copies but cannot consult the originals.
Researchers may consult the letters without taking possession of the originals.
Researchers may authorize the archive to dispose of the original letters.
questions.explanation: 'Access to' describes availability for consultation here, while the second clause preserves custody.
feedback: Access to the letters does not transfer possession, and the originals remain in the archive.
The agreement says nothing about ownership of copies and allows access to the letters.
'Access to' describes availability for consultation here, while the second clause preserves custody.
Access grants no stated authority over disposal or ownership.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that preserves an evidential basis without identifying the people who wrote the report.
questions.prompt: The report is based on interviews with former tenants.
options: Interviews with former tenants provide the basis for the report.
Former tenants wrote the report on the basis of interviews.
The report provides a basis for interviewing former tenants.
The report is addressed to former tenants who were interviewed.
questions.explanation: 'Based on' identifies supporting material; 'with former tenants' identifies the interview participants.
feedback: 'Based on' identifies supporting material; 'with former tenants' identifies the interview participants.
This turns interview participants into authors, which the original does not establish.
This reverses the direction: the interviews support the report, not the report the interviews.
This changes participants in the evidence into the report's intended audience.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that distinguishes representation from support for a policy.
questions.prompt: Aisha spoke on behalf of the residents, some of whom opposed the proposal she presented.
options: Aisha spoke in favour of the proposal because the residents had unanimously endorsed it.
Aisha represented the residents, including opponents of the proposal.
Aisha replaced the residents' proposal with one that she personally preferred.
Aisha spoke about the residents rather than representing them.
questions.explanation: 'On behalf of' expresses representation. Residents who opposed the proposal could still be included in the group represented.
feedback: 'On behalf of' names whom she represented; the second clause rules out unanimous support.
'On behalf of' expresses representation. Residents who opposed the proposal could still be included in the group represented.
Representation does not establish substitution of a proposal or Aisha's personal preference.
Speaking about a group would make it the topic; 'on behalf of' assigns a representative role.

questions.setup: Choose the assessment of the change in relationship, not a claim about which policy is better.
questions.prompt: Original: 'In contrast to the earlier policy, the new policy covers temporary staff.' Edit: 'Contrary to the earlier policy, the new policy covers temporary staff.'
options: The edit merely shortens the wording while preserving a neutral comparison.
The edit presents coverage as conflicting with the earlier policy, rather than simply contrasting the policies.
The edit says the earlier policy caused the new coverage.
The edit changes temporary staff from beneficiaries into the writers of the policy.
questions.explanation: Changing 'in contrast to' to 'contrary to' adds an oppositional relationship, not just a comparison.
feedback: 'Contrary to' presents opposition or inconsistency; 'in contrast to' can simply compare a difference.
Changing 'in contrast to' to 'contrary to' adds an oppositional relationship, not just a comparison.
Neither phrase expresses causation by the earlier policy.
The staff remain those covered; the edit changes the relationship between policies.

questions.setup: Choose the revision that clearly makes the camera the journalist's tool, not something the visitor possessed.
questions.prompt: Ambiguous draft: 'The journalist photographed the visitor with a borrowed camera.'
options: Using a borrowed camera, the journalist photographed the visitor.
The journalist photographed the visitor who had a borrowed camera.
The visitor with a borrowed camera was photographed by the journalist.
The journalist photographed a visitor's borrowed camera.
questions.explanation: Moving the instrument phrase to a clause about the journalist makes its role explicit.
feedback: Moving the instrument phrase to a clause about the journalist makes its role explicit.
This assigns the camera to the visitor, the reading the edit must avoid.
This attaches the camera phrase to the visitor and preserves the unwanted reading.
This makes the camera the photographed object rather than the instrument.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves both the restriction and the possibility left open.
questions.prompt: The voucher is valid for travel within the city, but not for journeys beyond its boundary.
options: It covers trips that begin inside the city, wherever they end.
It covers journeys towards the city but not journeys away from it.
It covers only trips along the city's outer boundary.
It covers travel inside the city, not trips extending outside it.
questions.explanation: 'Within' sets a geographical limit, reinforced by the exclusion of travel beyond it.
feedback: This ignores the exclusion of journeys beyond the city's boundary.
Direction is not the stated criterion; geographical limits are.
'Within' includes the interior; it does not restrict travel to the boundary itself.
'Within' sets a geographical limit, reinforced by the exclusion of travel beyond it.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that presents the new evidence as a reason to reconsider, not as something disregarded.
questions.prompt: The editor reopened the inquiry ___ the newly discovered letters.
options: regardless of
in spite of
in light of
in the absence of
questions.explanation: 'In light of' means taking the letters into account as grounds for reconsideration.
feedback: This makes the decision independent of the letters rather than responsive to their evidential significance.
This presents the letters as a possible obstacle to reopening, not the stated reason.
'In light of' means taking the letters into account as grounds for reconsideration.
This presents the letters as unavailable, not as evidence taken into account in reopening the inquiry.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that preserves the review's intended aim without saying the aim was achieved.
questions.prompt: The team met with a view to reducing delays.
options: The team met with the aim of reducing delays.
The team met as a result of reduced delays.
The team met after reducing delays.
The team met and thereby reduced delays.
questions.explanation: 'With a view to' expresses an aim and takes a noun or gerund complement; it does not guarantee success.
feedback: 'With a view to' expresses an aim and takes a noun or gerund complement; it does not guarantee success.
This turns an intended result into an already achieved cause of the meeting.
This makes the reduction an earlier event rather than the meeting's purpose.
'Thereby' claims an achieved result, which the purpose phrase does not establish.

questions.setup: Choose the reading that keeps the comparison's reference group.
questions.prompt: For a first-time presenter, Leo handled the questions confidently.
options: Leo handled the questions on behalf of another first-time presenter.
Leo became confident because another first-time presenter helped him.
Leo handled only questions intended for first-time presenters.
Leo's handling of questions was confident when judged against expectations for a first-time presenter.
questions.explanation: Initial 'for a first-time presenter' qualifies the evaluation by naming the relevant comparison group.
feedback: 'For' here sets the standard of comparison; it does not assign a representative role.
The phrase supplies a comparison frame, not a cause or helper.
The initial phrase evaluates Leo; it does not restrict which questions were asked.
Initial 'for a first-time presenter' qualifies the evaluation by naming the relevant comparison group.

questions.setup: Choose the version matching this editing brief: the museum changed the label at the artist's request; the artist did not write the new text.
questions.prompt: Which revision preserves both facts?
options: By the artist's hand, the museum label was rewritten.
At the artist's request, the museum rewrote the label.
On the artist's behalf, the museum displayed the artist's new label.
With the artist's permission, the museum commissioned a new label.
questions.explanation: 'At someone's request' identifies the prompt for an action without making that person its agent.
feedback: This attributes the writing to the artist, contrary to the brief.
'At someone's request' identifies the prompt for an action without making that person its agent.
This adds artist authorship and changes rewriting into displaying.
Permission is not the same as a request, and commissioning does not preserve who rewrote it.

questions.setup: In the original, 'of' names the target of the criticism. Choose the assessment of what the edit changes.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The article contains criticism of the agency.' Edit: 'The article contains criticism by the agency.'
options: The edit preserves the target but makes the criticism more severe.
The edit says the agency commissioned the article but did not supply criticism.
The edit makes the agency the source of criticism instead of its target.
The edit narrows criticism of the agency to criticism of its director.
questions.explanation: With 'criticism', 'of the agency' identifies what is criticized; 'by the agency' identifies who voices it.
feedback: Changing 'of' to 'by' changes a participant's role, not the degree of criticism.
'Criticism by the agency' attributes the criticism to it; commissioning is not stated.
With 'criticism', 'of the agency' identifies what is criticized; 'by the agency' identifies who voices it.
Neither phrase singles out the director; the change is source versus target.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that preserves the stated reason for setting aside the account without treating lack of support as proof of falsity.
questions.prompt: The editor set the account aside for want of corroboration, not because it had been disproved.
options: The account was set aside in order to obtain proof that it was false.
The account was set aside despite having received independent confirmation.
The account was set aside pending the expected arrival of confirmation.
The account was set aside because supporting confirmation was lacking.
questions.explanation: 'For want of' means because of a lack of something. The final clause distinguishes missing support from disproof.
feedback: 'For want of' identifies an existing lack; it does not express a purpose of disproving the account.
This changes lack of corroboration into its presence and replaces a cause with a concession.
'Pending' would present a temporary waiting state and expected event, neither of which the original specifies.
'For want of' means because of a lack of something. The final clause distinguishes missing support from disproof.

questions.setup: Choose the formal revision that identifies an inconsistency between two accounts without saying which is true.
questions.prompt: The witness's account conflicts with the station log.
options: The witness's account is at variance with the station log.
The witness's account takes precedence over the station log.
The witness's account is derived from the station log.
The witness's account is verified against the station log.
questions.explanation: 'At variance with' expresses inconsistency without deciding which source should be accepted.
feedback: 'At variance with' expresses inconsistency without deciding which source should be accepted.
This gives the account priority or authority instead of simply reporting a conflict.
This identifies the log as the account's source, not an inconsistent account to compare it with.
This describes checking the account using the log; it does not preserve the finding that they conflict.

questions.setup: Choose the editorial advice that preserves a natural conversational question.
questions.prompt: A dialogue contains: 'Which proposal were you referring to?' An editor wants to remove the final 'to' because sentences should not end with a preposition.
options: Delete to; referring takes the proposal as a direct object in this meaning.
Keep to: refer to needs it here, and a final preposition is natural in this dialogue.
Replace to with about because final to is not allowed in direct questions.
Move to before which because only indirect questions permit a final preposition.
questions.explanation: Preposition stranding is normal in English questions. 'To which proposal were you referring?' is possible but more formal.
feedback: For mentioning or alluding to a proposal, the construction is 'refer to', not 'refer a proposal'.
Preposition stranding is normal in English questions. 'To which proposal were you referring?' is possible but more formal.
The position is allowed, and 'referring about' is not the required construction.
Direct questions also allow final prepositions; fronting is a style choice here, not a grammatical requirement.

questions.setup: Choose the phrase that says the researcher is examining the assumption critically, not using it as an accepted starting point.
questions.prompt: The new study proceeds ___ the assumption that remote work reduces collaboration.
options: on
from
in accordance with
by questioning
questions.explanation: 'By questioning' identifies critical examination as the method of proceeding.
feedback: 'Proceeds on the assumption' takes it as a starting premise rather than examining it critically.
'Proceeds from the assumption' also treats it as a basis for further work.
This presents the study as following the assumption, not challenging it.
'By questioning' identifies critical examination as the method of proceeding.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that does not confuse the object of risk with its source.
questions.prompt: The report describes the risk to historic buildings from heavy traffic.
options: Historic buildings are presented as a threat to heavy traffic.
The report treats historic buildings as a means of reducing heavy traffic.
Heavy traffic is presented as a threat to the historic buildings.
The report identifies heavy traffic as a result of damage to historic buildings.
questions.explanation: 'Risk to' names what is endangered; 'from' identifies the source of that danger.
feedback: This reverses the threatened thing and the threat's source.
A risk relation does not describe a traffic-reduction measure.
'Risk to' names what is endangered; 'from' identifies the source of that danger.
This turns a potential source of harm into an effect of damage, which the sentence does not say.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that keeps the limitation on the review's remit, not on whether a problem exists.
questions.prompt: Questions about staff pay fall outside the scope of this safety review.
options: This review does not cover staff pay, whether or not pay issues exist.
The review has established that staff pay presents no problems.
Staff pay will be reviewed after the safety work is finished.
Staff pay is too difficult for any review to address.
questions.explanation: 'Outside the scope of' limits the subjects examined; it does not make a finding about excluded subjects.
feedback: 'Outside the scope of' limits the subjects examined; it does not make a finding about excluded subjects.
Excluding a subject from a review does not establish that the subject is problem-free.
'Outside the scope' does not schedule a later review.
The limitation concerns this review's remit, not what any review could handle.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the proposed edit is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The observations are consistent with the proposed explanation, though they are equally consistent with two rival explanations.' Edit: 'The observations provide evidence in favour of the proposed explanation over its rivals.'
options: The edit adds a comparative evidential preference that the original explicitly leaves unsupported.
The edit simply unpacks consistent with into a fuller description of the same preference.
The edit excludes the rival explanations as incompatible with the observations.
The edit weakens the original preference by allowing the rival explanations to remain possible.
questions.explanation: The original allows all three explanations to fit; in favour of one over its rivals makes the observations discriminate between them.
feedback: The original allows all three explanations to fit; in favour of one over its rivals makes the observations discriminate between them.
The original does not establish a preference: consistent with expresses compatibility.
Evidence favouring one explanation over others does not itself make those others incompatible.
The original already allows the rivals and expresses no comparative preference to weaken.

questions.setup: How does the proposed edit change the condition for release?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The release is contingent on completion of the independent review.' Edit: 'The release is contingent on a favourable recommendation from the independent review.'
options: The edit merely states what completion of an independent review necessarily means.
The edit makes the review's conclusion a reason for release rather than a condition of it.
The edit requires a completed review but allows either recommendation.
The edit replaces completion of a process with a specified outcome of that process.
questions.explanation: What follows contingent on defines the condition: completion and a favourable recommendation impose different requirements.
feedback: A review can be completed with an unfavourable recommendation; completion does not guarantee a positive outcome.
Contingent on still expresses a condition, not merely an explanatory reason.
That describes the original requirement; the edit specifically requires a favourable recommendation.
What follows contingent on defines the condition: completion and a favourable recommendation impose different requirements.

questions.setup: Which interpretation is supported by both clauses?
questions.prompt: 'Applicants remain eligible for assistance irrespective of whether they appeal; an appeal may, however, delay payment.'
options: Appealing does not determine eligibility, although it can affect when eligible applicants are paid.
Appealing neither affects eligibility nor changes the timing of payment.
Applicants who appeal retain eligibility, but applicants who do not appeal may lose it for that reason.
Appeals can delay eligibility, though payment follows once eligibility returns.
questions.explanation: Irrespective of whether qualifies remaining eligible, while the next clause permits a distinct effect on payment timing.
feedback: Irrespective of whether qualifies remaining eligible, while the next clause permits a distinct effect on payment timing.
The second clause permits a delay in payment, so the independence claim cannot be extended to timing.
Irrespective of whether they appeal covers both alternatives; not appealing cannot itself remove the stated eligibility.
The text allows payment to be delayed while eligibility remains; it does not describe interrupted eligibility.

questions.setup: Choose the most faithful paraphrase of the statement.
questions.prompt: 'The archive is analogous to a library in respect of access arrangements, not in the ownership of its contents.'
options: The archive is effectively a library, except that ownership details have not yet been checked.
The access arrangements match, while the ownership arrangements are known to differ.
The archive and a library have comparable access arrangements; the ownership comparison is excluded.
The archive is comparable to a library only where access depends on ownership.
questions.explanation: In respect of restricts the analogy to access; the final phrase expressly excludes ownership from it.
feedback: The sentence limits an analogy; it neither classifies the archive as a library nor reports an unfinished ownership check.
Excluding ownership from the comparison does not itself establish how the ownership arrangements differ.
In respect of restricts the analogy to access; the final phrase expressly excludes ownership from it.
This combines access and ownership into one condition, although the sentence compares the first dimension and excludes the second.

questions.setup: Compare the original and the edit. Which assessment is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The photographs were removed in compliance with the artist's request, despite the curator's objections.' Edit: 'The photographs were removed with the artist's consent and the curator's support.'
options: The edit preserves both relationships but uses less formal prepositions.
The edit downgrades the request to permission and reverses the curator's stated opposition.
The edit strengthens the artist's permission into a requirement while leaving the curator's stance unchanged.
The edit preserves the curator's objections but makes the artist's consent conditional on them.
questions.explanation: In compliance with reports following the request. With consent reports permission, while the curator's objections are replaced by support.
feedback: Following a request is not merely receiving consent, and support does not preserve the stated objections.
In compliance with reports following the request. With consent reports permission, while the curator's objections are replaced by support.
The original reports a request being followed; the edit gives consent and changes the curator's objection to support.
The edit states curator support, not objections, and introduces no condition linking the artist's consent to them.

questions.setup: The editor wrote the review, and the historian wrote the book. Choose a clear revision of the draft.
questions.prompt: Draft: 'The journal published a review of a book by the historian by the editor.'
options: The journal published the historian's review of the editor's book.
The journal published a book by the historian reviewing the editor.
The journal published a review by the historian of a book edited by the editor.
The journal published the editor's review of the historian's book.
questions.explanation: Separate possessives make the reviewer and book author explicit, replacing the awkward chain of by phrases.
feedback: This reverses the two authorship roles.
This turns the published item into a book and the editor into the subject of a review.
This makes the historian the reviewer and reduces the editor's role to editing the book.
Separate possessives make the reviewer and book author explicit, replacing the awkward chain of by phrases.

questions.setup: Which summary is supported by the full statement?
questions.prompt: 'Publication has been suspended pending a review of the disputed passages; the review may recommend either revision or withdrawal.'
options: Publication will resume as soon as the review is complete, regardless of its recommendation.
Publication is on hold while the review is awaited, with its eventual course unresolved.
Publication has been withdrawn following a review of the disputed passages.
Publication is postponed solely to let the reviewers choose a resumption date.
questions.explanation: Pending marks an interim state awaiting an event. The possible recommendations leave the later decision open.
feedback: Pending describes the current wait; it does not guarantee resumption after a review that may recommend withdrawal.
Pending marks an interim state awaiting an event. The possible recommendations leave the later decision open.
This turns suspension pending a review into withdrawal following a completed review.
The review may recommend withdrawal, so its role is not limited to scheduling a resumption.

questions.setup: The editor still has reservations but recommends publication. The factual errors must be corrected before publication. Choose a concise recommendation matching this brief.
questions.prompt: Which recommendation meets the brief?
options: In view of my reservations, I recommend publication irrespective of correction of the factual errors.
Subject to my reservations, I recommend publication notwithstanding the uncorrected factual errors.
Following the resolution of my reservations, I recommend publication in advance of any factual corrections.
Notwithstanding my reservations, I recommend publication subject to correction of the factual errors.
questions.explanation: 'Notwithstanding' concedes the continuing reservations; 'subject to' makes correction a condition of the recommendation.
feedback: This makes the reservations grounds for publication and removes correction as a condition.
This exchanges the roles: reservations become the qualification while uncorrected errors become an obstacle publication proceeds despite.
This claims the reservations were resolved and permits publication before corrections, reversing both parts of the brief.
'Notwithstanding' concedes the continuing reservations; 'subject to' makes correction a condition of the recommendation.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that preserves the original comparison.
questions.prompt: 'As against the earlier edition's fuller notes, the new edition offers a more accurate text.'
options: The new edition is preferable to the earlier one because accuracy matters more than notes.
The earlier edition has fuller notes, whereas the new edition has a more accurate text.
The new edition improves both the text and the notes supplied by the earlier edition.
The new edition's more accurate text compensates for its less extensive notes.
questions.explanation: The contrast preserves the distinct quality attributed to each edition without ranking those qualities against each other.
feedback: This adds a weighting of the two qualities and an overall preference.
The contrast preserves the distinct quality attributed to each edition without ranking those qualities against each other.
The original attributes fuller notes to the earlier edition, not improvement in both areas to the new one.
Compensates for adds a judgment that one advantage offsets the other; the original simply contrasts the two features.

questions.setup: Which revision preserves the original claim?
questions.prompt: 'The journalist completed the interview without asking about the disputed donation.'
options: The journalist completed the interview to prevent discussion of the disputed donation.
The journalist completed the interview despite being forbidden to ask about the disputed donation.
The interview was completed with no question from the journalist about the disputed donation.
The journalist completed the interview before being able to ask about the disputed donation.
questions.explanation: This preserves the absent action and its agent without assigning a motive or ruling out other ways the subject arose.
feedback: 'To prevent' adds an intention; 'without asking' reports an omission without explaining it.
This adds a prohibition and presents it as an obstacle, neither of which is stated.
This preserves the absent action and its agent without assigning a motive or ruling out other ways the subject arose.
This adds lack of opportunity and implies an intended later question rather than simply reporting the omission.

questions.setup: The author's brief is to evaluate only the book's treatment of sources, praising its clarity and criticizing its brevity. Choose a clear revision.
questions.prompt: Draft: 'The review praises the book's clarity and criticizes its brevity in its treatment of sources.'
options: The review praises the book's overall clarity but criticizes the brevity of its treatment of sources.
The review praises the clarity of the book's treatment of sources but criticizes the book's overall brevity.
In assessing the book's treatment of sources, the review praises its clarity and criticizes its brevity.
In assessing the book as a whole, the review praises its clarity and criticizes its brevity.
questions.explanation: The initial phrase makes source treatment the frame for both evaluations.
feedback: This extends the praise to the whole book while restricting only the criticism to source treatment.
This restricts the praise but extends the criticism to the entire book.
The initial phrase makes source treatment the frame for both evaluations.
This applies both judgments to the whole book, exceeding the author's restricted brief.

questions.setup: Which summary accurately represents the speaker's position?
questions.prompt: 'I object to the proposal only to the extent that it transfers editorial decisions to the sponsor; I have no objection to the funding arrangement itself.'
options: The speaker opposes sponsorship unless the sponsor makes the editorial decisions.
The speaker's objection grows whenever the amount of sponsorship increases.
The objection concerns the transfer of editorial decisions, not sponsorship as such.
The speaker accepts the transfer of editorial decisions but objects to its funding.
questions.explanation: The phrase restricts the objection to a particular feature, reinforced by explicit acceptance of the funding arrangement itself.
feedback: This reverses the concern: transferring those decisions is the objectionable feature.
'To the extent that' here limits the grounds of objection; it does not set a financial scale.
The phrase restricts the objection to a particular feature, reinforced by explicit acceptance of the funding arrangement itself.
This reverses both the disputed and accepted parts of the proposal.

questions.setup: The writer confirms that both the budget and travel costs were discussed. Choose an explicit revision of the draft.
questions.prompt: Draft: 'Apart from the budget, we discussed travel costs.'
options: Excluding the budget, we discussed travel costs.
Instead of the budget, we discussed travel costs.
With regard to the budget, we discussed travel costs.
In addition to the budget, we discussed travel costs.
questions.explanation: 'Apart from' can be additive or exceptive; 'in addition to' makes the intended inclusion explicit.
feedback: This chooses the exception reading of apart from rather than the intended addition.
This replaces the budget as a topic rather than retaining it alongside travel costs.
This treats travel costs as a budget-related subtopic, not explicitly as an additional topic discussed.
'Apart from' can be additive or exceptive; 'in addition to' makes the intended inclusion explicit.

questions.setup: Which summary accurately represents the editor's offer?
questions.prompt: 'Short of withdrawing the essay from the collection, I can accommodate the changes you propose,' the editor wrote.
options: The editor can accommodate the changes only after the author withdraws the essay.
The editor offers accommodation in exchange for the author's promise to withdraw the essay.
The editor offers to accommodate changes that stop short of withdrawing the essay.
The editor predicts that the proposed changes will fall short of preventing withdrawal.
questions.explanation: Here 'short of' marks the boundary of the offer: lesser changes can be accommodated, but withdrawal is not included.
feedback: This turns the excluded step into a prior condition of accommodating changes.
This invents a reciprocal bargain; 'short of' identifies a limit, not an exchange.
Here 'short of' marks the boundary of the offer: lesser changes can be accommodated, but withdrawal is not included.
This takes short of as insufficiency for an outcome and turns an offer into a prediction about withdrawal.

questions.setup: How does the proposed edit affect the meaning?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The studio received a grant in recognition of its contribution to local theatre.' Edit: 'The studio received a grant in return for its contribution to local theatre.'
options: The edit presents the grant as an exchange for the contribution, rather than simply an acknowledgement of it.
Both versions give the same reason for the grant; the edit changes only the level of formality.
The edit changes a past contribution into a promise of future theatre work.
The edit changes a reward for past work into payment under a previously agreed bargain.
questions.explanation: In recognition of marks acknowledgement; in return for frames one thing as given in exchange for another.
feedback: In recognition of marks acknowledgement; in return for frames one thing as given in exchange for another.
Recognition and reciprocal exchange are different meanings, not merely different levels of formality.
In return for does not by itself determine whether the contribution is past or future.
An exchange framing does not establish that a bargain was agreed in advance.

questions.setup: Edit the draft to state when the meeting began. Do not add an explanation for the chair's decision.
questions.prompt: Draft: 'With two members still absent, the chair began the meeting.'
options: The chair began the meeting because two members were still absent.
The chair began the meeting while two members were still absent.
The chair began the meeting despite two members still being absent.
The chair began the meeting after two members had left.
questions.explanation: The with phrase supplies a concurrent circumstance; 'while' makes simultaneity explicit without specifying a motive.
feedback: This makes the absences the cause of beginning, which the brief leaves open.
The with phrase supplies a concurrent circumstance; 'while' makes simultaneity explicit without specifying a motive.
This presents absence as an obstacle overridden; the brief asks to make timing explicit without adding that relationship.
This adds an earlier departure. The with phrase does not establish that the absent members had previously been there.

questions.setup: Choose the revision that preserves the statement's meaning.
questions.prompt: 'In the critic's reading of the novel, the narrator's politeness is a form of resistance.'
options: The novelist presents politeness as resistance in the critic's account of the novel.
The critic interprets the narrator's politeness as a form of resistance.
The critic reports that the novelist explicitly described politeness as resistance.
The novel confirms the critic's claim that the narrator intended resistance.
questions.explanation: In the critic's reading frames the proposition as an interpretation and identifies whose interpretation it is.
feedback: This attributes the position to the novelist; the original establishes the critic's interpretation without assigning it to the author.
In the critic's reading frames the proposition as an interpretation and identifies whose interpretation it is.
This changes the critic's reading into a report of something the novelist expressly said.
This adds confirmation and character intention beyond the attributed interpretation.

questions.setup: The storage manager is describing a view the archivist would take. Choose a faithful revision of the draft.
questions.prompt: Draft: 'From the archivist's perspective, retaining the duplicate files is prudent.'
options: As the archivist would see it, retaining the duplicate files is prudent.
From my perspective as storage manager, retaining the duplicate files is prudent.
According to the archivist's explicit instructions, the duplicate files must be retained.
In agreement with the archivist, I regard retention of the duplicate files as prudent.
questions.explanation: This preserves the attributed standpoint and its hypothetical framing without claiming the archivist has actually stated the view.
feedback: This preserves the attributed standpoint and its hypothetical framing without claiming the archivist has actually stated the view.
This transfers the evaluation from the archivist's standpoint to the writer's own professional standpoint.
This turns an attributed perspective into documented instructions and changes an evaluation into a requirement.
This adds the writer's endorsement. Attributing a standpoint does not establish agreement with it.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the change is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'On reading the manuscript, the editor requested a second opinion.' Proposed edit: 'For the purpose of requesting a second opinion, the editor read the manuscript.'
options: The edit changes a response following the reading into a purpose attributed to the reading.
The edit keeps the sequence and merely makes the editor's original purpose explicit.
The edit changes a request made after reading into a request made before reading.
The edit preserves two completed actions while making their connection more explicit.
questions.explanation: On reading links the request to the occasion of reading; the purpose phrase instead supplies an aim motivating the reading.
feedback: On reading links the request to the occasion of reading; the purpose phrase instead supplies an aim motivating the reading.
The original reports a request on reading; it does not say the editor read with that purpose already in mind.
The purpose phrase does not establish that a request was actually made before the reading.
Reading for the purpose of requesting does not itself report that the request was subsequently made.

questions.setup: The curator discussed the loans with the northern and southern museums. Only the northern museum was involved in correspondence.
questions.prompt: Which sentence accurately combines these facts?
options: The curator discussed the loans and corresponded with both museums.
With both museums, the curator discussed the loans and maintained correspondence.
The curator discussed the loans with the northern museum and corresponded with both museums.
The curator discussed the loans with both museums and corresponded with the northern museum.
questions.explanation: Repeating 'with' assigns each verb its own participants: both museums for discussion, only the northern one for correspondence.
feedback: The shared final phrase makes correspondence involve both museums, exceeding the brief.
The fronted phrase frames both coordinated activities with both museums, losing the unequal coverage.
This reverses which activity involves both museums and narrows the discussion incorrectly.
Repeating 'with' assigns each verb its own participants: both museums for discussion, only the northern one for correspondence.

questions.setup: Choose the pronoun that refers to the book, not Mina.
questions.prompt: Mina has a book. ___ is on the desk.
options: They
It
Them
She
questions.explanation: It refers to the one book and agrees with is.
feedback: They would refer to more than one book and would need are.
It refers to the one book and agrees with is.
Them is an object form; this sentence needs a subject before is.
She would refer to Mina, not the book specified in the task.

questions.setup: Choose the form for the person speaking, using standard English.
questions.prompt: Hello. ___ am your new neighbour.
options: Me
My
Mine
I
questions.explanation: I is the subject form for the speaker and pairs with am.
feedback: Me is used as an object; a subject is needed before am.
My introduces a noun, as in my name; it cannot stand as the subject here.
Mine refers to something belonging to the speaker, not the speaker introducing themself.
I is the subject form for the speaker and pairs with am.

questions.setup: Choose the subject pronoun referring to the photos.
questions.prompt: Here are the holiday photos. ___ are ready to print.
options: They
Them
Their
It
questions.explanation: They is the plural subject pronoun referring to the photos.
feedback: They is the plural subject pronoun referring to the photos.
Them can be the object of print, but not the standard subject of are.
Their shows possession before a noun; it does not replace the photos by itself.
It would refer to one photo and require is, not are.

questions.setup: Choose the pronoun for the speaker after 'call', in standard English.
questions.prompt: I finish work at six. Please call ___ after that.
options: I
me
my
mine
questions.explanation: 'Me' is the object of 'call' and refers to the speaker.
feedback: 'I' is the subject form, but the speaker receives the call here.
'Me' is the object of 'call' and refers to the speaker.
'My' needs a following noun, such as 'my phone'.
'Mine' refers to something belonging to the speaker, not the person being called.

questions.setup: Choose the form meaning that the keys belong to the person being addressed.
questions.prompt: Are these ___ keys, Mr Shah?
options: your
you
yours
yourself
questions.explanation: Your goes before keys and identifies the listener as their owner.
feedback: Your goes before keys and identifies the listener as their owner.
You names the listener but cannot introduce the noun keys as a possessive.
Yours stands alone; before keys, use your.
Yourself refers back to the listener as a person, not to ownership before a noun.

questions.setup: Choose the word that means 'my bag' without repeating 'bag'.
questions.prompt: The blue bag belongs to me. It is ___.
options: my
mine
me
I
questions.explanation: 'Mine' replaces 'my bag' and can stand after 'is'.
feedback: 'My' must introduce a noun, as in 'my bag'.
'Mine' replaces 'my bag' and can stand after 'is'.
'Me' refers to the speaker, not to something the speaker owns.
'I' is a subject pronoun and does not express bag ownership here.

questions.setup: Choose the subject pronoun for the speaker and her husband together.
questions.prompt: My husband and I live near the station. ___ walk to work.
options: Us
They
Our
We
questions.explanation: We includes the speaker and the other person, her husband.
feedback: Us is an object form; a subject is needed before walk.
They would exclude the speaker from the group described.
Our needs a following noun, such as our office, and cannot replace the two people alone.
We includes the speaker and the other person, her husband.

questions.setup: Choose the object pronoun for the speaker and her friend.
questions.prompt: My friend and I cannot find the address. Can you help ___?
options: us
we
our
ours
questions.explanation: Us is the object pronoun for the speaker and her friend together.
feedback: Us is the object pronoun for the speaker and her friend together.
We is the subject form; the group receives help here.
Our would need a noun naming something belonging to the group.
Ours expresses ownership, not the people needing help.

questions.setup: Choose the word that means 'her coat' without repeating 'coat'.
questions.prompt: This coat belongs to my sister. It is ___.
options: her
she
hers
herself
questions.explanation: 'Hers' can stand alone to mean 'her coat'.
feedback: 'Her' shows possession before a noun, but the noun 'coat' is omitted here.
'She' refers to the sister as a person, not her coat.
'Hers' can stand alone to mean 'her coat'.
'Herself' refers back to the sister, not to a possession.

questions.setup: Choose the word showing that the tickets belong to both neighbours.
questions.prompt: Our neighbours are going to a concert. These are ___ tickets.
options: them
theirs
they
their
questions.explanation: Their introduces tickets and links ownership to the neighbours.
feedback: Them is an object pronoun, not the form used before an owned noun.
Theirs would stand alone after are; before tickets, use their.
They is a subject pronoun and cannot show ownership before tickets.
Their introduces tickets and links ownership to the neighbours.

questions.setup: Choose the pronoun that refers to the two parcels as the things to bring.
questions.prompt: Two parcels are at reception. Please bring ___ upstairs.
options: they
their
it
them
questions.explanation: Them is the plural object pronoun referring to the two parcels.
feedback: They is a subject form, not the object of bring.
Their introduces a possessed noun; it does not replace parcels on its own.
It would refer to one parcel rather than both of them.
Them is the plural object pronoun referring to the two parcels.

questions.setup: Choose the form that refers to my father as the subject, in standard English.
questions.prompt: My father is a bus driver. ___ starts work early.
options: Him
His
He
Himself
questions.explanation: He is the subject pronoun referring back to my father.
feedback: Him is an object form, not a subject before starts.
His can show ownership, but it does not replace the father as the person starting work.
He is the subject pronoun referring back to my father.
Himself normally refers back to a subject or adds emphasis; it is not the ordinary subject pronoun needed here.

questions.setup: Choose the word for the woman receiving the invitation.
questions.prompt: My aunt lives nearby. I invited ___ to dinner.
options: her
she
hers
herself
questions.explanation: Her is the object form for the aunt who receives the invitation.
feedback: Her is the object form for the aunt who receives the invitation.
She would be a subject; after invited, use the object form her.
Hers means something belonging to the aunt, not the aunt herself.
The subject is I, so herself does not express the speaker inviting the aunt in this sentence.

questions.setup: Choose the word that means 'his phone' without repeating 'phone'.
questions.prompt: This phone belongs to my brother. The phone is ___.
options: he
him
himself
his
questions.explanation: 'His' can stand alone to mean 'his phone'; its form does not change when the noun is omitted.
feedback: 'He' refers to the brother as a person and does not express ownership here.
'Him' is an object pronoun, not a possessive form.
'Himself' refers to the brother, not to an object belonging to him.
'His' can stand alone to mean 'his phone'; its form does not change when the noun is omitted.

questions.setup: Choose the word for the person I am speaking to.
questions.prompt: Hello, Ms Chen. Are ___ here for the interview?
options: your
you
yours
yourself
questions.explanation: You addresses Ms Chen directly and works as the subject after are.
feedback: Your must introduce a noun, such as your interview.
You addresses Ms Chen directly and works as the subject after are.
Yours refers to something belonging to the listener, not the listener attending.
Yourself is not the ordinary personal subject in this question; use you.

questions.setup: Choose the standard word used as the subject in this weather sentence.
questions.prompt: Take an umbrella. ___ is raining.
options: This
There
It
They
questions.explanation: Weather expressions use it as a subject even though it does not stand for a particular object.
feedback: This would point to an identified thing; the ordinary weather sentence uses it without such a reference.
There is raining is not the standard weather construction; use it is raining.
Weather expressions use it as a subject even though it does not stand for a particular object.
They needs are and refers to people or things, not the weather subject here.

questions.setup: Choose the question asking for the new person's identity, not a place, time or choice of object.
questions.prompt: Someone has just joined our table. ___ is that?
options: Where
When
Who
Which
