options: I'm not feeling great, but I'll be there today.
I'm unwell and can't come to work today.
I might take some time off next month.
Things are a bit difficult at the moment.
questions.explanation: This gives a brief reason and states the absence clearly; contractions can be appropriate in a routine work message.
feedback: This reports illness but says you will attend, contrary to the situation.
This gives a brief reason and states the absence clearly; contractions can be appropriate in a routine work message.
This discusses a possible future absence, not today's illness.
This is too vague to tell the supervisor you cannot work today.

questions.setup: You write to a customer: 'Thanks for the info.' You want a more formal version with the same meaning.
questions.prompt: Choose the best replacement.
options: Please send me the information.
Thanks for all that stuff.
Thank you for the information.
Sorry about the information.
questions.explanation: 'Thank you' and the full word 'information' make the wording more formal while preserving the thanks.
feedback: This requests information instead of thanking the customer for information already sent.
'Stuff' is vaguer and more informal than 'info', so this moves away from the requested style.
'Thank you' and the full word 'information' make the wording more formal while preserving the thanks.
This changes gratitude into an apology.

questions.setup: A neighbor invites you to dinner on Friday, but you must work that evening.
questions.prompt: Choose a friendly refusal that thanks the neighbor and explains why you cannot come.
options: Thanks, Friday is fine. See you then.
Thanks for asking, but I'm working on Friday.
You should have asked me about my work first.
I don't know. Ask someone else instead.
questions.explanation: This acknowledges the invitation warmly and gives a clear reason for declining.
feedback: This accepts Friday even though you must work.
This acknowledges the invitation warmly and gives a clear reason for declining.
This criticizes the neighbor and does not thank them for the invitation.
This gives neither thanks nor your actual reason and sounds dismissive.

questions.setup: You introduce your colleague Sam to a new employee. Sam manages the shop.
questions.prompt: Choose a friendly introduction that gives Sam's name and role.
options: Sam, please introduce me to the manager.
Are you Sam, the shop manager?
This is Sam, our shop manager.
I used to manage the shop with Sam.
questions.explanation: 'This is' introduces someone present, and the following phrase explains Sam's role.
feedback: This asks Sam to introduce you to someone else, reversing the intended action.
This checks the listener's identity rather than introducing Sam to the new employee.
'This is' introduces someone present, and the following phrase explains Sam's role.
This describes your past work and does not identify Sam's current role.

questions.setup: A visitor is about to touch a very hot pan. You need to warn them immediately.
questions.prompt: Choose a direct warning that stops the action and names the danger.
options: You might want to be careful.
The pan should be cool enough now.
Could you check whether the pan is hot?
Don't touch it! It's hot!
questions.explanation: An urgent danger calls for a brief direct warning; the command is appropriate because it helps prevent harm.
feedback: This vague advice does not clearly say to stop touching the pan or explain that it is hot.
This reassures the visitor that the pan is cool instead of warning that it is very hot.
This asks the visitor to investigate the temperature rather than immediately stopping contact.
An urgent danger calls for a brief direct warning; the command is appropriate because it helps prevent harm.

questions.setup: A colleague suggests opening the shop at six. You think there will be too few customers that early.
questions.prompt: Choose a respectful disagreement that explains your concern.
options: I agree that six is a sensible time to open.
You don't understand our customers as well as I do.
I'm concerned that we won't have many customers at six.
We can discuss the opening time when everyone arrives.
questions.explanation: This states a reservation about the proposal without attacking the person who suggested it.
feedback: This expresses agreement and leaves your concern unstated.
This criticizes the colleague's knowledge instead of explaining the concern about demand.
This states a reservation about the proposal without attacking the person who suggested it.
This postpones discussion but does not communicate your disagreement or its reason.

questions.setup: You need a supplier's price list no later than Wednesday. Your email should be courteous and keep the deadline clear.
questions.prompt: Which request meets both requirements?
options: Could you send the price list by Wednesday, please?
Could you send the price list whenever you have time?
You need to get that price list to me already.
Could you send the price list sometime after Wednesday?
questions.explanation: The request form is courteous, and 'by Wednesday' preserves the latest acceptable date.
feedback: The request form is courteous, and 'by Wednesday' preserves the latest acceptable date.
This is polite but removes the Wednesday deadline.
This sounds impatient and does not specify the actual deadline.
This politely requests delivery after the latest acceptable day.

questions.setup: A delivery was due on Monday. It is Wednesday and it has not arrived. You do not know why.
questions.prompt: Choose a professional complaint that states the known facts without guessing the cause.
options: Your driver has clearly forgotten to deliver our order.
Our delivery was due on Monday and has not arrived.
You seem to have decided our order can wait.
The delivery may be late, but I'm not sure.
questions.explanation: This records the missed date and current position without assigning an unsupported cause.
feedback: This assumes the driver forgot, but the cause is unknown.
This records the missed date and current position without assigning an unsupported cause.
This attributes a decision to the supplier without evidence.
This weakens a fact you know: the Monday delivery has not arrived by Wednesday.

questions.setup: You emailed the wrong file to a client. You now send the correct one.
questions.prompt: Choose an apology that accepts your error and identifies the correction.
options: Sorry if you found the previous attachment rather confusing.
You opened the wrong file; please use this one instead.
The correct file will follow when I have located it.
Sorry I sent the wrong file. The correct one is attached.
questions.explanation: This owns the mistake and directs the client to the replacement.
feedback: This apologizes conditionally for the client's experience without acknowledging that you sent the wrong file.
This blames the client, although you sent the wrong file.
This delays the correction instead of identifying the correct file you are sending now.
This owns the mistake and directs the client to the replacement.

questions.setup: An official notice needs a more formal version of 'We have put off the workshop until May.'
questions.prompt: Choose the replacement that keeps the same meaning.
options: We have cancelled the workshop planned for May.
We have arranged another workshop before May.
We have brought the workshop forward to May.
We have postponed the workshop until May.
questions.explanation: 'Postponed' is a more formal alternative to 'put off' for moving an event to a later date.
feedback: 'Cancelled' means it will not take place as planned; the original moves it to May.
This adds a different workshop and changes the time relationship.
'Brought forward' moves an event earlier, the opposite direction from 'put off'.
'Postponed' is a more formal alternative to 'put off' for moving an event to a later date.

questions.setup: You asked a venue about wheelchair access a week ago. You have not received a reply.
questions.prompt: Choose a courteous follow-up that repeats the question without accusing the venue of ignoring you.
options: Why have you ignored my question about wheelchair access?
I take it your silence means wheelchair access is unavailable.
I'm following up to ask whether the venue has wheelchair access.
Thank you for confirming that your venue has wheelchair access.
questions.explanation: This refers to the earlier contact and repeats the needed question without assigning blame.
feedback: 'Ignored' assumes deliberate neglect, which you cannot infer just from the missing reply.
This treats the lack of a reply as an answer and may lead to a false conclusion.
This refers to the earlier contact and repeats the needed question without assigning blame.
This claims you received confirmation even though no reply arrived.

questions.setup: A customer asks for delivery today. Today is fully booked, but tomorrow morning is available.
questions.prompt: Choose a polite refusal that offers the available alternative.
options: We can't deliver today, but we can come tomorrow morning.
We should be able to deliver today if you keep waiting.
You left it too late; tomorrow is your only chance.
We can't deliver today, so please contact a different company.
questions.explanation: This clearly declines today's request while offering the specific available time.
feedback: This clearly declines today's request while offering the specific available time.
This creates an expectation of today's delivery despite the full schedule.
This blames the customer and adds an unsupported claim that no later delivery is possible.
This refuses the request but omits the alternative your own company can provide.

questions.setup: Your invoice shows two charges for one room. You want the hotel to check whether there is an error.
questions.prompt: Choose a neutral subject line that describes the problem without alleging dishonesty.
options: Your hotel's dishonest billing practices
Please explain why you overcharged me deliberately
Invoice query: two charges for one room
Thanks for correcting the room charges
questions.explanation: This identifies the document and the discrepancy while leaving the cause open.
feedback: This accuses the hotel of dishonesty before the charges have been checked.
'Deliberately' assumes an intention not established by the invoice.
This identifies the document and the discrepancy while leaving the cause open.
This presents the correction as completed when you are only requesting a check.

questions.setup: You change 'I'll get back to you about your application tomorrow' into a more formal email sentence.
questions.prompt: Which version keeps the promise to reply tomorrow?
options: I will return your application to you tomorrow.
I will approve your application by tomorrow morning.
I will respond about your application tomorrow.
I will contact you about your application next week.
questions.explanation: 'Respond' expresses the intended meaning of 'get back to you' in more formal wording.
feedback: This promises to send the application back, not to reply about it.
This adds approval and a morning deadline, neither of which the original promises.
'Respond' expresses the intended meaning of 'get back to you' in more formal wording.
This keeps future contact but changes the promised day.

questions.setup: During a meeting, the chair says, 'It would help if we kept our comments brief; we have ten minutes left.'
questions.prompt: What is the chair politely asking people to do?
options: Leave the meeting ten minutes before it finishes.
Make their remaining comments short.
Stop making comments for the rest of the meeting.
Write a short report after the meeting ends.
questions.explanation: The indirect wording softens a request to limit speaking time; the ten-minute limit explains its purpose.
feedback: The time explains the need for shorter comments, not an instruction to leave early.
The indirect wording softens a request to limit speaking time; the ten-minute limit explains its purpose.
'Keep our comments brief' allows comments but asks that they be short.
The chair refers to comments during the meeting, not a later written task.

questions.setup: Your team is discussing ways to reduce printing. You want to suggest sharing files online, leaving the decision open.
questions.prompt: Choose a tentative, cooperative suggestion.
options: We have decided to share every file online from now on.
You must share your files online as I have explained.
Why haven't you started sharing the files online yet?
Perhaps we could share the files online instead.
questions.explanation: 'Perhaps we could' offers a possible shared action without presenting it as an order or settled decision.
feedback: This presents the idea as a decision already made.
This gives a requirement and invokes your authority instead of inviting discussion.
This criticizes people for not implementing an idea they are still discussing.
'Perhaps we could' offers a possible shared action without presenting it as an order or settled decision.

questions.setup: A colleague says, 'Send it to the other office.' You are unsure whether they mean the North Street office.
questions.prompt: Choose a polite question that checks that meaning.
options: I'll send it to North Street, as you requested.
Do you mean the office on North Street?
Why can't you give clear instructions for once?
Could you send it to North Street for me?
questions.explanation: This offers a possible interpretation and asks the speaker to confirm it.
feedback: This acts on an uncertain interpretation as if it were confirmed.
This offers a possible interpretation and asks the speaker to confirm it.
This criticizes the colleague instead of checking the intended office.
This is polite, but it transfers the task to the colleague instead of clarifying the destination.

questions.setup: You write a team memo about a printer: 'It's playing up again, so don't count on it.' The memo needs neutral, clear wording.
questions.prompt: Which version preserves the warning about an unreliable printer?
options: The printer has been repaired and is ready to use.
The printer has been removed from the office permanently.
The printer is faulty again, so it may not work reliably.
The printer is acting weird again, so don't bank on it.
questions.explanation: This replaces the informal idioms with a clear statement of the fault and its practical consequence.
feedback: This changes the warning into reassurance that the problem is resolved.
This adds permanent removal, which the original does not state.
This replaces the informal idioms with a clear statement of the fault and its practical consequence.
This retains conversational idioms instead of making the wording neutral and clear.

questions.setup: A customer said the queue was too long. A staff member wrote, 'The customer whined about the wait.'
questions.prompt: Choose a neutral report that preserves the customer's dissatisfaction without judging their manner.
options: The customer enjoyed talking about the waiting time.
The customer complained about the length of the queue.
The customer complained in a childish way about the wait.
The customer asked where the queue started that morning.
questions.explanation: 'Complained' records dissatisfaction without the dismissive judgment carried by 'whined'.
feedback: This reverses the negative reaction by presenting the conversation as enjoyable.
'Complained' records dissatisfaction without the dismissive judgment carried by 'whined'.
'In a childish way' retains the judgment about manner that the task asks you to remove.
This changes a complaint about length into a question about location.

questions.setup: A close colleague covered your shift when you needed help. You send a warm personal text.
questions.prompt: Choose an appreciative message suited to that relationship.
options: Your assistance with the shift has been noted for the record.
Thanks for covering my shift. I really appreciate it.
Thanks, but you could have offered to cover sooner.
I'll need you to cover the same shift next week.
questions.explanation: This names the favor and expresses personal gratitude in a natural, warm tone.
feedback: This sounds like an administrative record and does not convey the personal warmth requested.
This names the favor and expresses personal gratitude in a natural, warm tone.
The added criticism undermines the intended appreciative message.
This makes a new demand rather than thanking the colleague for the favor.

questions.setup: You work at a sports center's reception. Only the bookings team can change a group reservation.
questions.prompt: Choose a helpful, polite response that directs the customer to the right team without promising a change.
options: Please contact our bookings team about changing the reservation.
I'll change your reservation myself this afternoon.
That's not my job. Find someone from bookings.
The bookings team will definitely approve the change.
questions.explanation: This courteously identifies the team that handles changes without promising what it will decide.
feedback: This courteously identifies the team that handles changes without promising what it will decide.
This promises an action your reception role cannot carry out.
This identifies another team but sounds dismissive instead of helpful.
This guarantees an outcome that the situation does not establish.

questions.setup: At a work social event, someone asks how much you earn. You prefer to keep that private.
questions.prompt: Choose a polite refusal to discuss your salary.
options: I don't remember, but I can check for you.
You must be earning less than I do here.
I'll tell everyone my salary when the others arrive.
I'd rather not discuss my salary, if you don't mind.
questions.explanation: This states your preference and sets a boundary without criticizing the questioner.
feedback: This suggests you will provide the information later, rather than declining to discuss it.
This speculates about the other person's pay and may sound competitive or insulting.
This offers to disclose the information, contrary to your wish for privacy.
This states your preference and sets a boundary without criticizing the questioner.

questions.setup: A shop wants simpler customer instructions. Its draft says, 'Retain your receipt in case you wish to return the item.'
questions.prompt: Which version uses everyday language and keeps the same advice?
options: Keep your receipt in case you want to return the item.
Return your receipt if you decide to keep the item.
Keep the receipt because the item must be returned.
Preserve the receipt should you elect to return the item.
questions.explanation: 'Keep' and 'want' make the instruction plainer while preserving the possible reason for keeping the receipt.
feedback: 'Keep' and 'want' make the instruction plainer while preserving the possible reason for keeping the receipt.
This reverses both the receipt action and the reason for it.
This turns a possible future return into a requirement.
This retains a formal style with 'preserve', 'should you', and 'elect', rather than simplifying it.

questions.setup: A venue's email says your group has twelve people. Your booking confirmation says ten, which is correct.
questions.prompt: Choose a polite correction that clearly gives the right number.
options: Just to clarify, our booking is for ten people, not twelve.
Thank you for confirming our booking for twelve people.
I suppose either ten or twelve people would be fine.
You really need to read your booking information properly.
questions.explanation: This introduces the correction courteously and states both the correct number and the error being corrected.
feedback: This introduces the correction courteously and states both the correct number and the error being corrected.
This accepts the incorrect number instead of correcting it.
This treats both numbers as acceptable, although the booking is for ten.
This criticizes the reader without clearly supplying the correct number.

questions.setup: A meeting speaker is about to move to a new topic. You need to ask about the date they just mentioned.
questions.prompt: Choose a polite interruption that asks for that clarification.
options: Stop there. You haven't explained anything clearly today.
I'll explain the dates after you've finished your presentation.
Please carry on; I don't have any questions about that.
Sorry to interrupt, but which date did you mean?
questions.explanation: This briefly acknowledges the interruption and asks the specific question before the topic changes.
feedback: This attacks the speaker's overall explanation rather than politely asking about the date.
This announces your own later explanation instead of asking the question now.
This gives the speaker permission to continue and hides the clarification you need.
This briefly acknowledges the interruption and asks the specific question before the topic changes.

questions.setup: A small trial found fewer booking errors after a software change, but other factors may have contributed. You are writing a cautious report.
questions.prompt: Choose the conclusion whose certainty matches that evidence.
options: The software change may have contributed to the reduction in booking errors.
The trial establishes the software change as the reason for fewer errors.
The reduction in errors probably reflects factors unrelated to the software change.
The trial provides little reason to connect the change with the error reduction.
questions.explanation: 'May have contributed' reports a possible influence while leaving room for the other factors.
feedback: 'May have contributed' reports a possible influence while leaving room for the other factors.
'Establishes ... as the reason' asserts a causal conclusion the trial cannot isolate.
This favors a competing explanation that the evidence does not establish as more likely.
This dismisses a possible connection instead of reporting it cautiously.

questions.setup: You ask a colleague at the same level to review a long draft as a favor. You want to make clear that they can decline if busy.
questions.prompt: Which request leaves that choice genuinely open?
options: I'd appreciate your review and will include your comments in tomorrow's version.
Please review the draft; let me know how much time you'll need.
Would you have time to review this, or is your schedule too full?
Thank you in advance for taking the time to review this draft.
questions.explanation: This asks about availability and explicitly allows a busy colleague to decline the favor.
feedback: This presumes the review will arrive by tomorrow without first securing agreement.
This negotiates timing but still assumes the colleague will undertake the review.
This asks about availability and explicitly allows a busy colleague to decline the favor.
This thanks the colleague for a favor as if they have already agreed.

questions.setup: You have reported a faulty office lock twice. A third email must be firm, request repair by Friday, and avoid accusations about anyone's motives.
questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that meets those requirements.
options: Your continued disregard for our security requires you to repair the lock by Friday.
Following my previous messages, please repair the lock whenever your schedule permits.
Please explain by Friday why you consider the faulty lock acceptable for our office.
As previously reported, the lock remains faulty; please arrange repair by Friday.
questions.explanation: This records the unresolved fault and prior reports, then gives a clear action and deadline without speculating about intent.
feedback: 'Continued disregard' interprets the delay as a dismissive attitude rather than stating the known facts.
This maintains courtesy but removes the required Friday deadline.
This asks for an explanation rather than a repair and assumes the recipient considers the fault acceptable.
This records the unresolved fault and prior reports, then gives a clear action and deadline without speculating about intent.

questions.setup: Residents say a contractor damaged a wall. An inspection has not yet established the cause. A local newsletter needs a neutral report.
questions.prompt: Which sentence reports the residents' account without adopting it as a confirmed fact?
options: Residents say the contractor damaged the wall; the cause has not been confirmed.
The contractor's damage to the wall was reported by several residents.
Residents have discovered how the contractor damaged the wall during the work.
The contractor apparently damaged the wall, as concerned residents have now confirmed.
questions.explanation: This attributes the account to residents and explicitly preserves the unresolved status of the cause.
feedback: This attributes the account to residents and explicitly preserves the unresolved status of the cause.
'The contractor's damage' presents responsibility as an established fact despite the pending inspection.
'Discovered how' implies the contractor's responsibility and the mechanism are already known.
Calling the residents' account confirmation overstates what has been established, despite 'apparently'.

questions.setup: Your company entered a customer's address incorrectly. A draft apology says, 'An error occurred in the address.' The company wants to acknowledge its own action clearly.
questions.prompt: Which replacement makes responsibility explicit without blaming the customer?
options: The address supplied by the customer appears to have been incorrect.
Your address was entered incorrectly, and the inconvenience is regrettable.
We entered your address incorrectly, and we apologize for the error.
We apologize if the address error has caused you any concern.
questions.explanation: Naming 'we' and the action identifies the company's responsibility and directly apologizes.
feedback: This shifts the source of the error to the customer, contrary to the known facts.
The passive form leaves the responsible party unnamed, and 'regrettable' avoids a direct apology.
Naming 'we' and the action identifies the company's responsibility and directly apologizes.
This names the company's apology but still does not say the company entered the address incorrectly.

questions.setup: A help page says, 'Local changes will not propagate until connectivity is restored.' Here, this means offline edits reach other devices only after the internet reconnects.
questions.prompt: Choose a plain-language version that preserves that condition.
options: Your offline changes will disappear from this device once you reconnect to the internet.
Your changes will appear on other devices even while this device remains offline.
Your offline changes will appear on other devices once you reconnect to the internet.
Your local modifications will propagate following restoration of network connectivity.
questions.explanation: This replaces the technical terms with familiar actions while preserving the need to reconnect.
feedback: This changes spreading the edits to other devices into deleting them from the current device.
This removes the connection requirement and gives the opposite timing.
This replaces the technical terms with familiar actions while preserving the need to reconnect.
This retains the technical vocabulary and dense noun phrases instead of making the guidance plain.

questions.setup: A staff survey found that several employees considered the new rota inconvenient. A manager drafts, 'Staff are making a fuss about the rota.'
questions.prompt: Choose a neutral summary limited to what the survey supports.
options: The staff's objections show that the new rota is unsuitable for the organization.
Several employees reluctantly accepted that the new rota was necessary for operations.
Staff have raised serious concerns about the safety of the new rota.
Several employees reported that the new rota was inconvenient for them.
questions.explanation: This retains the survey's limited group and their stated experience without the dismissive 'making a fuss'.
feedback: This converts several employees' inconvenience into a judgment about the rota's organizational suitability.
This adds acceptance and necessity that the survey did not report.
This changes inconvenience into a safety concern and implies a wider group.
This retains the survey's limited group and their stated experience without the dismissive 'making a fuss'.

questions.setup: A colleague says, 'We might get turned down because the form's late.' You record this possibility in a formal project update.
questions.prompt: Which version changes the register while preserving uncertainty and the reason?
options: Our application will be rejected because the form was submitted late.
Our application may be rejected because the form was submitted late.
Our application was rejected before the form could be submitted.
Our application may be accepted despite the late submission of the form.
questions.explanation: This replaces conversational 'get turned down' with a formal passive while retaining 'may' and the reason.
feedback: 'Will' changes a possible rejection into an expected outcome stated as certain.
This replaces conversational 'get turned down' with a formal passive while retaining 'may' and the reason.
This reports a completed rejection and a different sequence of events.
This expresses a possible acceptance instead of the original warning about possible rejection.

questions.setup: In a meeting, Mara says, 'I'm not keen on closing on Sundays, but I'll support a one-month trial.' You write neutral minutes.
questions.prompt: Choose the summary that preserves both Mara's reservation and her limited support.
options: Mara opposed Sunday closure and declined to support a trial.
Mara supported Sunday closure as the shop's new permanent policy.
Mara expressed reservations about Sunday closure but supported a one-month trial.
Mara reluctantly admitted that Sunday closure was necessary for the business.
questions.explanation: This replaces conversational wording with neutral reporting while keeping both parts of her position.
feedback: This preserves opposition but reverses her agreement to a trial.
This removes her reservation and changes one month into a permanent arrangement.
This replaces conversational wording with neutral reporting while keeping both parts of her position.
This adds reluctant admission and necessity, neither of which she stated.

questions.setup: A site's written policy makes an identification badge compulsory in the secure area. The editor wants to state the rule plainly, without presenting it as advice.
questions.prompt: Which wording preserves the policy's force?
options: Visitors should consider wearing an identification badge in the secure area.
Visitors must wear an identification badge in the secure area.
Visitors may wear an identification badge while using the secure area.
Visitors are welcome to wear an identification badge in the secure area.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses the stated requirement directly; it is appropriate for a compulsory rule.
feedback: This recommends considering the action rather than requiring the badge.
'Must' expresses the stated requirement directly; it is appropriate for a compulsory rule.
'May' grants permission and makes wearing the badge sound optional.
This friendly invitation does not preserve the compulsory nature of the policy.

questions.setup: A supplier needs to explain a technical specification. Your team cannot approve the order until it understands that specification.
questions.prompt: Choose a professional clarification request that explains the dependency without implying the specification is wrong.
options: Please correct the specification so that we can approve the order.
Could you clarify the specification so we can assess the order?
Please clarify the specification; our team will approve the order regardless.
Could you explain why your team supplied an unsuitable specification?
questions.explanation: This requests understanding and explains why it matters without alleging an error or promising approval.
feedback: 'Correct' assumes an error; you need an explanation before judging the specification.
This requests understanding and explains why it matters without alleging an error or promising approval.
This contradicts the stated dependency by promising approval without understanding it.
'Unsuitable' prejudges the specification instead of neutrally requesting clarification.

questions.setup: A funder replies, 'We appreciate the proposal, but we are not in a position to support it this year.'
questions.prompt: Which interpretation best respects both the courteous wording and its limits?
options: The funder has declined support this year without promising support later.
The funder has accepted the proposal and will arrange payment later.
The funder will support the proposal as soon as next year's budget begins.
The funder considers the proposal unsuitable for any future funding round.
questions.explanation: The courteous opening softens the refusal; 'this year' limits it but does not promise future funding.
feedback: The courteous opening softens the refusal; 'this year' limits it but does not promise future funding.
Appreciation does not amount to acceptance; the second clause declines support this year.
The reply leaves future support open and supplies no promise for next year.
The time-limited refusal does not establish a permanent judgment of suitability.

questions.setup: A report reads, 'The revised procedure improves record keeping. However, the handover arrangements are still a bit of a mess.' The report needs a consistently formal, factual tone.
questions.prompt: Which replacement for the second sentence preserves the criticism in that tone?
options: However, the handover arrangements are now broadly satisfactory.
However, the people doing handovers are making a mess of things.
However, the handover arrangements will improve in the coming months.
However, the handover arrangements remain poorly organized.
questions.explanation: This retains the criticism of organization while replacing conversational 'a bit of a mess' with neutral formal wording.
feedback: This changes the continuing criticism into a positive assessment.
This keeps informal wording and shifts criticism from arrangements to people.
This replaces the current problem with an unsupported prediction.
This retains the criticism of organization while replacing conversational 'a bit of a mess' with neutral formal wording.

questions.setup: You can offer a client a 5% discount only if they order at least 100 units. You want a courteous offer that preserves the condition.
questions.prompt: Which sentence does that?
options: We can offer a 5% discount on orders of 100 units or more.
We are pleased to offer 5% off your order, whatever quantity you choose.
We can offer a 5% discount if you order fewer than 100 units.
We may consider a discount after you place an order for 100 units.
questions.explanation: This states the available discount clearly and keeps the minimum quantity as a condition.
feedback: This states the available discount clearly and keeps the minimum quantity as a condition.
This makes the discount unconditional and removes the minimum order.
This reverses the threshold: the discount requires at least 100 units.
This turns a defined offer into an unspecified possibility after ordering.

questions.setup: A partner proposes a launch next week. You value the idea but cannot agree to that date because testing needs another month.
questions.prompt: Choose a diplomatic response that supports the idea while firmly rejecting next week's date.
options: The idea has merit, but testing rules out a launch next week.
The idea has merit, so we can launch next week and test afterwards.
The idea may have merit, though next week is probably worth considering.
The testing schedule makes the proposal itself unsuitable for further discussion.
questions.explanation: This acknowledges the proposal's value while making the timing objection definite and specific.
feedback: This acknowledges the proposal's value while making the timing objection definite and specific.
This accepts the date and changes the requirement that testing come first.
This keeps the rejected date under consideration instead of clearly ruling it out.
This rejects the whole idea rather than only the proposed timing.

questions.setup: Checked attendance records show that 48 of 60 members attended. You are writing a factual annual report, and this figure is not an estimate.
questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that reports the verified figure without unnecessary doubt or added judgment.
options: It seems that perhaps 48 of the 60 members may have attended.
Of the 60 members, 48 attended the meeting.
An impressive 48 of the 60 members made the effort to attend.
About 48 members are believed to have attended the meeting.
questions.explanation: This gives the verified figure directly; a factual report does not need a hedge when the number is known.
feedback: The stacked uncertainty markers make a checked fact sound doubtful.
This gives the verified figure directly; a factual report does not need a hedge when the number is known.
'Impressive' and 'made the effort' add evaluations not required by a factual attendance record.
'About' and 'are believed' turn an exact checked count into an estimate and omit the total.

questions.setup: A service survey should invite both positive and negative views of a new booking system without assuming either.
questions.prompt: Choose the neutral question.
options: How much easier has the new system made booking for you?
What problems has the new system caused when you book?
Why do you prefer the new system to the previous one?
How would you describe your experience of the new booking system?
questions.explanation: This invites the respondent's own evaluation without building a positive or negative answer into the question.
feedback: This assumes the system has made booking easier and asks only about the degree.
This assumes the system has caused problems.
This assumes a preference for the new system.
This invites the respondent's own evaluation without building a positive or negative answer into the question.

questions.setup: A staff update must say that the company will close two branches in June. The editor wants plain, respectful wording that names the action.
questions.prompt: Which version avoids both casual slang and wording that hides the closures?
options: Two branches will undergo a strategic footprint adjustment in June.
The company will close two branches in June.
The company is ditching a couple of branches come June.
The company will review the future of two branches in June.
questions.explanation: This names the action, number, and timing plainly without slang or an evasive substitute.
feedback: 'Strategic footprint adjustment' obscures the concrete fact that the branches will close.
This names the action, number, and timing plainly without slang or an evasive substitute.
'Ditching' sounds casual and dismissive for a staff announcement about closures.
This presents a future review rather than the decided closures.

questions.setup: Engineers estimate a website will be available again at 3 p.m., but the time is not confirmed. You write a customer update.
questions.prompt: Choose clear professional wording that communicates the estimate without promising it.
options: We confirm that the website will be available again at 3 p.m.
The website might return at some point; please check back later.
We aim to begin investigating the website problem at 3 p.m.
We expect the website to be available at 3 p.m.; this is an estimate.
questions.explanation: This gives the useful expected time while explicitly marking its uncertain status.
feedback: 'Confirm' presents the estimate as a settled restoration time.
This avoids a promise but withholds the useful 3 p.m. estimate.
This changes the estimate for restoration into a time for starting the investigation.
This gives the useful expected time while explicitly marking its uncertain status.

questions.setup: A report draft says, 'The pilot reduced costs. That said, it required extra staff time.' The editor wants a more formal linking expression.
questions.prompt: Which version preserves the contrast between the benefit and the limitation?
options: The pilot reduced costs. Therefore, it required extra staff time.
The pilot reduced costs. For example, it required extra staff time.
The pilot reduced costs. However, it required extra staff time.
The pilot reduced costs. In other words, it required extra staff time.
questions.explanation: 'However' provides a formal contrast, preserving the shift from a benefit to a limitation.
feedback: 'Therefore' makes the extra time a consequence of lower costs rather than a contrasting limitation.
Extra staff time is not presented as an example of a cost reduction; it is a limitation.
'However' provides a formal contrast, preserving the shift from a benefit to a limitation.
'In other words' signals a restatement, but the two sentences express different points.

questions.setup: An organization has established that its late cancellation cost participants money. It wants a formal apology acknowledging that specific harm, without making a compensation promise.
questions.prompt: Which apology best meets that brief?
options: We apologize if our cancellation caused participants any inconvenience.
We apologize for the financial loss our late cancellation caused participants.
We regret that participants believe the cancellation caused them financial loss.
We apologize for the cancellation and will reimburse the losses participants incurred.
questions.explanation: This acknowledges the organization's action and its established consequence directly without promising reimbursement.
feedback: 'If' treats harm as uncertain, and 'inconvenience' avoids the established financial consequence.
This acknowledges the organization's action and its established consequence directly without promising reimbursement.
This makes participants' belief the object of regret and distances the organization from the established harm.
This adds a compensation commitment that the brief does not authorize.

questions.setup: An internal review found no evidence that files were copied, but incomplete logs prevent ruling copying out. You draft a careful incident summary.
questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps the distinction between missing evidence and proof of non-occurrence?
options: We confirmed that no files were copied, although some logs were incomplete.
The incomplete logs indicate that files were probably copied during the incident.
We found no evidence of copying and can therefore rule out that possibility.
We found no evidence of copying, although the incomplete logs limit that conclusion.
questions.explanation: This reports the review's finding and its evidential limit without claiming copying did not occur.
feedback: 'Confirmed that no files were copied' makes a stronger claim than the incomplete record supports.
Missing records do not themselves establish that copying was probable.
This treats absence of evidence as sufficient proof of absence despite the stated limitation.
This reports the review's finding and its evidential limit without claiming copying did not occur.

questions.setup: A reviewer correctly notes that your study cannot establish causation. You still think its association finding is useful and must respond constructively.
questions.prompt: Choose a response that accepts the limitation while preserving the narrower contribution.
options: We appreciate the comment, but the strength of the association establishes the causal claim.
We agree that causation is not established; the association nevertheless merits further investigation.
We accept the limitation and have removed the association finding from our discussion.
We regret that the reviewer has interpreted our causal evidence as a mere association.
questions.explanation: This concedes the valid limitation while identifying a defensible role for the remaining finding.
feedback: The polite opening does not fix the unsupported move from association to causation.
This concedes the valid limitation while identifying a defensible role for the remaining finding.
This gives up the narrower finding instead of explaining its continuing value.
This challenges the reviewer on a point the scenario says is correct and upgrades the evidence to causal.

questions.setup: Asked specifically about a candidate's strategic leadership, a referee writes only, 'She is unfailingly punctual and keeps meticulous attendance records.'
questions.prompt: What is the most careful reading of this limited reference?
options: It directly establishes that she lacks the strategic leadership skills required for the role.
It strongly endorses her leadership through specific examples of strategic decision-making.
It praises reliability while leaving the requested leadership assessment unanswered.
It criticizes her reliability by using language that is clearly sarcastic in this context.
questions.explanation: The positive details concern reliability; their failure to address leadership may be telling, but no explicit leadership judgment is made.
feedback: The omission may raise a question but does not prove she lacks the skill.
Punctuality and attendance records are not examples of strategic decision-making.
The positive details concern reliability; their failure to address leadership may be telling, but no explicit leadership judgment is made.
The context supports a limited endorsement, but it does not establish sarcasm about reliability.

questions.setup: Researchers write, 'The estimate is imprecise and should not be interpreted as evidence of no effect.' For this task, that means the result cannot settle whether an effect exists.
questions.prompt: Choose the plain-language public summary that preserves that uncertainty.
options: The result shows no effect, although its exact size remains uncertain.
The result points to an effect that a larger study will probably confirm.
The result is uncertain because the researchers chose an unsuitable method.
The result is too uncertain to tell us whether there is an effect.
questions.explanation: This translates the limitation into everyday language without treating uncertainty as either proof or disproof.
feedback: This asserts no effect while leaving only its size uncertain, which changes the finding.
This introduces a positive direction and an expected confirmation not given in the source.
This adds a methodological cause and criticism absent from the supplied statement.
This translates the limitation into everyday language without treating uncertainty as either proof or disproof.

questions.setup: After several interruptions, a meeting chair says, 'Could we allow Leila to finish her explanation before returning to questions?'
questions.prompt: Which interpretation best captures the chair's immediate communicative purpose?
options: The chair is asking Leila whether she is capable of finishing her explanation.
The chair is inviting a vote on whether Leila's explanation deserves to continue.
The chair is directing the group to postpone questions until Leila has finished.
The chair is suggesting that Leila finish privately after the meeting has ended.
questions.explanation: The interrogative 'Could we' softens a chair's direction about turn-taking; 'before' specifies the order.
feedback: The request is addressed to the group, and its purpose is to manage interruptions rather than test Leila's ability.
The wording manages the speaking order; it does not propose a vote on Leila's contribution.
The interrogative 'Could we' softens a chair's direction about turn-taking; 'before' specifies the order.
Nothing moves the explanation outside the meeting; questions are simply to wait.

questions.setup: A draft says, 'With respect, your calculation ignores the delivery charge.' You want to challenge the omission while reducing the personal edge.
questions.prompt: Which revision keeps the criticism specific and directs attention to the calculation?
options: With all due respect, you appear to have overlooked a fairly obvious delivery charge.
The calculation omits the delivery charge; could that cost be included?
Your calculation is quite interesting, and delivery charges are sometimes worth considering.
I would not question your calculation, although the delivery charge is missing.
questions.explanation: This identifies the specific omission and requests a correction without evaluating the person's competence.
feedback: 'Fairly obvious' sharpens the personal criticism; the courtesy phrase does not cancel it.
This identifies the specific omission and requests a correction without evaluating the person's competence.
This softens the message until the known omission becomes an optional general consideration.
The disclaimer conflicts with the criticism that follows and makes the position less direct.

questions.setup: A handbook says, 'Employees may request a review of the decision.' In this handbook, 'may' grants permission; it does not predict what employees will do.
questions.prompt: Which plain-language version preserves that function?
options: Employees will probably ask for the decision to be reviewed.
Employees should ask for the decision to be reviewed.
Employees are allowed to ask for the decision to be reviewed.
Employees can have the decision changed by requesting a review.
questions.explanation: This makes the permission explicit without promising the outcome of a review.
feedback: This reads 'may' as a prediction of behavior instead of a permission.
This turns permission into advice or an expectation.
This makes the permission explicit without promising the outcome of a review.
This promises a changed decision, whereas the handbook only permits asking for review.

questions.setup: A company mistakenly deleted customer records. A draft says, 'A data housekeeping exercise resulted in some records becoming unavailable.' The company wants a candid statement of what it did.
questions.prompt: Which replacement removes the obscuring language without adding an unsupported motive?
options: We mistakenly deleted customer records during a data-cleaning operation.
Customer records were deliberately removed to reduce the company's storage costs.
Some customers experienced a temporary reduction in record accessibility.
A data-cleaning operation left customers with concerns about record availability.
questions.explanation: This names the actor and action, describes the error, and retains the operational context without hiding the deletion.
feedback: This names the actor and action, describes the error, and retains the operational context without hiding the deletion.
This adds a motive and intention, while the deletion is described as a mistake.
This retains evasive language and suggests the loss was temporary, which is not established.
This shifts the focus to customers' concerns instead of acknowledging the company's actual deletion.

questions.setup: You summarize an author's argument without signaling either approval or skepticism. The draft says, 'The author purports to explain the decline in participation.'
questions.prompt: Which revision neutrally describes the author's attempt without asserting that it succeeds?
options: The author convincingly explains the decline in participation.
The author seeks to explain the decline in participation.
The author pretends to explain the decline in participation.
The author establishes the reasons for the decline in participation.
questions.explanation: 'Seeks to explain' describes the aim without the skepticism often conveyed by 'purports' or a claim of success.
feedback: 'Convincingly' endorses the explanation rather than neutrally identifying the aim.
'Seeks to explain' describes the aim without the skepticism often conveyed by 'purports' or a claim of success.
'Pretends' accuses the author of an insincere attempt and is more skeptical than the draft.
'Establishes' reports a successful demonstration, which the neutral brief does not authorize.

questions.setup: A consumer leaflet must explain a supplied policy: customers are entitled to a refund if an item arrives damaged. A conversational draft says, 'We'll sort you out if it turns up broken.'
questions.prompt: Choose a clear revision that states the entitlement rather than merely expressing willingness to help.
options: We will consider helping customers whose items arrive damaged.
Customers should contact us if they believe their item is damaged.
You are entitled to a refund if your item arrives damaged.
We may replace damaged items as a gesture of goodwill.
questions.explanation: This replaces the vague assurance with the exact remedy and the condition under which customers have a right to it.
feedback: This turns an entitlement into a discretionary decision to consider assistance.
This gives a contact instruction but does not state the refund entitlement.
This replaces the vague assurance with the exact remedy and the condition under which customers have a right to it.
This changes a refund entitlement into an optional replacement.

questions.setup: A report arrived after the deadline. Its accuracy has not yet been checked. You need to criticize the lateness without implying anything about accuracy.
questions.prompt: Which formal evaluation respects that boundary?
options: The report was submitted late; its accuracy remains to be assessed.
The report's lateness raises doubts about the reliability of its findings.
Although submitted late, the report provides a reliable account of the evidence.
The report should be treated as provisional because it missed the submission deadline.
questions.explanation: This records the process failure and separates it from the still-open question about content.
feedback: This records the process failure and separates it from the still-open question about content.
This links late delivery to questionable accuracy, which has not been assessed.
This uses concession to endorse accuracy before it has been checked.
This makes the content's status depend on lateness rather than the uncompleted accuracy review.

questions.setup: You invite an external expert to a panel. They have not agreed. You want a courteous closing that leaves participation optional.
questions.prompt: Which closing avoids treating attendance as already settled?
options: We would be delighted if you were able to join the panel.
We look forward to welcoming you to the panel next month.
Thank you for agreeing to share your expertise with our audience.
Please confirm your travel arrangements so we can finalize your attendance.
questions.explanation: The conditional wording expresses enthusiasm while making participation depend on the expert's ability and choice.
feedback: The conditional wording expresses enthusiasm while making participation depend on the expert's ability and choice.
In this invitation, that closing anticipates attendance as if agreement were already in place.
This explicitly states agreement that has not been given.
This moves to travel planning and presumes acceptance rather than leaving the invitation open.

questions.setup: A report describes a scheme's temporary suspension, followed by an inquiry that found no misconduct. Applications were delayed by the suspension. The next sentence must link back to that cause without confusing it with the later finding.
questions.prompt: Choose the precise continuation for the formal report.
options: This finding delayed applications by requiring the committee to suspend the scheme.
The absence of misconduct meant that applications had proceeded without interruption.
This decision to abolish the scheme delayed applications despite the inquiry's conclusions.
The suspension nevertheless delayed applications, irrespective of the inquiry's subsequent finding.
questions.explanation: Naming 'the suspension' identifies the cause precisely; the later finding of no misconduct does not undo the earlier delay.
feedback: This makes the later inquiry finding cause the earlier suspension and reverses the chronology.
This treats the inquiry's conclusion as erasing the actual delay during the suspension.
'Abolish' changes a temporary suspension into a permanent ending not stated in the report.
Naming 'the suspension' identifies the cause precisely; the later finding of no misconduct does not undo the earlier delay.

questions.setup: A colleague tells you privately that a close friend has died. You want to express sympathy without claiming to know their feelings or asking them to explain.
questions.prompt: Choose a restrained, compassionate response.
options: I know exactly how you feel; you should talk it through with me.
I'm sorry, but these experiences tend to make people stronger in time.
That's sad news. Could you tell me precisely what happened to your friend?
I'm sorry to hear that. There's no need to reply to this message.
questions.explanation: This expresses sympathy while removing pressure to continue the conversation.
feedback: This claims exact knowledge of the colleague's feelings and directs them to disclose more.
This adds an unsolicited positive interpretation of the loss rather than simply acknowledging it.
This asks for details that the colleague has not offered and does not respect the no-explanation brief.
This expresses sympathy while removing pressure to continue the conversation.

questions.setup: Your mixed British and American team uses 'table a proposal' differently: some mean introduce it for discussion, others mean set it aside. You intend to delay discussion until June.
questions.prompt: Choose wording that states that intention unambiguously for this team.
options: We propose to postpone discussion of the proposal until June.
We propose to table the proposal at the June meeting.
We propose to put the proposal on the table before June.
We propose to shelve the proposal without setting a return date.
questions.explanation: This states the action and return date directly, avoiding the team's conflicting uses of 'table'.
feedback: This states the action and return date directly, avoiding the team's conflicting uses of 'table'.
The team's stated difference in usage leaves it unclear whether the proposal will be introduced or set aside then.
This suggests bringing the proposal into consideration before June, not postponing discussion until then.
This removes the June return point and makes the postponement indefinite.

questions.setup: An essay says, 'Arguably, the reform shifted power toward local councils.' The writer considers the interpretation defensible but open to dispute.
questions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves that stance in formal prose?
options: It is established that the reform shifted power toward local councils.
A case can be made that the reform shifted power toward local councils.
There is little basis for saying the reform shifted power toward local councils.
It has been alleged that the reform shifted power toward local councils.
questions.explanation: This expresses a supportable interpretation while leaving room for reasoned disagreement.
feedback: 'Established' treats the interpretation as settled rather than disputable.
This expresses a supportable interpretation while leaving room for reasoned disagreement.
This rejects the interpretation instead of presenting it as defensible.
This attributes an allegation to others rather than expressing the writer's own qualified judgment.

questions.setup: You review a report that discusses benefits but omits implementation costs. You have no evidence about the author's intention.
questions.prompt: Choose a precise professional criticism of the report itself.
options: The author avoids implementation costs to make the proposal appear more attractive.
The report's benefits are questionable because implementation costs are omitted.
The author seems unfamiliar with the costs involved in implementing the proposal.
The report discusses benefits but does not address implementation costs.
questions.explanation: This identifies the report's imbalance directly without alleging a reason for the omission.
feedback: This assigns a strategic motive that the available evidence does not establish.
This challenges the benefits themselves, although the known problem is missing cost analysis.
This infers a lack of knowledge from the omission rather than describing the text's limitation.
This identifies the report's imbalance directly without alleging a reason for the omission.

questions.setup: A museum label should foreground a vase's restoration date. The conservator's identity is unknown, and the label should not invent one.
questions.prompt: Which sentence best fits that informational focus?
options: The vase was restored in 1986.
Our conservators restored the vase in 1986.
The vase underwent a controversial restoration in 1986.
The vase's restorer appears to have been working around 1986.
questions.explanation: The passive keeps the vase and its known restoration date central while leaving the unknown actor unnamed.
feedback: The passive keeps the vase and its known restoration date central while leaving the unknown actor unnamed.
This supplies an institutional actor that the museum does not know to be responsible.
This adds a judgment of controversy absent from the information provided.
This shifts attention to an unknown person and makes the known restoration date uncertain.

questions.setup: In a friendly private chat, a collaborator writes, 'I'm swamped; can we park this until Tuesday?' You need to summarize the agreed temporary pause in a formal project log.
questions.prompt: Choose a faithful summary without carrying over the informal idioms or implying rejection.
options: The collaborator declined the task because it falls outside their responsibilities.
The collaborator was swamped, so the discussion has been parked for the time being.
Further discussion was deferred until Tuesday because of the collaborator's workload.
Further discussion was suspended pending the collaborator's approval of the project.
questions.explanation: This preserves the temporary pause and reason while replacing the conversational idioms with neutral project language.
feedback: This turns workload and temporary delay into refusal on grounds of role.
This retains the informal idioms and drops the agreed Tuesday return point.
This preserves the temporary pause and reason while replacing the conversational idioms with neutral project language.
This invents an approval condition instead of the stated workload and return date.

questions.setup: An attachment summarizes only the changes made to a report, not the report's full revised argument. An editor must describe its scope accurately in formal correspondence.
questions.prompt: Which description makes that distinction explicit without overstating the attachment's coverage?
options: The attachment provides a concise account of the report in its revised form.
The attachment replaces the report with a concise statement of its conclusions.
The attachment summarizes the revisions made to the report.
The attachment sets out the reasoning behind each revision to the report.
questions.explanation: 'The revisions made to' identifies the changes as the object of the summary, preserving the limited scope.
feedback: This suggests a summary of the revised report as a whole rather than its changes alone.
This changes both the attachment's function and its coverage: it neither replaces the report nor summarizes its conclusions.
'The revisions made to' identifies the changes as the object of the summary, preserving the limited scope.
This promises reasons for every change, whereas the attachment only summarizes the changes themselves.

questions.setup: In a casual chat, friends have agreed that Jo will bring biscuits to their picnic. One friend jokes, 'I hereby appoint Jo custodian of the biscuits.'
questions.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for the deliberately formal wording in this friendly exchange?
options: It humorously applies ceremonial appointment language to an ordinary task the friends already agreed on.
It establishes the speaker's authority to assign duties the group has not yet accepted.
It creates social distance by replacing the group's shared plan with an official instruction.
It makes the arrangement easier to understand by replacing colloquial words with precise technical terms.
questions.explanation: The mismatch between official-sounding wording and an everyday shared task creates the joke; formal language can serve an informal social purpose.
feedback: The mismatch between official-sounding wording and an everyday shared task creates the joke; formal language can serve an informal social purpose.
The practical arrangement is already agreed, and the speaker is joking rather than asserting real authority.
The supplied friendly, joking context supports playful formality, not an attempt to create distance.
'Hereby appoint' and 'custodian' add mock ceremony, not needed technical precision about bringing food.

questions.setup: A transport researcher addresses both local residents and specialists. She wants to explain access to jobs through familiar journeys, without treating non-specialists as less capable or promising to omit the analysis.
questions.prompt: Which opening creates that inclusive relationship with the audience?
options: For those who lack the relevant expertise, I'll keep the opening examples suitably simple.
Let's begin with two familiar journeys to work, then examine what the travel data reveal.
The specialists here will recognize the real issues; the journeys are for everyone else.
Rather than burden you with analysis, I'll offer a few journeys we can all relate to.
questions.explanation: This gives everyone a shared starting point and invites the whole audience into the analysis without ranking their abilities.
feedback: This singles out part of the audience by an assumed deficit and can sound patronizing.
This gives everyone a shared starting point and invites the whole audience into the analysis without ranking their abilities.
This divides the audience into people who understand the substance and people offered only examples.
This treats analysis as a burden the audience cannot welcome and promises to omit it, contrary to the brief.

questions.setup: A company calls its new system a 'partnership model'. A neutral account needs to attribute that label without endorsing or mocking it.
questions.prompt: Which wording handles the label most precisely?
options: The company's so-called partnership model changes how suppliers are selected.
The system the company calls its 'partnership model' changes how suppliers are selected.
The company's genuine partnership model changes how suppliers are selected.
The company's partnership with suppliers has changed how suppliers are selected.
questions.explanation: This identifies the company as the source of the label without evaluating whether the label is deserved.
feedback: 'So-called' can cast doubt on the legitimacy of the label, introducing skepticism the brief excludes.
This identifies the company as the source of the label without evaluating whether the label is deserved.
'Genuine' endorses the company's label rather than simply attributing it.
This recasts the contested label as an actual partnership and changes what is said to cause the change.

questions.setup: An engineer begins a conference talk: 'My first prototype worked beautifully, provided nobody switched it on.' She intends a self-deprecating joke before explaining what the failure taught her.
questions.prompt: What does this choice of register achieve in the opening?
options: It reassures the audience that the prototype's technical performance was largely successful.
It shifts responsibility for the failure to people who operated the prototype incorrectly.
It establishes that the remaining presentation will be a comic performance without technical content.
It makes her own failed design a shared joke, building rapport before a technical explanation.
questions.explanation: The playful qualification turns apparent praise into self-directed humor, making the speaker approachable while leaving room for serious analysis.
feedback: The condition undercuts the apparent praise: a prototype that cannot be switched on is not being presented as successful.
The supplied self-deprecating purpose makes her own work the object of the joke, not operators' misuse.
A humorous opening does not determine the whole talk's genre; she will explain the technical lesson next.
The playful qualification turns apparent praise into self-directed humor, making the speaker approachable while leaving room for serious analysis.

questions.setup: A client writes, 'After three unanswered emails and six weeks of delay, your service has been a model of efficiency.' The client intends the praise ironically.
questions.prompt: Choose a neutral internal summary of the intended criticism without copying the irony.
options: The client praised the service's efficiency despite delays in correspondence.
The client found the service efficient but objected to the staff's writing style.
The client questioned whether six weeks was the normal service target.
The client criticized the service for delayed responses and prolonged handling.
questions.explanation: This translates the ironic praise into its intended complaint and preserves the reasons supplied.
feedback: This reads the ironic praise literally and misrepresents the stated intention.
This retains literal praise and substitutes a writing-style issue for the delay.
This turns a critical assertion into a factual enquiry about a target not mentioned in the message.
This translates the ironic praise into its intended complaint and preserves the reasons supplied.

questions.setup: A cautious review concludes, 'The proposal is not without merit, though its practical implications remain largely unexplored.'
questions.prompt: Which summary best preserves the restrained praise and the substantial reservation?
options: The reviewer finds the proposal meritorious enough to proceed despite minor practical questions.
The reviewer regards the proposal as having little practical value and no theoretical interest.
The reviewer identifies some value in the proposal while withholding a full endorsement.
The reviewer believes the practical implications confirm the proposal's considerable strengths.
questions.explanation: 'Not without merit' offers limited praise, and the unresolved practical implications prevent reading it as a full endorsement.
feedback: This upgrades restrained praise to a recommendation and downgrades largely unexplored implications to minor questions.
This turns a concession of merit into a broadly negative conclusion not stated in the review.
'Not without merit' offers limited praise, and the unresolved practical implications prevent reading it as a full endorsement.
The implications are unexplored, so they cannot be presented as confirmation of considerable strengths.

questions.setup: Minutes confirm that a committee excluded two representatives from consultation by mistake. A draft says, 'We regret that the representatives felt excluded.' The committee wants to acknowledge the recorded action.
questions.prompt: Which revision corrects the shift from an established event to a subjective reaction?
options: We regret any impression that the consultation did not include the representatives.
We regret that we mistakenly excluded the representatives from the consultation.
We regret the representatives' response to the consultation arrangements we adopted.
We regret that the representatives were unable to take part in the consultation.
questions.explanation: This identifies the committee's action as the object of regret and states the mistake directly.
feedback: This still treats exclusion as an impression rather than the established event.
This identifies the committee's action as the object of regret and states the mistake directly.
This makes the representatives' response the problem and leaves the exclusion unacknowledged.
This can imply a difficulty on the representatives' side, obscuring the committee's confirmed exclusion.

questions.setup: In this audit, a 'material discrepancy' means a difference significant enough to affect a decision, even if its numerical size is small. The summary is for non-specialists.
questions.prompt: Choose the paraphrase that preserves that specialized threshold without carrying over the term.
options: The audit found a difference significant enough to affect the decision.
The audit found a difference large enough to be noticed without close examination.
The audit found a small difference that was unlikely to affect any decision.
The audit found a difference affecting presentation rather than the decision itself.
questions.explanation: This translates the stated technical threshold accurately without equating significance with numerical size.
feedback: This translates the stated technical threshold accurately without equating significance with numerical size.
This substitutes visual or numerical prominence for significance to a decision.
This contradicts the supplied meaning by treating the discrepancy as inconsequential.
This limits the discrepancy to presentation, excluding the decision-level significance in the supplied definition.

questions.setup: An editor says publication depends on resolving the methodological concern, then writes, 'The paper would benefit from a fuller account of how participants were selected.'
questions.prompt: In this exchange, how should the author understand the softened wording?
options: As optional stylistic advice that can be ignored without affecting publication.
As confirmation that participant selection was unsuitable and the study must be repeated.
As permission to remove the selection procedure from the paper's main argument.
As a required substantive clarification expressed in a tactful form.
questions.explanation: The conditional-sounding phrase softens the request, but the stated publication condition gives it substantive force.
feedback: The preceding statement makes resolution a condition of publication, so the softened phrasing does not make it optional.
The editor asks for a fuller account; the exchange does not establish invalid selection or require a new study.
The requested direction is fuller explanation, not removal of the methodological detail.
The conditional-sounding phrase softens the request, but the stated publication condition gives it substantive force.

questions.setup: A review concludes, 'We recommend acceptance subject to the corrections listed below; no further review is required.' A summary must distinguish this from both unconditional acceptance and a request for resubmission.
questions.prompt: Which summary preserves the recommendation's procedural status?
options: The reviewers have accepted the paper and offered corrections for the author's consideration.
The reviewers invite a corrected submission so that they can reconsider whether to recommend acceptance.
The reviewers recommend acceptance once the listed corrections are made, without another review.
The reviewers recommend acceptance but require the corrected paper to pass a second review.
questions.explanation: This preserves the recommendation, the correction condition, and the explicit absence of a further review requirement.
feedback: This upgrades a conditional recommendation to completed acceptance and makes required corrections optional.
This adds a new review and withholds the positive recommendation already given.
This preserves the recommendation, the correction condition, and the explicit absence of a further review requirement.
This keeps a condition but contradicts the explicit statement that no further review is required.

questions.setup: A negotiation brief authorizes a firm promise: the company will accept the new price if delivery is guaranteed by 1 June. It does not authorize changing that date or promising more than acceptance of the price.
questions.prompt: Which courteous sentence conveys exactly that conditional commitment?
options: We will accept the new price, provided delivery by 1 June is guaranteed.
We would be pleased to consider the new price if delivery by 1 June were guaranteed.
We can accept the new price and would appreciate a guarantee of delivery by 1 June.
We will accept the new price, provided delivery is scheduled for early June.
questions.explanation: This commits to accepting the price once the stated delivery guarantee is in place, without adding another promise.
feedback: This commits to accepting the price once the stated delivery guarantee is in place, without adding another promise.
'Consider' keeps acceptance undecided; the brief authorizes a firm conditional promise to accept.
This separates acceptance from the guarantee and presents the guarantee as an appreciated extra rather than a condition.
A schedule is weaker than a guarantee, and 'early June' loosens the exact 1 June deadline.

questions.setup: A council favors a cycle-lane plan but is inviting residents to influence it. Its draft says, 'We must educate residents about the benefits so that they accept the plan.' The editor wants a respectful consultation tone while retaining the council's stated preference.
questions.prompt: Which revision treats residents as participants rather than an audience to be brought into agreement?
options: We favor the cycle lanes and will help residents understand why their concerns need not stand in the way.
We favor the cycle lanes and invite residents' views on how the plan should develop.
We have no preference on the cycle lanes and will simply adopt whichever plan residents select.
We favor the cycle lanes and invite residents to hear how their concerns have already been resolved.
questions.explanation: This states the council's preference openly while allowing residents' contributions to shape the plan; agreement is not treated as a foregone conclusion.
feedback: This treats the concerns as obstacles to acceptance, rather than possible grounds for changing the plan.
This states the council's preference openly while allowing residents' contributions to shape the plan; agreement is not treated as a foregone conclusion.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that preserves both facts.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that describes the day of the meeting, not a day someone remembered or chose.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence in standard written English.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that preserves the reason for cancelling.

questions.setup: Choose the option that preserves the intended group.

I is the lender and Rosa the recipient inside the relative clause I lent Rosa.

questions.setup: Choose the description that preserves the missing tool's use.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that describes a station's location, not a visit to it.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that keeps the reason unknown and the departure certain.

questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence in standard written English.

Who already serves as the subject of speaks, making he redundant.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that preserves the relationship between the company and its logo.

questions.setup: Choose the word that completes the sentence grammatically in standard written English.

who

questions.setup: Choose the description that preserves both facts.

questions.setup: Choose the version that preserves the meaning in ordinary English.

questions.setup: Choose what the relative clause tells us about the applicant.
