questions.setup: Choose the grammatically correct sentence in standard written English.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that identifies which emails to print.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that uses a defining relative to select the affected residents, not to add information about an already selected group.
questions.prompt: A leak damaged six flats in a block of thirty. The residents of those six flats will receive hotel vouchers.

The residents whose flats were unaffected will receive hotel vouchers.

questions.setup: Choose what 'which' refers to in this sentence.

The museum's evening visitors
The museum's location

questions.setup: Choose the version suited to a formal report that keeps 'to' immediately before the relative pronoun.

'Whom' is the formal object form after the fronted preposition 'to'; the recipient remains the officer.

questions.setup: Choose the relative phrase that preserves the plan as the subject of negotiations, not as a method or source of opposition.

to which the teams attached their agreement
about which the teams negotiated

feedback: Through which presents the plan as a means of exchanging proposals, not their subject.
To which describes attaching agreement to the plan, not negotiations about it.
About which identifies the plan as the topic of the negotiations, preserving the original relationship.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that clearly identifies the reason for the rejection.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that presents the clinic's free service as extra information about the already identified clinic.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of the time relationship.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that keeps the source of the judgment clear.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that expresses a mechanism rather than a setting.

A physical location for receiving charges is different from a process for contesting them.
Whereby means by which here: the procedure is the means enabling tenants to challenge charges.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that explicitly makes the delay, rather than the permit, the cause of increased costs.
questions.prompt: The contractor received the permit late, which increased costs.
options: The contractor received the permit, which increased costs, late.
The contractor received a permit whose cost had increased.
The contractor received the permit late, a delay which increased costs.
The contractor received the permit for the work which increased costs.
questions.explanation: A delay provides an explicit antecedent for which and assigns the cost increase to late receipt.
feedback: Placing the relative after permit makes the permit the described source of costs, rather than explicitly naming the delay.
This states that the permit became more expensive, not that late receipt caused increased costs.
A delay provides an explicit antecedent for which and assigns the cost increase to late receipt.
This attaches the relative to work and does not isolate the delay as the cause.

questions.setup: Choose the conclusion that follows without adding an unstated claim.
questions.prompt: The delegates, three of whose proposals were adopted, asked for feedback on the remaining proposals.
options: Three delegates each had all their proposals adopted.
Each delegate had exactly three proposals adopted.
Three adopted proposals were submitted by other delegates.
Three proposals submitted by the delegates were adopted.
questions.explanation: Three of whose proposals quantifies proposals belonging to the delegate group, not the delegates themselves.
feedback: The number applies to proposals; the sentence does not distribute success across three individual delegates.
There is no each in the relative, so three cannot be read as a per-delegate total.
Whose connects the proposals to the delegates being discussed, not an outside group.
Three of whose proposals quantifies proposals belonging to the delegate group, not the delegates themselves.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that preserves the difference between method and result.
questions.prompt: The audit examined the way in which complaints were handled, not whether complainants were satisfied.
options: The audit tested how satisfied complainants were with each outcome.
The audit established why complainants accepted the decisions.
The audit checked whether complaints had produced favourable decisions.
The audit investigated the process used to deal with complaints.
questions.explanation: The way in which introduces manner or method; it identifies the handling process as the object of examination.
feedback: Satisfaction is explicitly outside the stated focus of the audit.
Reasons for accepting decisions concern reactions, not the handling method identified by the way in which.
Whether decisions were favourable evaluates outcomes rather than how complaints were processed.
The way in which introduces manner or method; it identifies the handling process as the object of examination.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that correctly identifies who was interviewed.
questions.prompt: The analyst whose supervisor the committee interviewed was subsequently invited to submit a written response.
options: The supervisor was interviewed; the analyst was later asked to respond in writing.
The analyst was interviewed, then asked to send the supervisor a response.
The committee interviewed the analyst and invited the supervisor to respond.
The supervisor interviewed the committee before inviting the analyst to respond.
questions.explanation: The committee interviewed the analyst's supervisor inside the relative clause; the main-clause invitation went to the analyst.
feedback: The committee interviewed the analyst's supervisor inside the relative clause; the main-clause invitation went to the analyst.
Whose supervisor is the object of interviewed; the analyst is the owner of that relationship, not the interviewee.
This swaps the interviewee and the recipient of the invitation.
The committee is the interviewer, not the group interviewed by the supervisor.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation of 'setting where' in context.
questions.prompt: The training created a setting where junior staff could question established practice without embarrassment.
options: The training provided circumstances favourable to open questioning.
The training prescribed a procedure specifying how questions should be worded.
The training designated a room in which questions had to be submitted privately.
The training introduced a requirement to revise practices once they were questioned.
questions.explanation: 'Where' introduces an abstract setting: circumstances in which staff felt able to question practice.
feedback: 'Where' introduces an abstract setting: circumstances in which staff felt able to question practice.
A setting permits questioning; it does not itself prescribe the wording or method of questions.
'Setting' can describe circumstances rather than a physical room, and privacy is not the same as freedom from embarrassment.
'Could question' creates an opportunity, not a requirement that each questioned practice be revised.

questions.setup: Choose the reading that preserves the scope of 'none'.
questions.prompt: The panel interviewed four candidates, none of whom had managed a merger, before choosing its new director.
options: The interview panel lacked merger-management experience.
The panel selected someone outside the four interviewees.
The four interviewees lacked merger-management experience.
The four candidates had managed mergers but not as directors.
questions.explanation: 'None of whom' applies the lack of merger-management experience to the four interviewees, without extending it to the panel or other candidates.
feedback: 'Whom' refers to the candidates, not the panel members assessing them.
The relative describes the interviewees' experience; it does not show that the eventual selection came from elsewhere.
'None of whom' applies the lack of merger-management experience to the four interviewees, without extending it to the panel or other candidates.
'None had managed a merger' denies that experience; it does not restrict the denial to experience as a director.

questions.setup: Choose the revision that preserves an uncertain identity without making the accusation a fact.
questions.prompt: Investigators are looking for a contractor who may have removed the equipment.
options: Investigators are looking for the contractor who removed the equipment.
Investigators are seeking a contractor suspected of removing the equipment.
Investigators know which contractor removed the equipment and are seeking that person.
Investigators are seeking the contractor whose removal of the equipment they confirmed.
questions.explanation: A contractor leaves identity open, and suspected preserves the uncertainty carried by may have.
feedback: The definite head and unqualified removed turn the possible accusation into an identifying fact.
A contractor leaves identity open, and suspected preserves the uncertainty carried by may have.
Know which asserts identified responsibility, exceeding the original uncertainty.
Confirmed removes the uncertainty expressed by may have and presents the removal as established.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase of the relative phrase.
questions.prompt: The review assessed the extent to which the new rota reduced overtime.
options: The review measured how far the rota reduced overtime.
The review identified the date on which the rota changed.
The review explained the method by which overtime was recorded.
The review determined the reason why staff requested a new rota.
questions.explanation: The extent to which asks about degree: how much reduction the rota produced, including the possibility of little or none.
feedback: The extent to which asks about degree: how much reduction the rota produced, including the possibility of little or none.
A date concerns time, not the degree of the rota's effect.
A recording method is a means, not the magnitude of a reduction.
Staff's reason for requesting a rota is a motive, not the degree of its effect.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that makes it explicit that the mentor, not the trainees, left early.
questions.prompt: The trainees spoke to their mentor, who left before the final session.
options: The trainees spoke to their mentor, and it was the mentor who left early.
The trainees, who left early, spoke to their mentor before the final session.
The trainees spoke to their mentor before leaving the final session.
The trainees spoke to the mentor who had left with them before the final session.
questions.explanation: The repeated noun and identifying who clause explicitly assign the departure to the mentor.
feedback: The repeated noun and identifying who clause explicitly assign the departure to the mentor.
The relative now modifies trainees, assigning the departure to them.
The understood subject of leaving is the trainees, not the mentor.
With them adds the trainees to the departure group and does not preserve the intended contrast.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that keeps the counterfactual consequence tied to the stated safeguard.
questions.prompt: The archive introduced a backup system without which the recent power failure would have destroyed years of work.
options: The backup system prevented the power failure from destroying the work.
The power failure destroyed the backup system and the archived work.
The archive had already lost the work before the backup system was introduced.
The archive introduced the backup system because the power failure had destroyed the work.
questions.explanation: Without which refers to the backup system and frames destruction as what would have happened in its absence.
feedback: Without which refers to the backup system and frames destruction as what would have happened in its absence.
Would have destroyed under without which describes the hypothetical loss without the safeguard, not an actual loss of both.
The sentence presents the system as effective during the recent failure, not as arriving after the work was lost.
This turns the unrealized destruction into an actual earlier cause of introducing the system.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning that preserves the relationship between the request and the response.
questions.prompt: The application was returned with a request for evidence, in response to which the applicant supplied bank statements.
options: The application was returned because the applicant had supplied statements.
The applicant supplied statements in response to the request for evidence.
The applicant supplied statements in response to a bank's request.
The return of the statements prompted the original request for evidence.
questions.explanation: Which follows in response to and refers to the request for evidence.
feedback: This reverses the sequence, making the statements the reason for returning the application.
Which follows in response to and refers to the request for evidence.
The bank supplies the statements but is not identified as making the evidence request.
The application was returned; the sentence does not report returned bank statements.

questions.setup: Choose the sentence that unambiguously refers to the organization's recommendations, not its members' personal recommendations.
questions.prompt: The association issued recommendations. Several of those recommendations were adopted by the council.
options: The association's members, several of whom made recommendations, advised the council.
The association, several of whose members' recommendations were adopted, advised the council.
The association, several of whose recommendations were adopted, advised the council.
The association, whose members adopted several recommendations, advised the council.
questions.explanation: Whose attaches recommendations directly to association, and several of counts the adopted recommendations.
feedback: This counts members who made recommendations, not recommendations adopted from the association.
Members' places the recommendations with individual members, rather than explicitly with the association.
Whose attaches recommendations directly to association, and several of counts the adopted recommendations.
This makes the members the adopters and does not preserve adoption by the council.

questions.setup: Choose the reading supported by the sentence.
questions.prompt: We funded a workshop that the organizers promised would be accessible to wheelchair users.
options: The workshop's accessibility was independently confirmed by the funders.
The organizers promised to fund a workshop that was already accessible.
Wheelchair users promised the organizers that they would attend the workshop.
The organizers committed themselves to making the funded workshop accessible.
questions.explanation: The relative links workshop to the accessibility promised by the organizers, keeping the commitment attributed to them.
feedback: The relative reports the organizers' promise, not independent confirmation that it was fulfilled.
We funded assigns funding to the speaker's group; the organizers' promise concerns accessibility.
Wheelchair users are the intended beneficiaries of accessibility, not the people making the promise.
The relative links workshop to the accessibility promised by the organizers, keeping the commitment attributed to them.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that preserves both the target of the criticism and the document containing it.
questions.prompt: The editor sent the author a review which criticized the publisher's decision. The review, not the editor's covering message, contained the criticism.
options: The editor sent a review in which the author criticized the covering message.
The editor's message to the author criticized the publisher's review.
The editor sent the publisher a review whose author criticized the covering message.
The editor sent the author a review in which the publisher's decision was criticized.
questions.explanation: In which locates criticism inside the review; the passive keeps the publisher's decision as its target.
feedback: This assigns criticism to the author and targets the covering message rather than the publisher's decision.
This moves criticism into the message and makes a review, not a decision, its target.
This changes the recipient to the publisher and the criticized object to the covering message.
In which locates criticism inside the review; the passive keeps the publisher's decision as its target.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase of the reservation expressed by the relative clause.
questions.prompt: The new software retained its familiar menus, such as they were, while replacing the underlying database.
options: The menus were retained as examples of other familiar features that were removed.
The menus were retained, though the speaker implies they were of limited quality.
The menus were retained in whatever form users might choose in future.
The menus were retained because their quality made other changes unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Such as they were refers back to the menus with a qualified, often dismissive assessment of their adequacy.
feedback: Such as they were is a parenthetical qualification here, not an example list headed by such as.
Such as they were refers back to the menus with a qualified, often dismissive assessment of their adequacy.
They were refers to the menus as they existed, not a future free choice of form.
The phrase qualifies the menus' merits; it does not praise them as making further changes unnecessary.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that clearly distinguishes the conditions authorizing access from the means of obtaining it.
questions.prompt: The protocol specifies when researchers are entitled to access records; a separate portal provides access.
options: The protocol describes the portal through which researchers are entitled to apply for access.
The protocol sets out the conditions under which researchers may access records.
The protocol supplies the means whereby researchers obtain access to records.
The protocol records the occasions on which researchers accessed the portal.
questions.explanation: Under which introduces the circumstances governing permission; it does not identify the delivery mechanism.
feedback: This makes the protocol a description of the application portal instead of the conditions of entitlement.
Under which introduces the circumstances governing permission; it does not identify the delivery mechanism.
Whereby presents the protocol as the enabling mechanism, conflating the rule with the separate portal.
On which introduces recorded past occasions, not the conditions authorizing access.

questions.setup: Choose the statement that preserves the narrator's commitments.
questions.prompt: The tribunal, whose jurisdiction the claimant continues to dispute, has not yet ruled on the admissibility of the evidence.
options: The tribunal lacks jurisdiction, so the evidence is inadmissible.
The tribunal has rejected the jurisdictional challenge but reserved the evidence issue.
A claimant disputes the tribunal's authority; admissibility remains undecided.
The claimant accepts jurisdiction while disputing the tribunal's evidence ruling.
questions.explanation: Whose identifies the tribunal's authority as the object of the claimant's dispute; has not yet ruled leaves the evidence decision open.
feedback: A reported dispute does not establish lack of jurisdiction, and no admissibility ruling has been made.
The sentence reports an ongoing challenge, not its rejection by the tribunal.
Whose identifies the tribunal's authority as the object of the claimant's dispute; has not yet ruled leaves the evidence decision open.
Continues to dispute contradicts acceptance, and an evidence ruling is still pending.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that preserves which group was recalled.
questions.prompt: The witnesses whose accounts the analyst questioned, several of whom had already left the country, were recalled for further testimony.
options: The witnesses with questioned accounts were recalled, including some who had left.
The witnesses who had left the country were the only ones recalled.
The analyst recalled witnesses without questioning their accounts.
The questioned accounts came only from witnesses who remained in the country.
questions.explanation: The defining whose clause selects the recalled group; the supplementary partitive describes some members within it.
feedback: The defining whose clause selects the recalled group; the supplementary partitive describes some members within it.
Several of whom adds information about some members; it does not restrict recalled to that subgroup.
Whose accounts the analyst questioned explicitly defines the witness group by the questioned accounts.
Several of whom refers back to that defined group, so some with questioned accounts had left.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that makes clear that only the order's interpretation is disputed.
questions.prompt: The lawyer discussed the notice and the order, the interpretation of which remains disputed.
options: The lawyer discussed the notice and the order, the interpretations of both of which remain disputed.
The lawyer discussed the notice and, separately, the order whose interpretation remains disputed.
The lawyer discussed the disputed interpretation of the notice and the order together.
The lawyer discussed the notice whose interpretation remains disputed and the order.
questions.explanation: Separately separates order from notice, and whose attaches the disputed interpretation directly to order.
feedback: Both of which extends the interpretation dispute to both documents, contrary to the stated editing goal.
Separately separates order from notice, and whose attaches the disputed interpretation directly to order.
Together leaves the disputed interpretation associated with the pair instead of isolating the order.
Whose places the disputed interpretation with notice rather than order.

questions.setup: Choose the distinction between the two that-clauses.
questions.prompt: Compare: 'the allegation that the auditor repeated' and 'the allegation that the auditor falsified the figures'.
options: Both clauses state that the auditor made a false allegation.
The first gives the allegation's content; the second identifies its source.
The first identifies an allegation by an action; the second states its content.
Both clauses identify allegations by actions performed on them.
questions.explanation: In the first, allegation is the understood object of repeated in a relative; in the second, the that-clause supplies what is alleged.
feedback: Neither wording by itself establishes that the allegation is false; the second reports what is alleged.
The functions are reversed: repeated takes the allegation as its missing object, while falsified the figures supplies a full proposition.
In the first, allegation is the understood object of repeated in a relative; in the second, the that-clause supplies what is alleged.
Only repeated has allegation as an understood object; the second clause already has the figures as its object.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation supported by the policy.
questions.prompt: Whoever is appointed to chair the inquiry must disclose any previous work for the contractor.
options: The speaker knows the appointee but declines to identify that person.
The disclosure requirement applies regardless of who becomes chair.
An appointee may decide whether previous work is relevant enough to disclose.
The inquiry must appoint the person who has already disclosed previous work.
questions.explanation: Whoever is appointed supplies the eventual role-holder as the subject of must disclose.
feedback: Whoever makes the requirement independent of identity; it does not establish concealed knowledge of an appointment.
Whoever is appointed supplies the eventual role-holder as the subject of must disclose.
The stated duty covers any previous work, not just work the appointee chooses to consider relevant.
Disclosure is a duty of the chair, not a stated rule for selecting the chair.

questions.setup: Choose the reading of 'whatever support' in context.
questions.prompt: Whatever support the redevelopment proposal once enjoyed has ebbed away during the prolonged consultation.
options: The proposal's renewed support depends on shortening the consultation.
The proposal's earlier support, of unspecified extent, has diminished.
The proposal necessarily had little support before consultation began.
The amount of remaining support is being investigated during consultation.
questions.explanation: 'Whatever support' gathers the earlier support without quantifying it, while 'has ebbed away' reports its decline.
feedback: 'Whatever support' is the subject of 'has ebbed away', not a conditional promise of renewed support.
'Whatever support' gathers the earlier support without quantifying it, while 'has ebbed away' reports its decline.
'Whatever' leaves the earlier amount unspecified; it need not have been little.
The clause identifies the earlier support and reports decline; it is not a question or investigation into an amount.

questions.setup: Choose the inference warranted by the relative clause under 'need'.
questions.prompt: The team needs an adviser who can reconcile the two datasets without discarding the disputed observations.
options: The sentence specifies required expertise without establishing that a suitable adviser exists.
The team has identified an adviser who has already reconciled the datasets.
An existing adviser has agreed to retain the disputed observations.
The team believes that the disputed observations should be discarded before reconciliation.
questions.explanation: Under 'needs', 'an adviser who can...' describes a requirement; it does not assert an actual person's existence or availability.
feedback: Under 'needs', 'an adviser who can...' describes a requirement; it does not assert an actual person's existence or availability.
'Can' states a required ability, not an identified person's completed reconciliation.
No existing adviser or agreement is reported by the need statement.
'Without discarding' makes retention part of the required solution, not an obstacle to remove first.

questions.setup: Choose the statement that accurately contrasts the two reports.
questions.prompt: A: Few submissions that challenged the policy received a reply. B: The submissions, few of which challenged the policy, received a reply.
options: Both reports say that challenges made replies unlikely.
A counts challenges among replied-to submissions; B counts replies among challenges.
A says most submissions challenged the policy; B says most replies challenged it.
A limits replies within the challenging group; B reports replies to the stated submission set.
questions.explanation: A's defining relative restricts the domain of few; B's partitive gives the number of challenges while the main clause applies to the stated submissions.
feedback: Neither report establishes causation; B does not even restrict replies to a subset of the stated submissions.
This reverses the scope: A counts replies within challenges, while B counts challenges within the submission set.
A does not give the share of all submissions that challenged the policy, and B describes submissions rather than replies as challenging it.
A's defining relative restricts the domain of few; B's partitive gives the number of challenges while the main clause applies to the stated submissions.

questions.setup: Choose the contribution of 'what little' in this sentence.
questions.prompt: What little evidence survived the deletion was insufficient to reconstruct the transaction history.
options: The phrase selects a small part of a larger surviving body of evidence.
The phrase asks how much evidence survived before judging its quality.
The phrase gathers the small surviving amount as the sentence's subject.
The phrase limits insufficiency to evidence deleted rather than evidence retained.
questions.explanation: The phrase means the small amount of evidence that survived, and that amount is the subject of 'was insufficient'.
feedback: 'What little evidence survived' denotes the small surviving total, not a selected fraction of a larger surviving collection.
This is a noun-like relative construction, not an indirect question about quantity.
The phrase means the small amount of evidence that survived, and that amount is the subject of 'was insufficient'.
'Survived' identifies retained evidence; insufficiency is predicated of that evidence, not the deleted material.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that clearly keeps the unexpected element as the difficulty, not the negotiations.
questions.prompt: A difficulty arose during the negotiations which neither party had anticipated.
options: During negotiations that neither party had anticipated, a difficulty arose.
Negotiations arising from an unforeseen difficulty have begun.
Neither party had anticipated the negotiations during which a difficulty arose.
During the negotiations, a difficulty arose that neither party had anticipated.
questions.explanation: Fronting the time phrase leaves the relative attached to difficulty, removing the intervening competing noun.
feedback: This makes the negotiations, rather than the difficulty, the unanticipated event.
This makes the difficulty predate and prompt the negotiations, instead of arising during them.
The object of had anticipated becomes negotiations, not difficulty.
Fronting the time phrase leaves the relative attached to difficulty, removing the intervening competing noun.

questions.setup: Choose what the narrator still asserts despite the negative main clause.
questions.prompt: The chair, who had opposed the merger from the outset, did not attend the meeting at which it was approved.
options: The chair's opposition is denied together with attendance at the meeting.
The meeting's approval of the merger is only something the chair suspected.
The chair's opposition is presented as a fact, although attendance is denied.
The chair attended a different meeting where the merger was rejected.
questions.explanation: The supplementary who clause asserts opposition independently of the main clause's did not attend.
feedback: The main negation governs attendance, not the supplementary assertion about earlier opposition.
At which it was approved identifies the meeting through approval; no suspicion is attributed to the chair.
The supplementary who clause asserts opposition independently of the main clause's did not attend.
Not attending this meeting does not establish attendance at another one or a different vote.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that treats prior committee approval as confirmed by the minutes, not merely claimed in them.
questions.prompt: The proposal had already received committee approval. The minutes corroborate that fact.
options: The minutes, which had received committee approval, mentioned the proposal.
The proposal had received approval from the committee that drafted the minutes.
The proposal, whose approval the minutes questioned, went to the committee.
The proposal had already received committee approval, as the minutes confirm.
questions.explanation: As refers to the preceding proposition, and confirm presents the minutes as corroboration of that proposition.
feedback: This makes the minutes, rather than the proposal, the thing approved and weakens corroboration to mention.
This identifies the committee through authorship of the minutes but does not make the minutes confirm the approval.
Questioned reverses corroboration into doubt about the approval.
As refers to the preceding proposition, and confirm presents the minutes as corroboration of that proposition.

questions.setup: Choose the inference that keeps both possessive relationships intact.
questions.prompt: The foundation supported two laboratories, the directors of both of which had trained under the scientist whose methods the review criticized.
options: The review criticized the two laboratory directors' methods, which the scientist had taught them.
Both laboratories had directors trained by a scientist whose methods were criticized.
The foundation's directors trained the scientist whose laboratory methods were reviewed.
The review criticized the foundation's support for the scientist's two laboratories.
questions.explanation: Both of which refers to the laboratories, their directors underwent the training, and whose methods refers to the scientist.
feedback: The relative whose methods assigns the criticized methods to the scientist; it does not explicitly attribute their use to the directors.
Both of which refers to the laboratories, their directors underwent the training, and whose methods refers to the scientist.
Directors belongs to laboratories, not foundation, and had trained under makes the scientist the trainer, not the trainee.
The review's stated object is the scientist's methods, not the foundation's funding decision or laboratory ownership.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that correctly identifies the missing prerequisite.
questions.prompt: The panel requested an independent valuation, in the absence of which it said it could not recommend a sale.
options: The panel's absence from the sale would prevent an independent valuation.
The sale could not be valued until the panel issued its recommendation.
The panel requested a valuation because the sale had already been recommended.
The panel said a valuation was necessary before it could recommend a sale.
questions.explanation: In the absence of which refers to the requested valuation, and it said attributes the prerequisite to the panel.
feedback: Which refers to valuation, not panel; the absence concerns evidence, not attendance.
This reverses the prerequisite: the valuation is required for the recommendation, not produced after it.
Could not recommend without the valuation leaves the recommendation unavailable, not already made.
In the absence of which refers to the requested valuation, and it said attributes the prerequisite to the panel.

questions.setup: Choose the distinction between the two uses of 'what'.
questions.prompt: A: We archived what the inspector submitted. B: We asked what the inspector submitted.
options: A refers to submitted material; B presents a question about its identity.
A questions whether submission occurred; B confirms that the material was archived.
Both uses ask the reader to identify the inspector's submission.
Both uses refer to material that the speaker physically stored.
questions.explanation: In A, 'what...' functions like 'the material that' and is archived; in B, it supplies the content of an indirect question.
feedback: In A, 'what...' functions like 'the material that' and is archived; in B, it supplies the content of an indirect question.
'Archived' reports an action on material, while 'asked' does not establish any archiving.
Only 'asked' introduces a question; 'archived' takes the submitted material as its object.
Storage is asserted in A, not in B, where the action is asking.

questions.setup: Choose the conclusion licensed by the sentence alone.
questions.prompt: No applicant who lacked the required certification was shortlisted.
options: Any applicant who was shortlisted had the required certification.
Every applicant with the certification was shortlisted.
Applicants who lacked certification did not apply.
The panel shortlisted applicants according to how recently they were certified.
questions.explanation: The negative statement rules out a shortlisted applicant lacking certification, so shortlisted applicants had it.
feedback: The negative statement rules out a shortlisted applicant lacking certification, so shortlisted applicants had it.
The relative-based exclusion makes certification necessary for shortlisting, not sufficient to secure it.
The sentence excludes such applicants from the shortlist, not from applying.
The relative distinguishes possession from absence of certification, not recency.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that explicitly means a different physical copy with matching terms, not the very document signed earlier.
questions.prompt: The witness was shown the same contract as the director had signed.
options: The witness was shown the contract that bore the director's original signature.
The witness was shown the signed contract, which the director had kept in the file.
The witness was shown the very contract that the director had signed.
The witness was shown a separate copy whose terms matched those of the signed contract.
questions.explanation: Separate copy fixes physical non-identity, while whose terms matched preserves equivalence of contractual content.
feedback: The original signature identifies the signed document, not explicitly a separate matching copy.
This again identifies the shown document as the signed contract rather than clarifying a different copy.
The very contract emphasizes identity of the physical document, contrary to the editing goal.
Separate copy fixes physical non-identity, while whose terms matched preserves equivalence of contractual content.

questions.setup: Choose the reading of 'such information as' in context.
questions.prompt: The reviewer assessed the project using such information as the organizers were willing to release.
options: The reviewer worked within the information the organizers were prepared to make available.
The reviewer chose information similar to material the organizers had withheld.
The organizers released the information that the reviewer had already assessed.
The reviewer assessed examples of information rather than the project itself.
questions.explanation: The 'as' clause restricts the available information to what the organizers were willing to release; it need not mean a complete record.
feedback: The 'as' clause restricts the available information to what the organizers were willing to release; it need not mean a complete record.
'Such...as' identifies the available information here; it does not describe similarity to withheld material.
The relative limits the information by willingness to release it, not by an earlier review of that information.
'Such information as' is not an examples list here, and 'project' remains the object of 'assessed'.

questions.setup: Choose the wording that makes the limit apply to which proposal was rejected, not to who rejected it.
questions.prompt: Of several proposals, the board rejected only the proposal requiring an outside audit.
options: The proposal that required an outside audit was rejected only by the board.
Only the board rejected the proposal that required an outside audit.
The only proposal that the board rejected was the one requiring an outside audit.
The proposal that only the board rejected required an outside audit.
questions.explanation: The only proposal places exclusivity on the head restricted by that the board rejected, singling out one rejected proposal.
feedback: Only by the board limits the rejecting agent, not the set of rejected proposals.
Only the board again focuses on the agent and leaves open what else it rejected.
The only proposal places exclusivity on the head restricted by that the board rejected, singling out one rejected proposal.
Only inside the relative attaches to the board as agent rather than limiting how many proposals it rejected.

questions.setup: Daniel says, 'I am ready.' Choose the report about Daniel, not about yourself.
questions.prompt: Daniel says that ___ is ready.
options: I
him
he
his
questions.explanation: He refers to Daniel as the person who is ready.
feedback: I would refer to the person reporting the message, but Daniel is talking about himself.
Him is an object form; the person before is needs a subject form.
He refers to Daniel as the person who is ready.
His shows possession and cannot stand as the subject meaning Daniel here.

questions.setup: The cashier tells me, 'You are early.' Choose my report of her message.
questions.prompt: She says that ___.
options: I am early
she is early
they are early
we are early
questions.explanation: The cashier's you refers to the person reporting, so my report uses I am.
feedback: The cashier's you refers to the person reporting, so my report uses I am.
She would make the cashier the early person, but her you refers to me.
They introduces other people whom the cashier did not mention.
We adds the cashier or other people to the early group; the message addresses only me.

questions.setup: My two neighbors say, 'We live nearby.' I am not part of their household.
questions.prompt: My neighbors say that ___ live nearby.
options: we
they
he
she
questions.explanation: They refers to both neighbors without including the reporter.
feedback: We would include me, but the neighbors are speaking about their own household.
They refers to both neighbors without including the reporter.
He refers to one man and does not keep the two neighbors together.
She refers to one woman, not the two people who spoke.

questions.setup: My brother says, 'My bike is outside.' Choose the report keeping the bike as his.
questions.prompt: My brother says that ___ bike is outside.
options: his
my
her
our
questions.explanation: His keeps the bike as the brother's possession when I report his words.
feedback: His keeps the bike as the brother's possession when I report his words.
My would make the bike mine rather than my brother's.
Her assigns the bike to a woman who is not the stated owner.
Our would make the bike a shared possession, which the message does not say.

questions.setup: Choose the report with the same meaning as the customer's words.
