Promised to replace keeps the seller as the person committed to replacing the mug.
This attributes the promise to me rather than to the seller.

questions.setup: A neighbor said, 'Be careful. The stream may flood tonight.' Choose a report keeping the warning and its uncertainty.
questions.prompt: Our neighbor ___.
options: promised that the stream would flood tonight
warned us that the stream might flood tonight
confirmed that the stream had flooded
warned us that the stream could not flood
questions.explanation: Warned us preserves the caution, and might keeps flooding as possible rather than certain.
feedback: Promised misrepresents a caution as a commitment, and would removes the original may possibility.
Warned us preserves the caution, and might keeps flooding as possible rather than certain.
Confirmed ... had flooded turns a possible future danger into an established past event.
Could not flood denies the danger rather than warning that it is possible.

questions.setup: The guest said, 'I'm sorry I arrived late.' Complete the apology report.
questions.prompt: The guest apologized ___.
options: to arrive late
for arriving late
that arriving late
for arrive late
questions.explanation: Apologized for takes an -ing phrase naming the action the guest regrets.
feedback: To arrive would not give the normal complement naming the reason for this apology.
Apologized for takes an -ing phrase naming the action the guest regrets.
That arriving is not a complete clause and does not fit this apology pattern.
After for, use arriving rather than the base form arrive.

questions.setup: The musician was asked to sign a poster and answered, 'No, I won't sign it.' Choose the report of that response.
questions.prompt: The musician ___.
options: denied signing the poster
offered to sign the poster
refused to sign the poster
asked whether the poster was signed
questions.explanation: Refused to sign reports the unwillingness to perform the action requested.
feedback: Denied signing would reject a claim that signing happened, not refuse a requested future action.
Offered would show willingness instead of the expressed refusal.
Refused to sign reports the unwillingness to perform the action requested.
Asked whether would seek information about the poster rather than reject the request.

questions.setup: It is still the same week. On Monday a colleague said, 'The exhibition ends this week.' Compare two reports made on Wednesday.
questions.prompt: A: 'She said the exhibition ended this week.' B: 'She said the exhibition ended that week.'
options: Both can refer to the same week in this context.
A must be wrong because this always changes to that after said.
B must mean a week later than the exhibition's final week.
A means the exhibition has already ended, while B means it has not.
questions.explanation: The shared week allows this week, while that week can refer back to the week being reported.
feedback: The shared week allows this week, while that week can refer back to the week being reported.
This week can remain accurate when the original speaker and the reporter are within the same week.
That week can point back to the week of the original statement; it does not automatically mean a later week.
This versus that does not by itself establish whether the ending has already happened at Wednesday's reporting time.

questions.setup: Choose what the sentence establishes, without treating the manager's message as independent proof.
questions.prompt: The manager said that the coffee machine was broken.
options: The sentence reports the manager's statement that it was broken.
The sentence proves that the machine was broken.
The sentence says the manager broke the machine.
The sentence says the manager was unsure whether it was broken.
questions.explanation: The sentence attributes the broken-machine claim to the manager without independently establishing it.
feedback: The sentence attributes the broken-machine claim to the manager without independently establishing it.
Reporting what someone said does not itself provide independent proof of the content.
The manager is the speaker, not an identified cause of the fault.
The reported statement contains no uncertainty such as might or perhaps.

questions.setup: Leah tells Victor, 'I'll send you my recipe.' Choose Victor's report, preserving both people and the recipe's owner.
questions.prompt: Victor says: 'Leah told me that ___.'
options: I would send her my recipe
she would send him my recipe
he would send me her recipe
she would send me her recipe
questions.explanation: She refers to Leah, me to Victor as reporter, and her recipe remains Leah's recipe.
feedback: This makes Victor the sender and recipe owner, reversing the original roles.
Him fails to keep Victor's first-person reporting viewpoint, and my changes the owner to Victor.
He changes the sender from Leah to a male person not identified as the original sender.
She refers to Leah, me to Victor as reporter, and her recipe remains Leah's recipe.

questions.setup: Choose the interpretation that does not treat backshift alone as evidence of a later change.
questions.prompt: The technician said that the casing was waterproof. No later test is mentioned.
options: The past was proves that the casing is no longer waterproof.
Was can reflect the past reporting viewpoint; it does not establish a later loss of waterproofing.
The sentence independently confirms that the casing is still waterproof now.
The technician said that the casing had stopped being waterproof before she spoke.
questions.explanation: Was can locate the reported property at the speaking time without saying whether it has since changed.
feedback: Backshift after said does not itself imply that the reported property has ceased.
Was can locate the reported property at the speaking time without saying whether it has since changed.
The sentence reports the technician's statement and does not independently verify a current property.
Was waterproof reports the property, not its ending before the conversation.

questions.setup: Choose what the report says without adding an outcome.
questions.prompt: The curator announced that the gallery would reopen after the repairs.
options: The repairs were complete when the announcement was made.
The gallery certainly reopened, although the announcement date is unknown.
Reopening was presented as later than the repairs; the report does not confirm that it happened.
The gallery was already open when the curator announced the repair plan.
questions.explanation: The report presents the reopening prospectively and keeps the after-repairs sequence without confirming fulfillment.
feedback: After the repairs sets the condition or sequence for reopening; it does not establish completion at announcement time.
Would reopen reports a future event from a past viewpoint, not a verified later outcome.
The report presents the reopening prospectively and keeps the after-repairs sequence without confirming fulfillment.
Was already open reverses the future orientation of would reopen.

questions.setup: Report 'How long have you been waiting?' using a past-perfect continuous clause in standard written order.
questions.prompt: The dispatcher asked us ___.
options: how long we had been waiting
how long had we been waiting
how long we had being waiting
how long we have been waiting
questions.explanation: We had been waiting preserves the duration question with embedded order and the requested aspect.
feedback: We had been waiting preserves the duration question with embedded order and the requested aspect.
Had we is direct-question inversion; the indirect clause requires we had.
Had must be followed by been, not being, in the perfect continuous.
Have been waiting can be used in some current reports, but the instruction specifically requires past perfect continuous.

questions.setup: The host asked me, 'Who invited you?' Choose the report keeping the unknown person as the inviter.
questions.prompt: The host asked ___.
options: whom I had invited
who I had sent an invitation to
who had invited me
whether I had invited anyone
questions.explanation: Who is the inviter, and me remains the person who received the invitation.
feedback: This makes me the inviter and asks for the person I invited, reversing the original roles.
Sending an invitation also makes me the inviter rather than the recipient.
Who is the inviter, and me remains the person who received the invitation.
This changes a who question about my inviter into a yes/no question about my own invitations.

questions.setup: Choose the linker used before a to-infinitive when reporting a choice in standard written English.
questions.prompt: The tenants discussed ___ to renew the lease or move elsewhere.
options: if
that
what
whether
questions.explanation: Whether to renew introduces the choice between renewal and moving.
feedback: If does not normally introduce a to-infinitive choice in this standard written construction.
That introduces a finite content clause, not this choice followed by a to-infinitive.
What would ask which thing to renew, whereas the sentence asks whether renewal should happen.
Whether to renew introduces the choice between renewal and moving.

questions.setup: The customer asserted a right to immediate repayment: 'I insist that you refund me now.' Choose the report preserving that force.
questions.prompt: The customer ___.
options: suggested that a refund might be useful
wondered whether a refund was available
demanded an immediate refund
offered to refund the payment
questions.explanation: Demanded captures the explicit insistence, and immediate preserves now.
feedback: Suggested ... might be useful weakens the insistence into a tentative proposal.
Wondered whether turns an asserted demand into uncertainty about availability.
Demanded captures the explicit insistence, and immediate preserves now.
Offered to refund makes the customer the person returning money rather than requesting it.

questions.setup: A passenger said to the driver, 'You ignored my stop.' Complete a report attributing that accusation to the passenger.
questions.prompt: The passenger accused the driver ___.
options: to ignore the stop
for ignoring the stop
that he ignored the stop
of ignoring the stop
questions.explanation: Accused the driver of ignoring names the person blamed and the alleged action without confirming the accusation.
feedback: Accuse someone does not take a to-infinitive for the alleged act in this construction.
The conventional preposition after accused the driver is of, not for.
A that clause cannot directly replace the of-phrase after accused the driver here.
Accused the driver of ignoring names the person blamed and the alleged action without confirming the accusation.

questions.setup: The coach said to the runners, 'Well done on finishing your first marathon!' Complete the congratulation report.
questions.prompt: The coach congratulated the runners ___.
options: for to finish their first marathon
on finishing their first marathon
to finish their first marathon
that finishing their first marathon
questions.explanation: Congratulated them on finishing reports praise for the achievement already completed.
feedback: For to finish incorrectly combines a preposition and to-infinitive in this compliment pattern.
Congratulated them on finishing reports praise for the achievement already completed.
To finish sounds like an intended action, but congratulate does not take this direct infinitive complement.
That finishing is not a complete content clause and does not fit this pattern.

questions.setup: Choose the comparison keeping a proposed action distinct from an assertion about the past.
questions.prompt: A: 'She insisted on paying the bill.' B: 'She insisted that she had paid the bill.'
options: Both report her assertion that payment had already happened.
A reports her determination to pay; B reports her firm claim of earlier payment.
A reports a demand that someone else pay; B reports her own refusal to pay.
Both independently prove that she paid the bill.
questions.explanation: On paying presents her insistence on the action, whereas that she had paid supplies the content of an assertion about earlier payment.
feedback: Only B explicitly reports the claim that payment had already occurred; A concerns insisting on doing it.
On paying presents her insistence on the action, whereas that she had paid supplies the content of an assertion about earlier payment.
She is the intended payer in A, and B asserts payment rather than refusing it.
Neither the insistence on an action nor the report of a claim independently proves the payment outcome.

questions.setup: The electrician reassured the residents: 'The supply is safe.' Choose the report of reassurance, not a claim that he carried out safety work.
questions.prompt: The electrician ___.
options: ensured that the supply was safe
assured the residents that the supply was safe
made the supply safe for the residents
required the residents to make the supply safe
questions.explanation: Assured the residents reports reassurance addressed to people while retaining its stated content.
feedback: Ensured says he made certain of safety; it does not specifically report reassuring speech to the residents.
Assured the residents reports reassurance addressed to people while retaining its stated content.
Made the supply safe asserts an intervention that the quoted reassurance does not establish.
Required ... to make changes reassurance into an instruction assigning safety work to residents.

questions.setup: Choose the report that leaves the existence of a fault open, as the original question does.
questions.prompt: The engineer asked, 'Is the sensor faulty?'
options: The engineer asked why the sensor was faulty.
The engineer explained that the sensor was faulty.
The engineer asked when the sensor had become faulty.
The engineer asked whether the sensor was faulty.
questions.explanation: Whether preserves the open question of whether a fault exists.
feedback: Why treats a fault as the basis for asking its cause, rather than asking whether there is a fault.
Explained that reports a statement about a fault instead of a yes/no inquiry.
When asks for the onset of a fault and treats becoming faulty as given.
Whether preserves the open question of whether a fault exists.

questions.setup: The librarian said, 'You ought to keep a record of your sources.' Keep 'ought to' unchanged in the report.
questions.prompt: The librarian said that we ___.
options: ought to keep a record of our sources
ought kept a record of our sources
had ought to keep a record of our sources
would ought to keep a record of our sources
questions.explanation: 'Ought to' is retained, with the base form 'keep', while 'our' adjusts the possessive to the reporting group.
feedback: 'Ought to' is retained, with the base form 'keep', while 'our' adjusts the possessive to the reporting group.
'Ought' needs 'to' plus the base verb here, not the past form 'kept'.
'Had' cannot be added as a backshift auxiliary before 'ought' in this standard construction.
'Would' cannot be stacked before 'ought' to make the intended report.

questions.setup: A resident says angrily, 'The drilling starts before dawn every day.' Choose a report of the complaint without adding an order or a remedy.
questions.prompt: The resident ___.
options: ordered the builders to finish before dawn
promised to stop the drilling before dawn
asked what time the drilling started
complained that the drilling started before dawn each day
questions.explanation: Complained preserves the angry statement and its repeated early starting time.
feedback: The resident states a grievance about starting time, not an instruction about finishing time.
A promise to stop the work adds both a commitment and control over the work that the source does not state.
The resident already states the time; the utterance is not an information question.
Complained preserves the angry statement and its repeated early starting time.

questions.setup: A friend recommends a cheaper route: 'Why don't you go by coach?' Choose a report of that recommendation, not a literal question about past reasons.
questions.prompt: My friend ___.
options: suggested that I go by coach
asked why I had not gone by coach
denied that I could go by coach
confirmed that I had gone by coach
questions.explanation: Suggested that I go preserves the recommendation made through the conventional why-don't-you form.
feedback: Suggested that I go preserves the recommendation made through the conventional why-don't-you form.
This turns the recommendation into a question about why I failed to travel that way in the past.
Denied that I could rejects an option that the friend is recommending.
Confirmed ... had gone reports a completed journey, not a proposed choice.

questions.setup: The equipment clerk said, 'Don't forget to return your helmet.' Choose the report of a reminder about a pending action.
questions.prompt: The clerk ___.
options: reminded me that I had returned my helmet
remembered returning my helmet
asked why I had returned my helmet
reminded me to return my helmet
questions.explanation: Reminded me to return keeps me as the person who still needs to carry out the action.
feedback: Reminded me that I had returned recalls a completed event, not the action still required.
Remembered returning makes the clerk the person recalling an action rather than someone reminding me to act.
Asked why seeks a reason for an earlier return rather than prompting a pending return.
Reminded me to return keeps me as the person who still needs to carry out the action.

questions.setup: Both sentences report the same caution about an unfamiliar website. Choose the accurate comparison.
questions.prompt: A: 'They warned me not to share my password.' B: 'They warned me against sharing my password.'
options: Only A contains a warning; B says I have already shared the password.
A prohibits sharing, while B encourages sharing with caution.
Both advise against the same action; their complement patterns differ.
B is ungrammatical because warn cannot be followed by against.
questions.explanation: Not to share and against sharing are both standard ways to report this warning, using different complement forms.
feedback: Against sharing does not assert that sharing has already happened.
Both discourage sharing; against does not convert the warning into cautious encouragement.
Not to share and against sharing are both standard ways to report this warning, using different complement forms.
Warn someone against doing something is an established complement pattern.

questions.setup: Choose the report retaining both willingness and lack of ability.
questions.prompt: The neighbor said, 'I wanted to help, but I couldn't lift the cabinet.'
options: The neighbor said he had wanted to help but had been unable to lift the cabinet.
The neighbor refused to help because he could lift the cabinet.
The neighbor admitted that he had been able to help but had not wanted to.
The neighbor claimed that he had lifted the cabinet without help.
questions.explanation: Had wanted keeps the intention positive, while had been unable preserves the practical limitation.
feedback: Had wanted keeps the intention positive, while had been unable preserves the practical limitation.
Refused replaces willingness with unwillingness, and could reverses the stated lack of ability.
This reverses both parts: ability becomes positive and willingness negative.
This asserts successful lifting and introduces working alone, neither of which the source states.

questions.setup: Choose the report preserving the upper limit without turning it into a minimum or a fixed duration.
questions.prompt: The repair shop said, 'Delivery can take up to six weeks.'
options: The shop said delivery could take as long as six weeks.
The shop said delivery would take at least six weeks.
The shop guaranteed delivery in exactly six weeks.
The shop said delivery would take more than six weeks.
questions.explanation: Could take as long as preserves the possibility of the upper duration without requiring every delivery to take that long.
feedback: Could take as long as preserves the possibility of the upper duration without requiring every delivery to take that long.
At least makes six weeks a lower limit, reversing the up-to limit.
Exactly fixes the duration, and guaranteed strengthens the original can statement.
More than places the duration beyond the limit given in the source.

questions.setup: Nora tells Leila, 'I can lend you my tent.' Choose the report that makes the lender and owner unambiguous by naming them.
questions.prompt: Which report preserves the arrangement?
options: Nora said that Leila could lend Nora's tent to her.
Leila said that Nora could borrow Leila's tent.
Nora said that Leila could borrow Nora's tent.
Nora told Leila that she could borrow her tent.
questions.explanation: Leila remains the borrower, and repeating Nora identifies the tent's owner clearly.
feedback: This makes Leila the lender rather than the borrower and leaves her ambiguous.
This reverses the speaker, owner, and borrower of the tent.
Leila remains the borrower, and repeating Nora identifies the tent's owner clearly.
The two female pronouns leave their references open in isolation; the instruction requires names that make the roles unambiguous.

questions.setup: Choose the report preserving the condition rather than making the move unconditional.
questions.prompt: The organizer said, 'If it rains, we'll move the picnic indoors.'
options: The organizer said they would move the picnic indoors whether or not it rained.
The organizer said they would move the picnic indoors if it rained.
The organizer said rain had forced them to move the picnic indoors.
The organizer said they would cancel the picnic if it rained.
questions.explanation: If it rained preserves rain as the condition for the planned move, using a past reporting viewpoint.
feedback: Whether or not removes the condition and makes the move independent of the weather.
If it rained preserves rain as the condition for the planned move, using a past reporting viewpoint.
Had forced reports rain and a move as completed events rather than a conditional plan.
Canceling is a different response from moving the picnic indoors; the source plans to hold it in another place.

questions.setup: Which report of the jeweler's response is supported by this account?
questions.prompt: Asked whether she had copied the design, the jeweler declined to answer.
options: The jeweler did not admit to copying the design.
The jeweler denied having copied the design.
The jeweler admitted that she had not copied the design.
The jeweler conceded that the design had been copied.
questions.explanation: Did not admit accurately withholds an admission and does not turn silence into a denial.
feedback: Did not admit accurately withholds an admission and does not turn silence into a denial.
A denial would assert that she had not copied it; declining to answer does not supply that assertion.
Admitted that she had not copied attributes a negative assertion to her, whereas she gave no answer.
Conceded asserts an acknowledgment of copying, which the refusal to answer does not establish.

questions.setup: Which summary accurately represents the planner's position?
questions.prompt: The planner said, 'The junction is inconvenient, I accept that, but the route is still the best available.'
options: The planner conceded that the route was no longer the best available.
The planner denied that the junction was inconvenient while defending the route.
The planner acknowledged the junction's inconvenience but maintained that the route was the best available.
The planner conceded that the route was the best available because the junction was convenient.
questions.explanation: Acknowledged captures the limited concession, while maintained keeps the main claim in place.
feedback: The concession concerns the junction's inconvenience, not abandonment of the preferred route.
Denied reverses the explicit acceptance of inconvenience.
Acknowledged captures the limited concession, while maintained keeps the main claim in place.
This moves the concession to the route claim and reverses the stated inconvenience into a supporting convenience.

questions.setup: Which report matches the editor's statement?
questions.prompt: 'I recommend that the final chapter end with the interview.'
options: The editor confirmed that the final chapter ended with the interview.
The editor recalled that the final chapter had ended with the interview.
The editor recommended ending the final chapter with the interview.
The editor assumed that the final chapter ended with the interview.
questions.explanation: Recommended ending reports the proposed action and does not assert that the chapter already has that ending.
feedback: Confirmed presents the ending as established rather than proposed.
Recalled places the ending in a remembered earlier version rather than recommending a change.
Recommended ending reports the proposed action and does not assert that the chapter already has that ending.
Assumed attributes a belief about the chapter's state, not a recommendation about how to revise it.

questions.setup: Which report most precisely captures the treasurer's response to the assignment?
questions.prompt: After being assigned the task, the treasurer said, 'I undertake to provide the figures before the review.'
options: The treasurer intended to provide the figures before the review.
The treasurer offered to provide the figures before the review.
The treasurer reported having provided the figures before the review.
The treasurer undertook to provide the figures before the review.
questions.explanation: Undertook records acceptance of responsibility for the future action, matching the explicit commitment.
feedback: Intended records a plan but does not by itself preserve the undertaking given to others.
Offered presents the work as volunteered for possible acceptance rather than an assignment already accepted as a commitment.
Reported having provided asserts earlier completion instead of the undertaking to provide figures.
Undertook records acceptance of responsibility for the future action, matching the explicit commitment.

questions.setup: Which report accurately represents the sponsor's position?
questions.prompt: The sponsor said, 'Reduce the entry fee, or I will withdraw my support.'
options: The sponsor threatened to withdraw support unless the fee was reduced.
The sponsor promised to withdraw support if the fee was reduced.
The sponsor announced withdrawal regardless of whether the fee was reduced.
The sponsor warned that reducing the fee would make support impossible.
questions.explanation: Threatened captures the use of withdrawal as pressure; unless preserves fee reduction as the way to avoid it.
feedback: Threatened captures the use of withdrawal as pressure; unless preserves fee reduction as the way to avoid it.
This makes reduction trigger withdrawal, reversing the offered way to avoid it, and promise mislabels the pressure tactic.
Regardless removes the condition and turns the threat into an unconditional decision.
This treats reduction as a cause preventing support, whereas the speaker wants the fee reduced in order to continue support.

questions.setup: Which report matches the apprentice's statement in this context?
questions.prompt: Seeing a light in the workshop, the apprentice said, 'The carpenter must be inside.'
options: The apprentice said the carpenter was required to remain inside.
The apprentice instructed the carpenter to stay inside.
The apprentice inferred that the carpenter was inside.
The apprentice confirmed from direct sight that the carpenter was inside.
questions.explanation: Inferred preserves the evidential meaning of must in the stated context.
feedback: Required to remain treats must as an obligation, but the light is being used as evidence for an inference.
The speaker draws a conclusion about location rather than addressing an instruction to the carpenter.
Inferred preserves the evidential meaning of must in the stated context.
The apprentice sees a light, not the carpenter directly, so this strengthens the source of knowledge.

questions.setup: An editor needs a neutral account of this exchange. Which report adds no unsupported attitude?
questions.prompt: In response to a routine biography question, the photographer said simply, 'I trained in Madrid.'
options: The photographer said that she had trained in Madrid.
The photographer boasted that she had trained in Madrid.
The photographer confessed that she had trained in Madrid.
The photographer conceded that she had trained in Madrid.
questions.explanation: Said attributes the information without adding an unsupported attitude to the photographer.
feedback: Said attributes the information without adding an unsupported attitude to the photographer.
Boasted adds an attitude of pride or self-praise not supplied by the routine answer.
Confessed presents the training as an admission of something blameworthy or previously concealed, which the source does not support.
Conceded suggests yielding a point, often reluctantly, rather than simply supplying biographical information.

questions.setup: What did the coordinator commit to in this statement?
questions.prompt: The coordinator said, 'I promise to check whether an accessible entrance is available.'
options: The coordinator promised that an accessible entrance would be available.
The coordinator promised to check the availability of an accessible entrance.
The coordinator confirmed that an accessible entrance was available.
The coordinator promised to make an accessible entrance available.
questions.explanation: The promised action is checking; availability remains the unresolved question to be checked.
feedback: This moves the promise from an inquiry to a guaranteed positive outcome.
The promised action is checking; availability remains the unresolved question to be checked.
Confirmed replaces a promised future check with an established answer.
Making an entrance available is an intervention, not the promised inquiry into whether one already is available.

questions.setup: The source words were 'The rooms feel unusually cramped.' Which mixed report accurately handles the quoted wording?
questions.prompt: The travel writer described the rooms to an interviewer.
options: The writer said the rooms were 'far too small.'
The writer said the rooms felt 'unusually cramped.'
The writer said the rooms were 'unfit for guests.'
The writer said the rooms 'needed rebuilding.'
questions.explanation: Unusually cramped reproduces an exact phrase while the surrounding report adjusts the verb from feel to felt.
feedback: Far too small may be a possible paraphrase, but quotation marks wrongly present those different words as exact speech.
Unusually cramped reproduces an exact phrase while the surrounding report adjusts the verb from feel to felt.
Unfit for guests introduces a stronger judgment and falsely quotes it as the writer's wording.
Needed rebuilding adds a remedy not stated in the source and presents invented words as a quotation.

questions.setup: What should an editor conclude about the reference of 'we' in this transcript?
questions.prompt: A chair told visiting delegates, 'We must revise our position.' The surrounding transcript does not identify whether 'we' includes the delegates.
options: We must become they because a report can never include its audience.
We must become you because the chair was addressing delegates.
We proves that the chair and delegates held the same position.
The included group needs clarification before a report can replace we with a specific group name.
questions.explanation: The missing group membership cannot be recovered from pronoun form alone; clarification avoids inventing who shares the position.
feedback: A reported 'we' may include or exclude the original audience; there is no automatic 'they' rule that resolves membership.
Addressing delegates does not make 'we' refer to the delegates alone.
'We' alone does not settle whether the delegates belong to the group whose position is discussed.
The missing group membership cannot be recovered from pronoun form alone; clarification avoids inventing who shares the position.

questions.setup: Which report accurately represents the forecaster's degree of confidence?
questions.prompt: The forecaster said, 'I don't think the fog will lift before noon.'
options: The forecaster ruled out the fog lifting before noon.
The forecaster confirmed that the fog had persisted until noon.
The forecaster expressed doubt that the fog would lift before noon.
The forecaster predicted that the fog would lift before noon.
questions.explanation: Expressed doubt preserves the negative expectation while allowing the possibility that the speaker's expectation is wrong.
feedback: Ruled out makes non-lifting certain or excludes the alternative more strongly than don't think does.
Confirmed ... had persisted replaces a prospective judgment with a verified retrospective outcome.
Expressed doubt preserves the negative expectation while allowing the possibility that the speaker's expectation is wrong.
This gives the positive prediction that the speaker explicitly doubts.

questions.setup: What is the difference between these two reports?
questions.prompt: A: 'The witness did not say that the door was locked.' B: 'The witness said that the door was not locked.'
options: Both report the witness's denial that the door was locked.
A withholds the positive statement; B attributes a negative statement to the witness.
A establishes an unlocked door, while B leaves its condition unmentioned.
Both imply that the witness refused to answer a question about the door.
questions.explanation: Negation scopes over saying in A and over the door's being locked in B.
feedback: Only B attributes the negative statement; A merely says the positive statement was not made.
Negation scopes over saying in A and over the door's being locked in B.
A does not establish the door's condition, and B explicitly reports a statement about that condition.
Neither sentence requires a refusal to answer; A could reflect a conversation about something else, and B gives a negative statement.

questions.setup: An examiner is discussing marks on an old canvas. Which report best captures this statement?
questions.prompt: 'These marks may indicate that the canvas is older than the frame.'
options: The examiner recommended recording the canvas as older than the frame.
The examiner suggested that the canvas might be older than the frame.
The examiner established that the canvas was older than the frame.
The examiner instructed the cataloguer to date the frame before the canvas.
questions.explanation: Suggested here introduces a tentative interpretation, and might preserves the examiner's uncertainty.
feedback: Recommended recording turns an evidential possibility into an administrative proposal.
Suggested here introduces a tentative interpretation, and might preserves the examiner's uncertainty.
Established upgrades may indicate into a firm finding.
An instruction about the order of dating objects is not the proposed explanation of the marks.

questions.setup: Which report of the composer's diary entry is supported?
questions.prompt: In her diary the composer wrote, 'I wish I hadn't discarded those sketches.' No apology to anyone is mentioned.
options: The composer apologized to her collaborators for discarding the sketches.
The composer expressed regret about discarding the sketches.
The composer denied having discarded the sketches.
The composer promised her collaborators not to discard the sketches.
questions.explanation: The wish expresses regret about the earlier action without requiring an apology or an audience.
feedback: An apology to collaborators adds both a speech act and recipients absent from the diary entry.
The wish expresses regret about the earlier action without requiring an apology or an audience.
The regret concerns discarding them; it is not a denial that discarding occurred.
A future promise to collaborators replaces retrospective regret and invents an addressee.

questions.setup: Which report is warranted by the mentor's words and the available context?
questions.prompt: The mentor said, 'I strongly advise you not to abandon the apprenticeship.' The apprentice's response is unknown.
options: The mentor dissuaded the apprentice from abandoning the apprenticeship.
The mentor persuaded the apprentice to continue the apprenticeship.
The mentor prevented the apprentice from abandoning the apprenticeship.
The mentor advised the apprentice against abandoning the apprenticeship.
questions.explanation: Advised against reports the counsel without committing to whether the apprentice followed it.
feedback: Dissuaded normally presents the discouragement as successful, but the response is unknown.
Persuaded presents a successful change of decision rather than advice with an unknown response.
Prevented asserts that abandonment was stopped, going beyond what the speech establishes.
Advised against reports the counsel without committing to whether the apprentice followed it.

questions.setup: Which paraphrase preserves the captain's account?
questions.prompt: The captain reported asking the crew to check the lifeboat ropes.
options: The captain reported that the crew had checked the ropes.
The crew asked the captain to report on the checked ropes.
The captain asked the crew to report that he had checked the ropes.
The captain said he had asked the crew to check the ropes.
questions.explanation: Reported asking means he reported his own earlier request; the crew's checking remains the requested action.
feedback: This moves the content from a request to a completed crew action that the source does not assert.
This reverses the requesting roles and treats checking as completed.
This makes reporting the crew's requested action and makes the captain the checker, changing both layers.
Reported asking means he reported his own earlier request; the crew's checking remains the requested action.

questions.setup: In this passage the delegate is rejecting the allocation's fairness. Which report captures the purpose of the question?
questions.prompt: Looking at the unequal allocation, the delegate exclaimed, 'How could anyone call this fair?'
options: The delegate asked which person had used the word fair.
The delegate sought instructions on how to make the allocation fair.
The delegate admitted that the allocation could reasonably be called fair.
The delegate challenged the claim that the allocation was fair.
questions.explanation: Challenged captures the objection to describing the allocation as fair without inventing an information request.
feedback: A search for a named person would treat the rhetorical anyone question as a literal identity inquiry.
How could anyone call this fair challenges a description; it is not a request for a procedure to improve the allocation.
Admitted that it could be fair reverses the rejection conveyed in the supplied rhetorical context.
Challenged captures the objection to describing the allocation as fair without inventing an information request.

questions.setup: A reporter needs a neutral account of this disagreement. Which version keeps the disputed description attributed?
questions.prompt: The authority called the six-month closure 'a minor adjustment.' Residents rejected that description.
options: The authority described the closure as 'a minor adjustment,' a description residents rejected.
The minor adjustment announced by the authority was rejected by residents.
Residents rejected the authority despite its closure being only a minor adjustment.
The closure was a minor adjustment, although residents denied that fact.
questions.explanation: Described ... as keeps the evaluative label with the authority, and the final phrase records residents' rejection.
feedback: Described ... as keeps the evaluative label with the authority, and the final phrase records residents' rejection.
The minor adjustment uses the label as the reporter's identifying description rather than clearly attributing it.
Only a minor adjustment adopts the authority's evaluation and adds despite as the reporter's contrast.
Was a minor adjustment asserts the label, and that fact further treats it as established rather than disputed.

questions.setup: Which report asks for the same information as the visitor's question?
questions.prompt: The visitor asked the curator, 'Who do you believe repaired the telescope?'
options: The visitor asked who the curator believed had repaired the telescope.
The visitor asked who believed that the curator had repaired the telescope.
The visitor asked whether the curator believed the telescope had been repaired.
The visitor asked whom the curator had persuaded to repair the telescope.
questions.explanation: The curator remains the holder of the belief, and who asks for the repairer within that belief.
feedback: The curator remains the holder of the belief, and who asks for the repairer within that belief.
This makes the unknown person a believer and the curator the repairer, reversing the question's roles.
Whether changes the question from the repairer's identity to whether any repair occurred.
Persuaded introduces a causal speech act and a chosen repairer absent from the original belief question.

questions.setup: Which report accurately captures the organizer's response?
questions.prompt: The organizer said, 'I never suggested that the volunteers were unreliable.'
options: The organizer denied that the volunteers were unreliable.
The organizer admitted having suggested that the volunteers were reliable.
The organizer denied having suggested that the volunteers were unreliable.
The organizer said that nobody had ever questioned the volunteers' reliability.
questions.explanation: Denied having suggested keeps the negation over the earlier speech act and preserves its embedded content.
feedback: This changes the target of the denial from the organizer's earlier speech to the volunteers' actual reliability.
The source denies a particular suggestion; it does not admit making the opposite suggestion.
Denied having suggested keeps the negation over the earlier speech act and preserves its embedded content.
Nobody broadens the denial from the organizer alone to every possible speaker, and questioned is broader than the specified suggestion.

questions.setup: A journalist is combining the hiker's account with independently established information. Which version accurately represents both sources?
questions.prompt: The hiker said, 'A masked volunteer rescued me.' The reporter knows the volunteer was the mayor; the hiker did not recognize the mayor.
options: The hiker identified the mayor as the masked volunteer who had rescued him.
The hiker said the masked volunteer who rescued him was the mayor.
The hiker said a masked volunteer had rescued him; the volunteer was the mayor, whom he had not recognized.
The hiker recognized his rescuer as the mayor but described the mayor as a volunteer.
questions.explanation: The speech report retains the hiker's description, while the separate clause supplies the reporter's identification and the hiker's lack of recognition.
feedback: Identified attributes recognition of the mayor to the hiker, contrary to the stated limit of his knowledge.
This places the identity claim inside what the hiker said, attributing information he did not have.
The speech report retains the hiker's description, while the separate clause supplies the reporter's identification and the hiker's lack of recognition.
Recognized asserts the very recognition the context rules out and invents a deliberate choice of description.

questions.setup: An arts journalist is summarizing the dancer's response. Which report is supported?
questions.prompt: The dancer said, 'I have no recollection of agreeing to an encore.'
options: The dancer denied having agreed to an encore.
The dancer said she could not recall agreeing to an encore.
The dancer acknowledged agreeing to an encore but said the agreement had been forgotten.
The dancer denied having forgotten her agreement to an encore.
questions.explanation: Could not recall preserves the speaker's stated memory limit without settling the underlying event.
feedback: Denied agreeing asserts a negative position on the event, stronger than the absence of recollection.
Could not recall preserves the speaker's stated memory limit without settling the underlying event.
Acknowledged agreeing adds acceptance that agreement occurred; the original memory claim does not supply it.
Denied having forgotten presents a defense of retained memory and treats an agreement as given, neither of which matches the source.

questions.setup: Which conclusion about the historian's position follows from this statement?
questions.prompt: The historian said, 'I withdraw my earlier statement that the letter was forged; I cannot currently establish its authenticity either way.'
options: The historian admitted knowingly inventing the forgery allegation.
The historian established that the letter was authentic.
The historian ceased endorsing the forgery claim while leaving authenticity unresolved.
The historian maintained the forgery claim but declined to provide evidence.
questions.explanation: The withdrawal removes the earlier endorsement, while the stated evidence limit leaves both authenticity possibilities open.
feedback: Withdrawing a claim does not itself admit that the earlier statement was knowingly false.
The historian explicitly leaves authenticity open rather than establishing it.
The withdrawal removes the earlier endorsement, while the stated evidence limit leaves both authenticity possibilities open.
Maintained contradicts withdraw; the source relinquishes the claim rather than merely withholding evidence for it.

questions.setup: A novelist uses this passage to convey Mara's unspoken response. Which account explains how the viewpoint is handled?
questions.prompt: Mara shut the ledger. How could they expect her to pay for this? She would challenge it tomorrow.
options: The third-person her assigns the rhetorical complaint to the narrator's own voice rather than Mara's.
Tomorrow dates the narrator's act of composition rather than Mara's imagined next step.
Would challenge reports a spoken promise whose exact words are recoverable from the passage.
Third-person past narration carries Mara's rhetorical reaction and her prospective tomorrow without quoting an actual speech event.
questions.explanation: The third-person past frame combines with the character's expressive question and forward-looking time word, a characteristic free-indirect presentation.
feedback: Free indirect thought can use third-person reference while conveying the character's question rather than the narrator's independent complaint.
Tomorrow can be oriented to the character's experienced moment; it need not date the narrator's act of writing.
The specified passage presents unspoken thought and does not provide either a speech event or an exact quotation.
The third-person past frame combines with the character's expressive question and forward-looking time word, a characteristic free-indirect presentation.

questions.setup: Which account best captures what the climber communicates?
questions.prompt: The climber wrote, 'To say the ascent was demanding would be an understatement.'
options: The climber presented demanding as too weak, without reporting an actual use of the description.
The climber reported having used demanding earlier and now judged that description inadequate.
The climber presented demanding as too strong while acknowledging that the ascent was difficult.
The climber considered whether demanding was adequate but left that question unresolved.
questions.explanation: Calling the formulation an understatement communicates a stronger assessment while leaving the formulation itself hypothetical.
feedback: Calling the formulation an understatement communicates a stronger assessment while leaving the formulation itself hypothetical.
To say ... would be evaluates a hypothetical formulation; it does not report an earlier use of that wording.
An understatement falls short of the intended strength; it is not a description judged too strong.
Would be an understatement supplies the evaluation rather than leaving adequacy as an unresolved question.

questions.setup: A review editor is summarizing the critic's position. Which summary follows from the sentence?
questions.prompt: The critic wrote, 'I wouldn't call the performance a failure, but that is not an endorsement.'
options: The critic refused an earlier request to describe the performance as a failure.
The critic endorsed the performance as a qualified success.
The critic resisted the failure label while withholding endorsement.
The critic had called the performance a failure but later withdrew that judgment.
questions.explanation: The report keeps both the resistance to calling it a failure and the explicit limit on positive commitment.
feedback: Wouldn't call expresses a qualified evaluative stance here; it does not report an earlier request and refusal.
The second clause explicitly withholds endorsement, so a qualified-success endorsement goes beyond the stated position.
The report keeps both the resistance to calling it a failure and the explicit limit on positive commitment.
The source gives no earlier use of the failure label or later withdrawal of it.

questions.setup: How are the prediction and the correction attributed in this sentence?
questions.prompt: The fare would fall, the operator said, which was untrue: it rose instead.
options: The operator supplies the prediction; the narrator supplies its correction and the contrasting outcome.
The operator is reported as saying both that the fare would fall and that this prediction was untrue.
The narrator endorses a fare reduction but attributes the rise to the operator's account.
The narrator reports the operator as correcting an earlier prediction while leaving the actual fare unspecified.
questions.explanation: The parenthetical assigns the prediction to the operator, while the supplementary clause and final explanation correct it from the narrator's viewpoint.
feedback: The parenthetical assigns the prediction to the operator, while the supplementary clause and final explanation correct it from the narrator's viewpoint.
The supplementary correction follows the parenthetical attribution and belongs to the narrator's account, not to the operator's quoted prediction.
The narrator rejects the fare-reduction prediction and asserts a rise, not the reverse.
The operator is attributed the prediction, not its correction, and it rose instead supplies an actual outcome.

questions.setup: Which reading of the investigator's account is supported by the sentence?
questions.prompt: As far as the investigator knew, the harbor master had said that no vessel was missing.
options: The harbor master is quoted as qualifying the no-missing-vessel claim by her own limited knowledge.
The investigator independently establishes that no vessel was missing but is uncertain who said so.
The investigator qualifies only the speaker's identity, treating the statement and its content as established.
The investigator qualifies the speech account; the harbor master's own certainty is unspecified.
questions.explanation: The initial qualification is anchored to the investigator and scopes over the account of the harbor master's speech, not over a qualification uttered by the harbor master.
feedback: As far as the investigator knew is the reporter's framing, not wording attributed to the harbor master about her own knowledge.
The sentence does not independently establish vessel status; that content remains inside the account of the harbor master's statement.
The qualification scopes over the whole account of what was said; the sentence does not confine uncertainty to the speaker's identity or verify the content.
The initial qualification is anchored to the investigator and scopes over the account of the harbor master's speech, not over a qualification uttered by the harbor master.

questions.setup: An editor is preparing a formal account of a dialectal transcript. Which editorial judgment is sound?
questions.prompt: A man says, 'She don't owe me nothing,' using a dialect in which the negatives combine to express one negation.
options: An indirect report may say that she owed him nothing; an exact quotation should retain his wording.
Changing the quote to 'She doesn't owe me anything' preserves an exact quotation because the meaning is unchanged.
A formal paraphrase should say that she owed him something, applying logical cancellation to the negatives.
Retaining the dialect in a quotation commits the editor to using that dialect in the surrounding narrative.
questions.explanation: Formal indirect reporting can render the negative meaning in standard English while keeping the boundary between paraphrase and exact quotation clear.
feedback: Formal indirect reporting can render the negative meaning in standard English while keeping the boundary between paraphrase and exact quotation clear.
Preserving meaning does not make edited wording an exact quotation; grammatical standardization changes the words actually spoken.
The stipulated dialectal construction expresses a single negation; logical cancellation would reverse its meaning.
Quoted source language can differ from the register of the editor's own prose without changing the editor's narrative voice.

questions.setup: An editor is comparing an owner's announcement with a later review. Which account of their wording and stance is supported?
questions.prompt: The owner sincerely called the hotel's opening 'a triumph.' A review used 'a triumph' as its heading, listed double bookings and missed meals, and concluded, 'A triumph, then, provided one was not a guest.'
options: The reviewer attributes the ironic judgment to the owner by repeating the owner's exact phrase.
The exact repetition makes both writers responsible for the same positive evaluation, despite the review's complaints.
The reviewer preserves the owner's words while reversing their evaluative force in the review.
The ironic echo withdraws the attribution, suggesting that the owner never actually used the phrase.
questions.explanation: The original wording remains accurately attributed, while its ironic re-use signals the reviewer's opposing evaluation.
feedback: The owner used the words sincerely; the irony arises in the reviewer's re-use, not in the owner's original announcement.
Repeating words preserves lexical material, but the new context can change their pragmatic force rather than reproduce endorsement.
The original wording remains accurately attributed, while its ironic re-use signals the reviewer's opposing evaluation.
Irony can reject an evaluation while still accurately quoting its source; it does not deny that the owner used the phrase.

questions.setup: A reporter is summarizing this exchange. Which account accurately represents what each person said?
questions.prompt: The manager asked the employee, 'Why did you leak the roster?' The employee replied, 'I didn't leak it.'
options: After leaking the roster, the employee denied doing so when asked for a reason.
The manager asked why the employee had leaked the roster; the employee denied having leaked it.
The manager asked whether the employee had leaked the roster, and the employee declined to answer.
The employee explained why the roster had been leaked while denying responsibility for its contents.
questions.explanation: The two speech acts remain attributed to their respective speakers, and the contested leak is not separately asserted as narrator fact.
feedback: After leaking puts the leak into the narrator's factual account, despite the employee's explicit rejection of that premise.
The two speech acts remain attributed to their respective speakers, and the contested leak is not separately asserted as narrator fact.
Whether replaces the manager's premise-bearing why question, and declined to answer erases the actual denial.
The employee supplies no explanation for a leak and denies the act, not merely responsibility for the roster's contents.

questions.setup: Which paraphrase asks the same question?
questions.prompt: Which accusation did the witness say the curator had denied making?
options: Which accusation did the witness deny having made about the curator?
Which accusation did the curator say the witness had denied making?
Which accusation did the witness say the curator had disproved?
According to the witness's account, which accusation did the curator deny having made?
questions.explanation: The witness remains the source of the account, while the curator denies being the maker of the accusation being asked about.
feedback: This makes the witness the person denying authorship and turns the curator into the target of the accusation.
This exchanges the source of the report and the person denying that they made the accusation.
Disproved changes a denial of making an accusation into a successful refutation of the accusation's content.
The witness remains the source of the account, while the curator denies being the maker of the accusation being asked about.

questions.setup: How should a minute-taker summarize the delegate's argument?
questions.prompt: The delegate said, 'Even if your cost estimate is correct, it does not follow that we should cancel the festival.'
options: The delegate accepted the estimate as correct but reluctantly agreed to cancel the festival.
The delegate rejected the cost estimate because canceling the festival would be undesirable.
The delegate rejected cancellation as a necessary conclusion even on the assumption that the estimate was correct.
The delegate conceded both the estimate's accuracy and the need to cancel, while questioning the timing.
questions.explanation: Even if grants the estimate hypothetically, while does not follow rejects the necessity of the cancellation conclusion.
feedback: The source neither accepts the estimate as fact nor agrees to cancellation; it challenges the proposed inference.
The argument does not reject the estimate or make its truth depend on the desirability of cancellation.
Even if grants the estimate hypothetically, while does not follow rejects the necessity of the cancellation conclusion.
This turns a hypothetical concession and rejected inference into acceptance of both claims and invents a timing concern.

questions.setup: Which conclusion is supported by this sentence?
questions.prompt: Had the inspector been asked, she would have said that the bolts were unsafe.
options: The inspector made the unsafe-bolts statement, but whether she had been asked remains uncertain.
The narrator confirms unsafe bolts and leaves only the inspector's exact wording hypothetical.
The inspector refused to state that the bolts were unsafe because no one had asked her.
The saying is hypothetical and does not independently verify the condition of the bolts.
questions.explanation: The conditional governs would have said, and the unsafe-bolts claim remains embedded within that hypothetical speech.
feedback: Would have said places the saying itself within the unreal scenario rather than asserting that it occurred.
The bolts' condition is inside the content of the hypothetical saying; the narrator does not separately verify it.
The sentence gives a counterfactual response, not an actual refusal or a reason for refusing.
The conditional governs would have said, and the unsafe-bolts claim remains embedded within that hypothetical speech.

questions.setup: An editor wants to characterize the original conditional. What does the surviving report allow the editor to conclude?
questions.prompt: The porter said that if the guests left, he would follow them. No original quotation or wider context survives.
options: The report preserves an originally remote left/would conditional.
The original condition could have been open or more hypothetical.
The report backshifts an original leave/will conditional.
The report treats the guests' departure as an established event.
questions.explanation: Both an original open leave/will conditional and an original left/would conditional can produce this report, so the original stance is not uniquely recoverable.
feedback: An original left/would conditional is possible, but the same report could result from backshifting an open condition.
Both an original open leave/will conditional and an original left/would conditional can produce this report, so the original stance is not uniquely recoverable.
An original leave/will conditional is possible, but backshift is not the only route to the surviving form.
If the guests left does not by itself assert a completed departure, and would follow remains conditional.

questions.setup: What does this sentence establish about the result of the mediation?
questions.prompt: The mediator persuaded both teams to state publicly that the joint plan was workable. Their private opinions were not recorded.
options: The mediator convinced both teams that the plan was workable, and they reported that shared belief.
The mediator established that the plan was workable because both teams sincerely endorsed it.
The mediator reported that both teams had privately believed the plan workable before the discussion.
The mediator secured public statements; the teams' private convictions remain unspecified.
questions.explanation: Persuaded them to state concerns a successful action commitment; it does not establish sincere acceptance of the statement's content.
feedback: Convinced that changes the effect from producing a statement to producing a belief.
Neither the plan's actual workability nor the sincerity of the teams' public wording is established.
The sentence records no private beliefs or their earlier timing; it reports the mediator's success in obtaining statements.
Persuaded them to state concerns a successful action commitment; it does not establish sincere acceptance of the statement's content.

questions.setup: Which summary accurately captures the architect's correction?
questions.prompt: The architect said, 'I called the design "unprecedented", not "unacceptable".' No further evaluation was given.
options: The architect denied finding the design unacceptable.
The architect corrected the word attributed to her, without settling whether she considered the design acceptable.
The architect withdrew a judgment that the design was unprecedented and endorsed it as acceptable.
The architect admitted disapproving of the design but preferred a less direct expression.
questions.explanation: The contrast corrects which description she used; 'unprecedented' does not itself mean 'acceptable' or 'unacceptable'.
feedback: Not having used 'unacceptable' does not establish that she did not privately judge it unacceptable.
The contrast corrects which description she used; 'unprecedented' does not itself mean 'acceptable' or 'unacceptable'.
She maintains 'unprecedented' as her wording and supplies no endorsement of acceptability.
The statement does not admit disapproval or say 'unprecedented' was an indirect substitute for it.

questions.setup: Which conclusion follows from this sentence?
questions.prompt: Not all the witnesses denied seeing the cyclist.
options: There was at least one non-denial, which need not have been an admission.
Some witnesses admitted seeing the cyclist.
None of the witnesses denied seeing the cyclist.
At least one witness saw the cyclist, whether or not that witness admitted it.
questions.explanation: Negating all requires at least one non-denial but does not identify the person's response as an admission.
feedback: Negating all requires at least one non-denial but does not identify the person's response as an admission.
Failure to deny can include silence or another response; it does not necessarily constitute an admission.
Not all leaves open that some witnesses did deny it, so none is stronger than the source.
The sentence quantifies over denials, not over verified sightings; a non-denial does not prove the sighting occurred.

questions.setup: How does the narrator present the newsletter's account?
questions.prompt: If the newsletter's account is accurate, the choir has withdrawn from the festival.
options: The newsletter says the choir will withdraw if the newsletter's account is accurate.
The narrator's conclusion about withdrawal is conditional on accepting the newsletter's account.
The narrator confirms withdrawal and merely doubts the newsletter's explanation for it.
The newsletter makes its own accuracy conditional on whether the choir withdraws.
questions.explanation: The if clause marks the narrator's evidential reservation about drawing the withdrawal conclusion from the source.
feedback: This moves the narrator's source-accuracy condition into the content of the newsletter and changes a reported withdrawal into a future one.
The if clause marks the narrator's evidential reservation about drawing the withdrawal conclusion from the source.
The condition qualifies the conclusion that withdrawal occurred, not just an explanation for a confirmed event.
This reverses the dependency and assigns the condition to the newsletter rather than the narrator.

questions.setup: Which report of the director's position is justified?
questions.prompt: The director said, 'My objection is not to those remarks themselves, but to your making them in front of the clients.'
options: The director criticized the audience choice without settling the remarks' truth.
The director denied the remarks' truth because clients had heard them.
The director endorsed the remarks as true but wanted the clients to believe something different.
The director objected to anyone making the remarks in any setting, including before clients.
questions.explanation: The contrast places the objection on the public audience; absence of an objection to the remarks themselves does not settle their truth.
feedback: The contrast places the objection on the public audience; absence of an objection to the remarks themselves does not settle their truth.
The director does not deny the remarks or make their truth depend on who heard them.
No truth endorsement or wish to mislead clients is stated; both would add motives or commitments.
Any setting removes the speaker's explicit distinction between the remarks themselves and making them before clients.

questions.setup: You work in a shop. Your sister is a driver. Keep both facts in two complete sentences.
questions.prompt: Which version separates the two statements correctly?
options: I work in a shop my sister is a driver.
I work in a shop. My sister is a driver.
I work. In a shop my sister is a driver.
I work in a shop, my sister is a driver.
questions.explanation: Each statement has its own subject and verb. A full stop separates them while keeping 'in a shop' with your work.
feedback: The second statement starts at 'my sister'; it needs a sentence boundary.
Each statement has its own subject and verb. A full stop separates them while keeping 'in a shop' with your work.
This moves 'in a shop' to the statement about your sister and loses the stated location of your work.
A comma alone does not separate these two statements into sentences.

questions.setup: Write a complete sentence, not a label.
questions.prompt: Which sentence tells us where the keys are?
options: The keys on the table.
On the table the keys.
Are on the table.
The keys are on the table.
questions.explanation: 'The keys' is the subject and 'are' completes the statement about their location.
feedback: This names the keys and their location but is missing 'are'.
Moving the place phrase does not supply the missing verb.
'Are' needs a subject here: 'The keys are...'
'The keys' is the subject and 'are' completes the statement about their location.

questions.setup: A sign gives visitors an instruction.
questions.prompt: Which is a complete, correctly written instruction?
options: Your name here.
Writing your name here.
To write your name here.
Write your name here.
questions.explanation: A command can begin with 'Write'; the person being addressed is understood.
feedback: This could be a form label, but it is not a complete instruction sentence.
The -ing phrase does not give the instruction as a sentence.
'To write' introduces an infinitive phrase rather than the command needed here.
A command can begin with 'Write'; the person being addressed is understood.

questions.setup: Use standard sentence punctuation in an email.
questions.prompt: Which version correctly asks about the price?
options: How much is the ticket?
How much is the ticket.
How much? Is the ticket.
How much is? The ticket.
questions.explanation: The whole question ends after 'ticket' and takes a question mark.
feedback: The whole question ends after 'ticket' and takes a question mark.
This is a direct question, so use a question mark rather than a full stop.
The mark splits the question before its verb and leaves 'Is the ticket' unfinished.
The subject belongs inside the question; do not separate 'the ticket' from 'is'.

questions.setup: Write a short introduction using standard capitals and full stops.
questions.prompt: Which introduction starts each sentence correctly?
options: My name is Adil. i live in Leeds.
my name is Adil. I live in Leeds.
My name is Adil. I live in Leeds.
My name is Adil i live in Leeds.
questions.explanation: Both sentences start with capitals, and the first ends before 'I'.
feedback: The pronoun 'I' is always capitalized, including at the start of a sentence.
Start the first sentence with a capital 'M'.
Both sentences start with capitals, and the first ends before 'I'.
A new statement needs a boundary before 'I', which also needs a capital.

questions.setup: The email needs a complete statement about an appointment.
questions.prompt: Which option is a complete statement on its own?
options: At ten tomorrow.
My appointment tomorrow.
My appointment is at ten.
Is at ten tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The subject 'My appointment' and the verb 'is' form a complete statement.
feedback: This can answer 'When?', but it is not the complete statement requested.
The noun and time word need a verb to make a statement.
The subject 'My appointment' and the verb 'is' form a complete statement.
The reader needs to know what 'is at ten'; add a subject.

questions.setup: Tell a colleague about two things you sell. Use one sentence.
questions.prompt: Which version keeps the two objects together correctly?
options: We sell bread. And milk.
We sell. Bread and milk.
We sell bread milk.
We sell bread and milk.
questions.explanation: 'And' joins two objects of the single verb 'sell'.
feedback: 'And milk' is separated from the verb it depends on; the task asks for one sentence.
The full stop breaks the verb away from its objects.
The two separate items need a link such as 'and'.
'And' joins two objects of the single verb 'sell'.

questions.setup: Use ordinary written English, not note form.
questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes today's weather?
options: Is cold today.
It cold today.
Cold today it.
It is cold today.
questions.explanation: A weather statement uses 'it' as the subject: 'It is cold'.
feedback: The weather verb needs 'it' in a complete statement.
The adjective 'cold' needs the verb 'is' here.
These words do not form the subject-verb order of the required statement.
A weather statement uses 'it' as the subject: 'It is cold'.

questions.setup: Two neighbours arrive at different times. Write two sentences.
questions.prompt: Where should the full stop go in 'Eva arrives at six Ben arrives at seven'?
options: Eva arrives at six. Ben arrives at seven.
Eva arrives. At six Ben arrives at seven.
Eva arrives at six Ben. Arrives at seven.
Eva arrives at six Ben arrives. At seven.
questions.explanation: The boundary comes before the second subject, 'Ben', keeping each time with its person.
feedback: The boundary comes before the second subject, 'Ben', keeping each time with its person.
This attaches 'at six' to Ben's sentence and does not preserve Eva's arrival time.
'Ben' belongs with 'arrives at seven', not with Eva's time.
'At seven' is only a time phrase, not a complete second sentence.

questions.setup: You want to say that a cafe is not open.
questions.prompt: Which option is a complete negative sentence?
options: The cafe not open.
The cafe not is open.
The cafe is not open.
Not open the cafe.
questions.explanation: 'Is not open' gives a complete negative description of the cafe.
feedback: 'Not' does not replace the verb; use 'is not open'.
Put 'not' after 'is': 'The cafe is not open'.
'Is not open' gives a complete negative description of the cafe.
This order does not form the negative statement requested.

questions.setup: Keep this as one ordinary sentence.
questions.prompt: Which version correctly says what the bus driver does?
options: The bus driver, checks the tickets.
The bus driver checks the tickets.
The bus driver. Checks the tickets.
The bus, driver checks the tickets.
questions.explanation: 'The bus driver' stays together as the subject of 'checks'.
feedback: Do not put a comma between this subject and its verb.
'The bus driver' stays together as the subject of 'checks'.
The full stop leaves the subject without its verb and the second part without a subject.
The comma splits 'bus driver', which names one job.

questions.setup: Write a complete sentence about your room.
questions.prompt: Which version correctly says that the room contains a desk?
options: There a desk in my room.
There is a desk in my room.
A desk there in my room.
Is a desk in my room.
questions.explanation: 'There is' introduces something that exists in a place.
feedback: 'There' needs 'is' before the thing being introduced.
'There is' introduces something that exists in a place.
These words name the object and place but give no complete predicate.
The introductory subject 'There' is missing.

questions.setup: Make one complete statement about two actions by the same person.
questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes Ruth's morning?
options: Ruth opens the shop. And checks the till.
Ruth opens the shop and checks the till.
Ruth opens. The shop and checks the till.
Ruth the shop opens and the till checks.
questions.explanation: Both actions share the subject 'Ruth'; repeating her name is unnecessary.
feedback: The full stop separates the second action from its shared subject.
Both actions share the subject 'Ruth'; repeating her name is unnecessary.
'The shop' belongs with 'opens'; the break interrupts that connection.
Ordinary statements put these objects after their verbs: 'opens the shop' and 'checks the till'.

questions.setup: Use two normally punctuated sentences in a message.
questions.prompt: Which version separates a greeting from a question correctly?
options: Hello. Are you free today?
Hello. are you free today?
Hello are. You free today?
