feedback: 'More than one' explicitly rules out an exact count of one; the agreement does not override that meaning.
This construction keeps singular grammatical agreement with 'one visitor' although it describes multiple visitors.
The display is inside the complement of 'about' and does not control the main auxiliary.
Whether visitors are identified does not determine this agreement pattern.

questions.setup: Two editors suggest 'None of the submitted designs is suitable' and 'None of the submitted designs are suitable.'
questions.prompt: Which comment avoids an overstrict agreement rule?
options: The singular version means one design is suitable, while the plural means none is.
Both agreements are established, with different ways of viewing the set.
The plural version must refer to a different set of designs from the singular version.
The singular version is possible only if one design was submitted.
questions.explanation: None with plural reference admits singular and plural agreement, with singular often favored in more formal styles.
feedback: Both versions negate suitability; number choice does not reverse none's meaning.
None with plural reference admits singular and plural agreement, with singular often favored in more formal styles.
Both can refer to exactly the same submitted set.
None of a plural set can take singular agreement emphasizing not one of its members.

questions.setup: A journal consistently treats 'data' as plural. A new sentence begins 'A complete set of these data ...'.
questions.prompt: Which explanation correctly identifies the number of the main subject?
options: The main subject must be plural because the journal requires plural agreement for data.
The demonstrative these makes the entire set phrase plural.
The main subject is singular because set is its head, even under the journal's plural-data rule.
The main subject is singular only if the set contains one datum.
questions.explanation: 'A complete set' is the head phrase; plural 'these data' belongs inside its of complement and does not determine the main verb.
feedback: That policy governs 'data' when it controls agreement, not every larger phrase containing the word.
'These' modifies 'data' inside the complement; it does not change 'a complete set' into several sets.
'A complete set' is the head phrase; plural 'these data' belongs inside its of complement and does not determine the main verb.
One set may contain many data points and still be grammatically singular.

questions.setup: A budget report describes the use of funding and the participation of named staff members.
questions.prompt: Choose the standard written pair: Sixty percent of the funding ___ allocated, and sixty percent of the staff members ___ enrolled.
options: are / are
is / is
are / is
is / are
questions.explanation: Percentage subjects take agreement suited to what is measured: funding is singular mass, staff members plural count.
feedback: Staff members takes are, but funding is an uncountable amount and takes is.
The funding clause is right, but the staff-member percentage refers to plural individuals.
This reverses the number of the mass funding and countable staff members.
Percentage subjects take agreement suited to what is measured: funding is singular mass, staff members plural count.

questions.setup: An article uses the phrase 'the unemployed' to refer to people without jobs.
questions.prompt: Which explanation supports 'The unemployed are eligible for the scheme'?
options: Are is required because eligible is a plural adjective.
The article the makes every following subject plural.
The adjective phrase names a group of people and takes plural agreement.
Are makes the phrase refer to several unemployment programmes.
questions.explanation: 'The unemployed' is a conventional adjective-based expression for people as a class, so the verb is plural.
feedback: English adjectives such as 'eligible' do not take plural endings or control the subject's number.
'The' occurs with singular and plural subjects; it does not determine number by itself.
'The unemployed' is a conventional adjective-based expression for people as a class, so the verb is plural.
The subject denotes people, not the schemes for which they may qualify.

questions.setup: A formal memoir says, 'Many a visitor has paused at that window.'
questions.prompt: Which account preserves both the grammar and the meaning?
options: The expression refers to many visitors but uses singular noun and verb forms.
The sentence refers to one unusually frequent visitor.
Has shows that many a must be changed to a single.
Many a is a plural noun phrase that requires have in a memoir.
questions.explanation: Many a is a formal distributive expression: the quantity is large, but each imagined visitor is grammatically singular.
feedback: Many a is a formal distributive expression: the quantity is large, but each imagined visitor is grammatically singular.
Many a distributes the experience over many visitors; it does not describe repeated visits by one person.
Singular agreement is normal in many a plus a singular noun and does not require reducing the number meant.
The formal construction conventionally uses a singular noun and singular agreement.

questions.setup: A house style uses agreement with the nearer alternative in either/or subjects of mixed number.
questions.prompt: Which sentence follows that stated convention?
options: Either the director or the assistants are attending.
Either the assistants or the director are attending.
Either the director or the assistants is attending.
Either the assistants or the director have confirmed.
questions.explanation: The nearer alternative assistants is plural, so are follows the stated proximity convention.
feedback: The nearer alternative assistants is plural, so are follows the stated proximity convention.
With the singular director nearest, that convention calls for is.
The nearer assistants is plural; is follows the farther singular alternative instead.
The nearer director is singular, so this convention requires has confirmed.

questions.setup: A report mentions the directors-general of two separate agencies.
questions.prompt: Which explanation supports 'The directors-general have approved the exchange'?
options: General refers to all the directors together, so it makes the subject singular.
Have agrees with the plural agencies mentioned in the context rather than the subject.
Directors is the plural head of the compound subject.
The hyphen makes have possible even if there is just one director-general.
questions.explanation: The compound title pluralizes director, so directors-general denotes multiple office-holders and takes have.
feedback: General is part of the title and does not override the plural head directors.
The actual subject directors-general already supplies plural number; agreement does not depend on an earlier contextual noun.
The compound title pluralizes director, so directors-general denotes multiple office-holders and takes have.
Punctuation does not create plural number; a single director-general takes has.

questions.setup: A tutor contrasts 'Planning and testing are separate stages' with 'Planning and testing is one integrated process in our workshop.'
questions.prompt: Which comment best explains the agreement contrast?
options: The singular version is possible only because workshop is singular.
The plural version refers to many workshops, and the singular to one.
Plural treats them as separate activities; singular presents their combination as one process.
The first sentence changes the activities into finished past events.
questions.explanation: Coordinated activities normally take plural agreement, but a clearly unified activity can receive singular notional agreement.
feedback: Workshop is inside a later prepositional phrase and does not control the subject's agreement.
The number contrast concerns the activities or their combination, not the number of workshops.
Coordinated activities normally take plural agreement, but a clearly unified activity can receive singular notional agreement.
Present are does not give the activities past time; both examples are present descriptions.

questions.setup: An editor is discussing the exact wording 'The offices are closed', not the events the sentence reports.
questions.prompt: Which sentence preserves that wording and gives the single quotation standard agreement?
options: 'The offices are closed' are printed at the top of the notice.
'The offices is closed' is printed at the top of the notice.
'The offices are closed' is printed at the top of the notice.
'The offices is closed' are printed at the top of the notice.
questions.explanation: The quotation is one piece of wording, so the outside verb is singular is. The original are remains inside the preserved quotation.
feedback: This preserves the words but incorrectly lets plural offices control the outside verb, whose subject is the single quotation.
The outside is is appropriate, but the option changes the supplied quotation. Quoting nonstandard wording is possible; preserving the specified wording is the requirement here.
The quotation is one piece of wording, so the outside verb is singular is. The original are remains inside the preserved quotation.
This changes the required quotation and uses plural outside agreement for one quoted sentence. Both conflict with the editing task.

questions.setup: The delayed issue is whether two venues can open, rather than the venues themselves.
questions.prompt: Choose the standard formal completion: Whether the venues can open ___ still uncertain.
options: is
are
have been
were
questions.explanation: The whether clause names one unresolved issue and takes singular main-clause agreement.
feedback: The whether clause names one unresolved issue and takes singular main-clause agreement.
Venues is the subject inside the whether clause, not the head of the main subject as a whole.
Have would give plural agreement to the single clausal subject; has been would be grammatical with a different tense.
Were would incorrectly treat this single factual issue as plural in the ordinary declarative reading.

questions.setup: Several engineers have worked offshore. Mara belongs to that group.
questions.prompt: Choose the formal present-perfect completion making 'who' refer to those engineers: Mara is one of the engineers who ___ worked offshore.
options: has
is
are
have
questions.explanation: 'Who' represents the plural 'engineers' in the stipulated reading, so the relative clause uses 'have worked'.
feedback: 'Has' would attach the experience specifically to a singular referent; the task makes 'engineers' the antecedent of 'who'.
'Is' does not form the intended active perfect with 'worked offshore'.
'Are' is plural but does not form this active present-perfect experience statement.
'Who' represents the plural 'engineers' in the stipulated reading, so the relative clause uses 'have worked'.

questions.setup: Among the engineers, Mara alone has worked on offshore platforms.
questions.prompt: Choose the standard formal completion preserving the exclusive claim: Mara is the only one of the engineers who ___ worked offshore.
options: have
are
having
has
questions.explanation: The intended relative clause identifies the only one, Mara; the singular antecedent takes has worked.
feedback: Plural have would describe the engineers as an experienced group rather than the stipulated unique person.
Are cannot form the intended active present perfect and would also be plural.
Having does not supply the finite verb needed after relative who.
The intended relative clause identifies the only one, Mara; the singular antecedent takes has worked.

questions.setup: An inventory sentence places the location first for emphasis.
questions.prompt: Choose the standard written completion: On the top shelf ___ two unopened boxes of stationery.
options: is
has
am
are
questions.explanation: With this location-first order, the subject follows the verb. Two unopened boxes requires are.
feedback: The singular shelf is in the fronted location phrase; the following two boxes is the plural subject.
Has neither agrees with boxes nor supplies the required location predicate.
Am cannot agree with the plural noun phrase naming the boxes.
With this location-first order, the subject follows the verb. Two unopened boxes requires are.

questions.setup: A draft says neither the reports nor the contract was available. The editor wants a straightforward plural subject while preserving the unavailability of both categories.
questions.prompt: Which rewrite achieves that goal?
options: The reports and the contract were not all available.
The reports were unavailable, unlike the contract.
The reports or the contract were unavailable.
The reports and the contract were all unavailable.
questions.explanation: And forms an unambiguous plural subject, while all unavailable preserves the denial of availability for both the reports and the contract.
feedback: Not all allows some items to be available; the original denies availability to both categories.
Unlike makes the contract available by contrast, reversing part of the original claim.
Or leaves open which category was unavailable; the original excludes both.
And forms an unambiguous plural subject, while all unavailable preserves the denial of availability for both the reports and the contract.

questions.setup: A report distinguishes 'This series of tests has finished' from 'These two series of tests have finished.'
questions.prompt: What determines agreement despite the unchanged spelling of 'series'?
options: The number of tests, since tests is the nearest plural noun
Whether the perfect construction describes a finished event or an ongoing one
The determiners identify the number of series, not the number of tests
Whether series is a subject in the first phrase but an object of tests in the second
questions.explanation: 'Series' has the same written singular and plural form; 'this' identifies one series, while 'these two' identifies more than one.
feedback: 'Tests' is inside the of-phrase in both examples. Its unchanged plural number does not explain the contrast between 'has' and 'have'.
Both versions use the present perfect of 'finish'. The auxiliary contrast expresses the subject's number, not a change from completed to ongoing action.
'Series' has the same written singular and plural form; 'this' identifies one series, while 'these two' identifies more than one.
'Series' heads the main subject in both sentences. The determiners change its number without reversing the relation between 'series' and 'tests'.

questions.setup: Two proposed sentences are 'What we need is more copies' and 'What we need are more copies.' No house style chooses between them.
questions.prompt: Which editorial assessment is accurate?
options: Is requires copies to be changed to copy in order to preserve agreement.
Both are established: is follows the what-clause; are can reflect the plural complement.
Are is justified only if more copies is a second subject coordinated with the what-clause.
The choice changes whether the copies are needed by one person or several.
questions.explanation: Such specifying what-clefts permit singular treatment of the clause or plural agreement influenced by the focused complement.
feedback: Singular is can follow the what-clause even when the focused complement names plural copies.
Such specifying what-clefts permit singular treatment of the clause or plural agreement influenced by the focused complement.
More copies is the specifying complement, not a second subject joined to the what-clause. Plural agreement is possible without that proposed coordination.
We identifies the people who need them in both versions; main-clause number does not change that reference.

questions.setup: One figure in the budget covers both repair work and inspection work. The report says, 'The cost of repairs and inspections has risen.'
questions.prompt: Which analysis fits the intended single-cost reading?
options: And joins repairs and inspections within the complement of singular cost.
And joins cost and inspections as two main subjects, so has must be plural.
Has agrees with inspections because inspection work is conceptually one service.
Repairs and inspections form a plural subject, while cost is its object.
questions.explanation: The cost covers two kinds of work, but one singular cost is what has risen.
feedback: The cost covers two kinds of work, but one singular cost is what has risen.
The stated single figure covers both services; inspections is coordinated with repairs inside the of phrase.
Has agrees with the head cost, not with inspections treated as an abstract activity.
The clause has no such object relation; cost heads the subject noun phrase.

questions.setup: Both the editor and the reviewers were concerned. A revision should give the editor a full clause and use an as-clause for the reviewers.
questions.prompt: Which sentence preserves that meaning and standard agreement?
options: The editor was concerned, as was the reviewers.
The editor was concerned, as were the reviewers.
The editor was concerned, as the reviewers were not.
The editor was not concerned, as were the reviewers.
questions.explanation: The first clause agrees with editor; the inverted as-clause has plural reviewers as its subject and repeats were concerned elliptically.
feedback: The postverbal subject reviewers is plural, so the as-clause needs were.
The first clause agrees with editor; the inverted as-clause has plural reviewers as its subject and repeats were concerned elliptically.
This denies concern among the reviewers, changing the stated shared reaction.
This denies the editor's concern and no longer expresses the required shared positive state.

questions.setup: A deliberately formal declaration reads, 'It is I who am responsible for the inventory.'
questions.prompt: Which comment explains the agreement without declaring everyday alternatives invalid?
options: The focused I supports am in this formal pattern; me with who's is an everyday alternative.
Who is grammatically third person here, so am should be changed to is.
The form am establishes a contrast with an unnamed second-person addressee.
Am attaches the relative clause to the opening it rather than to the focused pronoun.
questions.explanation: The formal I/who am pattern and the ordinary It's me who's responsible pattern are both established. Their different case and agreement choices belong to different constructions and registers.
feedback: The formal I/who am pattern and the ordinary It's me who's responsible pattern are both established. Their different case and agreement choices belong to different constructions and registers.
In this deliberately formal construction, who can take first-person agreement from the focused I. The proposed correction overlooks that pattern.
Am follows first-person I here, but the grammar does not establish that the intended contrast is specifically with you.
The opening it controls is in the cleft frame. The focused I, not it, supports am in the relative clause.

questions.setup: An editor compares 'The main problem is the travel expenses' with 'The travel expenses are the main problem.'
questions.prompt: Why need the two versions not use the same form of 'be'?
options: Each version agrees with its own subject: singular problem or plural expenses.
The version with is describes one expense, while the version with are describes several.
Be agrees with whichever noun phrase supplies the identifying information after it.
The singular version requires an understood one of before the travel expenses.
questions.explanation: Reversing the identifying sentence changes which noun phrase occupies the subject position and thus the ordinary agreement.
feedback: Reversing the identifying sentence changes which noun phrase occupies the subject position and thus the ordinary agreement.
Both sentences refer to the travel expenses as plural; singular agreement in the first does not reduce the expenses to one.
The noun phrase after 'be' is the complement. These examples show ordinary agreement with the preceding subject, not a rule based on which phrase supplies new information.
The first version can identify the expenses collectively as the problem. No omitted 'one of' is needed to select one expense.

questions.setup: A cashier says, 'Five dollars is enough for the fare.' Later, describing five separate one-dollar coins, she says, 'Five dollars were scattered across the counter.'
questions.prompt: Which explanation fits the different agreement choices?
options: Present tense requires singular money agreement, while past tense requires plural.
Enough makes any preceding subject singular, regardless of what it names.
The second sentence must describe a larger total because its verb is plural.
The first describes a total sum; the second describes individual monetary units.
questions.explanation: A monetary total can take singular agreement, while separately considered coins or monetary units can take plural agreement.
feedback: Tense does not impose that distinction; the difference is amount versus separate units.
Enough does not mechanically control agreement; the sum is being construed as one amount.
Both totals are five dollars; plural agreement need not imply a higher monetary value.
A monetary total can take singular agreement, while separately considered coins or monetary units can take plural agreement.

questions.setup: A financial note refers to the same money first as the proceeds of a sale and later as the income from that sale.
questions.prompt: Which standard written agreement contrast is appropriate?
options: The proceeds has been transferred; the income has been recorded.
The proceeds have been transferred; the income has been recorded.
The proceeds have been transferred; the income have been recorded.
The proceeds has been transferred; the income have been recorded.
questions.explanation: Proceeds is conventionally plural in this financial meaning, whereas income is an uncountable singular noun, even when they refer to the same money.
feedback: The shared amount does not remove the lexical plural agreement of proceeds.
Proceeds is conventionally plural in this financial meaning, whereas income is an uncountable singular noun, even when they refer to the same money.
Income is uncountable singular in this meaning and requires has.
This reverses the established number of both nouns: proceeds plural, income singular.

questions.setup: In conversation, an organiser says, 'There's a lectern and two chairs on the stage.'
questions.prompt: Which editing comment respects the spoken construction while offering straightforward formal agreement?
options: The singular indicates that the speaker considers the chairs part of the lectern itself.
The spoken wording is singular because two chairs is the object of there's.
The spoken singular is possible; a subject-first recast gives plural agreement.
The recast would need singular is because the first noun phrase remains a lectern.
questions.explanation: A clear formal recast is 'A lectern and two chairs are on the stage.' The original conversational list can begin with singular agreement when its first item is singular.
feedback: Singular agreement at the start of this existential list does not collapse the distinct objects into parts of one lectern.
Existential be does not take two chairs as an object. The two chairs are additional items introduced by the existential list.
A clear formal recast is 'A lectern and two chairs are on the stage.' The original conversational list can begin with singular agreement when its first item is singular.
Once the whole list is the ordinary preceding subject, its three separate objects support plural are; the first item's number is not enough.

questions.setup: One person holds both offices. The minutes say, 'Our secretary and treasurer has submitted her report.'
questions.prompt: Which account of 'has' fits this stipulated role arrangement?
options: Has agrees with report because the document, not its author, is singular.
And forces plural agreement even when both titles identify the same person.
The coordinated titles identify a single office-holder, so singular agreement is appropriate.
Has implies that only the treasurer submitted a report and the secretary did not.
questions.explanation: 'Secretary and treasurer' names two roles of the same person in this context, not two independent subjects.
feedback: 'Report' is the object; the subject's single-person reference explains 'has'.
Titles can jointly name one individual; such co-reference supports singular agreement.
'Secretary and treasurer' names two roles of the same person in this context, not two independent subjects.
Both roles belong to the same person; singular agreement does not exclude one role-holder.

questions.setup: A news draft says, 'An estimated five hundred residents have received the notice.'
questions.prompt: Which explanation correctly accounts for plural 'have' despite 'an'?
options: The phrase names one estimated total, so has is required even though residents is plural.
An should be removed because plural agreement rules out this estimated-number construction.
Estimated is a past-tense verb here, so the following have should be changed to had.
An belongs to the estimated-number expression; the residents remain a plural subject.
questions.explanation: 'An estimated' plus a numeral is an established quantity expression; the people counted still form a plural subject.
feedback: The sentence says that the residents received notices, not that an abstract estimated total received one. The quantity expression supports plural 'have'.
'An estimated' followed by a numeral is an established construction. The article can remain while the quantified residents take plural agreement.
'Estimated' modifies the number; it is not the sentence's finite past-tense verb. 'Have received' supplies the finite present-perfect predicate.
'An estimated' plus a numeral is an established quantity expression; the people counted still form a plural subject.

questions.setup: A researcher writes, 'The estimates have changed again, which is inconvenient for the planning team.'
questions.prompt: Why does 'is' not have to become 'are' to match 'estimates'?
options: Which takes singular agreement because its spelling does not contain a plural ending.
Which singles out one particular estimate from the set as the inconvenient one.
Is agrees with the singular planning team at the end of the sentence.
Which refers to the whole change just reported, not to the estimates as plural objects.
questions.explanation: A sentential relative can refer back to a complete event or proposition; that singular reference supports 'which is inconvenient'.
feedback: The form 'which' does not display number, but it can represent singular or plural antecedents. Its reference, not its spelling, matters.
The sentence comments on the estimates' changing again. It does not select one estimate as a singular antecedent.
'Planning team' is inside the for-phrase. It identifies who is inconvenienced, not the subject controlling 'is'.
A sentential relative can refer back to a complete event or proposition; that singular reference supports 'which is inconvenient'.

questions.setup: A review treats two separate facts as independent reasons for delay: the files were missing, and the backup failed.
questions.prompt: Which sentence reflects that two-fact structure with standard agreement?
options: That the files were missing and that the backup failed is two distinct reasons for the delay.
That the files were missing and that the backup failed is one combined reason for the delay.
That the files were missing is the only reason for the delay.
That the files were missing and that the backup failed are two distinct reasons for the delay.
questions.explanation: Each that clause contributes one fact; coordinating them as two distinct reasons supports plural agreement.
feedback: The explicitly separate that clauses are presented as two reasons, so the coordinated subject takes are.
This can express a unified construal, but the task explicitly preserves two independent reasons.
This drops the independently relevant backup failure and changes the number of reasons.
Each that clause contributes one fact; coordinating them as two distinct reasons supports plural agreement.

questions.setup: An editor asks, 'Which of these files are missing?' The assistant replies, 'Only the January file.'
questions.prompt: Which judgment of this exchange is most accurate?
options: The answer is inconsistent because are proves at least two files must be missing.
The question has to use is because which is inherently singular.
The question allows several files as an answer without ruling out just one.
The reply is an unfinished correction of the question rather than an answer to it.
questions.explanation: Plural agreement opens a potentially plural selection; the response can narrow the result to one file.
feedback: The question can anticipate several possibilities without asserting how many files will satisfy the description.
Which can introduce singular or plural selection; it has no fixed singular number.
Plural agreement opens a potentially plural selection; the response can narrow the result to one file.
Only the January file is a sufficient short answer identifying the missing member. It need not be treated as a correction simply because it supplies one file.

questions.setup: After inspecting an empty building, an officer says, 'All is quiet.' After checking the waiting guests, a host says, 'All are ready.'
questions.prompt: Which explanation accounts for the change in number?
options: Quiet requires a singular subject, whereas ready requires a plural subject.
All is an omitted form of all the guests in both statements.
All refers first to the overall situation, then to the waiting people.
Are means every guest is ready at a different time rather than together.
questions.explanation: Standalone all can mean everything in a situation or all the people or things in a set; that reference controls singular or plural agreement.
feedback: Both adjectives can describe singular or plural subjects. The different referents of all explain the number choices.
The first statement follows an inspection of an empty building and summarizes its overall condition, not the readiness of guests.
Standalone all can mean everything in a situation or all the people or things in a set; that reference controls singular or plural agreement.
Plural agreement identifies multiple people without specifying different readiness times.

questions.setup: A proposal says, 'If this room were larger, we could hold the rehearsal here.' A proofreader flags 'were' because 'room' is singular.
questions.prompt: Which response correctly distinguishes mood from ordinary number agreement?
options: Were indicates that this room is being treated as several connected rooms.
Were can mark an unreal condition with a singular subject, so this is not a plural-agreement error.
Were needs to become was because an unreal condition still requires ordinary singular agreement.
Were reports a past fact, so the proposal implies that the room used to be larger.
questions.explanation: Irrealis 'were', a form used for hypothetical or unreal situations, is licensed with singular subjects in this conditional pattern.
feedback: 'This room' remains singular. 'Were' marks the hypothetical construction rather than a plural reinterpretation of 'room'.
Irrealis 'were', a form used for hypothetical or unreal situations, is licensed with singular subjects in this conditional pattern.
That rule would exclude the established irrealis form. 'Was' also occurs in some usage, but singular 'room' does not make 'were' an error.
The if-clause considers an unreal possibility. The form does not establish a past period when the room actually was larger.

questions.setup: A careful report states, 'There appear to be several discrepancies in the ledger.' A reviewer proposes 'appears' solely because the sentence begins with 'there'.
questions.prompt: Which response best addresses that reasoning?
options: Appear can agree with the later discrepancies; there does not denote one object.
Appear should be singular because to be prevents discrepancies from affecting the finite verb.
Appear is an infinitive after there, so its form is not affected by number.
Discrepancies is the object of appear, so it cannot help explain the verb's number.
questions.explanation: In this existential raising construction, the later plural noun phrase supports plural agreement on 'appear'; 'there' does not refer to a single object.
feedback: In this existential raising construction, the later plural noun phrase supports plural agreement on 'appear'; 'there' does not refer to a single object.
The intervening infinitive does not block plural agreement in this construction. The later noun phrase can support 'appear'.
'Appear' is the finite verb here, and 'to be' is the infinitive. Compare the singular 'There appears to be a discrepancy.'
'Appear' does not take 'discrepancies' as a direct object. The existential construction links agreement to the postponed noun phrase.

questions.setup: A review says, 'It is surprising that the operating costs have fallen.'
questions.prompt: Which account correctly assigns the two agreement controllers?
options: Operating costs controls both verbs because the that-clause carries the main information.
It controls is in the main clause, while operating costs controls have in the that-clause.
The whole that-clause makes both finite verbs singular.
It refers to one operating cost considered separately from the remaining costs.
questions.explanation: Introductory it takes singular agreement outside the content clause; the embedded plural subject has its own agreement.
feedback: The informational importance of the costs does not merge the two clauses' grammatical subjects. Introductory it still supports is.
Introductory it takes singular agreement outside the content clause; the embedded plural subject has its own agreement.
The postponed clause supplies the surprising fact, but costs remains the plural subject inside that clause and takes have.
It is introductory here, not a reference to one selected cost. The entire fact that the costs have fallen is what is surprising.

questions.setup: A correction reads, 'It is the conservators who are responsible for moving the exhibits, not the guides.'
questions.prompt: Why can singular 'is' and plural 'are' both be correct?
options: The opening it-cleft stays singular, while who represents the plural conservators.
Is agrees with the singular job of moving exhibits, while are agrees with the guides.
Is should become are because conservators follows it immediately.
Are should become is because who repeats the opening it.
questions.explanation: The two clauses have distinct agreement patterns: 'it is' introduces the focus, and the relative clause agrees with the plural people identified.
feedback: The two clauses have distinct agreement patterns: 'it is' introduces the focus, and the relative clause agrees with the plural people identified.
The first verb belongs to the cleft frame, and the relative 'who' represents 'conservators', not the rejected guides.
A plural focus does not normally make the introductory 'it' + 'be' frame plural.
'Who' represents the focused conservators, not the introductory 'it'.

questions.setup: Compare two instructions: 'Whatever remains is to be archived' and 'Whatever documents remain are to be archived.'
questions.prompt: Which analysis accounts for both agreement patterns?
options: The second subject contains plural documents; the first has no such plural head.
Documents is the object of remain, so its number affects only the later passive.
The first instruction refers to one document, whereas the second refers to several.
The presence of to be archived licenses either agreement pattern in both instructions.
questions.explanation: Whatever remains means roughly 'anything that remains' and has singular agreement. In whatever documents remain, documents supplies plural number, also reflected in are.
feedback: Whatever remains means roughly 'anything that remains' and has singular agreement. In whatever documents remain, documents supplies plural number, also reflected in are.
Remain has no object here. Documents supplies the plural subject within the relative construction and supports both remain and are.
Singular agreement with whatever remains does not count the remaining material. It could include numerous documents.
The infinitival passive does not determine the subject's number. The difference lies in the structure of the two subjects.

questions.setup: An editor encounters: 'The cost of the repairs, the insurers estimate, exceeds the original budget.' A colleague proposes 'exceed' because 'insurers' is plural.
questions.prompt: Which response correctly analyses the proposed change?
options: The change is needed because insurers becomes the subject when inserted before exceeds.
Insurers belongs to the inserted reporting clause; cost controls exceeds.
The change is optional because either repairs or cost can head the main subject here.
Exceeds should remain, but estimate needs to become estimates to match cost.
questions.explanation: Removing the parenthetical gives 'The cost of the repairs exceeds the original budget.' The insurers estimate that proposition; their plural number controls 'estimate', not 'exceeds'.
feedback: Position alone does not make 'insurers' the subject of 'exceeds'. The inserted clause attributes an estimate to the insurers.
Removing the parenthetical gives 'The cost of the repairs exceeds the original budget.' The insurers estimate that proposition; their plural number controls 'estimate', not 'exceeds'.
The sentence concerns the cost exceeding a budget, not the repairs doing so. 'Repairs' is inside the of-phrase and is not an alternative head on this reading.
'Estimate' belongs to its own clause with the plural subject 'the insurers'. The two clauses have separate agreement controllers.

questions.setup: An editor reviews 'One in ten applicants have worked abroad.' A colleague proposes 'has'. Neither has checked the publication's house style.
questions.prompt: Which editorial advice is accurate?
options: Use has: one is singular, so the plural applicants cannot support have in an established one-in-ten construction.
Has follows the usual formal convention; have also occurs naturally, particularly in informal speech and writing.
Keep have: in ten applicants makes applicants the grammatical head of the entire subject, so has is an agreement error.
Choose by national variety: British English permits have here, whereas American English requires has even in conversational use.
questions.explanation: Formal prose commonly follows singular 'one', while informal usage often allows plural agreement with the population being discussed. Check the intended register and any house rule before presenting either choice as a required correction.
feedback: This extends a formal singular preference into an unrestricted prohibition. Plural agreement is established in informal one-in-N expressions with people.

Formal prose commonly follows singular 'one', while informal usage often allows plural agreement with the population being discussed. Check the intended register and any house rule before presenting either choice as a required correction.
The in-phrase does not simply replace 'one' with 'applicants' as the subject's head. Singular 'has' follows a conventional formal pattern and is not an error.
The variation is not a categorical British-versus-American division. Informal plural agreement is recognized in American usage guidance too; register and house convention matter.

questions.setup: A draft contains 'A range of objections have been raised' and 'The range of objections is unusually broad.' No house rule specifies singular agreement after 'a range of'.
questions.prompt: Which editorial comment best accounts for this contrast?
options: Have is defensible only if range is being used as an abbreviation for several ranges.
The first use is quantifying; the second describes the breadth of the range itself.
Is must become are because the earlier sentence has already established plural agreement.
Have makes objections the speakers who raised the issue, rather than the issues raised.
questions.explanation: 'A range of' can function as a quantity expression and occur with plural agreement; singular agreement is also used. In the second sentence, 'broad' describes the range itself, supporting 'is'.
feedback: Plural agreement with 'a range of objections' does not require an omitted plural word. It can reflect the quantity expression and its plural complement.
'A range of' can function as a quantity expression and occur with plural agreement; singular agreement is also used. In the second sentence, 'broad' describes the range itself, supporting 'is'.
The later sentence presents the range as the thing whose breadth is described. Agreement is not fixed for every occurrence of a noun by its first use.
Objections remain the things raised in the passive construction. Verb number does not convert them into the people doing the raising.

questions.setup: A writer wants to say that both the director and the auditors have already approved the proposal. Keep their subjects in separate coordinated clauses, use the present perfect in both, and share the final words 'approved the proposal'.
questions.prompt: Which sentence meets all three editing requirements?
options: The director and the auditors have approved the proposal.
The director had, and the auditors have, approved the proposal.
The director has approved the proposal, and so have the auditors.
The director has, and the auditors have, approved the proposal.
questions.explanation: 'Has' agrees with 'the director' and 'have' with 'the auditors'. The clauses share 'approved the proposal', while each retains its own present-perfect auxiliary.
feedback: This is grammatical and preserves the approval claim, but combines the subjects into one clause instead of retaining separate clauses.
Each auxiliary agrees with its subject, but 'had' changes the director's clause to the past perfect, contrary to the requested tense in both clauses.
This expresses the right facts and tense, but 'approved the proposal' occurs in the first clause rather than as the shared final wording.
'Has' agrees with 'the director' and 'have' with 'the auditors'. The clauses share 'approved the proposal', while each retains its own present-perfect auxiliary.

questions.setup: An archivist writes, 'The donor insisted that the original manuscript be returned before the exhibition.' An editor changes 'be' to 'is' solely because 'manuscript' is singular.
questions.prompt: Which assessment of that change is accurate?
options: Be shows that the donor is uncertain whether the manuscript is a single object.
Is preserves the same construction because insisted automatically makes the following verb subjunctive.
Be can express the demanded action; changing it to is is not a number-agreement repair.
Be is an infinitive whose understood subject is the donor rather than the manuscript.
questions.explanation: This is a mandative subjunctive: a base verb form used for an action being demanded. It can have a singular subject. 'Is' is an indicative form, so the proposed substitution concerns the construction and reading, not a missing singular ending.
feedback: The form does not express uncertainty about the noun's number. The subject still denotes the original manuscript.
'Insisted' can introduce a demand or an asserted claim. Its presence does not make the indicative form 'is' into a subjunctive.

This is a mandative subjunctive: a base verb form used for an action being demanded. It can have a singular subject. 'Is' is an indicative form, so the proposed substitution concerns the construction and reading, not a missing singular ending.
The that-clause has its own stated subject, the original manuscript. This use of 'be' is not a subjectless infinitive controlled by the donor.

questions.setup: Consider: 'Not one of the reports that the inspectors say were altered contains the original signature.'
questions.prompt: Which analysis correctly links all three finite verbs to their subjects?
options: Say follows inspectors, were refers back to reports, and contains follows not one.
Say follows reports, were follows inspectors, and contains follows the original signature.
Say follows inspectors, while were and contains both follow reports within the relative clause.
Say and were both follow inspectors, while contains agrees with the whole negative relative clause.
questions.explanation: The relative construction spans the intervening reporting words the inspectors say: the reports were altered. The main subject remains not one, giving contains, while inspectors controls say.
feedback: The relative construction spans the intervening reporting words the inspectors say: the reports were altered. The main subject remains not one, giving contains, while inspectors controls say.
The inspectors do the saying, the reports were altered, and not one is the main subject. Signature is the object of contains.
Were belongs to the relative construction about the reports. Contains is outside that construction and makes the main claim about not one.
The inspectors are not said to have been altered. The main subject is the noun phrase not one of the reports, not the relative clause that modifies reports.

questions.setup: A British report says, 'The committee disagree among themselves about the timetable.' A publisher asks for wording that avoids collective-noun agreement variation while preserving the disagreement described.
questions.prompt: Which rewrite best meets the publisher's request?
options: The committee disagrees with its members about the timetable.
The committees disagree with one another about the timetable.
The committee members disagree with one another about the timetable.
The committee's disagreement with the timetable remains unresolved.
questions.explanation: Members supplies an explicitly plural subject, and with one another preserves disagreement within the committee. The original plural collective agreement is possible in British English, not an error that must be corrected everywhere.
feedback: This contrasts the committee as a body with its own members. The original describes disagreement among the members themselves.
This makes several committees the disputing parties. The original concerns members within one committee.

Members supplies an explicitly plural subject, and with one another preserves disagreement within the committee. The original plural collective agreement is possible in British English, not an error that must be corrected everywhere.
This presents opposition to the timetable as the committee's position. It does not preserve the internal disagreement about it.

questions.setup: A partnership agreement says, 'Each partner and each supplier has its own account.' A reader argues that singular 'has' means that the partners and suppliers share one account.
questions.prompt: Which response best explains the grammar and its consequence for that reading?
options: Has treats partner and supplier as two job titles held by the same person.
Repeated each distributes the statement; singular has does not imply a shared account.
Has applies the account requirement only to each supplier, the nearer subject.
The sentence needs have before own can refer separately to partners and suppliers.
questions.explanation: 'Each partner and each supplier' supports singular agreement in formal usage. With 'its own account', the sentence assigns an account individually; it does not describe one account shared by everyone.
feedback: Nothing in the sentence requires a person to hold both roles. 'Each' distributes the requirement across members of both named categories.

'Each partner and each supplier' supports singular agreement in formal usage. With 'its own account', the sentence assigns an account individually; it does not describe one account shared by everyone.
The coordinated subject includes both 'each partner' and 'each supplier'. Agreement does not remove partners from the requirement.
The distributive 'each' construction already permits the individual reading with 'has'. A plural verb is not needed to create separate account holders.

questions.setup: A rulebook says, 'A majority is required for the motion to pass.' A meeting record says, 'A majority of the delegates are absent.'
questions.prompt: Which account explains the different agreement without changing either statement's meaning?
options: The rule concerns exactly one voter, whereas the record concerns several voters.
The record implies that each absent delegate personally holds a majority of votes.
The record should use is unless the meeting has more than one distinct majority.
The rule names a required threshold; the record predicates absence of people.
questions.explanation: In the rule, a majority is the requirement considered as one threshold. In the record, a majority of the delegates can take plural agreement because the delegates are the people described as absent.
feedback: A required majority is a threshold for support, not a single voter. The singular verb does not determine the number needed.
A majority of the delegates identifies a proportion of the people. It does not give a majority of voting power to each one.
Plural agreement with a majority of people does not require multiple majorities. It can reflect the people making up the majority.
In the rule, a majority is the requirement considered as one threshold. In the record, a majority of the delegates can take plural agreement because the delegates are the people described as absent.

questions.setup: A meeting secretary asks, 'No one has withdrawn their objection, have they?' A reviewer thinks 'has' and 'have' cannot both belong in this question.
questions.prompt: Which response correctly explains both agreement and the checking question's polarity?
options: Have shows that the secretary now assumes several people have withdrawn their objections.
The tag should use hasn't because the first clause contains no negative auxiliary.
No one takes has; the tag uses they with have and checks the negative claim.
The singular verb is appropriate only if their refers to someone outside the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'No one' has singular agreement in the main clause. 'They' can refer back without specifying gender and takes 'have' in the tag. Since 'no one' makes the statement negative, the positive tag is appropriate for checking it.
feedback: 'They' with 'have' does not assert a plural group of withdrawals. The tag checks the preceding claim that no person has withdrawn an objection.
'No one' makes the first clause negative even though 'has' is not contracted with 'not'. The ordinary opposite-polarity checking tag is therefore positive.

'No one' has singular agreement in the main clause. 'They' can refer back without specifying gender and takes 'have' in the tag. Since 'no one' makes the statement negative, the positive tag is appropriate for checking it.
'Their' can refer back to the people considered individually by 'no one'. No outside person is needed to license either 'their' or the tag's 'they'.

questions.setup: A writer means that the gardeners live nearby and that their niece manages the cafe. The draft says, 'The niece of the gardeners who lives nearby manages the cafe.'
questions.prompt: Which rewrite uses relative-clause agreement to express the intended relationships, without adding a claim about where the niece lives?
options: The niece of the gardeners who live nearby manages the cafe.
The niece, who lives near the gardeners, manages the cafe.
The gardeners whose niece lives nearby manage the cafe.
The niece and the gardeners, who live nearby, manage the cafe.
questions.explanation: Plural live links who to gardeners, while singular manages links the main claim to niece. The sentence no longer makes the relative clause describe the niece's residence.
feedback: Plural live links who to gardeners, while singular manages links the main claim to niece. The sentence no longer makes the relative clause describe the niece's residence.
This locates the niece near the gardeners. It does not say that the gardeners live nearby, and it adds a residence relation the writer did not intend.
This makes the gardeners the cafe managers and the niece the nearby resident, reversing both intended assignments.
This adds the gardeners as cafe managers and can include the niece among the nearby residents. The original goal assigns cafe management only to the niece.

questions.setup: A researcher writes, 'I am a linguist who studies workplace conversations.' An editor proposes 'study', arguing that 'who' ultimately refers to the first-person speaker.
questions.prompt: Which assessment correctly distinguishes reference from the relative clause's grammatical antecedent?
options: Who modifies a linguist here, so studies need not agree directly with I.
Study is required because two expressions referring to one person must share grammatical person.
Studies is appropriate only if the linguist is someone other than the writer.
Am makes the whole sentence first person, but studies is retained as reported speech.
questions.explanation: The relative clause is attached to 'a linguist', which supports third-person singular 'studies'. In a different construction such as 'I, who study these conversations, ...', 'who' would attach directly to 'I'.
feedback: The relative clause is attached to 'a linguist', which supports third-person singular 'studies'. In a different construction such as 'I, who study these conversations, ...', 'who' would attach directly to 'I'.
Different expressions for the same person need not have the same grammatical person. 'I' is first person, while 'a linguist' is a third-person noun phrase.
The sentence identifies the writer as a linguist. Third-person agreement inside the relative clause does not introduce a second person.
'Am' does not assign first-person agreement to every later clause, and no one is being quoted or reported here. The relevant fact is the attachment to 'a linguist'.

questions.setup: Compare 'A lot of defects have appeared' with 'The cause of the defects has become clear.' A learner proposes a rule: use the number of the noun immediately after 'of' in both constructions.
questions.prompt: Which evaluation best explains why that proposed rule is unreliable?
options: The rule works in the first sentence because have is active, but fails with become because it is passive.
The rule works whenever the of-phrase begins with an indefinite article rather than the.
The rule fails because both sentences should agree with the singular word before of.
A lot of quantifies defects; cause names a separate thing about which a claim is made.
questions.explanation: In the first subject, 'a lot of' means roughly 'many', and the defects are what have appeared. In the second, the cause is what has become clear. An of-phrase does not have one uniform effect on agreement.
feedback: 'Has become' is not passive. The difference concerns the subjects, not active versus passive voice.
An article alone does not settle the structure. 'A cause of the defects' would still name a cause and normally take singular agreement.
That would wrongly force singular agreement in 'a lot of defects have appeared'. 'A lot of' functions as a quantity expression here.

In the first subject, 'a lot of' means roughly 'many', and the defects are what have appeared. In the second, the cause is what has become clear. An of-phrase does not have one uniform effect on agreement.

questions.setup: A formal response reads, 'The redesign would save space. Be that as it may, the access problem remains.' An editor wants to replace 'be' with 'is' because 'that' is singular.
questions.prompt: Which comment best assesses this proposed agreement edit?
options: Be is simply the infinitive governed by the later may, with the same structure as may be.
Is is preferable because it strengthens the same concession without changing its grammatical construction.
Be is retained because the preceding would makes the following independent clause infinitival.
Be belongs to a fixed concessive expression, not an ordinary indicative statement needing is.
questions.explanation: 'Be that as it may' is an established formal expression that sets a point aside before continuing the argument. Its 'be' is not a missing singular indicative ending, so changing it to 'is' does not preserve the expression.
feedback: The opening 'be' belongs to the concessive frame, not a reordered ordinary 'may be' verb phrase. The expression cannot be explained by moving a modal's infinitive across its subject.
'Is that as it may' does not retain the conventional concessive construction. This is not merely a stronger version of the same wording.
'Would' governs 'save' in the preceding sentence. It does not turn a separate sentence's opening expression into its infinitival complement.

'Be that as it may' is an established formal expression that sets a point aside before continuing the argument. Its 'be' is not a missing singular indicative ending, so changing it to 'is' does not preserve the expression.

questions.setup: A formal narrative says, 'The last guests having left, the caretaker locks the courtyard.' A reviewer says 'having' should become 'have' because 'guests' is plural.
questions.prompt: Which response best diagnoses the proposed change?
options: Having left is nonfinite and has its own stated subject; it does not inflect for guests.
Having is singular because its subject is the later caretaker, while guests is its object.
Have would preserve the same nonfinite construction while making its plural agreement visible.
Having left is a shortened relative clause modifying guests, equivalent in structure to who have left.
questions.explanation: The opening is an absolute construction: a nonfinite clause with 'the last guests' as its subject. 'Having' does not change for number. Replacing it with 'have' creates a finite clause and would require different punctuation or linkage to the main clause.
feedback: The opening is an absolute construction: a nonfinite clause with 'the last guests' as its subject. 'Having' does not change for number. Replacing it with 'have' creates a finite clause and would require different punctuation or linkage to the main clause.
The guests are the people who have left; they are not an object of 'having'. The caretaker is the separate subject of 'locks'.
'Have left' with 'the last guests' as its subject is a finite present-perfect clause. It is not an inflected version of the original nonfinite construction.

The opening supplies a background circumstance in a separate nonfinite clause. It is not a relative modifier within a noun phrase; treating it as one would leave that opening noun phrase without a role in the main clause.

questions.setup: An inventory report says, 'Five thousand dollars' worth of paintings have been recovered.' A colleague objects that 'have' can be correct only if actual dollars, not paintings, were recovered.
questions.prompt: Which response best addresses that objection without imposing an unstated house style?
options: Have implies that each painting was individually worth five thousand dollars.
The sentence refers to both paintings and money, with have agreeing with their combined value.
Changing have to has would mean that only one painting had been recovered.
Plural agreement can reflect paintings; it does not turn their stated value into recovered cash.
questions.explanation: A monetary worth-of expression can occur with plural agreement reflecting the goods named after 'of'. It still denotes paintings of the stated total value. A singular amount-focused version is also possible; neither reading requires recovered banknotes.
feedback: The value expression describes the quantity of paintings collectively. Plural agreement does not distribute that full value to each painting.
The dollars specify how much the paintings are worth. They are not an additional recovered item coordinated with paintings.
Singular agreement can present the valued quantity as an amount. It need not reduce the number of paintings to one.

A monetary worth-of expression can occur with plural agreement reflecting the goods named after 'of'. It still denotes paintings of the stated total value. A singular amount-focused version is also possible; neither reading requires recovered banknotes.

questions.setup: Exactly one of the speaker and the addressee is to chair the session. Rewrite without making either 'you' or 'I' a shared subject before an agreement-sensitive verb; name both parties and keep the one-person restriction explicit.
questions.prompt: Which sentence meets the editing goal?
options: You and I will decide who chairs the session, but only one chair is needed.
Either you or I am to chair the session, but not both of us.
Either you will chair the session or I will, but not both of us.
Either you and I will chair the session or neither of us will.
questions.explanation: Each alternative has its own subject and 'will', whose form does not vary with person. The second clause omits the repeated predicate, and 'but not both of us' preserves the explicit one-person restriction.
feedback: This makes the two people decision-makers. It does not require either of them to be the chair; they could choose someone else.
This keeps the mixed-person shared subject that the editing brief asks you to avoid. The task is a structural recast, not a claim that this proximity-based form is never used.

Each alternative has its own subject and 'will', whose form does not vary with person. The second clause omits the repeated predicate, and 'but not both of us' preserves the explicit one-person restriction.
This offers both people together or neither person, excluding the intended exactly-one arrangement. Its agreement is grammatical but its alternatives are different.

questions.setup: A report says, 'The assistant of the curator who was interviewed has resigned.' The surrounding text has mentioned interviews with both people, but does not identify which interview this sentence concerns.
questions.prompt: What can an editor conclude from 'was' about the relative clause's attachment?
options: Was proves that the curator was interviewed, because the nearest noun controls relative agreement.
Was cannot settle the attachment, since both possible antecedents are singular.
Was proves that the assistant was interviewed, because the main subject controls relative agreement.
Was cannot help because past-tense be has the same form with singular and plural subjects.
questions.explanation: Both 'assistant' and 'curator' can support singular 'was'. Agreement therefore does not disambiguate this sentence; the editor should clarify which person's interview is intended rather than treating a preferred attachment as compulsory.
feedback: Proximity may encourage that reading, but it is not proof. The more distant 'assistant' is also singular and can support 'was'.

Both 'assistant' and 'curator' can support singular 'was'. Agreement therefore does not disambiguate this sentence; the editor should clarify which person's interview is intended rather than treating a preferred attachment as compulsory.
A relative clause inside a subject phrase need not modify the phrase's head. 'Curator' is also a possible antecedent here.
Past-tense 'be' does distinguish singular 'was' from plural 'were' in ordinary statements. It cannot help here because both candidate antecedents have the same number, not because it lacks agreement.

questions.setup: A policy draft says, 'The trustees, each of whom has signed a separate declaration, are eligible to vote.' An editor proposes 'have' in the relative clause to make both verbs plural like 'trustees'.
questions.prompt: Which response correctly evaluates the proposed change and the original declaration claim?
options: Has means one declaration was signed jointly, so have is needed to express separate declarations.
The main clause should use is because each of whom becomes the subject after the comma.
Each governs has within the relative clause; trustees governs are in the main clause.
Have is required because whom is plural, while each modifies declaration rather than the subject.
questions.explanation: In this formal draft, 'each of whom has' makes an individual statement about every trustee. The main subject 'the trustees' independently takes 'are'. Repeating one verb number across the sentence is not the agreement requirement.
feedback: 'Each' and 'a separate declaration' already distribute the signing across individual trustees. Singular agreement inside that clause does not make the declaration joint.
The relative clause supplements the trustees; it does not replace that plural main subject. Its singular 'each' governs only its own finite verb.

In this formal draft, 'each of whom has' makes an individual statement about every trustee. The main subject 'the trustees' independently takes 'are'. Repeating one verb number across the sentence is not the agreement requirement.
'Each' is the head of 'each of whom', not a modifier of 'declaration'. 'Whom' links the phrase to the trustees without making 'each' a plural subject in the formal pattern used here.

questions.setup: What does the traveler mean?
questions.prompt: I'd like a quiet seat, please.
options: I already have a quiet seat.
I want a quiet seat.
I usually sit in quiet places.
I do not want to sit down.
questions.explanation: Would like is a polite way to express this wish or request.
feedback: I'd like expresses what the traveler wants, not what the traveler already has.
Would like is a polite way to express this wish or request.
The request concerns a seat now, not a usual habit.
The traveler asks for a seat rather than refusing to sit.

questions.setup: Complete the polite order.
questions.prompt: I would ___ a bowl of soup, please.
options: likes
liked
like
liking
questions.explanation: Would like is the correct form for this polite order.
feedback: Would takes like without a third-person -s.
Liked is a past form; after would, use the base form like.
Would like is the correct form for this polite order.
Liking cannot follow would directly in this expression.

questions.setup: Complete the guest's request with an action.
questions.prompt: I'd like ___ a room for Saturday.
options: book
booking
to book
to booking
questions.explanation: To book names the action the guest would like to take.
feedback: Would like needs to before the requested action in this pattern.
Booking is not the to-infinitive used for the action the guest wants to take.
To book names the action the guest would like to take.
After to in this infinitive, use book rather than booking.

questions.setup: What does the speaker's sentence tell us?
questions.prompt: I hope the bus arrives soon.
options: The speaker knows the bus has arrived.
The speaker wants the bus to arrive late.
The speaker says the bus never arrives.
The speaker wants the bus to arrive soon.
questions.explanation: Hope expresses the desired arrival; it does not say the arrival has happened.
feedback: Has arrived would describe a completed arrival, which hope does not establish.
Soon expresses a wish for an early arrival, not a late one.
The sentence gives no claim that the bus never arrives.
Hope expresses the desired arrival; it does not say the arrival has happened.

questions.setup: The waiter is asking what you want now. Choose a polite order, not a statement about your usual taste.
questions.prompt: What would you like to drink?
options: I like tea.
I liked the tea yesterday.
I'd like some tea, please.
I don't usually drink tea.
questions.explanation: I'd like some tea politely names the drink wanted now.
feedback: I like tea describes a general preference rather than directly stating this order.
Liked ... yesterday comments on a past drink, not today's order.
I'd like some tea politely names the drink wanted now.
This states a usual habit and does not name a drink the customer wants now.

questions.setup: Complete the speaker's plan for learning a skill.
questions.prompt: I want to ___ how to cook rice.
options: learn
learning
learned
learns
questions.explanation: Want to learn expresses the skill the speaker wants to gain.
feedback: Want to learn expresses the skill the speaker wants to gain.
To in this infinitive needs the base form learn, not learning.
Learned is a past form and does not follow want to here.
Learns has a third-person ending, which is not used after to in this infinitive.

questions.setup: Choose the speaker's correct negative reply.
questions.prompt: A friend asks, 'Do you want to go to the party?' You do not want to go.
options: I don't want go to the party.
I not want to go to the party.
I don't want to go to the party.
I don't wanting to go to the party.
questions.explanation: Don't want to go correctly expresses the speaker's negative desire.
feedback: Want needs to before go in this action complement.
The present negative needs do: I do not want, not I not want.
Don't want to go correctly expresses the speaker's negative desire.
After don't, use the base form want rather than wanting.

questions.setup: A host holds a coffee pot. Which question offers you coffee now?
questions.prompt: Choose the host's offer.
options: Do you usually drink coffee?
Did you enjoy the coffee?
Would you like some coffee?
Where do you buy your coffee?
questions.explanation: Would you like some coffee offers a drink to the guest at this moment.
feedback: Usually asks about a habit rather than offering the coffee in the pot.
Did you enjoy asks about a drink already finished.
Would you like some coffee offers a drink to the guest at this moment.
Where do you buy asks for shopping information, not whether the guest wants a drink.

questions.setup: What does "I'd" mean in this sentence?
questions.prompt: I'd like two tickets for the concert.
options: I did
I would
I had
I do
questions.explanation: "I'd" expands to 'I would' before 'like' in this request.
feedback: 'I did like' would emphasize a past liking, not expand this polite request.
"I'd" expands to 'I would' before 'like' in this request.
'I had like' is not the construction used here; 'had' would need a different complement.
'I do like' expresses emphasis about liking, not the contraction "I'd".

questions.setup: Complete the group's polite request.
questions.prompt: We ___ like a table near the window.
options: would
woulds
would to
are would
questions.explanation: Would works with plural we without changing its form.
feedback: Would works with plural we without changing its form.
Would has no -s form, regardless of the subject.
To does not go between would and like.
Would is itself a modal auxiliary and does not need are before it.

questions.setup: Complete the good wish for another person.
questions.prompt: I wish ___ good luck in your new job.
options: your
yours
you're
you
questions.explanation: Wish you good luck uses you as the person receiving the good wish.
feedback: Your is a possessive form and cannot name the person receiving this wish by itself.
Yours refers to a possession, not the person being wished good luck.
You're means you are and does not fit after wish in this pattern.
Wish you good luck uses you as the person receiving the good wish.

questions.setup: What is the speaker doing?
questions.prompt: Have a good journey!
options: Saying that a trip has finished.
Asking which journey was best.
Saying that the journey is canceled.
Wishing someone an enjoyable trip.
questions.explanation: This common expression offers a good wish to someone who is traveling.
feedback: Have a good journey does not report a completed trip.
The expression is a wish, not a question comparing journeys.
It wishes the traveler well rather than announcing a cancellation.
This common expression offers a good wish to someone who is traveling.

questions.setup: Complete the friendly message about someone else's visit.
questions.prompt: I hope ___ your visit to the city.
options: you to enjoy
you enjoy
you enjoying
you enjoys
questions.explanation: You enjoy supplies a subject and present verb after hope.
feedback: Hope does not take you to enjoy as its direct complement in this pattern.
You enjoy supplies a subject and present verb after hope.
You enjoying lacks a finite verb needed for this clause.
Enjoys does not agree with the subject you.

questions.setup: Complete the speaker's hope about meeting again.
questions.prompt: I hope ___ you again soon.
options: to see
see
seeing
to seeing
questions.explanation: To see gives the action the speaker hopes to do.
feedback: To see gives the action the speaker hopes to do.
Hope needs to before the base verb when its own subject will perform the action.
Seeing is not the direct complement used in hope to see.
The infinitive uses to see, not to seeing.

questions.setup: Choose the complete short answer expressing a positive hope.
questions.prompt: Will the weather be sunny for our walk? I hope ___.
options: that
so
it
them
questions.explanation: I hope so means I hope the weather will be sunny.
feedback: That would need a following clause, such as that it will be sunny.
I hope so means I hope the weather will be sunny.
It does not replace the whole sunny-weather statement after hope here.
Them refers to plural things or people, not the whole hoped-for proposition.

questions.setup: Choose a polite refusal of the offer.
questions.prompt: Would you like another slice of cake?
options: Yes, please. Just a small one.
I'd love another slice.
That would be lovely, thanks.
No, thank you. I'm full.
questions.explanation: No, thank you declines politely, and I'm full gives a simple reason.
feedback: Yes, please accepts the offer rather than refusing it.
