The accounts demonstrated the analyst's ability to work analytically.
The analyst recommended that the accounts receive careful analysis.
The analyst carried out a careful analysis of the accounts.
questions.explanation: Analysis names the completed examination; carried out keeps the analyst as its agent and careful preserves the manner.
feedback: Preparation for analysis does not say the analyst actually examined the accounts.
This reports an ability demonstrated by the accounts rather than the specified examination.
A recommendation is not the completed action reported in the original.
Analysis names the completed examination; carried out keeps the analyst as its agent and careful preserves the manner.

questions.setup: Choose the adjective describing a process designed to involve people in making decisions.
questions.prompt: Residents helped design the survey questions, not just answer them. The researchers used a ___ approach.
options: participating
participatory
participant
participation
questions.explanation: Participatory describes a process in which the people concerned actively take part, here in designing the questions.
feedback: Participating normally describes those taking part; it does not identify this approach's design for involving them in decisions.
Participatory describes a process in which the people concerned actively take part, here in designing the questions.
Participant is a person noun and can modify some nouns, but participatory is the adjective describing this kind of involvement-based approach.
Participation names the act of taking part, not the usual descriptive adjective before approach in this meaning.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of 'calculated' in this business account.
questions.prompt: Opening the second shop was a calculated risk.
options: The owners discovered the risk only after opening the shop.
The owners established the precise financial value of every possible outcome.
The owners opened the shop because the risk had already disappeared.
The owners considered the possible gains and losses before taking the risk.
questions.explanation: A calculated risk is taken after considering its possible consequences; it need not involve an exact numerical calculation.
feedback: 'Calculated' presents the choice as considered in advance, not recognized only afterwards.
The adjective does not require exact figures for every outcome.
A calculated risk remains a risk, even when it has been considered carefully.
A calculated risk is taken after considering its possible consequences; it need not involve an exact numerical calculation.

questions.setup: Which summary preserves the director's response?
questions.prompt: The director gave an approving nod but said the application still needed written approval.
options: The director's nod replaced the need for written approval.
The application had already been approved before the director nodded.
The director withheld any positive reaction until the application was approved.
The director reacted positively without yet granting the required written approval.
questions.explanation: Approving describes a favourable reaction; approval names the authorization still required.
feedback: The second clause explicitly says written approval is still needed.
An approving reaction does not establish prior formal approval.
The nod is described as approving, so a positive reaction has already occurred.
Approving describes a favourable reaction; approval names the authorization still required.

questions.setup: Choose the word meaning that the datasets can be fairly compared, not merely that someone has compared them.
questions.prompt: Because the surveys used the same definitions, their results are ___.
options: comparative
comparable
compared
comparing
questions.explanation: Comparable describes things sufficiently similar in relevant respects for a meaningful comparison.
feedback: Comparative describes work based on comparison, such as a comparative study, not the results' suitability for comparison.
Comparable describes things sufficiently similar in relevant respects for a meaningful comparison.
Compared reports an action performed on the results, not their suitability for it.
Comparing describes an action; the results are not themselves carrying out the comparison.

questions.setup: Choose the description of evaluative writing rather than merely descriptive writing.
questions.prompt: The review should be evaluative, not just descriptive.
options: It should list features without commenting on their quality.
It should be valuable to readers by being shorter than the product guide.
It should record whether another reviewer has already evaluated the product.
It should judge strengths and weaknesses, not only describe features.
questions.explanation: Evaluative means concerned with judging quality or value, whereas descriptive gives an account of features.
feedback: That would be descriptive; evaluative writing also makes judgments.
Valuable means useful or important; it is not equivalent to evaluative, and no length limit is stated.
A record of someone else's review does not itself meet the request to evaluate strengths and weaknesses.
Evaluative means concerned with judging quality or value, whereas descriptive gives an account of features.

questions.setup: Choose the role named by 'distributor' in this supply-chain description.
questions.prompt: The company acts as a distributor for several small manufacturers.
options: It designs the products that the manufacturers then produce.
It combines the manufacturers into a single new business.
It buys the manufacturers' products only for use by its own employees.
It supplies the manufacturers' products to shops or other buyers.
questions.explanation: A distributor is a person or business that supplies goods to retailers or other buyers; 'distribution' names that activity.
feedback: Designing products is not the distribution role identified here.
Distribution concerns supplying products, not merging companies.
That describes an end user, not a business acting as their distributor.
A distributor is a person or business that supplies goods to retailers or other buyers; 'distribution' names that activity.

questions.setup: Which interpretation of 'contributory' is supported here?
questions.prompt: Poor lighting was a contributory factor in the mistake.
options: The mistake could not have happened if the lighting had been good.
Poor lighting made the mistake inevitable regardless of the other circumstances.
Poor lighting helped bring about the mistake.
Poor lighting accompanied the mistake but did not affect whether it occurred.
questions.explanation: 'Contributory' means helping to cause a result, without specifying necessity or sufficiency.
feedback: 'Contributory' does not establish that poor lighting was a necessary condition.
A contribution to a mistake does not establish that it guaranteed the mistake.
'Contributory' means helping to cause a result, without specifying necessity or sufficiency.
'Contributory' attributes a causal role, not mere coincidence without an effect.

questions.setup: Choose the form saying the table's height can be changed, without saying someone has already changed it.
questions.prompt: The new worktable is height-___.
options: adjusted
adjusting
adjustable
adjustment
questions.explanation: Adjustable means capable of being adjusted; it does not report that adjustment has occurred.
feedback: Adjusted describes a change already made, not the continuing possibility of changing height.
Adjusting describes the process of changing height, not this capability adjective.
Adjustable means capable of being adjusted; it does not report that adjustment has occurred.
Adjustment is the noun for a change, not the adjective completing the compound.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of 'demanding' when it describes a role.
questions.prompt: Managing the evening service is a demanding role.
options: Someone has formally requested that the role be created.
The role requires considerable effort, attention, or skill.
Many applicants have already demanded to receive the role.
The role consists mainly of making requests to other departments.
questions.explanation: 'Demanding' is an adjective meaning requiring a great deal from the person doing the work.
feedback: That concerns a demand for a role, not the adjective describing how difficult it is.
'Demanding' is an adjective meaning requiring a great deal from the person doing the work.
'Demanding' here describes the work's requirements, not applicants' requests.
The adjective does not specify requesting as the main task; it describes the role's difficulty.

questions.setup: Choose the word saying the work received no payment, not merely too little payment.
questions.prompt: Although the exhibition was successful, the assistants' work remained ___.
options: unpaid
underpaid
repayable
payable
questions.explanation: Unpaid means not paid; un- negates the payment state rather than describing an insufficient amount.
feedback: Unpaid means not paid; un- negates the payment state rather than describing an insufficient amount.
Underpaid means paid less than is appropriate; the requested meaning is that no payment was made.
Repayable describes money that can or must be paid back, not work receiving no payment.
Payable describes an amount due for payment, not the absence of payment for work.

questions.setup: Choose the edit that describes the journalist's investigative work, not a journalist who is the subject of an investigation.
questions.prompt: The newspaper wants to describe someone who researches hidden facts for stories.
options: She is a journalist under investigation.
She is an investigative journalist.
She is an investigated journalist.
She is the journalist named in the investigation.
questions.explanation: Investigative describes journalism concerned with discovering and examining facts, especially those not readily available.
feedback: This makes the journalist the subject being investigated, reversing the intended role.
Investigative describes journalism concerned with discovering and examining facts, especially those not readily available.
Investigated presents her as someone examined in an investigation, not the person doing the investigative work.
Being named in an investigation does not identify her professional method or make her its investigator.

questions.setup: Which statement is supported by the description?
questions.prompt: The map shows the proposed station beside the hospital.
options: A station beside the hospital has already opened for passengers.
A station beside the hospital has been put forward as a plan.
Construction of the station has been formally approved.
The existing station beside the hospital will be demolished.
questions.explanation: Proposed identifies a suggestion or plan, not an approved or completed project.
feedback: Proposed does not establish completion or operation.
Proposed identifies a suggestion or plan, not an approved or completed project.
A proposal can exist before approval; the adjective does not settle that stage.
The word proposed does not establish an existing station or a demolition plan.

questions.setup: What does the observer's description mean?
questions.prompt: After she answered the criticism, an observer praised her 'measured response'.
options: She answered with deliberation and restraint.
She answered only after deciding that the criticism was entirely justified.
She gave precise figures instead of an argument about the criticism.
She had rehearsed the exact wording before the criticism was made.
questions.explanation: Measured is an evaluative adjective here, describing a controlled, considered response.
feedback: Measured is an evaluative adjective here, describing a controlled, considered response.
A measured response can disagree with criticism; the adjective does not imply conceding that it is justified.
This treats measurement literally; the observer is evaluating the manner of her response.
Deliberation in a response does not establish prior rehearsal or an already prepared script.

questions.setup: What does 'interpretation' refer to in this passage?
questions.prompt: The guide argues that the poem's last line rejects despair, calling this 'one possible interpretation of the ending'.
options: A proposed understanding of what the final line means.
A version of the final line in a different language.
An account of the way a performer delivered the final line.
A reconstruction of wording missing from the poet's original draft.
questions.explanation: The argument about rejecting despair offers a reading of the line; 'interpretation' names that account of its meaning.
feedback: The argument about rejecting despair offers a reading of the line; 'interpretation' names that account of its meaning.
'Interpretation' can concern language transfer in other settings, but this passage discusses the line's meaning, not another language.
A performance can be an interpretation, but the guide here argues for a meaning rather than describing delivery.
The passage does not report missing wording; it proposes an understanding of the existing ending.

questions.setup: Choose the adjective praising the team's quick and helpful reactions, not assigning accountability.
questions.prompt: The technical support team is very ___.
options: responsible
respondent
responsive
response
questions.explanation: Responsive describes reacting readily and appropriately to requests or needs.
feedback: Responsible concerns duty or accountability, not specifically quick reactions to requests.
A respondent is a person who answers a survey or responds in another defined role, not this quality adjective.
Responsive describes reacting readily and appropriately to requests or needs.
Response is the noun for a reaction, not an adjective after very.

questions.setup: Choose the word meaning that the rule is relevant to this case, without saying it has been put into practice.
questions.prompt: Does this rule remain ___ when the office is closed?
options: applied
applicant
applicable
application
questions.explanation: Applicable means relevant or able to be applied to the case under discussion.
feedback: Applied reports the rule being used; it does not ask whether the rule covers the case.
An applicant is someone making an application, not a quality of a rule.
Applicable means relevant or able to be applied to the case under discussion.
Application names a request or use of something; it cannot describe the rule after remain in this way.

questions.setup: Which interpretation of the compound adjective is supported?
questions.prompt: The brochure describes the window frame as maintenance-free.
options: The supplier promises to carry out its maintenance without charging.
The frame can be maintained only when it is not in use.
The frame is described as not needing maintenance.
The maintenance has already been completed before the frame is sold.
questions.explanation: In maintenance-free, -free means without a need for maintenance, not a zero price for maintenance work.
feedback: That would be free maintenance; maintenance-free describes not needing the service.
The compound gives no such timing restriction.
In maintenance-free, -free means without a need for maintenance, not a zero price for maintenance work.
Maintenance-free is a claimed property, not a report of an earlier completed service.

questions.setup: Which summary preserves the committee's role?
questions.prompt: The committee is consultative; final decisions remain with the board.
options: The committee provides advice, while the board retains decision-making authority.
The committee must approve a decision before the board can act.
The board advises the committee, which makes the final decision.
The committee implements decisions without contributing views to their formation.
questions.explanation: Consultative describes an advisory role. The second clause confirms that providing advice does not transfer final authority.
feedback: Consultative describes an advisory role. The second clause confirms that providing advice does not transfer final authority.
A consultative role provides advice; the sentence reserves final decision-making for the board rather than giving the committee approval power.
This reverses the two bodies' roles.
Implementation is not the consultative function: consultation concerns supplying views or advice.

questions.setup: Which statement is supported by 'revised' in this account?
questions.prompt: The builder sent a revised estimate after receiving the final measurements.
options: The builder sent an estimate that had been changed.
The builder sent a cheaper estimate than before.
The builder sent the first estimate for the work.
The builder corrected an error made in the original estimate.
questions.explanation: 'Revised' means altered or updated; new information can prompt revision without proving the earlier version mistaken.
feedback: 'Revised' means altered or updated; new information can prompt revision without proving the earlier version mistaken.
'Revised' does not state the direction of any change in price.
'Revised' indicates a change to an earlier version, not simply an initial estimate.
A correction is one reason for revision, but receiving final measurements can also lead to an update without an earlier error.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the edit is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The procedure is still unvalidated.' Edit: 'The procedure is invalid.'
options: The edit merely replaces a participle with an equivalent adjective.
The edit reports that earlier validation has expired.
The edit turns absence of validation into a negative judgment about validity.
The edit weakens a definite negative judgment into a statement that testing is incomplete.
questions.explanation: The negative prefix has different scope: unvalidated negates having been validated, while invalid negates validity itself.
feedback: Unvalidated describes a lack of completed validation; invalid judges the procedure not valid. These are not equivalent claims.
Neither unvalidated nor invalid specifies that validation once existed and later expired.
The negative prefix has different scope: unvalidated negates having been validated, while invalid negates validity itself.
That is the reverse of the change: the original leaves validity unestablished, while the edit judges it negatively.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that preserves both adverbs' contributions.
questions.prompt: Mina and Omar were appointed chair and treasurer, respectively. They responded respectfully to the outgoing committee.
options: Mina became treasurer and Omar chair; both replied courteously to the outgoing committee.
Mina became chair and Omar treasurer; both replied courteously to the outgoing committee.
Mina and Omar received equally respected positions and replied together to the outgoing committee.
Mina became chair and Omar treasurer; the outgoing committee replied to them with respect.
questions.explanation: Respectively connects names and positions in sequence; respectfully describes their courteous manner. Similar-looking adverbs perform different functions.
feedback: Respectively pairs each name with the role in the same order, so reversing the appointments changes the account.
Respectively connects names and positions in sequence; respectfully describes their courteous manner. Similar-looking adverbs perform different functions.
Respectively maps the ordered pairs, not their prestige; respectfully describes courtesy, not simultaneous speaking.
The appointments are preserved, but the direction of the response is reversed: Mina and Omar responded to the committee.

questions.setup: Choose the faithful rewrite using a verb from the 'coherence' family.
questions.prompt: The coherence of the essay's ideas makes its argument convincing.
options: The essay's ideas cohere because readers already find its argument convincing.
The essay's ideas might cohere if the argument became convincing.
Readers made the essay's ideas cohere by accepting its argument.
The argument is convincing because the essay's ideas cohere.
questions.explanation: 'Cohere' is the verb meaning fit together as a unified whole; the rewrite keeps coherence as the reason the argument convinces.
feedback: This reverses the stated explanatory direction.
This changes an asserted quality into a conditional possibility.
This adds reader agency and a process of creating coherence.
'Cohere' is the verb meaning fit together as a unified whole; the rewrite keeps coherence as the reason the argument convinces.

questions.setup: Choose the description supported by the comparison.
questions.prompt: Both filters achieve the required cleaning result, but Filter A uses much more electricity to do the same work than Filter B.
options: Filter A is effective but less efficient than Filter B.
Filter A is efficient but less effective than Filter B.
Filter A is ineffective and therefore consumes more electricity.
Filter A is more effective because it consumes more electricity.
questions.explanation: Effective concerns achieving the intended result; efficiency concerns the resources used to achieve it.
feedback: Effective concerns achieving the intended result; efficiency concerns the resources used to achieve it.
This reverses the comparison: A achieves the result but uses more resources.
A achieves the required result, and the source does not give ineffectiveness as a cause of consumption.
Higher resource use does not establish a better cleaning result; both meet the stated requirement.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the revision is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The team made consistent progress throughout the season.' Edit: 'The team's performance remained constant throughout the season.'
options: The edit preserves the improvement but specifies that it happened at a fixed speed.
The edit changes a steady pattern into one interrupted by setbacks.
The edit says the team trained continuously rather than competing regularly.
The edit replaces steady progress with an unchanged level of performance.
questions.explanation: Consistent progress describes a sustained pattern of improvement; constant performance describes a level that does not change.
feedback: Constant performance means an unchanged level, not a fixed rate of improvement.
Neither version introduces interruptions or setbacks.
The edit concerns performance, not the frequency of training or competition.
Consistent progress describes a sustained pattern of improvement; constant performance describes a level that does not change.

questions.setup: How does the substituted adjective change the description?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The buyer was credible.' Edit: 'The buyer was credulous.'
options: The edit changes believability into a judgment that the buyer deserves praise.
The edit strengthens the judgment that other people can trust the buyer's account.
The edit describes readiness to believe others rather than being believable oneself.
The edit describes the buyer's ability to obtain credit rather than the truth of an account.
questions.explanation: Credible means believable or convincing; credulous means too ready to believe what one is told.
feedback: Deserving praise is creditable; credulous describes believing too readily.
Credulous concerns the buyer's susceptibility to belief, not stronger support for the buyer's own account.
Credible means believable or convincing; credulous means too ready to believe what one is told.
Ability to obtain credit is creditworthiness, not credulity.

questions.setup: Choose the accurate summary of the manager's position.
questions.prompt: Anita, the manager, wants a reliable supplier but does not want the firm to become reliant on a single supplier.
options: She wants the supplier to depend on the firm while remaining free to provide unreliable service.
She thinks a dependable supplier must become dependent on the firm.
She rejects suppliers whose services the firm can rely on.
She wants dependable service without dependence on one provider.
questions.explanation: Reliable describes trustworthiness in providing service; reliant describes depending on someone or something.
feedback: This reverses the direction of reliance and contradicts the request for reliability.
Reliability and reliance are different relationships; the sentence imposes no dependence on the supplier.
The first clause seeks a reliable supplier; the concern is dependence on a single provider, not dependability itself.
Reliable describes trustworthiness in providing service; reliant describes depending on someone or something.

questions.setup: What does 'transparently' contribute to this description?
questions.prompt: The spokesperson repeated a transparently false claim.
options: The spokesperson openly admitted that the claim was false.
The spokesperson made the claim available for independent checking.
The claim's falsity was readily apparent.
The spokesperson was unaware that the claim was false.
questions.explanation: 'Transparently' modifies 'false' here and means plainly or obviously, not candidly admitting the claim.
feedback: The adverb describes how apparent the falsity is; it does not report an admission.
That would concern openness of procedure; the phrase instead characterizes the obvious falsity.
'Transparently' modifies 'false' here and means plainly or obviously, not candidly admitting the claim.
The writer calls the falsity apparent; the phrase does not establish what the spokesperson did or did not recognize.

questions.setup: The course involves building models rather than just reading about them. Assess the proposed edit to its description.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The course is practical.' Edit: 'The course is practicable.'
options: The edit strengthens the claim that students work with real materials rather than theory.
The edit says the course has already been put into practice.
The edit describes feasibility rather than the hands-on character intended in the original.
The edit narrows the course to preparing students for a specific occupation.
questions.explanation: Practical has the hands-on meaning fixed by the scenario; practicable instead means possible to carry out.
feedback: Practicable means capable of being carried out; it does not intensify the hands-on sense of practical.
Practicable expresses feasibility, not a completed implementation.
Practical has the hands-on meaning fixed by the scenario; practicable instead means possible to carry out.
Neither the suffix nor the adjective practicable specifies an occupational purpose.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the change is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'These costs approximate our budget.' Edit: 'These costs are approximate.'
options: The edit preserves the budget comparison but makes the costs more precise.
The edit changes closeness to the budget into a claim that the stated costs are inexact.
The edit says that the budget was calculated from these costs.
The edit turns an estimate into a statement that the costs exceed the budget.
questions.explanation: Approximate as a verb means come close to; as an adjective after are, it means not exact.
feedback: The budget comparison disappears, and approximate as an adjective does not mean more precise.
Approximate as a verb means come close to; as an adjective after are, it means not exact.
Neither sentence establishes how the budget was calculated.
The original expresses closeness, not an estimate, and the edit gives no above-or-below comparison.

questions.setup: Choose the meaning of 'complicity' in this report.
questions.prompt: The inquiry examined the supervisor's complicity in the deception.
options: It examined how difficult the supervisor found the investigation.
It examined the supervisor's involvement in the wrongdoing.
It examined an unexpected problem that disrupted the supervisor's work.
It examined whether the supervisor followed the new reporting procedure.
questions.explanation: 'Complicity' means involvement with others in an improper or wrongful act.
feedback: Difficulty or intricacy concerns complexity, not complicity in wrongdoing.
'Complicity' means involvement with others in an improper or wrongful act.
An additional obstacle is a complication, not complicity.
Following requirements concerns compliance; complicity concerns involvement in the deception.

questions.setup: How do the two uses of 'objective' differ?
questions.prompt: Our objective is an objective assessment of the service.
options: Both describe the assessment as free from personal bias.
The first names an aim; the second describes an assessment not driven by personal bias.
The first describes impartiality; the second names the aim of the assessment.
Both name outcomes the assessment has already achieved.
questions.explanation: 'Objective' can be a count noun meaning 'goal' or an adjective meaning 'unbiased'; the sentence uses both.
feedback: The first follows 'our' as a noun naming what is to be achieved, not as an adjective describing assessment.
'Objective' can be a count noun meaning 'goal' or an adjective meaning 'unbiased'; the sentence uses both.
This reverses their grammatical roles and meanings.
An objective is a goal, not necessarily an achieved outcome, and the second 'objective' is an adjective.

questions.setup: Choose the accurate assessment of the rewrite.
questions.prompt: Original: 'The engineers began stabilizing the platform.' Edit: 'The engineers achieved stability in the platform.'
options: The edit adds a successful result to an action that the original only says began.
The edit simply replaces the verb with its noun while preserving the same stage of work.
The edit weakens an achieved result into an intention to start work.
The edit changes lasting stability into a temporary improvement.
questions.explanation: Stability names the state sought; combining it with achieved claims that the stabilizing process reached its goal.
feedback: Stability names the state sought; combining it with achieved claims that the stabilizing process reached its goal.
Achieved stability reports a result, while began stabilizing reports the start of a process.
That reverses the change: the original reports beginning and the edit reports achieving.
Neither version specifies duration. The contrast is between starting stabilization and achieving its result.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite using an adverb from the 'subtle' family that preserves the evaluation.
questions.prompt: The difference between the two readings remains important despite its subtlety.
options: Because the readings matter, the difference between them must be subtle.
The readings differ substantially because the distinction matters.
The readings differ only in importance, not in their interpretation of the text.
Although the readings differ subtly, the difference still matters.
questions.explanation: 'Subtly' describes how the readings differ; the contrast preserves the claim that a hard-to-notice difference can matter.
feedback: This adds a causal link from importance to subtlety, which the original does not claim.
Importance does not make the difference large or conspicuous; the original calls it subtle.
This changes the dimension of difference rather than preserving its subtle character and importance.
'Subtly' describes how the readings differ; the contrast preserves the claim that a hard-to-notice difference can matter.

questions.setup: Choose the adjective that specifically describes automatic adjustment in response to changing conditions.
questions.prompt: The display changes its brightness whenever the surrounding light changes. It uses ___ controls.
options: adaptive
adapted
adaptable
adopted
questions.explanation: Adaptive describes a system that changes in response to its conditions, matching the automatic brightness behaviour.
feedback: Adaptive describes a system that changes in response to its conditions, matching the automatic brightness behaviour.
Adapted says controls have been modified for a purpose; it does not itself describe continuing responses to changing conditions.
Adaptable describes a capacity to be adjusted or suit different circumstances, not necessarily automatic adjustment as conditions change.
Adopted says the controls have been selected or taken into use, not how they respond.

questions.setup: Which interpretation of 'robustly' is supported here?
questions.prompt: The councillor robustly disagreed with the proposed closure.
options: The councillor expressed disagreement forcefully.
The councillor proved that the closure proposal contained factual errors.
The councillor expressed disagreement in a deliberately uncertain way.
The councillor insulted the people who proposed the closure.
questions.explanation: 'Robustly' describes a strong, vigorous manner of disagreeing, not the truth of the councillor's position.
feedback: 'Robustly' describes a strong, vigorous manner of disagreeing, not the truth of the councillor's position.
Forceful disagreement does not establish that the proposal was disproved.
That does not match the forceful manner conveyed by 'robustly'.
Robust disagreement can be forceful without being personally insulting; the adverb does not establish insults.

questions.setup: How does the adjective change affect the description?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The review contains a moral argument about consumption.' Edit: 'The review contains a moralistic argument about consumption.'
options: The edit says the argument improves the readers' morale.
The edit removes ethical concerns and describes a practical calculation.
The edit adds a suggestion of preachy moral judgment, not merely an ethical subject.
The edit confirms that the argument reaches the ethically correct conclusion.
questions.explanation: Moralistic commonly carries disapproval of excessive or self-righteous moralizing, unlike the more neutral moral argument.
feedback: Morale concerns confidence or spirits; moralistic concerns the manner of judging morality.
Moralistic still concerns moral judgment; it does not turn the subject into a calculation.
Moralistic commonly carries disapproval of excessive or self-righteous moralizing, unlike the more neutral moral argument.
Moralistic evaluates the manner of moralizing, not whether the conclusion is ethically correct.

questions.setup: Which summary follows from the verb form used?
questions.prompt: Before publication, the editor anonymized the quotations.
options: The editor established that the speakers' identities had never been known.
The editor removed identifying information from the quotations.
The editor published quotations whose sources had volunteered to be named.
The editor verified the quotations' wording while retaining identifying details.
questions.explanation: Anonymize is the verb for making material anonymous by removing identifying information; the past form reports that action.
feedback: Anonymized reports a process applied to the quotations, not that identities were never known.
Anonymize is the verb for making material anonymous by removing identifying information; the past form reports that action.
That concerns identification and permission, not the removal of identifying information.
Verification is different from anonymizing; retaining identifying details does not preserve the stated action.

questions.setup: Choose the summary that keeps both judgments.
questions.prompt: The restaurant's menu is varied, but the quality of its cooking is variable.
options: The menu changes unpredictably, but every dish is of the same quality.
The dishes differ in quality because there are too many choices.
The menu offers few choices, although the cooking uses several techniques.
There is a wide choice of dishes, but cooking quality is inconsistent.
questions.explanation: Varied describes diversity; variable here describes a quality that changes rather than remaining dependable.
feedback: This assigns variability to the menu and consistency to the cooking, reversing the contrast.
The original does not give variety as the cause of inconsistent quality or say the choice is excessive.
That reverses varied's wide-range meaning and changes quality into technique.
Varied describes diversity; variable here describes a quality that changes rather than remaining dependable.

questions.setup: What does the sentence-initial adverb add?
questions.prompt: Significantly, the interviewees did not mention the booking fee.
options: The writer presents the omission as important.
The writer reports that the fee was unusually large.
The writer reduces confidence that the omission occurred.
The writer says the interviewees deliberately concealed the fee.
questions.explanation: Sentence-initial significantly marks the following observation as noteworthy; it does not measure a quantity here.
feedback: Sentence-initial significantly marks the following observation as noteworthy; it does not measure a quantity here.
The adverb comments on the following observation, not the amount of the fee.
Significantly is not a hedge such as apparently; it evaluates importance rather than weakening the claim.
An important omission is not necessarily deliberate concealment; the adverb supplies no motive.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the edit is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'Her reply was noncommittal about the proposal.' Edit: 'She was uncommitted to the proposal.'
options: The edit gives the same information but moves it from the reply to its speaker.
The edit says she communicated her opposition more directly than before.
The edit turns a description of her reply into a claim about her commitment.
The edit replaces a claim about her private intentions with one about public wording.
questions.explanation: Noncommittal describes avoiding a definite position in what is communicated. Uncommitted describes the person's lack of commitment, which the reply alone need not establish.
feedback: A noncommittal reply does not reveal a definite position; a committed supporter could still give one. The change adds a claim about her actual stance.
Uncommitted does not mean opposed, and the edit does not describe a more direct reply.
Noncommittal describes avoiding a definite position in what is communicated. Uncommitted describes the person's lack of commitment, which the reply alone need not establish.
That reverses the direction: the original describes the reply; the edit attributes a stance to the person.

questions.setup: A copy editor proposes this rewrite. What is the strongest linguistic objection?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The manager inferred agreement from Lea's silence.' Edit: 'Lea implied agreement by remaining silent.'
options: It replaces an indirect expression of agreement with an explicit statement by Lea.
It recasts the manager's interpretation as something conveyed by Lea's silence.
It makes the manager, rather than Lea, responsible for expressing agreement.
It transfers the act of drawing a conclusion from the manager to Lea.
questions.explanation: Infer concerns drawing a conclusion; imply concerns conveying or suggesting it. An inference can be mistaken, so the rewrite is not automatically equivalent. Implying need not be deliberate.
feedback: Implied agreement remains indirect; the edit does not give Lea an explicit statement.
Infer concerns drawing a conclusion; imply concerns conveying or suggesting it. An inference can be mistaken, so the rewrite is not automatically equivalent. Implying need not be deliberate.
The manager interprets in the original; the edit attributes the implication to Lea's silence, not to the manager.
Imply does not assign the act of inference to Lea; it attributes a suggestion of agreement to her silence.

questions.setup: How does the revised description affect the reviewer's judgment?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The novel draws on the author's family diaries.' Edit: 'The novel is derivative, drawing on the author's family diaries.'
options: It merely uses an adjective to restate where the novel's material came from.
It changes the stated source from family diaries to another published novel.
It praises the novelist's skill in transforming private documents into fiction.
It adds a criticism of originality to the statement about source material.
questions.explanation: Derivative in an artistic evaluation commonly criticizes dependence on existing ideas. Drawing on diaries identifies a source without by itself making that criticism.
feedback: The evaluative adjective derivative carries a judgment about originality that the neutral source description does not supply.
The edit still identifies the diaries; derivative does not require a previously published novel as the source.
Derivative is normally disparaging in this reviewing context, not praise for the transformation.
Derivative in an artistic evaluation commonly criticizes dependence on existing ideas. Drawing on diaries identifies a source without by itself making that criticism.

questions.setup: Choose the nominal rewrite that preserves the estimator's position.
questions.prompt: Assuming the deliveries arrive on time, I estimate completion by Friday.
options: My estimate of completion by Friday establishes that the deliveries will arrive on time.
Timely deliveries are a requirement imposed by my estimate of completion by Friday.
My estimate of completion by Friday rests on the assumption of timely deliveries.
My assumption of completion by Friday rests on an estimate of timely deliveries.
questions.explanation: Assumption names the provisional premise introduced by assuming; rests on preserves its role in the estimate, and by Friday keeps the deadline rather than fixing the exact day.
feedback: The rewrite turns a premise used for estimating into a conclusion supposedly established by the estimate.
A working assumption does not impose a delivery requirement; this changes the estimator's role.
Assumption names the provisional premise introduced by assuming; rests on preserves its role in the estimate, and by Friday keeps the deadline rather than fixing the exact day.
This exchanges what is assumed with what is estimated: the original assumes timely deliveries and estimates completion.

questions.setup: Which reading is supported by the opening phrase?
questions.prompt: Not uncharacteristically, Leo claimed credit for a success he had helped bring about.
options: The writer presents Leo's behaviour as in keeping with his usual manner.
The writer doubts whether Leo actually claimed credit on this occasion.
The writer presents Leo's claim as a departure from his usual modesty.
The writer questions whether claiming credit reveals anything about Leo's usual behaviour.
questions.explanation: Not negates uncharacteristically, producing an understated way to describe characteristic behaviour rather than an unusual departure.
feedback: Not negates uncharacteristically, producing an understated way to describe characteristic behaviour rather than an unusual departure.
The negative phrase comments on how characteristic the behaviour is; it does not cast doubt on the reported event.
That would fit uncharacteristically without not; the combined negatives point the other way.
The opening does connect the claim with Leo's usual behaviour; its double negation does not withdraw that connection.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the paraphrase is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The evidence remained equivocal.' Paraphrase: 'The researchers continued to equivocate.'
options: The paraphrase reports the same uncertainty, changing only the word class.
The paraphrase attributes evasive communication to people instead of uncertainty to evidence.
The paraphrase locates uncertainty in the researchers' understanding rather than in the evidence.
The paraphrase narrows the claim to researchers disagreeing with one another.
questions.explanation: Equivocal evidence does not settle an interpretation. Researchers who equivocate avoid clear expression; inconclusive evidence alone does not establish that behaviour.
feedback: Equivocal evidence can be inconclusive without the researchers speaking evasively; changing the subject and form changes the claim.
Equivocal evidence does not settle an interpretation. Researchers who equivocate avoid clear expression; inconclusive evidence alone does not establish that behaviour.
Equivocating concerns how people express themselves; it need not mean their own understanding is uncertain.
Researchers can equivocate without disagreeing with one another; the verb concerns unclear or evasive communication.

questions.setup: Which edit preserves the copy editor's report?
questions.prompt: The editor made a substantial number of corrections to spelling and punctuation, without changing the content.
options: The editor made numerous surface corrections, leaving the substance unchanged.
The editor made substantive corrections while preserving the original spelling and punctuation.
The editor substantially changed the substance through corrections to spelling and punctuation.
The editor made a few substantial corrections rather than many minor ones.
questions.explanation: Substantial modifies number here. It reports quantity, whereas substantive corrections would concern content rather than just spelling and punctuation.
feedback: Substantial modifies number here. It reports quantity, whereas substantive corrections would concern content rather than just spelling and punctuation.
This exchanges surface corrections for changes to substance and says the corrected features were preserved.
This relocates substantial from the number of corrections to their effect on substance, contradicting their stated limitation.
The original explicitly describes a substantial number, not a small set of major interventions.

questions.setup: What is lost in the revised evaluation?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The repeated reminders proved counterproductive.' Edit: 'The repeated reminders proved unproductive.'
options: The edit no longer conveys that the reminders produced no effect of any kind.
The edit no longer conveys that the reminders worked against their intended goal.
The edit removes the judgment that sending reminders was unnecessary.
The edit removes a positive result and leaves only criticism of how it was achieved.
questions.explanation: Counterproductive describes effects contrary to the intended result; unproductive describes lack of useful results without necessarily asserting that opposing effect.
feedback: Counterproductive can describe a definite harmful effect, not an absence of effects.
Counterproductive describes effects contrary to the intended result; unproductive describes lack of useful results without necessarily asserting that opposing effect.
Counterproductive judges their effects as contrary to the goal, not merely whether they were needed.
Counterproductive is already a negative evaluation of the reminders' effects, not praise for a result.

questions.setup: An editor changes one adjective in a book notice. Which assessment is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'An authorized biography of the actor is forthcoming.' Edit: 'An authoritative biography of the actor is forthcoming.'
options: The edit exchanges a claim about authorization for a claim about authority as a source.
The edit keeps the permission claim but makes the actor's personal endorsement more emphatic.
The edit removes a judgment of reliability and substitutes confirmation that permission was granted.
The edit identifies the actor, rather than the biographer, as the authority behind its account.
questions.explanation: Authorized concerns approval or permission; authoritative presents the work as informed and dependable. Either description can apply without the other.
feedback: Authorized concerns approval or permission; authoritative presents the work as informed and dependable. Either description can apply without the other.
Authoritative concerns the work's standing as a source; it does not retain permission or specify a stronger endorsement by the actor.
That reverses the meanings of authoritative and authorized.
Authoritative evaluates the biography; it does not identify the source of its information or give that role to the actor.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the revised description is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The mayor-elect met the transport planners.' Edit: 'The elected mayor met the transport planners.'
options: The edit says the meeting occurred before the election rather than after it.
The edit no longer explicitly places the meeting before the mayor takes office.
The edit explicitly places the meeting after the mayor has taken office.
The edit changes an appointed mayor into one chosen by a public vote.
questions.explanation: Mayor-elect identifies an elected successor who has not yet taken office. Elected mayor states the selection status but does not itself fix whether the term has begun.
feedback: Elected still describes someone selected by an election; it does not place the meeting before that event.
Mayor-elect identifies an elected successor who has not yet taken office. Elected mayor states the selection status but does not itself fix whether the term has begun.
Elected mayor can also describe someone awaiting office. The edit loses the precise stage; it does not necessarily assert the opposite stage.
Mayor-elect already indicates election; the original does not describe appointment instead.

questions.setup: Choose the rewrite that preserves the narrator's account.
questions.prompt: Although Rafi oversaw the repairs, he overlooked the damage behind the cupboard and only noticed it afterwards.
options: Rafi's failure to supervise the repairs explains why he did not notice the hidden damage.
Rafi's supervision ensured that the hidden damage was noticed but deliberately left unrepaired.
Rafi's inspection of the hidden damage made supervision of the repairs unnecessary.
Despite supervising the repairs, Rafi failed to notice the hidden damage until afterwards.
questions.explanation: Oversaw means supervised; the later discovery fixes overlooked as failed to notice here. The rewrite retains the concession and the timing of that discovery.
feedback: He did oversee the repairs. This changes the concession into a cause and denies the supervision.
Only noticed it afterwards fixes overlooked as an earlier failure to notice, not a choice to leave known damage unrepaired.
The sentence does not report an earlier inspection of that damage or dispense with supervision.
Oversaw means supervised; the later discovery fixes overlooked as failed to notice here. The rewrite retains the concession and the timing of that discovery.

questions.setup: What reading does the adjective 'studied' support?
questions.prompt: At the reception, his studied casualness sat oddly beside his elaborate courtesies.
options: His relaxed manner showed how little preparation he had given to the occasion.
His academic interests were evident despite his relaxed social manner.
His relaxed manner appeared carefully cultivated rather than spontaneous.
His courtesies made an originally deliberate manner become genuinely spontaneous.
questions.explanation: 'Studied' is an evaluative adjective meaning deliberately arranged here, not simply the past form of academic study. The apparent ease can therefore be calculated.
feedback: 'Studied' describes deliberate preparation or cultivation, not its absence; 'casualness' is the effect being cultivated.
The adjective does not identify an academic interest; it characterizes how the casual manner was produced.
'Studied' is an evaluative adjective meaning deliberately arranged here, not simply the past form of academic study. The apparent ease can therefore be calculated.
'Sat oddly beside' contrasts two observed features; it does not report one transforming the other.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the writer's meaning in this sentence.
questions.prompt: Mira's disinterested advocacy for the scheme was tireless; she would gain nothing personally from its adoption.
options: Mira tirelessly supported the scheme without a personal stake in its success.
Mira reluctantly promoted a scheme that she found too dull to care about.
Mira described the scheme impartially without supporting either outcome.
Mira supported the scheme tirelessly in exchange for benefits owed to her.
questions.explanation: Here disinterested means free from personal advantage, as the second clause confirms. It does not mean she lacked interest in the cause; that other established sense does not fit this sentence.
feedback: Here disinterested means free from personal advantage, as the second clause confirms. It does not mean she lacked interest in the cause; that other established sense does not fit this sentence.
That uses the uninterested sense of disinterested, but the tireless advocacy and absence of personal gain establish a different sense here.
She actively advocated its adoption; absence of personal gain does not erase that support.
An exchange of personal benefits contradicts the statement that she would gain nothing personally.

questions.setup: Which rewrite preserves the panel's position?
questions.prompt: The panel dismissed the critic's assessment as needlessly dismissive.
options: The panel accepted the assessment's conclusions while conceding that its tone was dismissive.
The critic rejected the panel's assessment because she found its attitude contemptuous.
The panel's contemptuous attitude was criticized for making a substantive assessment unnecessary.
The panel rejected an assessment it considered unduly contemptuous.
questions.explanation: Dismissed reports rejection of the assessment; dismissive characterizes its disparaging attitude. The rewrite also retains that the panel makes the judgment.
feedback: The source says the panel dismissed the assessment, not that it accepted the conclusions despite the tone.
This exchanges the critic and panel as the source of the assessment and the party rejecting it.
Dismissive describes the critic's assessment, not the panel's attitude; the original does not say that assessment was unnecessary.
Dismissed reports rejection of the assessment; dismissive characterizes its disparaging attitude. The rewrite also retains that the panel makes the judgment.

questions.setup: Which account best preserves the reviewer's two descriptions?
questions.prompt: An ingenious question elicited a disarmingly ingenuous answer.
options: A deceptively simple question received a reply crafted to conceal the speaker's intentions.
A clever question drew a candid reply that tended to ease suspicion.
A naive question received a strategically clever answer that defeated its premise.
A technically complex question received an answer praised mainly for its precision.
questions.explanation: Ingenious praises clever devising; ingenuous describes candid openness, sometimes with naivety. Disarmingly adds the effect of taking an edge off resistance or suspicion.
feedback: Ingenuous describes an open, unguarded reply, not a deliberately concealing one. Ingenious need not mean deceptively simple.
Ingenious praises clever devising; ingenuous describes candid openness, sometimes with naivety. Disarmingly adds the effect of taking an edge off resistance or suspicion.
This transfers ingenuity to the answer and ingenuousness to the question; neither a defeated premise nor that reversal is stated.
Ingenious is not necessarily technically complex, and ingenuous evaluates openness rather than technical precision.

questions.setup: In ordinary contemporary reviewing usage, what changes in this edit?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The recommendations are unexceptionable.' Edit: 'The recommendations are unexceptional.'
options: The edit strengthens the claim that the recommendations are unusually good.
The edit says the recommendations admit exceptions that the original ruled out.
The edit preserves the same criticism but expresses it less formally.
The edit substitutes a judgment of ordinariness for one of acceptability.
questions.explanation: Unexceptionable means not reasonably open to objection; unexceptional ordinarily means not remarkable. The different endings lead to distinct usual evaluations.
feedback: Unexceptional usually means not out of the ordinary, not an intensified compliment.
Unexceptionable concerns grounds for objection, not whether a recommendation permits exceptions.
The original is not a criticism of ordinariness; the edit changes the evaluation rather than just its formality.
Unexceptionable means not reasonably open to objection; unexceptional ordinarily means not remarkable. The different endings lead to distinct usual evaluations.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the proposed revision is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'The date of the undated letter remains undetermined.' Edit: 'The date of the letter is indeterminable.'
options: The edit weakens certainty about the letter's age by presenting a proposed date as approximate.
The edit preserves the same unresolved state but uses a more formal adjective.
The edit turns an unresolved date into one that cannot be established.
The edit reports disagreement between researchers rather than an absence of a settled date.
questions.explanation: Undetermined negates an achieved determination; indeterminable negates the possibility of determining it. The latter is a stronger claim, not a mere change of ending.
feedback: The original provides no proposed date; indeterminable does not simply qualify the precision of an estimate.
Indeterminable adds inability to determine the date, rather than merely changing the formality of undetermined.
Undetermined negates an achieved determination; indeterminable negates the possibility of determining it. The latter is a stronger claim, not a mere change of ending.
Indeterminable need not involve researchers disagreeing; they could agree that the date cannot be established.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the wording change is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'Ari, a self-styled expert, spoke at the meeting.' Edit: 'Ari, a self-taught expert, spoke at the meeting.'
options: The edit retains the writer's doubt about the title and specifies its official source.
The edit merely makes explicit that Ari's expertise has been independently verified.
The edit replaces a claim about Ari's title with one about how Ari learned.
The edit replaces an account of unsuccessful study with one of successful certification.
questions.explanation: Self-styled attributes the designation to Ari and can signal the writer's distance from it. Self-taught concerns learning without a teacher; the first description does not establish that history.
feedback: Self-taught neither names an official source for the title nor necessarily retains the scepticism conveyed by self-styled.
Self-styled does not establish verification, and self-taught describes education rather than an independent assessment.
Self-styled attributes the designation to Ari and can signal the writer's distance from it. Self-taught concerns learning without a teacher; the first description does not establish that history.
Neither version reports unsuccessful study or certification; both readings add events not encoded by the compounds.

questions.setup: Which assessment of the replacement is accurate?
questions.prompt: Original: 'Readers complained about discontinuities in the serialized narrative.' Edit: 'Readers complained about the discontinuation of the narrative.'
options: The edit merely makes the same complaint singular rather than plural.
The edit changes the complaint from a stopped series to flaws within a continuing story.
The edit specifies that the narrative resumed after readers had complained.
The edit changes breaks within the narrative into the stopping of its continuation.
questions.explanation: Discontinuity and discontinuation are related nouns with different event meanings. Discontinuation need not mean the narrative could never later resume.
feedback: Discontinuities are breaks or gaps in continuity; discontinuation names the act of stopping continuation. The issue is lexical meaning, not just number.
That reverses the change: internal breaks belong to the original, while stopping belongs to the edit.
The noun reports stopping, not resumption or its timing relative to the complaint.
Discontinuity and discontinuation are related nouns with different event meanings. Discontinuation need not mean the narrative could never later resume.

questions.setup: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the concession.
questions.prompt: Defensive though her reply sounded, its central claim was defensible.
options: Her reply sounded protective of her position, but its main claim could be justified.
Because her main claim could be justified, the reply did not sound defensive.
Her reply established its main claim by defending it against the criticism.
Although the reply sounded impartial, its main claim lacked a plausible defence.
questions.explanation: Defensive characterizes the stance or tone of the reply; defensible concerns whether a claim can be supported. Though preserves the contrast between these independent evaluations.
feedback: Defensive characterizes the stance or tone of the reply; defensible concerns whether a claim can be supported. Though preserves the contrast between these independent evaluations.
This makes justification remove the defensive tone, whereas the original allows the two to coexist.
Defensible expresses capacity for justification, not a report that the reply actually established the claim.
This reverses both evaluations: defensive is not impartial, and defensible does not mean lacking a defence.

questions.setup: Mina has a new job at a hotel. She starts on Monday.
questions.prompt: What does Mina have?
options: a room she has booked
a holiday she has planned
a visit to meet a friend
work she will be paid to do
questions.explanation: A job here is paid work at the hotel.
feedback: A guest books a room; a job is work, not accommodation.
Starting a job means starting work, not taking a holiday.
A social visit is not a job.
A job here is paid work at the hotel.

questions.setup: 'My boss is Ana,' says a cook at the restaurant.
questions.prompt: Who is Ana in relation to the cook?
options: a person who eats there
a person who delivers food
a person in charge of the cook's work
a person who works under the cook
questions.explanation: Your boss is the person you work under.
feedback: A person eating there is a customer, not necessarily the cook's boss.
Delivery work does not make someone the cook's boss.
Your boss is the person you work under.
That reverses the relationship: the boss directs the cook's work.

questions.setup: The garage will pay Luis for his work on Friday.
questions.prompt: What will the garage do?
options: give Luis money
ask Luis for money
give Luis another job
ask Luis to take a rest
questions.explanation: Pay someone for work means give that person money for doing it.
feedback: Pay someone for work means give that person money for doing it.
That reverses the payment: the garage is paying Luis.
Payment rewards work; it does not mean assigning more work.
A rest is a break, not payment.

questions.setup: A museum door says 'Staff only.'
questions.prompt: Who is this entrance for?
options: people visiting the museum
people buying tickets
people waiting for a tour
people who work at the museum
questions.explanation: Staff are the people employed to work in an organization.
feedback: Visitors are not staff simply because they enter the museum.
Buying admission makes someone a visitor, not a staff member.
Tour groups are visitors; this entrance is for workers.
Staff are the people employed to work in an organization.

questions.setup: Omar's shift at the bakery is from six until two.
questions.prompt: What do these times describe?
options: when Omar travels to work
when Omar is scheduled to work
when Omar takes his lunch break
when Omar buys his groceries
questions.explanation: A shift is a set period during which someone works.
feedback: The journey is separate from his scheduled work period.
A shift is a set period during which someone works.
A break is a pause within work, not the whole shift.
A work shift does not describe personal shopping.

questions.setup: 'The keys are in my office, beside my computer,' says the school manager.
questions.prompt: Where should you look?
options: in the room where meals are cooked
in the room where visitors sleep
in the room where the manager works
in the room where cars are kept
questions.explanation: An office is a room or place used for work such as administration.
feedback: That is a kitchen; office does not name a cooking room.
That is a guest room, not the manager's office.
An office is a room or place used for work such as administration.
A garage holds cars; an office is used for other work.

questions.setup: A factory needs three more workers to pack boxes.
questions.prompt: What does it need?
options: three more people to do the packing
three more people to buy the boxes
three more people to visit the factory
three more people to inspect a purchase
questions.explanation: A worker is a person doing work; the sentence specifies packing.
feedback: A worker is a person doing work; the sentence specifies packing.
Buyers are customers; workers do the packing.
Visitors need not do the factory's work.
Inspecting a purchase is not the packing role described.

questions.setup: Our team has a meeting about the new menu at ten.
questions.prompt: What will the team do at ten?
options: stop work to eat their own meals
serve the first customers
come together to discuss the menu
leave the restaurant for the day
questions.explanation: A meeting brings people together for discussion or shared business.
feedback: A meeting about a menu is a discussion, not necessarily a meal.
Serving customers is different from meeting to discuss work.
A meeting brings people together for discussion or shared business.
A meeting is an activity at work, not the end of the working day.

questions.setup: We take a ten-minute break at eleven, then return to work.
questions.prompt: What happens during the break?
options: We finish our jobs for the day.
We stop working for a short time.
We begin a different job.
We work faster than before.
questions.explanation: A break is a temporary pause, followed here by returning to work.
feedback: They return after ten minutes; the working day is not over.
A break is a temporary pause, followed here by returning to work.
A break pauses work rather than changing the task.
Working faster is still working, not taking a break.

questions.setup: 'Your first task is to put labels on these jars.'
questions.prompt: What does 'task' mean here?
options: the piece of work you must do
the person you work for
the place where you work
the time you can go home
questions.explanation: Putting labels on jars is a particular task within the job.
feedback: Putting labels on jars is a particular task within the job.
A task is work to do, not the person assigning it.
The jars may be at a workstation, but task names the activity.
A finishing time is not a task.

questions.setup: The hotel wants to meet Eva and ask her about her work before giving her a job.
questions.prompt: Eva is going for a job ___.
options: break
interview
shift
holiday
questions.explanation: A job interview is a meeting where an employer asks an applicant questions.
feedback: A break pauses work; this meeting is part of applying for work.
A job interview is a meeting where an employer asks an applicant questions.
A shift is scheduled work after someone has the job.
A holiday is time off, not a meeting to discuss getting a job.

questions.setup: Ben repairs shoes. A customer brings him a broken boot.
questions.prompt: Who is the customer?
options: the person who teaches Ben repairs
the person who works for Ben
the person who sells tools to Ben
the person using Ben's repair service
questions.explanation: A customer buys goods or uses a business's services, such as shoe repair.
feedback: A teacher may train Ben, but customer names the person using his service.
An employee works for him; a customer brings work to his business.
That person supplies Ben; the customer here brings a boot for repair.
A customer buys goods or uses a business's services, such as shoe repair.

questions.setup: I work in the cleaning team at the airport.
questions.prompt: What does 'team' name?
options: the list of things I need to clean
the building where I keep my tools
the group I work with
the hours when I do the cleaning
questions.explanation: A team is a group working together toward a shared purpose.
feedback: A list of tasks is not the people doing them.
A team is people, not their storage place.
A team is a group working together toward a shared purpose.
Work hours describe a shift, not a team.

questions.setup: Please put the papers on my desk, beside the keyboard.
questions.prompt: Which object is the desk?
options: the chair I sit on
the cupboard I hang clothes in
the bag I carry to work
the table I use for work
questions.explanation: A desk is a worktable, often holding papers or a computer.
feedback: The chair is a seat; the desk is the work surface.
A cupboard stores things; desk names the table here.
A bag may carry papers, but it is not a desk.
A desk is a worktable, often holding papers or a computer.

questions.setup: 'Please phone the driver. Do not send a text.'
questions.prompt: What should you do?
options: speak to the driver in a call
write the driver a short message
write down the driver's number
wait for the driver to call you
questions.explanation: Phone is a verb here: make a telephone call to someone.
feedback: Phone is a verb here: make a telephone call to someone.
The instruction explicitly asks for a call instead of a text.
Recording a number does not contact the driver.
The instruction asks you to make the call.

questions.setup: The blue file contains all the papers about the kitchen repairs.
questions.prompt: What is kept in this file?
options: documents about the repair work
tools for repairing the kitchen
food for the kitchen staff
money to pay the repair workers
questions.explanation: A paper file keeps related documents together.
feedback: A paper file keeps related documents together.
Tools do the repairs; this file holds information about them.
The file is for papers, not food storage.
Bills may be filed, but a file is not the payment itself.

questions.setup: On your first day, you receive a form with spaces for your name and address.
questions.prompt: What should you do to complete the form?
options: write a story about your first day
draw a map of the building
give the requested information
make a list of questions for your boss
questions.explanation: To complete this form, fill its spaces with the information requested.
feedback: A form asks for particular details, not a free-form story.
The spaces request a name and address, not a building map.
To complete this form, fill its spaces with the information requested.
Your questions do not complete the requested personal details.

questions.setup: 'Our summer sale ends today. Tomorrow these shirts go back to their usual prices.'
questions.prompt: What does 'sale' mean in this notice?
options: a day when the shop is closed
a time when goods cost less than usual
a delivery of new shirts
a change in the shop's owner
questions.explanation: A sale can mean a period of reduced prices, as the return to usual prices shows.
feedback: The shop is selling shirts; sale does not mean closure.
A sale can mean a period of reduced prices, as the return to usual prices shows.
A delivery brings stock; the notice concerns prices.
Nothing here concerns ownership of the business.

questions.setup: I work part-time at a bookshop: just two afternoons a week.
questions.prompt: What does 'part-time' tell you?
options: I work there for no money.
I work fewer hours than a full-time worker.
I work in two different shops.
I work there only while travelling.
questions.explanation: Part-time work uses only part of the usual full working week.
feedback: Part-time describes working hours, not whether the work is paid.
Part-time work uses only part of the usual full working week.
Two afternoons do not mean two employers; part-time concerns hours.
Part-time does not describe a travel arrangement.

questions.setup: 'I sent you an email with tomorrow's room number.'
questions.prompt: Where should you look for the room number?
options: on a paper notice by the door
in a recorded phone message
on a printed envelope in the post
in your email messages
questions.explanation: An email is an electronic message sent to an email address.
feedback: A notice is not the email the speaker sent.
An email is written electronic communication, not a voice recording.
Postal mail is different from an email message.
An email is an electronic message sent to an email address.

questions.setup: The deadline for sending your lunch order is 10 a.m.
questions.prompt: Which action meets the deadline?
options: Send the order by ten.
Start choosing lunch at 10:15.
Send the order when lunch arrives.
Wait until ten before reading the menu.
questions.explanation: A deadline is the latest time an action must be completed.
feedback: A deadline is the latest time an action must be completed.
Starting after ten is already too late for this deadline.
Delivery happens after ordering; it does not meet the stated sending time.
The order must be sent by ten, not merely considered then.

questions.setup: After repairing our printer, the engineer emailed an invoice for $80.
questions.prompt: What is this document for?
options: confirming that we have paid
offering us a new printer for $80
recording our request for a repair
telling us what we need to pay
questions.explanation: An invoice lists charges and requests payment; it is not itself proof of payment.
feedback: A receipt normally confirms payment; an invoice requests it.
This invoice charges for the completed repair, not a proposed new purchase.
The request came before the work; this document gives the charge afterwards.
An invoice lists charges and requests payment; it is not itself proof of payment.

questions.setup: Nora checks the packing team's work each day. She is their supervisor.
questions.prompt: Which description fits Nora's role?
options: She buys the boxes they pack.
She visits to learn about their jobs.
She oversees their day-to-day work.
She delivers supplies from another company.
questions.explanation: A supervisor checks and directs the work of other people.
feedback: A buyer purchases goods; a supervisor oversees the work.
A visitor observing the work is not necessarily responsible for it.
A supervisor checks and directs the work of other people.
A supplier provides materials, not day-to-day supervision.

questions.setup: The careers adviser can see me at three. I have an appointment with her.
questions.prompt: What has been arranged?
options: a job she has already offered me
a time for us to meet
a class that anyone can join
a deadline for paying her
questions.explanation: An appointment is an agreed meeting at a particular time.
feedback: An appointment to meet is not a job offer.
